# Majmu' al-Fatawa - Tome 12

## Page 6048

Part Twelve

The Book of the Quran: Truly the Speech of Allah

In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful.

All praise belongs to Allah alone, and blessings and peace be upon him after whom there is no prophet.

Shaykh al-Islām Abū al-‘Abbās Ahmad ibn Taymiyyah—may Allah be pleased with him—said:

In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful.

All praise belongs to Allah. We praise Him, seek His help, and ask His forgiveness. We seek refuge in Allah from the evil within ourselves and from our evil deeds. Whomever Allah guides, none can lead astray, and whomever He leads astray, none can guide. I bear witness that none has the right to be worshipped except Allah alone, without partner, and I bear witness that Muhammad is His servant and Messenger. He sent him with guidance and the religion of truth to make it prevail over all religion, and Allah is sufficient as a witness. May Allah bestow blessings and abundant peace upon him.

---

## Page 6049

A Principle Concerning the Quran and the Speech of Allah

The Muslim community fell into great turmoil over this matter, becoming divided and differing through conjecture and desires after the first three generations had passed, when the Jahmiyyah—an offshoot of the Sabians—arose among them. Allah Most High has said:

“Indeed, those who differ over the Scripture are in extreme dissension.”

And He Most High has said:

“Mankind was one community. Then Allah sent the prophets as bearers of glad tidings and warners, and sent down with them the Scripture in truth to judge between people concerning their disagreements. None differed over it except those who had been given it, after clear proofs had come to them, out of jealous animosity among themselves. Then Allah, by His permission, guided those who believed to the truth concerning which they had differed.”

Disagreement is of “two kinds”: disagreement over its revelation and disagreement over its interpretation. Those whom Allah censures for differing are those who differ over the truth: one group denies the truth held by the other, or vice versa. For it is obligatory to believe in all the truth that has been revealed.

But when some believe in it while others disbelieve in it, this is a disagreement in which one of the two groups is blameworthy, as Allah Most High has said:

“Those messengers—We favored some of them over others,”

up to His words:

---

## Page 6050

“But they differed: some of them believed, and some of them disbelieved.”

Disagreement over its revelation is more serious, and this is what we are concerned with here. We therefore say:

“Disagreement over its revelation” is between believers and disbelievers. Believers believe in what has been sent down, whereas disbelievers reject the Scripture and that with which Allah sent His messengers; they will soon know. Those among the Muslims, Jews, Christians, and Sabians who believe in scripture and messengers in general believe in this, whereas those among the polytheists, Magians, and Sabians who reject scripture and messengers in general disbelieve in it.

This is because Allah sent the messengers to convey to people the speech of Allah that He revealed to them. Whoever believes in the messengers believes in what they conveyed from Allah, and whoever rejects the messengers rejects it. Thus, belief in Allah’s speech forms part of belief in Allah’s message to His servants, and disbelief in the former is disbelief in the latter. Reflect, then, on this principle, for it provides the criterion for resolving this confusion.

For this reason, one who disbelieves in the messengers sometimes denies that Allah has speech which He has sent down to a human being, just as he may disbelieve in the Lord of the worlds—as did Pharaoh and his people. Allah Most High said:

“Is it astonishing to people that We have revealed to a man from among them, ‘Warn mankind’”—the verse.

And He Most High said concerning Noah and Hūd:

“Do you wonder that a reminder has come to you from your Lord through a man from among you, to warn you?”

And He said:

“They have not appreciated Allah as He deserves, when they said, ‘Allah has not sent down anything to a human being’”—to the end of the passage.

---

## Page 6051

for these verses establish fundamental principles. He also quoted al-Wahīd as saying:

“This is nothing but the speech of a human being.”

For this reason, the foundation of “faith” is belief in what He has sent down. He Most High said:

“Alif Lām Mīm. This is the Book about which there is no doubt, a guidance for the God-fearing, who believe in the unseen and establish prayer”—up to His words: “And who believe in what has been sent down to you and what was sent down before you.”

In the middle of the surah:

“Say, ‘We believe in Allah and what has been sent down to us and what was sent down to Abraham’”—to the end of the verse.

And at its end:

“The Messenger believes in what has been sent down to him from his Lord, as do the believers. All believe in Allah, His angels, His Books, and His messengers”—to the end of the two verses.

In the following surah:

“Alif Lām Mīm. Allah—there is no deity except Him, the Ever-Living, the Sustainer of all. He has sent down to you the Book in truth, confirming what came before it, and He sent down the Torah and the Gospel previously, as guidance for mankind, and He sent down the Criterion.”

He mentions belief in what has been sent down within the surah, and likewise at its end:

“Our Lord, we have heard a caller calling to faith, ‘Believe in your Lord,’ so we have believed”—up to His words: “Indeed, among the People of the Book are those who believe in Allah, in what has been sent down to you, and in what was sent down to them”—to the end of the verse.

For this reason, the Quran places great emphasis on establishing this principle. Sometimes He opens a surah with it, either by way of a statement, as in His words:

“This is the Book,”

and His words:

“Alif Lām Rā. These are the verses of the Book of wisdom,”

and His words:

“Alif Lām Rā. A Book whose verses have been perfected”—to the end of the verse.

The same applies to the surahs beginning with “Tā Sīn” and “Hā Mīm.” Most of the surahs beginning with “Alif Lām Mīm,” “Alif Lām Rā,” “Tā Sīn,” and “Hā Mīm” follow this pattern.

---

## Page 6052

or by praising Him for sending it down, as in His words:

“All praise is for Allah, who has sent down the Book to His servant and has placed no crookedness in it.”

“Blessed is He who sent down the Criterion to His servant”—to the end of the verse.

Within the surahs, such passages are very numerous. He repeatedly recounts the story of Moses and Pharaoh because they stand at opposite extremes of truth and falsehood. Pharaoh represents the utmost in unbelief and falsehood, having denied both divine lordship and messengership. Moses represents the utmost in truth and faith, in that Allah spoke to him directly, placing no created intermediary between Himself and him. Thus, Moses affirms the perfection of messengership and divine speech, and affirms the Lord of the worlds together with the attributes that rightfully belong to Him.

This differs from the situation of most prophets with the unbelievers they faced: most unbelievers do not deny Allah’s existence, nor were the messengers granted the same measure of direct speech from Allah as Moses. The story of Moses and Pharaoh is therefore the greatest of narratives and the richest in lessons for believers and unbelievers alike. For this reason, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, would spend most of his night relating accounts of the Children of Israel to his community, and he followed Moses’ example in many matters. When he received the good news that Abū Jahl had been killed on the day of Badr, he said, “This is the Pharaoh of this community.”

Pharaoh and his people were polytheistic, unbelieving Sabians. Hence, he worshipped gods besides Allah, as Allah tells us in His words:

“and leave you and your gods.”

Although he knew what Moses had brought and was certain of its truth, he was a defiant denier, doomed to destruction, as Allah tells us in His words:

“But when Our clear signs came to them, they said, ‘This is obvious magic.’”

“And they rejected them out of injustice and arrogance, though their souls were convinced of them”—to the end of the verse.

And He Most High said:

---

## Page 6053

“We certainly gave Moses nine clear signs”—up to His words:

“You know well that none but the Lord of the heavens and the earth has sent these down as clear proofs”—to the end of the verse.

Those who disbelieve in the messengers—from among the people of Noah, ʿĀd, Thamūd, the peoples of Lot, Shuʿayb, Abraham and Moses, and the polytheists among the Arabs, Indians, Romans, Berbers, Turks, Greeks, Chaldeans and all other nations, earlier and later—follow their conjectures and desires. They turn away from Allah’s reminder, which He has given them from Himself, as He said to them when Adam was sent down from Paradise:

“When guidance comes to you from Me, whoever follows My guidance will have no fear, nor will they grieve.”

“But those who disbelieve and reject Our signs will be the inhabitants of the Fire, remaining there forever.”

Elsewhere, He says:

“When guidance comes to you from Me, whoever follows My guidance will neither go astray nor suffer.”

“But whoever turns away from My remembrance will certainly have a life of hardship”—to the end of the verse.

In another passage:

“If messengers from among yourselves come to you, recounting My signs to you.”

Yet, although Allah has sent down no authority for what they follow, and “they follow nothing but conjecture and what their souls desire,” they claim to possess reason, sound judgment, rational inference and illustrative analogies. They call themselves sages and philosophers, and lay claim to dialectic and speculative theology, power, authority and wealth. They describe the followers of the messengers as fools, lowly people and misguided, and mock them. Allah Most High said:

---

## Page 6054

“When their messengers came to them with clear proofs, they exulted in the knowledge they possessed, and they were engulfed by what they used to mock.”

He also said:

“When they are told, ‘Believe as the people have believed,’ they say, ‘Should we believe as the fools have believed?’ Indeed, it is they who are the fools, but they do not know.”

Allah Most High said:

“Indeed, the wicked used to laugh at those who believed”—up to His words: “Yet they were not sent as guardians over them.”

Allah Most High said concerning the people of Noah:

“Should we believe in you when the lowliest have followed you?”

They also said:

“We see that none have followed you but the lowliest among us, at first glance.”

He said:

“The life of this world has been made alluring to those who disbelieve, and they ridicule those who believe.”

He also said:

“Whenever a group of chiefs from his people passed by him, they mocked him.”

Indeed, they accuse the prophets themselves of madness, foolishness, misguidance and other such things. Thus they said of Noah:

“‘A madman!’ And he was rebuffed.”

They also said:

“We certainly see you in clear error.”

And to Hūd:

“We certainly see you as foolish.”

Section

“Faith in the messengers” must be comprehensive, universal and consistent, admitting no division, partial acceptance or contradiction: one must believe in all the messengers and in everything revealed to them. Whoever believes in some messengers and disbelieves in others, or believes in some of what Allah has revealed and disbelieves in other parts, is a disbeliever. This is the condition of those among the Jews, Christians and Sabians who altered the religion and disbelieved; for

---

## Page 6055

these people, in their original state, may believe in Allah and the Last Day and do righteous deeds; such people shall have no fear, nor shall they grieve. As Allah Most High said:

“Indeed, those who believed, the Jews, the Christians and the Sabians—whoever believed in Allah and the Last Day and did righteous deeds—will have their reward with their Lord, and no fear shall be upon them, nor shall they grieve.”

A similar verse appears in Sūrat al-Mā’idah.

Among them are those who made distinctions, believing in some and disbelieving in others, as Allah Most High said concerning the Jews:

“When they are told, ‘Believe in what Allah has revealed,’ they say, ‘We believe in what was revealed to us,’ yet they disbelieve in what came after it”—and the following verses.

Allah Most High said:

“Indeed, those who disbelieve in Allah and His messengers, wish to make a distinction between Allah and His messengers, say, ‘We believe in some and disbelieve in others,’ and wish to pursue a way between the two—it is they who are truly disbelievers”—to the end of the verse.

Allah Most High said:

“Say, ‘We believe in Allah and what has been revealed to us, and what was revealed to Abraham and Ishmael’”—this verse and the next.

He said concerning the believers:

“The Messenger believes in what has been revealed to him from his Lord, as do the believers. All believe in Allah, His angels, His Books and His messengers: ‘We make no distinction between any of His messengers.’”

He also said:

“He has ordained for you of religion what He enjoined upon Noah, what We have revealed to you, and what We enjoined upon Abraham, Moses and Jesus: ‘Uphold the religion and do not become divided over it.’”

He condemned those who became divided and differed concerning the Scriptures. These are the people who believe in some parts but not others, so that one group holds to some parts and another group to others, as in His saying:

---

## Page 6056

“Indeed, those who differ over the Scripture are in profound discord.”

And His saying:

“None differed over it except those who were given it, after clear proofs had come to them, out of mutual rivalry.”

And His saying:

“Those who were given the Scripture did not become divided until after the clear proof had come to them.”

Allah Most High also said:

“Indeed, those who divided their religion and became sects—you have nothing to do with them.”

Section

Making distinctions and accepting only part may sometimes concern extent and sometimes attributes—that is, quantity or quality—just as it may sometimes concern revelation itself and at other times its interpretation. For everything that exists has a reality with particular attributes and a definite extent. Thus, making distinctions and accepting only part of what Allah revealed to His messengers may concern either its extent or its attributes.

The first is exemplified by the Jews’ statement: “We believe in what was revealed to Moses, but not in what was revealed to Jesus and Muhammad.” The same applies to the Christians in their belief in the Messiah but not in Muhammad. Whoever believes in some messengers and scriptures but not others falls into this category, for he has not believed in everything that was revealed. The same applies to anyone who identifies with this community and believes

---

## Page 6057

in some texts of the Book and the Sunnah but not others; for religious innovations derive from disbelief.

As for “attributes,” an example is the disagreement between the Jews and Christians concerning the Messiah. The former said that he was a created servant, but denied his prophethood and impugned his lineage. The latter acknowledged his prophethood and his mission as a messenger, but said that he was Allah. Thus, the two groups differed over his attributes, each describing him with a mixture of truth and falsehood.

Another example is the “Sabian philosophers,” whose description of Allah’s revelation to His messengers contains both truth and falsehood. They might say: “The messengers must be obeyed, and what they brought may be called the speech of Allah. However, it was only sent down to their hearts from the spirit, which is the active intellect in the lowest heaven, not from Allah Himself. What descends upon the hearts of others is likewise of the same kind. It is not truly the speech of Allah; rather, it is in reality the speech of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and is called the speech of Allah only figuratively.”

These people, too, accept only part and make distinctions, since they affirm some attributes of what Allah has revealed and some attributes of His messengers, but not others. The attributes they disbelieve in may be more numerous than those they believe in, just as what the Jews reject of Scripture is more extensive and weightier than what they accept. Yet these people are greater in disbelief than the Jews in one respect, though the Jews are greater in disbelief than they are in another.

---

## Page 6058

For any of these people who is a Jew or a Christian is a disbeliever on both counts. Likewise, anyone among them who does not consider following the Seal of the Messengers obligatory, but permits adherence to Judaism or Christianity, is a disbeliever on both counts. Thus, one of them may be greater in disbelief than the Jews and Christians who disbelieve in Muhammad and the Quran. Conversely, Jews and Christians may be greater in disbelief than those among these people who believe in most of the attributes of what Allah sent Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, to convey. Fundamentally, however, these people are greater in disbelief than Jews and Christians as a class: the latter acknowledge, in principle, the perfection of messengership and prophethood, whereas these people do not. Similarly, a righteous believer among the Jews and Christians of old was superior to a righteous believer among these people.

Likewise, someone who professes Islam and believes in some attributes of the Quran, of Allah’s speech and His sending it down to His messengers, and of His messengers themselves, but not others, stands in the same relation to these people as someone who believes in some texts of the Book and the Sunnah, but not others, stands to the Jews and Christians.

This makes clear the nature of the deviations arising from religious innovation within this community: they consist in believing in some of what the Messenger brought but not the rest, or in some attributes of Allah’s speaking, messengership, and prophethood but not others. Both forms may concern either the revelation itself or its interpretation.

---

## Page 6059

Section

The cause that led these people to disbelieve in part of what Allah revealed is, in many cases, of the same kind as that which led earlier peoples to disbelieve in all that Allah revealed. For anyone who reflects will find that, in many cases, the specious arguments used by the Jews, Christians, and those Sabians who followed them to reject what Allah revealed to Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, are of the same kind as those used by the polytheists, Magians, and the Sabians associated with them to reject scripture as such and what Allah revealed to His messengers.

They raise objections against his signs, the Scripture sent down with him, the law with which he was sent, and his conduct, much like the objections raised against the other messengers, such as Moses and Jesus. As Allah Most High said concerning them all:

“None dispute concerning the signs of Allah except those who disbelieve, so do not be deceived by their movement throughout the land.”

“Before them, the people of Noah denied, as did the factions after them. Every nation plotted against its messenger to seize him, and they argued with falsehood to overthrow the truth thereby.”

Up to His words:

“Thus Allah leaves astray whoever is a transgressor, full of doubt.”

“Those who dispute concerning the signs of Allah without any authority having come to them—it is greatly abhorrent to Allah and to those who believe.”

And in the other verse:

“There is nothing in their hearts but a desire for greatness they will never attain. So seek refuge in Allah.”

Up to His words:

“Have you not seen those who dispute concerning the signs of Allah? How are they turned away?”

“Those who deny the Scripture and that with which We sent Our messengers—they will soon know.”

---

## Page 6060

This is despite the fact that the authority with which Allah supported His Messenger—through miraculous proofs and dazzling displays of power—is greater than that with which He supported others. His prophethood is the one whose light has spread throughout the earth, east and west. Through him, the prophethood of those who preceded him was established, and truth was distinguished from falsehood. Without his message, people—both the People of the Book and those without scripture—would have been in layers of darkness, one above another, and in utter confusion, with those who were turned away diverted from it.

Since nothing is said to him except what was said to the messengers before him, Allah, glorified be He, commanded him to call upon the People of the Book to testify to the like of what he brought. This is part of the wisdom in allowing them to remain upon payment of the jizya, as in His words, Most High:

“So if you are in doubt about what We have revealed to you, ask those who have been reading the Scripture before you.”

And His words:

“Allah is sufficient as a witness between me and you, as is whoever possesses knowledge of the Scripture.”

And His words:

“We sent before you only men to whom We revealed—so ask the people of knowledge if you do not know—with clear proofs and scriptures. And We sent down to you the Reminder so that you may explain to people what was sent down to them.”

And in the other passage:

“We sent before you only men to whom We revealed, so ask the people of knowledge if you do not know. Nor did We give them bodies that did not eat food.”

And the rest of the verse. Likewise, His words:

“Say: Have you considered: if it is from Allah and you disbelieve in it, while a witness from the Children of Israel has testified to its like?”

The essence of these disbelievers’ specious arguments is that they drew an analogy between the Messenger and those from whom Allah had distinguished him, and denied the grace with which Allah had singled out His messengers. Their error thus arose

---

## Page 6061

from faulty analogy.

An analogy must involve something shared by the two things being compared, such as inspiration and descent in a general sense. For devils descend upon their allies and inspire them, as Allah says:

“Indeed, the devils inspire their allies to dispute with you.”

And He, glorified be He, says:

“Shall I inform you upon whom the devils descend? They descend upon every sinful liar. They pass on what is heard, and most of them are liars.”

The Most High also speaks in the Tā-Sīn surahs, each of which He begins with the account of Moses, Allah’s speaking to him, and his being sent to Pharaoh. This is the greatest of the accounts, as we have explained previously. Thus, in Surah al-Shu‘arā’, which recounts the stories of the messengers one after another—seven in all: Moses, Abraham, Noah, Hūd, Sālih, Lot, and Shu‘ayb—He then says concerning the Quran:

“Indeed, it is a revelation from the Lord of all worlds, brought down by the Trustworthy Spirit,”

through to His words:

“And they say what they do not do.”

He thus explained the distinction between the Messenger and those upon whom devils descend—soothsayers, claimants to prophethood, and the like—as well as the distinction between him and poets. A soothsayer may report something unseen in rhymed prose, while a poet likewise produces verse that stirs people’s souls. The devil’s companion draws his inspiration from the devil and assists the devil through his lying and wickedness. The poet draws his inspiration from within himself, though the devil may also assist him.

He therefore declares that devils descend only upon those who resemble them: those who lie in their speech and act wickedly, unlike those who are truthful and righteous; and that poets merely stir

---

## Page 6062

people’s souls to pursue their desires, so that the misguided follow them—those who follow whims and wayward passions. He thus ruled out both descriptions by showing the absence of what each necessarily entails, and explained what the devils among humans and jinn have in common.

Section

Once this principle is clear, it becomes apparent how religious innovations stem from disbelief. We therefore say:

Those among the Jews and Christians whom Allah praised were Muslims and believers: they neither altered what Allah had revealed nor disbelieved in any of it. Just as the Jews and Christians became disbelievers through altering what Allah had revealed and disbelieving in what was revealed to Muhammad, so too the Sabians became disbelievers through altering what Allah had revealed and disbelieving in what Allah revealed to Muhammad—even if they were hypocrites, just as a Jew or Christian may be a hypocrite. These are the later generations of Jews, Christians, and Sabians.

For the later Sabians did not believe that Allah has speech, that He speaks and says anything, that He sends down speech and a reminder from Himself to any human being, or that He speaks to any human being. Rather, in their view, Allah is not to be described by any positive attribute. They do not affirm that He has knowledge, love, or mercy, and they deny that

---

## Page 6063

Allah took Abraham as a close friend or spoke directly to Moses. In their view, He is described only through negation and denial—for example, that He is neither a body, a substance, nor an accident, and is neither within the world nor outside it—or through a relation, such as being the source of the world or the First Cause; or through an attribute combining negation and relation, such as being intellecting, intelligible, and intellect.

They hold that Allah does not single out Moses, rather than others, by speaking to him, nor Muhammad, rather than others, by sending him as a messenger. For they do not affirm that He has detailed knowledge of the things known, let alone a detailed will. Rather, what they affirm for Him—if they affirm anything—is general, universal knowledge and a general, universal purpose.

Those among them who affirm prophethood say that it is an emanation flowing into the prophet’s soul, of the same kind as that which flows into all other souls. The prophet, however—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—has a more perfect capacity to receive it, such that he knows what others do not know, hears what others do not hear, sees what others do not see, and his soul can accomplish what other souls cannot. The speech uttered by the prophets is thus their own speech and their own words. These are the ones who say of the Quran:

“This is nothing but the word of a human being.”

For “the solitary one,” namely al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīra, was one of their kind: he belonged to those polytheists who were also Sabians. For the Sabians, like the People of the Book, are sometimes classified by Allah as a group within the polytheists, and sometimes as a group distinct from them, as the Most High says:

“Those who disbelieved among the People of the Book and the polytheists were not to desist.”

---

## Page 6064

“Indeed, those who disbelieve among the People of the Book and the polytheists will be in the Fire of Hell.”

Likewise, when He mentioned the six religious communities in Surah al-Hajj, He said:

“Indeed, those who believe and those who are Jews…”—the verse.

And the Most High said:

“They have taken their rabbis and monks as lords besides Allah…”—the verse.

This follows His words:

“The Jews say, ‘Ezra is the son of Allah,’ and the Christians say, ‘The Messiah is the son of Allah,’”

and continues up to His words:

“Even though the disbelievers detest it.”

He also said:

“They have certainly disbelieved who say, ‘Allah is the Messiah, the son of Mary.’”

If Jews and Christians may be polytheists, then this applies even more readily to the Sabians. This is after they have altered their religion. Wherever they are described as polytheists, it is after that alteration; wherever they are classified as other than polytheists, it is because the original, authentic form of their religion contains no polytheism. Polytheism is an innovation among them. These distinctions should therefore be carefully understood.

“The solitary one” was among those Arabs distinguished by judgment, reasoning by analogy, and planning, and he was counted among their sages and philosophers. Thus Allah described him as being in a state resembling that of those who profess philosophy, saying:

“Indeed, he thought and calculated.
May he be destroyed! How he calculated!
Again, may he be destroyed! How he calculated!
Then he looked;
then he frowned and scowled;
then he turned away and grew arrogant,
and said, ‘This is nothing but magic passed down;
this is nothing but the word of a human being.’”

---

## Page 6065

Furthermore, these people are bewildered and confused about what the prophets say. The light of prophethood has dazzled them, yet prophethood does not accord with their corrupt principles. They have therefore taken “different approaches”: some do not believe much of what the prophets and messengers say, but instead turn away from it, doubt it, or deny it. Others say, “Lying is permissible for an overriding benefit, and the prophets did so.” Others say, “This is permissible for the benefit of the common people, but not the elite.” The best among them say, “Rather, these are imaginative representations and parables intended to make realities accessible to the hearts of the common people.” This is the approach of al-Fārābī and Ibn Sīnā, although Ibn Sīnā is closer to faith in certain respects, even though he is not a believer.

Anyone among them whom the message of Muhammad—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—has reached, who has been dazzled by its proofs and light, and who has seen the various kinds of beneficial knowledge and righteous deeds it contains—so much so that Ibn Sīnā said, “The philosophers of the world agree that no dispensation better than this dispensation has ever come into the world”—inevitably reinterprets the texts of the Book and the Sunnah, following his fellows’ practice of distorting words from their proper meanings. Thus they distort what the messengers have related concerning Allah’s speech, a distortion by which they become disbelievers in part of the Book’s meaning concerning certain attributes of its revelation.

When they saw that the messengers called this speech the speech of Allah, and stated that Allah’s angels, such as the Trustworthy Spirit, Gabriel, brought it down, they employed this

---

## Page 6066

expression outwardly while inwardly disbelieving in its meaning. They reinterpreted it according to their own foundational doctrine—that of the Sabians—and became hypocrites among the Muslims and among the adherents of other religions.

They say: “This Quran is the speech of Allah, and what the messengers brought is the speech of Allah. But this means that it emanated upon the soul of the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—from the Active Intellect.” Sometimes they say that this intellect is Gabriel, who is “not withholding knowledge of the unseen”—that is, not miserly—because it pours forth abundantly. They say that Allah spoke to Moses from the heaven of his intellect, and that those who practise spiritual discipline and attain purity can reach the point of hearing what Moses heard, just as Moses heard it. Many prominent figures were led astray by his words, including Abū Hāmid al-Ghazālī, who mentioned this idea in some of his books.

They composed the Epistles of the Brethren of Purity and other works, in which they claimed to reconcile the doctrines of the later Sabians—namely, their innovated philosophy—with what the messengers brought from Allah. They thus presented what they claimed was rationally established, although much of it has no supporting proof. Sometimes they claimed that it was based on transmitted reports.

It contains an enormous amount of falsehood and distortion. They lead many astray through it only by means of the matters of natural science and mathematics it contains, which have no bearing on prophethood and the divine message, either to negate or to affirm them. These matters do, however, serve worldly interests, as do crafts such as farming, weaving, building, sewing and the like.

---

## Page 6067

Once it is understood that the true substance of the position of these polytheist Sabians is that the Quran is human speech like any other, only superior to other speech just as some people are superior to others, and that it emanated upon the soul of the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—from the higher realm, just as all other sciences and knowledge emanate upon the souls of those who possess them, know that this view has become widespread among many later professed Muslims: philosophers, speculative theologians, Sufis and jurists. They are hypocrites and heretics, even if they claim perfect knowledge. One of them, such as al-Tilimsānī, goes so far as to say: “Our words lead to Allah, whereas the Quran leads to Paradise.” Some, such as Ibn ʿArabī, may say: “The saint draws from the same source as the angel who conveys revelation to the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace.” Many of them say: “The Quran is for the common people, whereas our words are for the elite.” Thus, they have divided the Quran into fragments and drawn comparisons for it, just as the polytheists before them did, and as they also did with the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace.

Some of these people regard the perfect saint and the perfect philosopher as superior to the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace. Others regard certain people whom they claim to be saints, or certain philosophers—such as themselves, their shaykhs or those they follow—as superior to the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace. They may say: “He is superior in one respect, while the Prophet is superior in another.” Their deviation and false allegations concerning Allah’s messengers parallel their deviation and false allegations concerning Allah’s messages: they compare the speech that the messengers conveyed from Allah with their own speech, and they compare Allah’s messengers with themselves.

Allah has explained the condition of such people in passages such as His words:

“They have not accorded

---

## Page 6068

Allah the reverence He is due when they said, ‘Allah has not sent down anything to any human being.’” He continues until He says:

“Who is more unjust than someone who fabricates a lie against Allah, or says, ‘Revelation has come to me,’ when nothing has been revealed to him, or someone who says, ‘I will send down the like of what Allah has sent down’?”

Allah thus mentions sending down the two Books—the Torah and the Quran—than which no Book sent down from Allah gives better guidance. He likewise mentions them together in His words:

“They said, ‘Two works of magic supporting one another!’ And they said, ‘We reject both.’”

“Say, ‘Then bring a Book from Allah that gives better guidance than these two, and I will follow it, if you are truthful.’”

Likewise, when the jinn listened to the Quran,

“They said, ‘O our people, we have heard a Book sent down after Moses’”—to the end of the verse.

Allah Most High also says:

“Say, ‘Consider: if it is from Allah and you disbelieve in it, while a witness from the Children of Israel testifies to its like and believes’”.

Hence, when the Negus heard the Quran, he said: “This and what Moses brought surely come from the same source.” Then Allah Most High describes the liar and the false claimant to prophethood, saying:

“Who is more unjust than someone who fabricates a lie against Allah, or says, ‘Revelation has come to me,’ when nothing has been revealed to him, or someone who says, ‘I will send down the like of what Allah has sent down’?”

Here He mentions together someone who attributes his fabrications to Allah and someone who claims to receive revelation without specifying who revealed it. Anyone claiming revelation necessarily falls into one of these two categories. The “second category” includes someone who falsely claims to have seen something in a dream

---

## Page 6069

and someone who falsely says, “It was cast into my heart,” “I was inspired,” or the like. The “first category” includes someone who says, “Allah said to me,” “Allah commanded me,” “Allah agreed with me,” “He said to me,” or the like, on the basis of fancies or inspirations he experiences within himself, without knowing that they come from Allah. Indeed, he may know that they come from Satan, as was the case with Musaylimah the Liar and others like him.

Then Allah Most High says:

“Or someone who says, ‘I will send down the like of what Allah has sent down.’”

This describes someone who claims that human beings can produce the like of Allah’s speech, or that this speech is human speech arising from its author’s exceptional qualities and powers, so that, with sufficient effort, another person could produce its like. This includes those who say that the Quran can be matched, such as Ibn Abī Sarh during his apostasy and various scattered individuals. It also includes the Sabaean philosophers—hypocrites and unbelievers—who claim that the message of the prophets is speech that emanated to them, and that its like may emanate to others. Such a person would thus have sent down the like of what, according to the messengers, Allah sent down. For someone who says, “I will send down the like of what Allah has sent down,” may say this without believing that Allah has sent down anything, or he may say it while believing that Allah has sent down something.

Section

For this reason, the first person to openly deny Allah’s speaking and His taking a close friend was al-Ja‘d ibn Dirham, in the early second century AH. The scholars of Islam—such as al-Hasan al-Basrī and others—ordered

---

## Page 6070

his execution; so Khālid ibn ‘Abd Allāh al-Qasrī, the governor of Iraq, offered him as a sacrifice at Wāsit. He said, “O people, offer your sacrifices—may Allah accept them from you. I am sacrificing al-Ja‘d ibn Dirham, for he has claimed that Allah did not take Abraham as a close friend and did not speak directly to Moses. Exalted is Allah, far above what al-Ja‘d says!” Then he stepped down and slaughtered him.

Al-Jahm ibn Safwān adopted this doctrine from him and denied that Allah speaks. Then, acting hypocritically toward the Muslims, he acknowledged the term “speech,” saying, “His speech is created in a medium such as air or the leaves of trees.” Some practitioners of speculative theology and disputation who professed Islam, among the Mu‘tazilites and others, adopted aspects of the doctrines of the Sabaeans and polytheists, following al-Ja‘d and al-Jahm.

This began with the Sabaeans holding two views concerning “creation.” Some maintain that the heavens were created after not having existed, as the messengers and the Books of Allah Most High have declared. Others introduced an innovation, saying instead that the heavens are eternal, without beginning, and have always existed by virtue of the existence of the First, whose existence is necessary in itself. Some of them may deny the Maker altogether. Their doctrines concerning creation and resurrection, the beginning and the final return, are highly contradictory, because they did not hold fast to the rope of Allah Most High, which would unite them. Conjectures cannot unite people on matters such as these, whose realities human judgment cannot grasp except through revelation from Allah Most High. Their debates with one another rely only on inferences whose premises are drawn from natural phenomena of the lower world and the natural powers present in earth, water, and air

---

## Page 6071

and animals, minerals, and plants. Through these premises drawn from the lower world, they seek knowledge of Allah, of what lies above the heavens, and of the beginning and end of all things. This is a manifest error. Their own leading authorities have acknowledged that this is impossible, that they have no way of attaining certainty, and that they follow nothing but conjecture.

Such was the condition of these misguided, innovating Sabaeans and the Jews and Christians whom they had led astray. Their teachings reached certain practitioners of speculative theology and disputation who had not followed the guidance with which Allah sent His messengers. These men then sought to follow their path, just as the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, foretold:

“You will surely follow the ways of the nations before you, span for span and cubit for cubit.” They asked, “O Messenger of Allah, Persia and Rome?” He replied, “Who else would it be but Persia and Rome?”

They therefore argued that the world had a beginning using methods similar to those of these Sabaeans: reasoning about bodies and accidents by first establishing the existence of accidents, then establishing that bodies cannot be without them, and then that these accidents have a beginning. They would then say, “Whatever does not precede things that have a beginning must itself have a beginning.” Many practitioners of disputation relied on this to establish that the world had a beginning. When they concluded that accidents—which are attributes—indicated, in their view, that the subject bearing them had a beginning, they committed themselves to denying such attributes of Allah, because affirming them would entail His having a beginning.

The invalidity of this argument for the world’s having a beginning—which they believed to be the only proof, and perhaps even believed that no one’s faith was valid without it—is necessarily known as part of the religion of Islam.

---

## Page 6072

These men differ, however, from the “Sabaean philosophers,” who maintain that the world is eternal and that prophethood is a perfection that emanates upon the prophet’s soul. These speculative theologians possess more of the truth and adhere more closely to rational and revealed evidence, because their hearts have been illuminated by the light of Islam and the Quran, even though they have gone astray regarding much of what the messengers brought. Nevertheless, they are better than those philosophers in other respects in which they agree with Ahl al-Sunnah.

Yet they agreed with those philosophers that Allah has not spoken, just as they agreed with them that He has neither knowledge nor power nor any other attribute. They considered that affirming Him as one who speaks would entail His being a body, and a body has a beginning. This is because speech is among the attributes indicating that its bearer has a beginning. Indeed, in their view, it indicates that the speaker has a beginning more decisively than other attributes do. Moreover, Allah, in their view, depends upon something external that others do not depend upon; and speech involves an ordering and succession of elements not found in other attributes.

When they saw that the messengers unanimously affirmed that He speaks, and that the Quran abounds in affirmations of this, they would sometimes say, “He speaks figuratively, not literally.” This was their initial position, when, despite their innovation, they still retained their natural disposition, before resorting to obstinacy and denial. Then they saw how objectionable this was and said, “Rather, He truly speaks.” Some of their speculative theologians would even claim consensus on this. Yet this is not what they actually hold. Rather, the true substance and foundation of their doctrine, as understood by those who knew it and devised it, is that Allah does not speak. They said, “A speaker is someone who produces speech, even if it is in a locus separate from himself.” Thus they interpreted the word “speaker” in the language

---

## Page 6073

in a sense unknown in the language of the Arabs or any other people, whether literal or figurative. This is the position of those who say that the Quran is created, and it is one of the two views held by the Sabaeans who agree with the messengers that the world had a beginning. Although it constitutes disbelief in what the messengers brought, it is not equal in disbelief to the first view; for these people do not say that Allah intended to send a particular messenger and to send down to him this speech which He created. They denied that He speaks in the manner indicated by the divine scriptures and unanimously acknowledged by people of sound natural disposition.

Disagreement arose between these people, who are offshoots of the Sabaeans, and the believers who follow the messengers. These people rejected part of what the messengers brought concerning Allah’s speaking and addressing others. They differed over Allah’s Book, believing in some of it and disbelieving in some.

The believers, however, followed what had been sent down to them from their Lord: that Allah spoke the Quran, that He spoke directly to Moses, and that He speaks. They did not distort words from their proper places as the former group had done. Rather, they refuted those distortions through the insight afforded by faith, through which they understood what the messengers meant when conveying Allah’s message and His speech. They followed this Quran, the hadith, and the consensus of the early generations—the Companions and their successors—and all the other followers of the prophets. They knew that these people’s position was more vile than that of the Jews and Christians, to the point that Ibn al-Mubārak, the imam of the Muslims, used to say:

“We can indeed recount what the Jews and Christians say, but we cannot recount what the Jahmiyyah say.”

---

## Page 6074

And these people—offshoots of the polytheists—and their followers among those who had altered the religion of the Sabaeans, and then those who had altered the religions of the Jews and Christians, had become increasingly prominent in the early second century and the early third century, during the rule of Abū al-'Abbās, known as “al-Ma'mūn.” This was due to the translation into Arabic of the books of the pagan Sabaean Romans who preceded the Christians, and of their counterparts in Persia and India. The sciences of the Sabaean astrologers and others like them also became widespread.

It has already been explained that the adherents of the innovated speculative theology within Islam are offshoots of the Sabaeans, as expressed in the saying:

“The Mu'tazilah are the effeminates of the philosophers.”

This doctrine thus spread among scholars and theologians, as well as among military and political leaders. It gained enough adherents among caliphs, governors, ministers, judges and jurists to enable them to persecute believing men and women and Muslim men and women who followed what had been sent down to them from their Lord, neither altering it nor introducing innovations. This was due to the shortcomings and negligence of most of them in understanding the true nature of what the Messenger brought and following it. Had such understanding and adherence been widespread among them, those who introduced innovations contrary to the religion of Islam would not have been able to gain power over them.

Section

Then came a group of theologians from among those who affirmed the divine attributes. They defended the position that Allah possesses knowledge, power, sight and life, using rational arguments consistent with the prophetic texts. They distinguished between attributes inhering in substances, which they classified as accidents, and attributes inhering in the Lord, which they did not call accidents. For an accident is that which neither endures nor remains, or that which inheres in something occupying space, or

---

## Page 6075

a body. The Lord’s attributes, however, are inseparable from Him and everlasting; they are not of the same kind as the accidents inhering in bodies.

These theologians who affirmed the divine attributes and relied on rational argument differed in many respects from those innovating Sabaeans who denied the attributes. They affirmed attributes for which rational arguments could be advanced, such as the seven attributes: life, knowledge, power, will, hearing, sight and speech. They disagreed over whether hearing, sight and speech are attributes established by reason or attributes known through prophetic reports and revelation. They also differed concerning everlastingness, beginninglessness and perception—that is, the perception of smells, tastes and tangible things.

They likewise differed concerning attributes conveyed through revelation in the Quran, such as the face and the hand. Most, if not all, of their early scholars affirmed these, whereas many of their later scholars did not. As for attributes mentioned only in hadith, most of them did not affirm them. Some then diverted the texts from their meanings because of rational arguments they considered to conflict with them, while others consigned their meaning to Allah. The purpose here is not to detail people’s positions concerning all the other attributes. Rather, the intended subject is

“Allah’s message and His speech,”

which His messengers conveyed. These people thus had a measure in common with the heirs of the prophetic tradition, alongside the Sabaean methods they followed concerning the Creator, His names and His attributes.

Their doctrine concerning the divine message therefore became a synthesis of the two legacies: they mingled the truth held by the heirs of the prophets with the falsehood held by the heirs of the Sabaeans’ followers. Similarly, the doctrine of those who espoused purely innovated speculative theology, such as the Mu‘tazilah, contained a synthesis, though not one between the prophetic legacy and the Sabaean legacy;

---

## Page 6076

but those theologians follow the prophetic legacy more closely and are nearer to the doctrine of Ahl al-Sunnah than the Mu‘tazilah and others like them in many respects. Hence, many scholars of jurisprudence, hadith and Sufism agreed with them in some of their innovations, for several reasons:

“First”: The considerable truth in what they say and the prominence of the prophetic legacy in their teachings.

“Second”: Their mingling of that truth with rational arguments, some inherited from the Sabaeans and others newly introduced within Islam; the hold that the specious arguments involved have over them; and their belief that people of reason and learning could adhere to the prophetic legacy only in this way.

“Third”: Their limited acquaintance with the prophetic legacy that dispels these specious arguments and makes the path of guidance clear.

“Fourth”: The shortcomings and negligence found among those who affiliate themselves with the Sunnah and hadith: sometimes they transmit reports whose authenticity they do not know; at other times they resemble the unlettered who know nothing of the Scripture beyond mere recitation, and they turn away from explaining how the Quran and Sunnah demonstrate the true nature of things.

---

## Page 6077

With this as their “method,” they affirmed that the Quran is uncreated, on the strength of the scriptural texts and the consensus of the early generations, and because they considered this consistent with the principle they had established concerning the divine attributes. They held that reconciling the transmitted prophetic texts with rational inference was possible only by regarding the Quran as a meaning subsisting in Allah Himself, exalted is He, like His other attributes—just as the earlier group had classified it among things made and created, rather than as eternal like the other attributes. They considered that it could only be either created or eternal, since affirming a third category subsisting in Allah would entail temporally originated events subsisting in His essence, which would demonstrate that the bearer of these events has a beginning and invalidate the argument for the world’s having a beginning.

They then held that it could not consist of many meanings, but must be either a single meaning, according to one group, or four meanings, according to another. On this basis, they committed themselves to the position that speech in its true nature is the meaning subsisting within the self, and that letters and sounds are not part of speech in its true nature, but merely signify it and are therefore given its name. According to one group, this designation is figurative; according to another, it is literal, with the same word bearing distinct meanings; and according to a third, it is figurative in the case of Allah’s speech but literal in the speech of others.

The earlier group, along with some who affiliate themselves with the Sunnah, disagreed with them, saying: “Speech consists of nothing but letters and sounds. Beyond these there is no meaning other than knowledge and what is of its kind, or will and what is of its kind.” Thus the dispute arose between the two groups.

---

## Page 6078

It was further put to this group that commands, prohibitions, and statements are relational attributes of speech, not its types or subdivisions, and that Allah’s speech is a single meaning: when expressed in Arabic, it is the Quran; in Hebrew, it is the Torah; and in Syriac, it is the Gospel. Most people told them, “This is self-evidently false.” Likewise, the earlier group had claimed that He created speech in the air and thereby became one who speaks it, and that a speaker is whoever brings speech into existence, even in an essence other than his own. Most people told them, “This is self-evidently false.”

The majority across all groups held that speech denotes both wording and meaning together, just as the designation “speaking human being” refers to both soul and body together. When it is applied to either one alone, this requires a contextual indication. The meanings of speech are diverse, just as its expressions are diverse, and are not confined to knowledge and will—even though meanings tend more toward unity and cohesion, while expressions tend more toward multiplicity and separation.

These people accepted the consequence that the letters of the Quran are created, even though what they regarded as Allah’s speech was not created. They distinguished between Allah’s Book and His speech, saying, “Allah’s Book consists of the letters and is created, while Allah’s speech is their meaning and is uncreated.” These people and the earlier group thus agree that the Quran which the earlier group declared created is indeed created. These people differed, however, over where these letters were created: were they created in the air, or within Gabriel himself? Or was it Gabriel who brought them into existence, or Muhammad?

---

## Page 6079

As for the majority of the Muslim community and the people of hadith, jurisprudence, and Sufism, they adhere to what the messengers brought and to the scriptures and transmitted knowledge handed down from them. They follow the revealed message purely, without mixing it with contrary doctrines of the Sabians. Their position is that the Quran is Allah’s speech: they do not regard part of it as Allah’s speech and another part as something other than His speech. The Quran is precisely what Muslims recognize as the Quran—both its letters and its meanings. Commands and prohibitions likewise comprise both wording and meaning.

For this reason, jurists who wrote on the principles of jurisprudence from all the schools—the Hanafī, Mālikī, Shāfi'ī, and Hanbalī schools—affirmed this when discussing commands and prohibitions, provided they did not depart from the positions of the imams and jurists. They opposed those who said that a command is an abstract meaning alone.

Those who preserve the knowledge transmitted from the Prophet—the people of the Sunnah and hadith, the general body of Muslims, who constitute the great majority of those who pray toward the qiblah—know that His words, Most High,

“Alif Lām Mīm.”

“This is the Book about which there is no doubt,”

and similar passages are Allah’s speech, not anyone else’s. Allah’s speech is what He has spoken, not something He created in something other than Himself without speaking it Himself.

---

## Page 6080

Shaykh al-Islām—may Allah sanctify his soul—was also asked about two men who disputed concerning “the letters that Allah revealed to Adam.” One said, “They are eternal, without beginning, while their vowel marks and dots are originated.” The other said, “They are not Allah’s speech; they are created, together with their vowel marks and dots. Allah is the Eternal, and His speech originated from Him and will return to Him; it is revealed, not created. Yet He wrote using these letters.” They asked which of them was more correct in his statement and sounder in his belief.

He replied:

All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds. The foundation of this question is understanding “the speech of Allah Most High.” The position of the early generations of this community and its imams—the Companions, those who followed them in righteousness, and the other imams of the Muslims, including the four imams—is what the Quran and Sunnah indicate and what accords with clear rational evidence: the Quran is Allah’s speech, revealed and not created; it originated from Him and will return to Him. He is the One who spoke the Quran, the Torah, the Gospel, and the rest of His speech; this is not

---

## Page 6081

something created and separate from Him. He, glorified be He, speaks by His will and power. His speech subsists in His essence; it is not something created and separate from Him. He speaks by His will and power. None of the early generations of this community said that Allah’s speech is created and separate from Him. Nor did any of them say that the Quran, the Torah, or the Gospel is inseparably inherent in His essence for all eternity, while He is unable to speak by His will and power. Nor did they say that His actual calling to Moses, or a particular word itself, is eternal and without beginning. Rather, they said that Allah has always spoken whenever He wills. His speech is therefore eternal in the sense that He has always spoken whenever He wills.

Allah’s words have no end, as He Most High says:

“Say, ‘If the sea were ink for the words of my Lord, the sea would be exhausted before the words of my Lord were exhausted, even if We brought another like it as a supplement.’”

Allah, glorified be He, spoke the Quran in Arabic and the Torah in Hebrew. The Arabic Quran is thus Allah’s speech, as He Most High says:

“So when you recite the Quran, seek refuge in Allah from Satan, the accursed,”

through to His words:

“a clear Arabic tongue.”

He, glorified be He, has thus explained that the Quran—in which He replaces one verse with another—was brought down in truth from Allah by the Holy Spirit, who is Gabriel. He is also the Trustworthy Spirit, as Allah mentions elsewhere. He then explained that some of the disbelievers said:

“It is only a human being who teaches him.”

Some of the polytheists claimed that a non-Arab man in Mecca was teaching him. So He Most High said:

“The tongue of the one to whom they allude is foreign,”

meaning that the one to whom they attribute this teaching is a non-Arab,

“while this is a clear Arabic tongue.”

---

## Page 6082

This therefore indicates that the verses expressed in a clear Arabic tongue were brought down in truth from Allah by the Holy Spirit, as He says in another verse:

“Then is it other than Allah I should seek as judge, when it is He who has sent down to you the Book explained in detail? Those to whom We have given the Scripture know that it has been sent down from your Lord in truth. So never be among the doubters.”

The Book sent down, explained in detail, is the Arabic Quran, as everyone agrees. He has stated that those to whom He gave the Scripture know that it was sent down from Allah in truth. Knowledge can only be true. Thus, He said, “they know,” not “they say,” for knowledge, unlike a statement, can only be true. Their knowledge is mentioned as supporting testimony.

He, glorified be He, distinguished between His revelation to those other than Moses and His speaking to Moses in His words:

“Indeed, We have revealed to you as We revealed to Noah,”

through to His words:

“an argument after the messengers.”

He, glorified be He, distinguished between His speaking to Moses and His revelation to others, and emphasized His speaking to Moses by using the corresponding verbal noun. He Most High also says:

“Those messengers—We favored some of them over others,”

through to His words:

“with the Holy Spirit.”

He Most High also says:

“It is not for any human being that Allah should speak to him except by revelation,”

through to the end of the surah.

He, glorified be He, has thus explained that Allah does not speak to any human being except in one of three ways: by revelation, from behind a veil, or by sending a messenger who reveals, by His permission, whatever He wills. He thus distinguished revelation from speaking, and it was from behind a veil that He spoke to Moses.

---

## Page 6083

He has also stated in several places that He called to Moses, as in His words:

“And We called him from the side of the Mount,”

to the end of the verse. He also says:

“When he came to it, he was called from the right bank of the valley,”

to the end of the verse. By the agreement of language scholars, a “call” can only be an audible sound. This is something upon which the early Muslims and the majority of Muslims agree.

The People of the Book say that Moses’s Lord called to him with a call that he heard with his own ears, and that He called to him with a voice that Moses heard. A voice can only be speech, and speech can only consist of letters arranged in sequence. Allah Most High says:

“The revelation of the Book is from Allah, the Exalted in Might, the Wise.”

He also says:

“Hā Mīm. A revelation from the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful.”

And He says:

“Hā Mīm. The revelation of the Book is from Allah, the Exalted in Might, the Wise.”

Thus, He has made clear in several places that the Book—the Arabic Quran—was sent down from Allah.

This is the meaning of the early Muslims’ statement: “From Him it originated.” Ahmad ibn Hanbal, may Allah have mercy on him, said: “From Him it originated”—that is, He is the One who spoke it. Those who said that it was created maintained that He created it in something other than Himself, so that it emerged from that created thing. The early Muslims therefore said: “From Him it originated”—meaning that He is the One who spoke it. He did not create it in something else, such that it would be the speech of the subject in which He created it.

For when Allah Most High creates an attribute in a subject, that attribute belongs to that subject, not to the Lord of all worlds. If He creates a taste or a color in a subject, it is that subject that moves and takes on color thereby. Likewise, if He creates life, will, power, knowledge, or speech in a subject, it is that subject that wills

---

## Page 6084

, has power, has knowledge, and speaks those words. The quality created in that subject is not an attribute of the Lord of all worlds. Rather, the Lord Most High is described by the attributes that subsist in Him, not by those He creates in other created beings. Thus, He is the Ever-Living, the All-Knowing, the All-Powerful, the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing, the Merciful, and the One who speaks the Quran and other speech, by virtue of His life, knowledge, power, and speech that subsist in Him—not by virtue of any of these qualities that He creates in others.

Whoever holds that His speech is created must consequently say that a created being is the one who said to Moses:

“Indeed, I am Allah. There is no deity except Me, so worship Me and establish prayer for My remembrance.”

This is impossible: these words can only be the speech of the Lord of all worlds. If Allah has spoken the Quran, the Torah, and the other scriptures, with their meanings and their words composed of letters, then none of that is created; rather, it is the speech of the Lord of all worlds.

Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal was told that so-and-so said: “When Allah created the letters, they prostrated to Him, except alif, which said, ‘I will not prostrate until I am commanded.’” He replied: “This is disbelief.” Thus, he rejected the claim that letters are created, because if letters as a class were created, it would follow that the Arabic Quran, the Hebrew Torah, and the other scriptures were created. This is false and contrary to the position of the early Muslims and the imams, as well as to rational and scriptural evidence, as has been explained at length elsewhere.

---

## Page 6085

People have disputed extensively concerning Allah’s speech. There are approximately six major groups. The view furthest removed from Islam is that of those philosophers and Sabians who say that Allah’s speech is merely what emanates into souls, whether from the Active Intellect or from something else. They say that Allah spoke to Moses only from the heaven of Moses’ own intellect—that is, through speech that arose within his soul, which he did not hear from outside himself.

The foundation of their position is that the celestial spheres are eternal and without beginning, and that Allah did not create them by His will and power in six days, as the prophets reported. Indeed, they say that Allah does not know particulars. When the prophets brought the astonishing things they brought, these people began interpreting them in ways that distorted words from their proper meanings, seeking to reconcile them with the doctrines of their heretical predecessors. Thus they made statements of this kind.

These people are more deeply immersed in disbelief than the Jews and Christians, and their contradictions are numerous. For example, they claim that an attribute is identical with the one it describes, and that one attribute is identical with another. They therefore say: He is intellect, the thinker, and the object of thought; the object of pleasure, the one who takes pleasure, and pleasure itself; the lover, the beloved, and love itself. They sometimes express this by saying that He is living, knowing, known, loving, and beloved. They say that knowledge itself is love itself and power itself; that knowledge itself is the knower himself; and that love itself is the beloved himself. They also say that He is a complete cause from eternity; hence its effect must accompany it in

---

## Page 6086

eternity in temporal terms, although it is prior to it causally, not temporally. They say that a complete cause and its effect coexist in time and necessarily accompany one another: no effect exists without a complete cause, and no complete cause exists without its effect accompanying it in time. Yet they acknowledge that events in the world occur successively, without anything newly arising from the First Originator that would make Him the cause of these successive events. In reality, their position amounts to saying that events arise without anyone bringing them into existence. Likewise, according to their principles, these events cease to exist after coming into existence without any cause necessitating their cessation. Opposing them were groups of speculative theologians who supposed that the effect of a fully operative cause could be delayed; that an agent endowed with power and choice favors one of two things within his power over the other without any determining factor; and that events have a beginning, having come into existence after not existing, without any newly occurring cause.

Neither group arrived at the middle position: a fully operative cause necessarily entails that its effect follows immediately upon its complete exercise of causation, neither accompanying that exercise nor occurring after a delay. As the Most High says:

“His command, when He wills a thing, is only to say to it, ‘Be,’ and it is.”

Thus He, glorified be He, brings everything into being, and it comes to be immediately upon His bringing it into being—not simultaneously with that act in time, nor after a delay. Similarly, becoming broken follows immediately upon the act of breaking; becoming severed follows immediately upon the act of cutting; and a divorce taking effect follows immediately upon its pronouncement, neither after a delay nor simultaneously with it in time. Those who maintain that there is a delay supposed that an infinite succession of events was impossible, which committed them to the conclusion that

---

## Page 6087

the Lord could not do this. They therefore committed themselves to the position that the Lord could not have always spoken by His will, nor could He have always had the power to act and speak by His will.

They then divided into different groups. Some said:

His speech can only be temporally originated, because speech can only be an object of power and will, and whatever is such can only be temporally originated. Whatever is temporally originated must be created and separate from Him, because, in their view, it is impossible for temporal events to subsist in Him or to form an infinite succession.

Others said:

Rather, His speech can only subsist in Him. Whatever subsists in Him cannot be subject to His will and volition, but must be eternal in its particular existence. For if it were an object of power and will, it would be temporally originated, and temporal events would thus subsist in Him. If they subsisted in Him, He would neither precede them nor be free of them. Whatever is not free of temporal events is itself temporally originated, because a succession of temporal events without a beginning is impossible.

Still others said:

Rather, He speaks by His will and power, but it is impossible for Him to have spoken in eternity, or to have always spoken by His will and power, because this would entail the existence of temporal events without a beginning, which is impossible.

“These groups” said:

Through this method we came to know that the world is temporally originated. We inferred that bodies are temporally originated from the fact that they are neither free of temporal events nor prior to them; and whatever does not precede temporal events is itself temporally originated. Then some of them supposed that this

---

## Page 6088

is a self-evident proposition, without recognizing its ambiguity. Others recognized the distinction between what does not precede a finite, bounded series of temporal events and what precedes the class of temporal events occurring one after another. The former is necessarily temporally originated, because those events have a definite beginning; whatever does not precede them must exist either alongside them or after them, and in either case it is temporally originated.

As for temporal events occurring one after another, people have disagreed about this. Some have held that such a succession is impossible in both the past and the future, as was the position of Jahm and Abū al-Hudhayl. Jahm therefore maintained that Paradise and Hellfire would cease to exist, while Abū al-Hudhayl maintained that the movements of their inhabitants would cease. Others have held that it is possible in the future but not in the past, because the past has come into existence, whereas the future has not. This is the position of many groups of speculative thinkers.

Still others have held that it is possible in both the past and the future. This is the position of the leading authorities of the religious communities and the imams of the Sunnah, such as ‘Abd Allāh ibn al-Mubārak, Ahmad ibn Hanbal, and others who maintain that Allah has always spoken whenever He wills, that His words have no end and subsist in His essence, and that He speaks by His will and power.

This is also the position of the leading philosophers. Aristotle and his followers, however, make this claim concerning the motions of the celestial sphere, which they hold to be beginninglessly eternal. In this they opposed the majority of philosophers, as well as the prophets, the messengers, and the great majority of rational people. For these all agree that Allah created the heavens and the earth; indeed, He is the Creator of everything, and everything other than Allah is created and temporally originated, coming into existence after not having existed. They also agree that it is Allah Most High who is beginninglessly eternal, together with His attributes of

---

## Page 6089

perfection. His attributes are not excluded from what His name denotes. Rather, whoever says, “I worshipped Allah and called upon Allah,” has worshipped His essence, endowed with the attributes of perfection that befit Him. His essence cannot exist without its inseparable attributes.

Then, when followers of Aristotle—such as Ibn Sīnā and others like him—discussed prophethood and considered what the prophets had taught—that Allah speaks, that He truly spoke to Moses, and that He is the Creator of everything—they began distorting the prophets’ words from their proper meanings. They say: “Origination is of two kinds: intrinsic and temporal. We hold that the celestial sphere is temporally originated, meaning that it is an effect, even though it is beginninglessly eternal and has always existed alongside Allah.” They also said that it is created in this sense. Yet the divine Scriptures state that Allah created the heavens and the earth in six days, whereas what is beginninglessly eternal cannot come into existence within a span of days.

It is known with certainty that when the messengers declared that Allah created everything, or that He created such and such, they meant that He created it and brought it into existence after it had not existed, as He said:

“I created you before, when you were nothing.”

Sound reason agrees with this and recognizes that what is acted upon, created, and fashioned cannot be simultaneous in time with its agent, but must come after it, and that acting necessarily entails bringing the object of the act into existence.

---

## Page 6090

They also said to these people: Your assertion, “He is a complete cause in beginningless eternity,” is ambiguous. It may mean universal causal efficacy extending to everything; causal efficacy in an unrestricted sense, producing one thing after another; or causal efficacy directed at one particular thing to the exclusion of others.

If you mean “the first,” it follows that nothing new can occur in the world, which contradicts observation. If you mean “the second,” it follows that everything other than Allah is created and originated, coming into existence after not having existed, while the Lord has always spoken by His will and done whatever He wills. This contradicts your position and entails that everything other than Him is created. It accords with what the messengers taught, and sound reason points to it. Thus it becomes clear that sound reason agrees with what the prophets taught.

If you mean “the third,” your position is invalid, because it entails that He wills them to come into existence after not having acted to produce them, without any new cause arising to necessitate their origination. This contradicts your position. If this is sound, then He could bring everything into existence after not having brought anything into existence. If it is not sound, the claim collapses. Your position is therefore false on either supposition.

Your position amounts to saying that a complete cause can exist only simultaneously with its effect, and that an effect can exist only simultaneously with its complete cause. It then follows from your position that nothing can come into existence; that everything which has come into existence has done so without a cause; and that any distinction between one effect and another is invalid. You cannot say that some effects are simultaneous with the complete cause while others arise later.

---

## Page 6091

Moreover, the notion that He produces a particular effect that coexists with Him eternally, without beginning or end, is plainly contrary to reason. Furthermore, you and all other rational people agree that what is merely possible, admitting both existence and nonexistence—what you designate as “the possible in the specific sense,” contrasted with the necessarily existent and the necessarily impossible—can only exist at one time and be nonexistent at another. You also agree that whatever is eternal and beginningless must be necessarily existent, such that its nonexistence is impossible. Aristotle and his followers agreed on this, including Ibn Sīnā, who stated it in his well-known works, such as al-Shifā and others.

He then contradicted himself, claiming that the celestial sphere is possible despite being eternal and beginningless, having always existed and continuing to exist forever. He also claimed that what is necessary through another—eternal and beginningless, with its nonexistence being impossible—can nevertheless be possible, admitting both existence and nonexistence. He further claimed that it has an essence distinct from its existence. The unsoundness and inconsistency of these people’s position have been discussed at length elsewhere.

The “second position” concerning the speech of Allah Most High is held by those who say that no attribute subsists in Allah: neither life, knowledge, power, speech, will, mercy, anger, nor anything else. Rather, He created speech in something other than Himself, and that created thing is His speech. This is the position of the Jahmiyyah and the Muʿtazilah.

This position likewise contradicts the Quran, the Sunnah, and the consensus of the early generations. It contradicts the prophets’ statements and explicit teachings. These people have no statement from the prophets that agrees with their position. Rather, they have flawed rational arguments whose unsoundness we have explained elsewhere than in this

---

## Page 6092

passage. These people claimed that their arguments established that the world came into existence, yet they neither championed Islam nor defeated its enemies.

The “third position” is that of those who say that He speaks independently of His will and power, with speech that subsists in His essence eternally, without beginning or end. They agree with the preceding group on the fundamental premise of their position, but say that attributes subsist in the Lord, whereas attributes exercised by choice, which relate to His will and power, do not subsist in Him. The first person within Islam widely known to have expressed this position was Abdullāh ibn Sa‘īd ibn Kullāb.

His followers then differed. Some said: That speech is a single meaning: it is the command to do everything commanded, the prohibition of everything forbidden, and the statement concerning everything spoken of. If expressed in Arabic, it is the Quran; if expressed in Hebrew, it is the Torah. They said that the meaning of the Quran, the Torah, and the Gospel is one, and that the meaning of the Verse of the Throne is the meaning of the verse on debt.

They also said: Commands, prohibitions, and statements are attributes of speech, not categories of it. Some of their more exacting thinkers reduced that meaning to declarative speech, and declarative speech to knowledge.
