The majority of rational people say: The unsoundness of this position is self-evident. Those who hold it say that His speaking to Moses consists only in creating a perception through which Moses understands that meaning.

They were therefore asked: Did he understand all of the speech, or only some of it? If he understood all of it,

---

## Page 6093

then he possessed Allah’s knowledge. If he understood only part of it, then it is divisible, whereas in their view Allah’s speech admits neither division nor multiplicity.

They were also told:

Allah has distinguished between His speaking to Moses and His conveying revelation to others. Yet according to your premise, there is no difference.

They were also told:

Allah has declared whoever considers the Arabic Quran to be the word of a human being a disbeliever. Yet He has attributed it, in one passage, to a human messenger and, in another, to an angelic messenger. In one passage He says:

“Indeed, it is the word of a noble messenger.”
“It is not the word of a poet—how little you believe!”
“Nor the word of a soothsayer—how little you reflect!”

This messenger is Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. In the other passage He says:

“Indeed, it is the word of a noble messenger,”
“Possessed of strength, held in honour with the Lord of the Throne,”
“Obeyed there and trustworthy.”

This is Gabriel. Thus, He attributes it in one passage to the angelic messenger and in another to the human messenger. Allah chooses messengers from among the angels and from among humankind.

Some of these people claimed that Gabriel or Muhammad originated the Arabic Quran. They were therefore told:

If either of them had originated it, it could not properly be attributed to the other. Yet Allah, glorified is He, attributed it to each of them using the designation “messenger,” which points to the One who sent him, rather than the designation “angel” or “prophet.” This indicates that it is the word of a messenger who conveyed it from the One who sent him, not the word of an angel or a prophet who originated it himself. Indeed, whoever says that it is the word of a human being has disbelieved.

---

## Page 6094

And the other group, who agreed with Ibn Kullāb that Allah does not speak by His will and power, said:

“Rather, eternal speech consists of letters, or letters and sounds, inseparable from the Lord’s essence, without beginning or end. He does not speak them by His will and power, nor does He utter them successively.”

These people failed to distinguish between letters and speech as general categories and particular letters that are eternal and beginningless. This, too, is something that most rational people regard as self-evidently false. For letters that follow one another cannot each be eternal and beginningless, even if their kind is eternal. Words without end and successive letters without end are possible, but each individual letter cannot be eternal and beginningless, since whatever is preceded by something else cannot be beginningless.

Some of them distinguished between their existence and their essence, saying:

“The sequence pertains to their essence, not their existence.”

The falsity of this statement is self-evident to anyone who reflects upon it. For the essence of speech consisting of letters does not occur successively, whereas sound can only occur successively. It is therefore impossible for the existence of the particular essence to be beginningless and thereby precede it, although the distinction between the two is clear—if a distinction between them is assumed. These two considerations entail that their existence must also follow a successive order.

Some among them further claim that this eternal speech is the sounds heard from people reciting the Quran, the Torah and the Gospel, or some of these. This was more manifestly

---

## Page 6095

false than the preceding view, for it is necessarily known that the sounds produced by human beings come into existence.

A “fifth group” said: “Rather, Allah speaks by His will and power, uttering the Quran in Arabic and other speech. However, it was not possible for Him to speak by His will in pre-eternity, because events without a beginning are impossible.” Like those others, they held that the Lord was unable in pre-eternity to speak by His will or to act. They then held that action and speech became possible and within His power without anything new occurring to bring about that ability and possibility—just as those others maintained concerning the effects of His acts that exist separately from Him.

As for the early generations, they maintained that Allah has always spoken whenever He wills; that speech is an attribute of perfection; and that one who speaks is more perfect than one who does not, just as one who knows and has power is more perfect than one who neither knows nor has power. One who speaks by his will and power is more perfect than one whose speech is inseparable from his essence, yet over which he has no power and in which he exercises no will. Perfection lies only in attributes subsisting in the one described by them, not in things separate from him. Someone can be described as speaking, knowing and possessing power only through speech, knowledge and power that subsist in him.

That being so, one who has always possessed the attributes of perfection is more perfect than one who acquired them after not possessing them—even if their coming into existence were possible. How much more so, then, if that is impossible? Thus it is clear that the Lord has always possessed, and will always possess, the attributes of perfection and the qualities of majesty. Among the greatest of these is speech. He has therefore always spoken whenever He wills and will always do so. He speaks in Arabic whenever He wills, as He spoke the Quran

---

## Page 6096

in Arabic. Whatever Allah has spoken subsists in Him; it is not something created and separate from Him. Thus, the letters that make up Allah’s most beautiful names and His revealed Books are not created, because Allah spoke them.

Section

Some later scholars then disputed the letters found in human speech. Their dispute arose for two reasons.

The first is that they did not distinguish between speech that Allah Himself utters and that is heard from Him, and that same speech when someone conveys it from Him and it is heard from that person. The Quran is Allah’s speech: He spoke it, both its wording and its meaning, with His own voice. When reciters recite it, however, they do so with their own voices.

When a reciter says:

“All praise is for Allah, Lord of all worlds,
the Most Compassionate, the Most Merciful,”

the speech heard from him is Allah’s speech, not his own, yet he has recited it with his own voice, not Allah’s voice. The speech is the Creator’s speech, while the voice is the reciter’s voice. As the Prophet (may Allah Most High bless him and grant him peace) said:

“Beautify the Quran with your voices.”

He also used to say:

“Is there a man who will take me to his people so that I may convey the speech of my Lord? For Quraysh have prevented me from conveying the speech of my Lord.”

Both hadiths are reliably established. He thus made clear that the speech he conveyed was the speech of his Lord, and he made clear that the reciter

---

## Page 6097

recites it in his own voice. The Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) said:

“He is not one of us who does not recite the Quran melodiously.”

Ahmad, al-Shāfi‘ī, and others said: “This means beautifying it with one’s voice.” Ahmad ibn Hanbal said: “He beautifies it with his own voice.” Ahmad thus made clear that the reciter beautifies the Quran with his own voice.

The second reason is that the early generations said: “The Quran is Allah’s speech, sent down and uncreated.” They also said: “He has always spoken whenever He wills.” They thus explained that Allah’s speech is eternal—that is, His speech as a kind is eternal and has always existed. None of them said that a particular utterance itself is eternal, nor did any of them say: “The Quran is eternal.” Rather, they said: “It is Allah’s speech, sent down and uncreated.”

Since Allah spoke the Quran by His will, the Quran is His speech, sent down from Him and uncreated. Yet this does not mean that it has existed eternally alongside Allah, even though Allah has always spoken whenever He wills, so that His speech as a kind is eternal.

Whoever understands the statements of the early generations and distinguishes between these positions will be freed from the doubts surrounding these difficult questions over which people throughout the world have been in turmoil.

Whoever says that all the letters of the alphabet are created and that Allah Most High’s speech is created has expressed a view contrary to sound reason and authentic transmitted evidence. Likewise, whoever says that people’s own voices, their ink, or anything of that sort is eternal has contradicted the statements of the early generations. The falsity of his view is apparent to everyone. He has introduced an innovated position that none of the imams of the Muslims ever held, nor has any major group among

---

## Page 6098

the Muslims. Rather, the four imams and the majority of their followers are free of that view. Whoever says that a particular letter or word is itself eternal has introduced an innovated position that is false according to both revelation and reason.

Whoever says that the letters with which Allah spoke the Quran and other speech, considered as a kind, are uncreated; that the Arabic speech He uttered is uncreated; and that the letters composing it are part of it and inseparable from it, and, since Allah spoke them, cannot be created—has spoken correctly.

Likewise, if he says that Allah guided His servants and taught them to express themselves, enabling them to utter these letters in different languages, and bestowed His favour upon them by enabling them to pronounce the letters that form His Books, His speech, and His names, then he has spoken correctly.

A human being, along with all the sounds, movements, and other things that subsist in him, is created, having come into existence after not existing. The Lord Most High, with His attributes, words, and actions that subsist in Him, is uncreated.

When His servants recite His speech, the speech they recite is His speech, not anyone else’s. His speech, which He uttered, cannot be created, whereas the movements and voices by which they recite His speech are created. Likewise, whatever of His speech is written in copies of the Quran is His speech, written in those copies, and His speech is uncreated. The ink used to write His speech or anything else is created.

---

## Page 6099

He, glorified and exalted, has distinguished His speech from the ink used for His words by saying:

“Say, ‘If the sea were ink for the words of my Lord, the sea would be exhausted before the words of my Lord were exhausted, even if We brought its like as a supplement.’”

Allah’s words are uncreated, whereas the ink used to write Allah’s words is created. The Quran written in copies of the Quran is uncreated, as is that written in the Preserved Tablet and elsewhere. The Most High says:

“Rather, it is a glorious Quran, in a Preserved Tablet.”

And He says:

“No! Indeed, it is a reminder—so whoever wills may take heed of it—in honoured pages, exalted and purified.”

And the Most High says:

“Reciting purified pages containing upright writings.”

And He says:

“Indeed, it is a noble Quran, in a well-guarded Book, which none touch except the purified.”

Section

As for the two disputants who disagreed over “the letters that Allah sent down to Adam,” one said: “They are eternal and have no beginning, whereas their vowel marks and dots came into being.”

The other said: “They are not Allah’s speech; rather, they are created, including their vowel marks and dots. It is Allah who is eternal, and His speech originated from Him and will return to Him; it is sent down and uncreated. But He wrote using them.”

They ask us to explain what is correct and which of them is sounder in belief. They should be told: Explaining what is correct requires clarifying the ambiguous language in the question.

---

## Page 6100

For much disagreement among rational people arises because they do not clearly understand the point at issue. In many disputes, the correct position may be a third view, different from either of the two advanced. Many disputes may also rest on a weak premise: once its invalidity is explained, the dispute falls away.

The first matter in this question is their expression, “the letters that Allah sent down to Adam.” Some have mentioned that Allah sent down to him the letters of the alphabet, written separately. Ibn Qutaybah mentioned this in al-Maʿārif. This and similar accounts appear in historical works such as the history of Ibn Jarīr al-Tabarī and others. Such accounts are related from those who transmit Israelite narratives and similar reports concerning earlier prophets, such as Wahb ibn Munabbih, Kaʿb al-Ahbār, Mālik ibn Dīnār, Muhammad ibn Ishāq, and others.

Muslims unanimously agree that what these people relate concerning earlier prophets may not be made a basis for the religion of the Muslims unless it is established through mass transmission or transmitted from the Seal of the Messengers. Moreover, this report is contradicted by another report:

“The first to write and sew was Idrīs.”

This is related from some of the early generations and is comparable to the former account—indeed, stronger. They mention in it that Idrīs was the first to sew clothes and write with a pen. Accordingly, Adam’s descendants before Idrīs neither wrote with pens nor read books. And what is stated in the well-known hadith of Abū Dharr, narrated from Abū Dharr, from

---

## Page 6101

the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, is: “Adam was a prophet to whom Allah spoke; Allah spoke to him directly.” It does not say that He sent down anything written to him. Thus, it does not say that Allah sent down a scroll or a book to Adam, nor is this known among the People of the Book. This indicates that the claim has no foundation. Even if it were known among the People of the Book, this report would still be found neither in the Quran nor in authentic hadiths from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. Rather, it would belong to the category of Israelite narratives that one is not obliged to believe; indeed, one may not affirm their authenticity without evidence. As the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said in an authentic hadith:

“When the People of the Book relate something to you, neither believe them nor disbelieve them, for they may tell you something true and you reject it, or tell you something false and you believe it.”

Allah, glorified be He, taught Adam all the names and enabled him to utter coherent speech. As for teaching isolated letters, especially when written, this is instruction that offers no benefit. However, when people wished to teach beginners to write, they began by teaching them the individual letters of the alphabet, then teaching them to combine these letters. Thus, the beginner is taught abjad, hawwaz, but this alone does not constitute speech.

Accordingly, this account that the letters of the alphabet were sent down to Adam is established neither by transmitted evidence nor by reason. Rather, the stronger indication of both is that it did not happen. It belongs to the same category as the reports they attribute to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, interpreting alif, bā, tā, thā, and interpreting abjad

---

## Page 6102

hawwaz and huttī. They also relate that the Messiah said this to his teacher at the elementary school. All these reports are feeble—indeed, fabricated. The scholars of transmitted reports agree that none of them may be cited as evidence, although some authors who wrote on this subject mentioned them, such as al-Sharīf al-Mazīdī, Shaykh Abū al-Faraj, his son 'Abd al-Wahhāb, and others. Some Quran commentators and historians also mention them. Yet specialists in this field regard all of this as false, and it cannot be relied upon in any matter of religion. Although Abū Bakr al-Naqqāsh and other Quran commentators mentioned it, and al-Sharīf al-Mazīdī al-Harrānī and others transmitted it from al-Naqqāsh and writers like him, the most eminent commentator to mention it was Abū Ja'far Muhammad ibn Jarīr al-Tabarī. He explained in his commentary that everything transmitted from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, on this subject is false.

At the end of his commentary, he mentioned people's differing interpretations of abjad, hawwaz and huttī. He cited a hadith transmitted through Muhammad ibn Ziyād al-Jazarī, from Furāt ibn Abī al-Furāt, from Mu'āwiya ibn Qurra, from his father, who said:

The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said, “Learn abājād and its interpretation. Allah. As for hā, it stands for the Abyss; as for wāw, woe to whoever is heedless; as for zāy, the corner; and as for hā, the remission of sins for those who seek forgiveness before dawn.” He related the remainder of the hadith along similar lines.

He mentioned a second report transmitted by ‘Abd al-Rahīm ibn Wāqid: “Al-Furāt ibn al-Sā’ib narrated to me, from Maymūn ibn Mihrān, from Ibn ‘Abbās, who said:

## Page 6104

of this kind, and he also related it as a statement of al-Rabī‘ ibn Anas himself.

Abū al-Faraj al-Maqdisī narrated, through al-Sharīf al-Mazīdī, a similar hadith from ‘Umar, from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, explaining the letters alif, bā, tā and thā.

Then Ibn Jarīr said:

I say: This Ismā‘īl ibn Yahyā is known as al-Taymī, a Kufan known for lying. The reports Ismā‘īl ibn ‘Ayyāsh narrates from non-Syrian transmitters cannot be used as evidence. Rather, he is weak in what he transmits from the people of the Hijaz and Iraq, unlike what he transmits from his Syrian teachers. He is accurate in preserving the hadith of his own region but makes frequent errors in the hadith of those others. The scholars of hadith transmitters agree on this. ‘Abd al-Rahmān ibn Wāqid cannot be relied upon as evidence, by agreement of the scholars, and Furāt ibn al-Sā’ib is also weak

---

## Page 6105

and cannot be relied upon as evidence; he is Furāt ibn Abī al-Furāt. Muhammad ibn Ziyād al-Jazarī is also weak.

People have disagreed about “Abjad, Hawwaz, Huttī.” One group said that these were people’s names: according to some, the names of the kings of Midian, or of people who were tyrannical kings.

It was also said that these were the names of the six days in which Allah created the world. Al-Tabarī preferred the first view. Those who held it claimed that the original forms were “Abū Jād,” like “Abī ‘Ād,” and “Hawāzz,” like “Rawādd” and “Jawwāb,” and that they were not inflected because of the absence of linkage and composition.

The correct view is that these are not names designating particular things. Rather, they were put together to teach how words are formed from the letters of the alphabet, once the letters themselves have been learned. Their actual wording is “Abjad, Hawwaz, Huttī,” not “Abū Jād, Hawāzz.” Subsequently, many arithmeticians began using them as symbols for numerical values, assigning one to alif, two to bā, three to jīm, and so on through yā. They then say: kāf is twenty … (1)

Others, among geometers and logicians, use them as symbols for drawn lines or for the terms of constructed syllogisms. For example, they say: “Every A is B, and every B is C; therefore every A is C.” They used these expressions in their examples because they indicate the form of the syllogistic figure, while a syllogism is not restricted to any particular subject matter. Similarly, morphologists use the pattern “fa‘ala” to correspond to the root letters,

> **Footnotes:**
> (1) A blank in the original.

---

## Page 6106

and pronounce the additional letters themselves. Thus they say that the pattern of istakhraja is “istaf‘ala.” Prosodists use combinations of these letters to represent metrical patterns, but consider only the metre, without distinguishing root letters from additional letters. Thus, when one of them was asked about the pattern of naktal, he answered, “naf‘al,” and the morphologists laughed at him. According to them, its pattern is naftal, since its original form is naktālu, whose underlying form is naktayilu. The yā carried a vowel and was preceded by a fathah, so it became an alif; then, when the verb became jussive, the alif was dropped. We give a similar explanation for na‘tadi and naftadi, from i‘tāda, ya‘tādu (“to be accustomed”), and iqtāda al-ba‘īra, yaqtāduhu (“to lead a camel”). Something similar applies to naqtayilu. When they omitted the alif, which is called the lām of the word, its pattern became … (1)

And they were made “eight.” It may carry a vowel, in which case it is hamzah, or carry no vowel. It counts as two letters under the first convention and one under the second. Alif is grouped with wāw and yā because they are the weak letters. This is why it was placed at the end of the alphabet. They pronounced the initial sound of each letter’s name, except alif: since they could not pronounce it at the beginning of an utterance, they placed lām before it and said “lā.” The one at the beginning is the vowelled hamzah, since hamzah occurs at the beginning of its name. Some people pronounce it “lām alif,” but the correct pronunciation is “lā.” A fuller discussion of this belongs elsewhere.

The point here is that knowledge requires authenticated transmission and soundly established reasoning. Weak reports, especially fabricated ones, cannot be relied upon. Likewise, unsound theories and false rational arguments rooted in ignorance cannot serve as evidence.

> **Footnotes:**

> Shaykh Nāsir ibn Hamad al-Fahd states (p. 102):
> There is an omission after the words, “When they deleted the alif called the lām of the word [the third root letter], its pattern became,” since the predicate of “became” is missing. It is “naftal”—meaning the pattern of “naktal.” The subsequent wording, “And they were made eight; it may carry a vowel …,” is disordered, n. However, I think another omission has also occurred. The correct wording is “And they were made twenty-eight,” referring to the number of letters in the alphabet, since the discussion concerned those letters.
> As for his words, “It may carry a vowel … or carry no vowel,” he apparently means alif. Its vowelled form is hamzah, placed at the beginning of the alphabet; its unvowelled form comes at the end and is represented by “lā.” The lām was placed before it solely to enable its pronunciation, because Arabs do not begin an utterance with an unvowelled letter. His subsequent discussion concerns this. Thus, it appears—and Allah knows best—that after mentioning the number of letters in the alphabet, he discussed alif and these forms of it. Accordingly, the corrected passage would read: “When they deleted the alif called the lām of the word, its pattern became [naftal]. And they were made eight [and twenty]; [and alif] may carry a vowel …,” or something similar. And Allah knows best.

## Page 6107

Second, it may be said:

Allah has spoken these letters found in the Arabic Quran by pronouncing their names, as in His sayings: “Alif Lām Mīm,” “Alif Lām Mīm Sād,” “Alif Lām Mīm,” “Tā Sīn,” “Hā Mīm,” “Kāf Hā Yā ‘Ayn Sād,” “Hā Mīm,” “‘Ayn Sīn Qāf,” “Nūn,” and “Qāf.” All of this is Allah’s speech, uncreated.

Third, when these letters occur in the speech of His servants—and likewise when names found in the Quran, such as Adam, Noah, Muhammad, Abraham, and others, occur in their speech—it is said:

Allah has spoken these names and letters, but He did not speak them in isolation, for a name alone does not constitute speech. Rather, He spoke them within His speech that He revealed, as in His saying:

“Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah,”

and His saying:

“And when Abraham said, ‘My Lord, make this city secure,’”

through to His saying:

“My Lord, make me steadfast in prayer, and some of my descendants as well,”

and His saying:

“Indeed, Allah chose Adam, Noah, the family of Abraham, and the family of ‘Imrān above all people,”

and other such passages.

When we speak and mention these names, our speech is created, and the letters of our speech are created. As Ahmad ibn Hanbal said to a man, “Are you not created?”

He replied, “Yes.”

Ahmad said, “Does your speech not come from you?”

He replied, “Yes.”

Ahmad said, “Is your speech not created?”

He replied, “Yes.”

Ahmad said, “Allah Most High, however, is uncreated, and His speech comes from Him and is not created.”

Thus Ahmad and others explicitly stated that the speech of Allah’s servants is created, and they merely

---

## Page 6108

speak using names and letters whose counterparts occur in the speech of Allah Most High. Yet Allah Most High spoke them with His own voice and His own letters, and that is uncreated. The attributes of Allah Most High do not resemble the attributes of His servants.

For nothing is like Allah Most High, whether in His essence, His attributes, or His acts. The voice with which He will call His servants on the Day of Resurrection, and the voice that Moses heard from Him, are unlike the voices of any created beings. The audible voice consists of letters arranged together, and nothing among the attributes of created beings resembles those letters, just as Allah’s knowledge, which subsists in His essence, is unlike the knowledge of His servants. Allah does not resemble created beings in any attribute. He, glorified is He, has taught His servants whatever He wills of His knowledge, as He Most High says:

“They encompass nothing of His knowledge except what He wills.”

When Allah teaches them whatever He teaches them of His knowledge, His knowledge itself, which is His attribute, is not created, whereas the servants themselves and their attributes are created. Someone may, however, consider what the term “knowledge” denotes without qualification. It must not then be said that such knowledge is created, since the Lord possesses this attribute, even though the knowledge possessed by a servant is created.

The underlying principle is that any attribute ascribed both to Allah and to His servants is ascribed to Allah in a manner befitting Him, and to His servants in a manner befitting them. Examples include life, knowledge, power, hearing, sight, and speech. Allah possesses life, knowledge, power, hearing, sight, and speech. His speech contains letters, and He speaks with His own voice. A servant likewise possesses life, knowledge, power, hearing, sight, and speech,

---

## Page 6109

and a servant’s speech contains letters, and he speaks with his own voice.

These attributes may be considered in three ways: as ascribed to the Lord, as ascribed to a servant, or without qualification, without being specific to either the Lord or a servant.

When a servant says, “Allah’s life, Allah’s knowledge, Allah’s power, Allah’s speech,” and the like, all of these are uncreated and do not resemble the attributes of created beings. When he says, “A servant’s knowledge, a servant’s power, a servant’s speech,” all of these are created and do not resemble the Lord’s attributes. But when he says, “Knowledge, power, speech,” these are general, unqualified terms. They cannot all be described indiscriminately as either created or uncreated. Rather, those attributes possessed by the Lord are uncreated, while those possessed by a servant are created. An attribute thus takes its status from the one who possesses it: if that is the Creator, His attributes are uncreated; if it is a created servant, his attributes are created.

Furthermore, when someone recites the Opening Surah and other passages of Allah’s speech, the Quran itself is Allah’s uncreated speech, even though the servants’ movements and voices are created.

If a person in a state of major ritual impurity says:

“All praise is for Allah, Lord of all worlds,”

intending it as Quranic recitation, he is prohibited from doing so, and it counts as Quran. But if he says it intending to praise Allah, without intending recitation, he is not reciting the Quran, and doing so is permissible for him. An example of this is the saying of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace: “The best speech after

---

## Page 6110

the Quran is four phrases, which are also part of the Quran: Glory be to Allah, praise be to Allah, there is no god but Allah, and Allah is the Greatest.” Muslim narrated it in his Sahīh.

He thus stated that they are the best speech after the Quran, while also saying that they are part of the Quran. They are therefore part of the Quran in one respect, but not in another. If someone says:

“O John, take the Book,”

intending Quranic recitation, he has spoken Allah’s words, and his prayer is not invalidated, by scholarly consensus. If he also intends thereby to alert someone else, his prayer is not invalidated according to the majority of scholars.

But if he says to a man named John, in whose presence there is a book, “John, take the book,” this would be created speech. Here, the name John refers to that particular person, and “the book” refers to that particular book; he does not intend what Allah intended by His words:

“O John, take the Book.”

This is the created being’s speech, in both its wording and its meaning.

People have disagreed over what “speech” fundamentally denotes. Some say it denotes the wording that conveys a meaning; others, the meaning conveyed by the wording. Others say it denotes each of the two as distinct meanings of the same word. Yet others say that it is an inclusive term for both together, encompassing both when used without qualification, although, when qualified, it may refer sometimes to one and sometimes to the other. This is the position of the early generations and the leading jurists, even though this position is not acknowledged in many books.

This resembles people’s disagreement over what “the human being” denotes: is it the soul alone or the body alone? The correct view is that it denotes both the soul and the body together, even though

---

## Page 6111

a contextual indication may make it refer sometimes to one and sometimes to the other. Their disagreement over what “speech” denotes thus resembles their disagreement over what “one who speaks” denotes.

If someone gives the names Muhammad and Abraham and says, “Muhammad has come, and Abraham has come,” these are not the Muhammad and Abraham mentioned in the Quran. If, however, he says, “Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, and Abraham is Allah’s close friend,” meaning the Seal of the Messengers and the close friend of the Most Merciful, then he has uttered the names of the Muhammad and Abraham mentioned in the Quran. Yet he has used these names to compose a statement of his own, so it is his speech; he has not uttered them as part of the Arabic Quran which Allah spoke.

This is further clarified by what the jurists have stated concerning the etiquette of relieving oneself: one should not take along anything bearing a mention of Allah. They cited as evidence the hadith in the Sunan collections:

“When the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, entered the privy, he would remove his ring. His ring was inscribed with ‘Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah.’”

“Muhammad” occupied one line, “Messenger” another, and “Allah” another. Yet no scholar has prohibited taking along material containing human speech and letters of the alphabet, such as the accounting sheets on which administrative clerks record accounts, the papers on which merchants record what they sell, and similar things.

The Prophet’s biography also relates:

“When the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, made a peace agreement with Ghatafān in return for half the dates of Medina, Saʿd came to him and asked, ‘Is this something Allah has commanded—in which case we hear and obey—or something you are doing for our benefit?’ The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, explained to him that he had not done this on the basis of revelation, but through his own judgment. Saʿd then said, ‘We were indeed living in the days of pre-Islamic ignorance

---

## Page 6112

and they would not eat a single one of our dates except as guests or by purchase. Now that Allah has granted us honour through Islam, do they want to eat our dates? They shall not eat even one date!’ Sa'd spat on the document and tore it up.” The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, approved of what he did. He did not say, “These are letters, so it is impermissible to treat them disrespectfully or spit on them.” Likewise, the early generations disapproved of erasing the Quran with one’s foot, but did not disapprove of erasing human speech.

As for someone saying, “Letters are eternal,” or “The letters of the alphabet are eternal”: if he means letters as a kind, this is correct. If, however, he means an individual letter, he is mistaken, for it has a beginning and an end and is preceded by something else. Whatever is like this can only have come into being.

Moreover, the term “letters” is ambiguous. It may refer to the spoken, audible letters that constitute speech, to written letters, or to letters imagined in the mind. Everyone agrees that sound cannot be speech without letters. Whether letters can constitute speech without sound, however, is disputed. A “letter” may mean a discrete segment of sound, or only the endpoint of a sound. “Letters” may also mean the ink, or the shape assumed by the ink.

The letters that Allah spoke are uncreated. When they are written in a copy of the Quran, it is said, “Allah’s speech written in this copy of the Quran is uncreated.” As for the actual voices of His servants, they are created. The ink is created, and the shape of the ink is created. Thus, the ink is created in both its substance and its form, while Allah’s speech written in ink is uncreated. Among Allah’s speech are

---

## Page 6113

the letters that Allah spoke. When they are written in ink, they are not created, although the ink is created. The forms of written letters vary according to the conventions of different peoples.

Arabic script is said to have originated in al-Anbār, from which it spread to Mecca and elsewhere. Arabic script varies in form: early Arabic script has a Kufic character, while later generations adopted changes to some of its letterforms. The people of the Maghrib have a third set of conventions, even in the placement of dots on letters and their alphabetical order. Allah’s speech written in these scripts, such as the Arabic Quran, does not itself vary with the different scripts in which it is written.

If it is asked:

“Is a letter, considered in itself, created or uncreated, irrespective of whether it occurs in the speech of the Creator or the speech of a creature? If you say that it is, in itself, uncreated, it follows that it is uncreated in the speech of His servants. If you say that it is created, it follows that it is created in Allah’s speech.”

The reply is:

To speak of “a letter considered in itself” is like speaking of “speech considered in itself,” “knowledge considered in itself,” “power considered in itself,” “existence considered in itself,” and so forth. The answer is that these things and others, when considered in absolute abstraction, without qualification or individuation, have no reality outside the mind

---

## Page 6114

except as something particular. Thus, there is no existence other than the existence of the Creator or the existence of a creature. Each creature’s existence is specific to it, although the term “existence” is general and encompasses all of these. Likewise, “knowledge” and “power” are general terms encompassing their individual instances. In external reality, however, there is only the Creator’s knowledge and the creature’s knowledge; each creature’s knowledge is specific to it and subsists in it.

The terms “speech” and “letters” encompass everything to which they apply, but in external reality there is only the speech of the Creator and the speech of creatures. Each creature’s speech is specific to it, while the term “speech” encompasses everything to which it applies. In external reality, there are only the letters Allah has spoken, which occur in the Creator’s speech, and the letters that occur in the speech of creatures.

Thus, if it is said that the Lord’s knowledge and power, together with His speech, are uncreated, and that the letters of His speech are uncreated, it does not follow that a servant’s knowledge, power, and speech are uncreated, or that the letters of his speech are uncreated.

Furthermore, the term “letter” encompasses both the spoken letter and the written letter. If it is said that Allah spoke the spoken letters, just as He spoke the Arabic Quran and His words “Alif Lām Mīm,” “Hā Mīm,” “Tā Sīn Mīm,” “Tā Sīn,” “Yā Sīn,” “Qāf,” “Nūn,” and the like, then this is His speech, and His speech is uncreated. When it is written in copies of the Quran, what is written of the Lord’s speech is uncreated, although the ink and the shapes it takes are created.

Furthermore, when people recite Allah’s speech, the speech itself is uncreated if Allah has spoken it. When someone conveying it recites it, it does not cease to be

---

## Page 6115

Allah’s speech; for speech belongs to the one who originally uttered it, whether as a command he issues or a report he conveys. It is not the speech of someone conveying it from another, for the messenger’s duty is only to convey the message clearly.

When someone recites it to convey it, he may refer to it as Allah’s speech and say, “This is Allah’s speech,” without considering the attributes of the servants through which they convey it. Or he may refer to the servant’s own attribute, such as his movement and life, or to both together. In the first case, what is referred to is uncreated; in the second, it is created; and in the third, it includes both what is created and what is uncreated. Anything comparable to this found in human speech is comparable to the servant’s attribute, never to the Lord’s attribute.

If someone says, “The letter qāf in His words, ‘And establish prayer for My remembrance,’ is like the qāf in the words, ‘Stop, you two, and let us weep at the memory of a beloved and a dwelling,’” the reply is: What Allah has spoken and what has been heard from Him does not resemble the attributes of created beings. However, when we convey Allah’s speech, we convey it only through our own attributes. Our attributes are created, and what is created resembles what is created.

This provides an answer to both groups—to those who compare the creature’s attribute to the Creator’s attribute and thus deem it uncreated. For the Jahmiyyah, who deny the divine attributes, resemble the Jews, while the proponents of divine indwelling who liken creation to the Creator

---

## Page 6116

resemble the Christians. They have fallen into these two errors: the former likened the Creator to created beings, attributing to Him deficiencies peculiar to creation, such as poverty and miserliness; the latter likened created beings to the Creator, attributing to them the distinctive qualities of lordship that belong to Allah alone.

Muslims describe Allah as He has described Himself and as His messengers have described Him, without distortion or denial, and without specifying how His attributes are or likening them to those of creation. Rather, they affirm for Him the attributes of perfection that He deserves and declare Him free of equals and likenesses. They neither deny His attributes nor liken them to the attributes of created beings. For whoever denies His attributes worships nonexistence, while whoever likens Him to creation worships an idol. Allah Most High says:

“There is nothing like unto Him, and He is the Hearing, the Seeing.”

It should also be understood that a speaker’s words are in themselves one and the same, although those conveying them do so in different voices. Thus, when someone recites the words of Labīd:

“Indeed, everything apart from Allah is vain,”

these words are Labīd’s, both in wording and meaning, even though those reciting them have different voices, none of which is Labīd’s voice. Likewise, when someone narrates a hadith of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, in its original wording, such as his saying:

“Actions are only according to intentions, and each person shall have only what he intended,”

these words are the words of Allah’s Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, both in wording and meaning, and its narrator is said to have transmitted the hadith in its original wording

---

## Page 6117

even though the voice of the person conveying it is not the Messenger’s voice. All the more, then, the Quran is Allah’s speech, in both its wording and its meaning; when reciters recite it, they do so in their own voices.

For this reason, Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal and other imams of the Sunnah used to say:

“Whoever says, ‘Utterance of the Quran is created,’ or ‘My utterance of the Quran is created,’ is a Jahmī; and whoever says that it is uncreated is an innovator.”

In some reports from him, the wording is:

“Whoever says, ‘My utterance of the Quran is created,’ meaning the Quran itself, is a Jahmī.”

This is because “utterance” can mean the act of uttering, as expressed by the verbal noun of the verb “to utter.” What it denotes in this sense is the servant’s action, and the servant’s action is created. But “utterance” can also mean the words that the speaker utters. Those are Allah’s speech, not the reciter’s speech. Whoever says that they are created has thereby said that Allah did not speak this Quran and that what Muslims recite is not Allah’s speech. It is well known that this contradicts what is necessarily known to be part of the Messenger’s religion.

As for the servant’s voice, it is created. Ahmad and others explicitly stated that the voice heard is the servant’s voice. Ahmad never said:

“Whoever says, ‘My voice when reciting the Quran is created,’ is a Jahmī.”

Rather, he said, “Whoever says, ‘My utterance of the Quran…’” The distinction between the wording of a statement and the voice of the person conveying it is clear. Anyone who conveys another person’s speech in that person’s own wording conveys the other person’s wording, not his own. Yet he conveys it in his own voice, not the other person’s voice.

Since the terms “utterance,” “recitation,” “reading,” “writing,” and the like can refer to the action denoted by the verbal noun, namely the movements of

---

## Page 6118

the servants and the resulting sounds of their voices and shapes traced in ink, and can also refer to the actual speech that a person reads, recites, utters, and writes, Ahmad and others prohibited unqualified negation or affirmation that would imply either that Allah’s attributes are created or that the servants’ attributes and their ink are uncreated.

Ahmad said:

“We say: The Quran is Allah’s speech, uncreated, however it is conveyed.”

That is, wherever it is recited, written, or read, whatever is in reality Allah’s speech remains His speech, and His speech is uncreated. Whatever belongs to the servants’ attributes and actions by which they read and write His speech, such as their voices and ink, is created.

Thus, whoever fails to grasp this distinction becomes confused. It is well known that the Quran is one, though many people recite it. The Quran itself does not multiply with the multitude of readers’ recitations; rather, what multiplies is that by which they recite the Quran. Whatever multiplies and comes into being in the servants is created. The Quran itself, however—its wording and meaning, which Allah spoke, which Gabriel heard from Allah and Muhammad heard from Gabriel, and which Muhammad conveyed to the people and used to warn the nations—is one Quran. As Allah Most High says:

“so that I may warn you thereby and whomever it reaches.”

It is Allah’s speech, uncreated.

This is not a case of something being one in kind but having multiple individual instances, like the humanity found in Zayd and ʿAmr. Nor is it a case of one person saying something like what another says, as Allah Most High says:

“Those before them likewise said the same as they say.”

For

---

## Page 6119

no one can produce the like of the Quran, as Allah Most High says:

“Say, ‘If mankind and the jinn gathered together to produce the like of this Quran, they could not produce its like, even if they supported one another.’”

Thus, even if mankind and the jinn gathered together, they could not produce the like of this Quran, although every reciter is able to recite it and convey it. It is therefore clear that what he recites is the Quran itself, not something like the Quran.

As for the letters found in the Quran, when their counterparts occur in someone else’s speech, the latter are not the very same letters, but their counterparts. When Allah speaks a name—such as Adam, Noah, or Abraham—and those letters and names which Allah has spoken are uttered, then, if they are recited as part of His speech, His speech has been conveyed. But when a person composes speech of his own, the letters and names that Allah spoke are not the very same as those spoken by the servant, such that one could say that these names and letters occurring in the speech of His servants are uncreated.

Some who maintain that the letters and names occurring in the speech of His servants are uncreated have claimed that only their arrangement and composition are created, not the individual elements. Yet whoever says this must also hold that their arrangement and composition are uncreated whenever their counterpart occurs in the Quran, as in His words:

“O John, take the Book.”

This would apply even if the speaker meant a person named John and a book before him. (If it is said, “This John and the book before him are not the John and the Book mentioned in the Quran, even though the wording is alike,” the reply is: “Likewise,

---

## Page 6120

all other names and letters have counterparts only in the speech of His servants, not in Allah’s speech.”) When we say that their counterparts occur in Allah’s speech, this is an approximate expression: we mean that they occur in what we read and recite. The sound heard when the names Muhammad, John, and Abraham are pronounced in the Quran resembles the sound heard when they are pronounced outside the Quran, and both sounds are created. As for the voice with which Allah speaks, nothing resembles it; it does not resemble the attributes of created beings. Allah’s speech is His speech in its arrangement, its prose, and its meanings. That speech does not resemble the speech of created beings.

Thus, when we say:

“Praise be to Allah, Lord of all worlds,”

intending thereby to recite the Quran which Allah spoke, Allah spoke that Quran in both its wording and its meaning, neither of which resembles the wording or meaning of created beings. But when we intend these words as remembrance in our own right, without intending to recite Allah’s speech, we intend only a remembrance that we ourselves initiate, whose meaning resides in our hearts and whose wording we utter with our tongues. The remembrance we initiate is not part of the Quran, even though its counterpart occurs in the Quran.

For this reason, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said in an authentic hadith:

“The best speech after the Quran consists of four phrases, and they are from the Quran: Glory be to Allah; praise be to Allah; there is no god but Allah; and Allah is the Greatest.”

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, thus described these phrases as the best speech after the Quran, placing them below the Quran in rank. This entails that they are not part of the Quran. Then he said:

“They are from the Quran.”

Both of his statements are true and correct. For this reason, Ahmad forbade saying, “Faith is created.”

---

## Page 6121

And he said: “‘There is no god but Allah’ is part of the Quran.”

This speech must not be described as created, even when it is not part of the Quran. Nor may the Torah and the Gospel be described as created, or the divine hadiths which the Prophet narrates from his Lord, such as His saying:

“My servants, I have forbidden oppression for Myself and have made it forbidden among you, so do not oppress one another.”

Allah’s speech may be Quran or something other than Quran, but prayer is permissible and valid only with the recitation of the Quran. All of Allah’s speech is uncreated.

Once this is understood in this instance, it should also be understood in comparable cases. Letters and names that occur both in Allah’s speech and elsewhere may be described as part of Allah’s speech in one respect and as not part of His speech in another, just as they may be part of the Quran in one respect and not part of it in another. Yet Allah’s speech, whether Quran or otherwise, is uncreated, while the speech of created beings is all created. Whatever is Allah’s speech is uncreated, and whatever is the speech of anyone else is created.

Those who argue that certain attributes and actions of Allah’s servants are uncreated or eternal, because their counterparts occur in what is ascribed to Allah, His speech, and faith in Him, share a corrupt premise with those who argue that Allah’s speech and attributes are created because their counterparts may occur in what is ascribed to His servants.

An example of this is the Quran which Muslims recite: it is Allah’s speech, which they recite through their own movements and voices. The Jahmī said: “The servants’ voices and their ink are created, and this

---

## Page 6122

is what is called Allah’s speech, or its counterpart is found in what is called Allah’s speech; therefore, Allah’s speech is created.”

The advocate of indwelling and union, who identifies the Creator’s attribute with the creature’s attribute, said: “What we hear from the reciters is Allah’s speech, yet we hear only the servants’ voices. Thus, the servants’ voices reciting the Quran are Allah’s speech. Allah’s speech is uncreated; therefore, the servants’ voices reciting the Quran are uncreated, and the letters heard from them are uncreated.” They then said: “The letters occurring in their speech are these very letters, or their counterparts; therefore, they are uncreated.” Some of their extremists went further, declaring the sounds of their ordinary speech uncreated. Similarly, some of them claimed that deeds are part of faith, that faith is uncreated, and that deeds are therefore uncreated.

Some extended this to both good and evil deeds, saying: “They are divine decree and prescribed law.” [And Umar said: “By deeds, we do not mean movements, but rather the reward that comes on the Day of Resurrection, as mentioned in the authentic hadith: ‘Al-Baqarah and Āl Imrān will come as though they were two clouds, or two canopies of shade, or two flocks of birds with wings outspread.’” He is to be told: “This reward, too, is created.” Ahmad and other imams explicitly stated that it is uncreated.] (*)

This was also their answer to anyone who cited such a hadith as evidence that the Quran is created. They told him: “What comes on the Day of Resurrection is the reward for the Quran, not the Quran itself, and the reward for the Quran is created.” These are among the many such statements introduced by various groups. Innovations arise little by little. This subject has been discussed at length elsewhere.

## Page 6123

We have explained that the correct position on this matter is the one established by the Book, the Sunnah, and the consensus of the earliest forerunners and those who followed them in righteousness. This was the position of Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal, the imams of Islam who preceded him, and those who agreed with them. The position of Imam Ahmad and the imams before him is the teaching brought by the Messenger and established by the Book and the Sunnah. However, when people were subjected to the Jahmiyyah’s inquisition and were required to deny the divine attributes and declare that the Quran is created, that Allah will not be seen in the Hereafter, and other such things, Allah kept Imam Ahmad steadfast throughout that ordeal.

He refuted the arguments of the opponents who denied the divine attributes, demonstrated what the Book and the Sunnah establish, and showed that the early generations affirmed those attributes. Allah granted him such patience and certainty that he became a leader for the God-fearing, as the Most High said:

“We made from among them leaders, guiding by Our command, when they were patient and had certainty in Our signs.”

Thus it was said of him, may Allah have mercy on him: “How steadfast he was in resisting worldly allurements, and how closely he resembled those who came before! Innovations came to him, and he rejected them; the world offered itself to him, and he refused it.”

Because of the extent to which the Sunnah was made manifest through him, his statements explaining and defending it were more numerous and substantial than those of others. Thus, adherents of the Sunnah across the various groups came to revere him and identify themselves with him.

Elsewhere, I have cited his statements and those of other imams, together with the texts of the Book and the Sunnah concerning these matters. We have explained that everything established by the Book and the Sunnah accords with sound reason, and that sound reason does not contradict

---

## Page 6124

authentic transmitted evidence. Yet many people err concerning one or the other. Whoever knows the Messenger’s words and what he intended by them knows the scriptural proofs; nothing established by reason contradicts transmitted revelation.

For this reason, the imams of the Sunnah held the position expressed by Ahmad ibn Hanbal, who said:

“Knowing hadith and understanding it are dearer to me than memorizing it.”

That is, “knowing it”—distinguishing its sound reports from its unsound ones—and “understanding it”—knowing what the Messenger intended and applying it to questions of religious fundamentals and subsidiary matters—are dearer to me than memorizing it without knowledge or understanding. Likewise, ʿAlī ibn al-Madīnī and other scholars expressed this view. Whoever cites as proof wording that is not reliably established from the Messenger, or wording that is reliably established from him but interprets it as conveying something it does not indicate, has only himself to blame.

Likewise, “sound rational arguments,” when their premises and logical structure are correct, can only yield truth and do not contradict anything the Messenger said. The Quran itself sets forth rational proofs through which the Creator, His oneness, His attributes, and the truthfulness of His messengers are known, and through which the possibility of resurrection is established.

The Quran explains the foundations of religion, whose premises are known through sound reason, in a manner unparalleled in anyone’s words. Indeed, the Quran presents the essence of most of the rational proofs advanced by accomplished thinkers, as well as proofs better than theirs. The Most High said:

“They bring you no argument without Our bringing you the truth and the best explanation.”

And He said:

“We have certainly presented to people in this Quran every kind of example.”

And He said:

“These are the examples We present to people so that they may reflect.”

---

## Page 6125

As for the invalid arguments advanced by the heretics, the Jahmiyya who deny the divine attributes, the Dahriyya, and others like them—such as those found in the writings of later authors who discuss innovated speculative theology and the doctrines of those who profess philosophy, claiming these to be rational arguments—they contain ignorance, contradiction, and error beyond the reckoning of anyone but the Lord of all servants. These people have been discussed at length elsewhere. Among the causes of their misguidance was both groups’ negligence or inability to understand what the Messenger brought, the way of the early generations, and sound reason.

For the former is the Book, and the latter the Balance. The Most High said:

“We certainly sent Our messengers with clear proofs and sent down with them the Scripture and the Balance so that people might uphold justice. And We sent down iron, in which there is great might and benefits for people, so that Allah may make evident those who support Him and His messengers unseen. Indeed, Allah is Powerful, Almighty.”

The present discussion does not permit a detailed treatment of these matters. The purpose here is merely to point out that these disputing groups agreed upon a false premise and then diverged. They agreed in identifying the very attribute of the Lord, the Creator, with the very attribute of the creature.

Then one group said: “The creature’s attribute is created; therefore, the Lord’s attribute is created.” The other said: “The Lord’s attribute is eternal; therefore, the creature’s attribute is eternal.” Each group then had to pursue its premise to its logical conclusion, arriving at manifestly erroneous positions. Those who deny the divine attributes came to hold that Allah did not speak the Quran or any of the divine scriptures—neither the Torah, nor the Gospel, nor any other—and that He did not

---

## Page 6126

call Moses Himself with a call that Moses heard from Him, nor speak the Arabic Quran or the Hebrew Torah. The other group, in turn, came to hold that what inheres in human beings and qualifies them is eternal and without beginning, and that what inheres in them and qualifies them does not actually subsist or dwell within them, but rather manifests itself from them without inhering in them.

When they discussed “the letters of the alphabet,” they divided into two positions. One group distinguished between things that were alike, saying: “There are two distinct letters: this one is eternal, and that one is created.” This was the position of Ibn Hāmid, Judge Abū Yaʿlā, Ibn ʿAqīl, and others. The majority objected, saying: “This contradicts sensory perception and reason, for the reality of this letter is the same as the reality of that letter.” They maintained that the letter is one and the same.

Judge Yaʿqūb al-Barzabīnī wrote a treatise on this subject in which he opposed his teacher, Judge Abū Yaʿlā, despite saying in that very work:

“It should be understood that what I have written on this question derives from what I learned from our teacher and imam, Judge Abū Yaʿlā ibn al-Farrāʾ, and the conclusions I drew from his teaching. Although he defended the opposite of what I have stated on this subject, he remains a scholar whose knowledge and religious devotion are exemplary. I have never seen anyone finer in bearing, more diligent, or more devoted to learning, despite his already extensive knowledge. He combined this with moral integrity, withdrawal from people, indifference to their possessions, and contentment with little in this world, while maintaining a dignified appearance and commanding great respect among both the elite and ordinary people. He would not exchange these virtues for anything, being averse to worldly life.”

---

## Page 6127

Judge Yaʿqūb also stated in his work that his position was that of Abū Bakr Ahmad ibn al-Musayyib al-Tabarī, and he attributed it to a number of the most distinguished scholars of Tabaristān. He also reported hearing the jurist ʿAbd al-Wahhāb ibn Halaba, the judge of Harrān, say: “This is the position of al-ʿAlawī al-Harrānī and a number of the people of Harrān.”

Abū ʿAbd Allāh ibn Hāmid also attributed it to a number of people from Tabaristān affiliated with our school, such as Abū Muhammad al-Kashfal and Ismāʿīl al-Kāwdharī, together with many of their followers, who held that the letters are eternal. Judge Abū Yaʿlā said: “I was likewise informed that a group in Syria held this view, including al-Nābulusī and others.” Judge Husayn mentioned that his father adopted this position toward the end of his life. They also attributed it to al-Sharīf Abū ʿAlī ibn Abī Mūsā. Shaykh Abū al-Faraj al-Maqdisī, his son ʿAbd al-Wahhāb, and all his other followers, as well as Abū al-Hasan ibn al-Zāghūnī and others like him, followed them in this. Judge Yaʿqūb stated that Ahmad’s words could bear either interpretation.

Those who held this view relied on Ahmad’s response when he was told that Sarī al-Saqatī had said: “When Allah created the letters, they prostrated before Him, except for the alif, which said, ‘I will not prostrate until I am commanded.’” Ahmad said: “This is disbelief.”

The other group relied on Ahmad’s statement: “Whatever comes from created beings, on the tongues of created beings, is created”; and on his statement: “If that were so, his prayer would not be valid through recitation of the Quran, just as it is not valid through other human speech”; and on Ahmad’s words

---

## Page 6128

to Ahmad ibn al-Hasan al-Tirmidhī:
“Are you not created?” He replied, “Yes.” Ahmad said, “Is not everything that comes from you created?” He replied, “Yes.” Ahmad said, “Your speech comes from you, and it is created.”

I say: What Ahmad said on this subject is correct; his statements confirm one another and contain no contradiction. He objected to the statement that Allah created the letters, for the implication of saying that the letters are created is that Allah did not speak an Arabic Quran and that the Arabic Quran is created. Ahmad also explicitly stated that human speech is created, without declaring any part of it uncreated. All of this is correct.

Al-Sarī, may Allah have mercy on him, merely related this account from Bakr ibn Khunays, the devout worshipper. Their point was that someone who worships Allah only according to His command is more perfect than someone who worships Him according to his own judgment, without a command from Allah. In support of this, they cited an account that had reached them:

“When Allah created the letters, they prostrated before Him, except for the alif, which said, ‘I will not prostrate until I am commanded.’”

A report of this kind cannot establish proof in any matter. Their intention, however, was to illustrate their point: the alif stands upright in writing, rather than lying horizontally like the bā’ and tā’. Thus, someone who does not act until commanded is more perfect than someone who acts without a command.

Ahmad objected to the words, “When Allah created the letters.” It is also reported that he said: “Whoever says that a single letter of the alphabet is created is a Jahmī, because he has taken a path leading to innovation. Whoever says that it is created has thereby said that the Quran is created.” Ahmad and other imams explicitly stated that Allah has never ceased to speak whenever

---

## Page 6129

He wills. Ahmad also explicitly stated that Allah speaks by His will. However, the followers of Ibn Kullāb, such as the Qādī and others, interpreted his words as meaning “whenever He wills to make His speech heard,” because, according to them, He does not speak by His will and power.

Ahmad and other early scholars explicitly stated that the Quran is the uncreated speech of Allah. None of the early scholars said that Allah spoke without His will and power. Nor did any of them say that a particular utterance itself—such as the Quran, His call to Moses, or any other particular utterance of His—is beginningless and eternal, having always existed and continuing forever; or that particular letters, or particular letters and sounds, subsist in Allah eternally, without beginning or end. Neither Ahmad nor any other imam of the Muslims said this, nor do their statements imply it. Rather, the statements of Ahmad and the other imams explicitly affirm the opposite: Allah speaks by His will and power, and He has never ceased to speak whenever He wills. At the same time, they affirm that Allah’s speech is uncreated and that it originated from Him; it is not something created that originated from someone other than Him.

Their explicit statements to this effect are numerous and well known in the works reliably transmitted from them. These include what Abū Bakr al-Khallāl compiled in his Kitāb al-Sunnah (The Book of the Sunnah) and elsewhere; what ʿAbd al-Rahmān ibn Abī Hātim compiled of the statements of Ahmad and others; and what was compiled by his students and their students, such as his two sons, Sālih and ʿAbd Allāh, Hanbal, Abū Dāwūd al-Sijistānī, the author of al-Sunan, al-Athram, al-Marwadhī, Abū Zurʿah, Abū Hātim, al-Bukhārī, the author of al-Sahīh, ʿUthmān ibn Saʿīd al-Dārimī, Ibrāhīm al-Harbī, and ʿAbd al-Wahhāb al-Warrāq,

---

## Page 6130

and ʿAbbās ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīm al-ʿAnbarī, Harb ibn Ismāʿīl al-Kirmānī, and countless other leading scholars and men of religion; and his students’ students who compiled his statements and reports about him, such as ʿAbd al-Rahmān ibn Abī Hātim, Abū Bakr al-Khallāl, Abū al-Hasan al-Banānī al-Asbahānī, and others like them. These also include those who followed him and other such imams in matters of doctrine and practical rulings, such as Abū ʿĪsā al-Tirmidhī, the author of al-Jāmiʿ, Abū ʿAbd al-Rahmān al-Nasāʾī, and others like them, as well as Abū Muhammad ibn Qutaybah and his peers. A detailed discussion of this belongs elsewhere.

In al-Masāʾil al-Tabaristāniyyah and al-Kīlāniyyah, we have given a detailed account of people’s positions and how they branched out and diverged on this fundamental issue. The point here is that many later scholars did not understand the true meaning of the statements of the early generations and the imams. Some revere them and claim to follow them, while unknowingly opposing them. Others suppose that they did not understand the fundamentals of religion or know how to establish them through demonstrative proofs. This is due to their ignorance of those scholars’ knowledge—indeed, their ignorance of the truth brought by the Messenger, which is supported by rational evidence as well as revelation.

Thus, many later scholars share a false premise, from which each group derives false conclusions to which it commits itself. This is exemplified by their explicit statements concerning Allah Most High’s speaking the Arabic Quran and the Hebrew Torah, and the letters of the alphabet contained in them, whether combined or separate: when they saw that this extended to the attributes of created beings, it became confused with the attributes of created beings, and so they failed to discern the proper basis for

---

## Page 6131

identifying what is shared and what is distinct. One group therefore said:

“What is recited and heard resembles the speech of created beings, so it is created.”

The other group said:

“This human speech resembles Allah’s speech, so it must be uncreated.”

Thus Ibn Aqīl related in Kitāb al-Irshād (The Book of Guidance), concerning some who held that the Quran is created:

“A specious objection was put to one of their imams, who said: ‘The least indication in the Quran that it originated is its resemblance to our speech, whereas what is eternal does not resemble what originates. Clearly, this cannot be denied. When someone says to his servant John, “O John, hold firmly to the Scripture,” his words match the words of Allah—glory be to Him—so closely that a listener cannot distinguish between them through his senses alone. Only when each speaker explains his intention can the listener distinguish between them, relying on the speaker’s explanation rather than his own senses.

“‘If they resemble one another to this extent, how can something that resembles what originates and serves the same purpose be claimed to be eternal? Moreover, if speech may be claimed to be eternal despite being perceptible to a created being, then resemblance may also be affirmed on the strength of the apparent meanings of the verses and transmitted reports, with nothing to prevent it. Since both we and you have resorted to denying resemblance, fearing the rejoinder that the Quran would thereby be subject to origination, you must likewise recoil from affirming eternity where resemblance exists. Indeed, the resemblance between the two has seemed so compelling to some of your companions that they say the speech is one and the same, and that the letters are uncreated. How, then, can one and the same thing be said to be both eternal and originated?’”

---

## Page 6132

I say:

Among the aforementioned adherents of the school from whom Ibn Aqīl related this view was Judge Yaʿqūb al-Barzabīnī, who stated in his work:

“A tenth proof: These letters, in their very identity, form, meaning, and function, are the same as those in the Book of Allah Most High and in His names and attributes. The Book, with its letters, is eternal; the same therefore applies here.”

He said:

“If it is objected, ‘We do not concede that those have sanctity while these have none,’ the reply is: ‘We do not concede this; rather, these too have sanctity.’

“If it is objected, ‘Were they sacred, menstruating women and women experiencing postnatal bleeding would have to be prohibited from touching and reciting them,’ the reply is: ‘They may have sanctity without such women being prohibited from reciting or touching them. This is like part of a verse: a woman is not prohibited from reciting it, yet it has sanctity and is eternal. She is not prohibited from reciting or touching it because of the need for instruction, just as a child is permitted to touch the written Quran without ritual purity because of the need to teach him.’

“If it is objected, ‘Then, if someone swears by them, his oath must be binding, and if he acts contrary to his oath, he must be deemed to have broken it,’ the reply is: ‘Our position here is exactly the same as concerning the letters of the Quran.’

“If it is objected, ‘Does not correspondence with them in these respects establish that they are identical? Do you not see that when someone utters a word intending to address a human being, its form may correspond to that of something in the Book of Allah Most High—for example, when he says, “O David,” “O Noah,” “O John,” and so forth? It corresponds to these names found in the Book of Allah, even though

---

## Page 6133

they are eternal in the Book of Allah but brought into being in human speech?’ The reply is: ‘Any speech that corresponds to the Book of Allah in its wording, arrangement, and letters is part of the Book of Allah, even if the speaker intends thereby to address a human being.’

“If it is objected, ‘Then, if someone uses these names to address a human being while praying, his prayer must not be invalidated,’ the reply is: ‘That is indeed our position. Something similar has been reported from Ali and others. A man from the Khawārij called out to him:

“‘“If you associate others with Allah, your deeds will surely come to nothing, and you will certainly be among the losers.”

“‘He related that Ali answered him while praying:

“‘“So be patient. Indeed, Allah’s promise is true. And do not let those who lack certainty shake your resolve.”

“‘It is also reported that when some of Ibn Masūd’s companions asked permission to enter his presence, he said:

“‘“Enter Egypt, Allah willing, in safety.”’

“He said: ‘If it is objected, “When someone says, ‘O John, hold firmly to the Scripture,’ intending to address a boy named John, is the utterance not created, whereas if he intends it as Quran, it is eternal?” the reply is: “It is eternal in both cases, because ‘eternal’ denotes what has always existed, whereas ‘brought into being’ denotes what came to exist after not existing. Intention does not make what was brought into being eternal, nor does it make what is eternal something brought into being.”’

“He said: ‘Anyone who says this has gone to extremes in ignorance and error.’
