## Page 6134

He also said:

“Anything compared to something else resembles it only in certain respects, not in others; it does not resemble it in every respect. For if it were like it in every respect, it would be that very thing, not something else. We have explained that these letters resemble the letters of the Quran; they are therefore distinct from them.” End of quotation.

I say:

These are the words of Judge Yaqūb and others like him, although he is the most eminent of those who discussed this question. Since his answer contained elements contrary to the scriptural texts, scholarly consensus, and reason, Ibn Aqīl and other leading scholars of the school, who were better versed in it, disagreed with him.

Ibn Aqīl answered the objection of those who said, “This is like that,” as follows:

“Sharing a common reality does not imply that both are brought into being. Likewise, His being knowing consists in His apprehending a thing, according to your principle, or His knowing it, according to our position, in the manner in which any one of us apprehends it; yet He is not like us in our being knowing. Similarly, His being powerful means that He—glorified and exalted—is capable of acting, but His power is not of the kind that we possess. Thus, there is no sharing of a common reality, while there is a distinction between eternity and being brought into being.”

He said:

“Another answer”:

We do not say that Allah speaks His speech in

---

## Page 6135

the manner in which Zayd speaks—that is, by saying, “O John,” then, when He has finished, moving on to say, “Hold firmly to the Scripture,” so that it comes into existence in that sequence. Rather, He—glorified and exalted—speaks it in a manner that our organs of speech cannot reproduce. Thus, the resemblance you mentioned in someone’s saying, “O John, hold to the Scripture,” is a resemblance between recitation and speech that is brought into being. It does not resemble the speech subsisting in His Essence.

Ibn Aqīl said:

They objected: “This is inconsistent with your position, for you hold that the recitation is itself what is recited, and the reading is itself what is read.”

The reply was:

When we say that it is what is recited, we do not mean these segmented sounds. Rather, we mean the eternal letters that become manifest in sounds brought into being. Their manifestation in what is brought into being necessarily gives them the characteristic of segmentation, owing to variations in breathing and the movement of the uvulas. For the instrument through which they become manifest can convey speech only in segmented form. The Creator’s speech subsists in His Essence, unlike this segmentation, beginning, ending, repetition, coming after, and coming before. Whoever maintains this has not understood the definition of the eternal, and has claimed that accidents are eternal and that the eternal undergoes segmentation. Yet segmentation of the eternal is an accident, which cannot subsist in anything eternal. Whoever believes that Allah’s speech subsisting in His Essence follows the pattern of a reciter’s recitation—with its separating and joining, drawing together and spacing apart, coming after and coming before—has likened Allah to His creation. Hence it is related in a report:

“The Children of Israel asked Moses, ‘How did you hear your Lord’s speech?’ He replied, ‘Like thunder that does not reverberate.’”

“Reverberate” here means “become interrupted,” because there are no interruptions for breath, nor any breath, vocal organs, or lips

---

## Page 6136

and uvulas. Whoever says otherwise and imagines that Allah spoke through the reciter’s tongue, or that the speech subsisting in His Essence has these characteristics of separation and joining, drawing together and spacing apart, has thereby judged it to have been brought into being. For coming together and separating are evidence that the world was brought into being, and these are characteristics of instruments. End of quotation.

I say: What Ibn Aqīl said here is less erroneous than what al-Barzabīnī said, for the latter plainly contradicts the revealed texts, scholarly consensus, and reason. The revealed texts and scholarly consensus establish that anyone who deliberately utters ordinary human speech during prayer, not for the benefit of the prayer and knowing that it is forbidden, invalidates his prayer by consensus—contrary to what Judge Ya‘qūb stated. Whenever he intends Quranic recitation by his words, his prayer is not invalidated, by consensus. If he intends both recitation and addressing someone, there is disagreement. The apparent position of Ahmad’s school is that his prayer is not invalidated, as is also the position of al-Shāfi‘ī and others. Another view holds that it is invalidated, as maintained by Abū Hanīfa and others. What they related from the Companions is evidence against them.

For the words spoken by ‘Alī ibn Abī Tālib:

“So be patient. Indeed, Allah’s promise is true. And do not let those who lack certainty unsettle you.”

are Allah’s speech. ‘Alī did not intend to say to the Khārijite, “Do not let the Khārijites unsettle you.” Rather, he intended to let him hear the verse and to show that he was acting upon it: remaining patient and not allowing those who lacked certainty to unsettle him.

Ibn Mas‘ūd, while in Kūfa, said to them:

“Enter Egypt, Allah willing, in safety.”

It is well known that Misr (Egypt), without nunation, denotes the city of that name, which was not in Kūfa. Ibn Mas‘ūd was in Kūfa. It is therefore clear that he intended to recite the verse and also intended

---

## Page 6137

at the same time to signal to those present that they could enter. When they heard him say, “Enter,” they understood that he had given them permission to enter, even though he was reciting the verse. So much for this point.

As for Ibn Aqīl’s answer, he based it on Ibn Kullāb’s principle, which he, his teacher, and others uphold. This is the principle on which they agreed with Ibn Kullāb and his followers, such as al-Ash‘arī and others: that Allah does not speak by His will and power, and that nothing subsisting in Him occurs by His will and power. In their view, matters dependent on choice cannot subsist in Him, because they come into being, and, according to them, nothing that comes into being can subsist in Allah.

For this reason, they interpreted away the revealed texts that contradict this principle, such as His saying, Most High:

“And say, ‘Act, for Allah will see your deeds, as will His Messenger and the believers.’”

This entails that He will see their deeds in the future. Likewise, His saying:

“Then We made you successors in the land after them, to see how you would act.”

And His saying:

“And Allah will see your deeds, as will His Messenger.”

Likewise, His saying:

“Say, ‘If you love Allah, then follow me; Allah will love you.’”

This entails that He loves them after they follow the Messenger. Likewise, His saying, Most High:

“And We certainly created you, then fashioned you, then said to the angels, ‘Prostrate before Adam.’”

This entails that He spoke to them after creating Adam. Likewise, His saying, Most High:

“Then, when he came to it, he was called.”

This entails that he was called when he came to it, and was not called before that. Likewise, His saying:

“His command, when He wills a thing, is only to say to it, ‘Be,’ and it is.”

There are many such passages in the Quran.

---

## Page 6138

This principle was among the things for which Imam Ahmad censured Ibn Kullāb and his followers—even al-Hārith al-Muhāsibī, despite his eminent standing. Ahmad instructed people to shun him and the Kullābiyyah, saying: “Beware of Hārith; the entire trouble comes from Hārith.” When al-Hārith died, only a few people attended his funeral prayer because of Imam Ahmad’s warning against him, even though his knowledge and religious commitment surpassed those of most who agreed with Ibn Kullāb on this principle. It has been said that al-Hārith recanted this view and acknowledged that Allah speaks with a voice, as reported by Abū Bakr Muhammad ibn Ishāq al-Kalābādhī, the author of al-Ta‘arruf li-madhhab al-tasawwuf (An Introduction to the Sufi Way). Many later followers of Mālik, al-Shāfi‘ī, Ahmad, and Abū Hanīfah agreed with Ibn Kullāb on this principle, as has been discussed at length elsewhere.

Ibn Aqīl’s statements on this principle varied. Sometimes he adopted Ibn Kullāb’s position, and sometimes he adopted the position of the early generations and the scholars of hadith: that matters dependent on choice subsist in Allah. He states that new acts of seeing subsist in Him as new objects of sight come into being—acts of seeing that did not exist before—and that knowledge that each thing has come into existence subsists in Him, distinct from His prior knowledge that it would come into existence. Several verses of the Quran indicate this, such as His saying, Most High:

“So that We may know who follows the Messenger.”

There are other such passages. His statements on this principle and others vary: sometimes he adopts one position, and sometimes another. For these are matters

---

## Page 6139

that are difficult and concerning which people have often erred because of the ambiguity and confusion involved.

The correct answer is that Allah’s speech is not like the speech of created beings, just as none of His attributes is like the attributes of created beings. The statement, “Sharing an essential reality does not entail sharing temporal origination,” is ambiguous. For if we say, “Allah has knowledge and we have knowledge,” or “He has power and we have power,” or “He has speech and we have speech,” or “He speaks with a voice and we speak with a voice,” and then say that the Creator’s attribute and the created being’s attribute share an essential reality, this may mean different things.

If what is meant is that their realities are numerically one and the same, this contradicts sensory perception, reason, and revelation. If what is meant is that they are alike in their essential reality and differ only in accidental attributes—as a group of speculative theologians have maintained, and as has been shown to be invalid in the discussion of al-Rāzī’s al-Arba‘īn and elsewhere—this too is utterly false. It entails that the essential reality of the Creator’s essence, Mighty and Majestic, is like the essential reality of the essences of created beings.

If, however, what is meant is that they share what is denoted by the terms knowledge, power, and speech, this is correct. Likewise, when it is said that He exists or that He has an essence, they share what is denoted by existence and essence. But this shared meaning is a universal, which exists as a universal only in minds, not in concrete entities. Thus, in external reality there is no single thing shared by two created beings in the way that particulars share their universals. This differs from the way parts share in a whole. For a distinction must be drawn between dividing a universal into its particulars—as in dividing the category of animal into

---

## Page 6140

rational and non-rational beings, dividing human beings into Muslims and disbelievers, or dividing nouns into inflected and indeclinable nouns—and dividing a whole into its parts, as in dividing real estate among co-owners or dividing speech into nouns, verbs, and particles. In the first case, the divisions share only a universal concept; still less could the Creator and created beings share anything existing in external reality. None of Allah’s attributes, as they exist in external reality, is like an attribute of a created being. Rather, everything attributed to the Lord Most High differs in definition and essential reality from what is attributed to created beings, far more than created beings differ from one another. If a created being differs from some other created beings in the definition and essential reality of its essence and attributes, then the Creator’s difference in essential reality from every created being is greater than the difference between any two created beings whatsoever. Nevertheless, His knowledge is knowledge in the true sense, His power is power in the true sense, and His speech is speech in the true sense, just as His essence is truly an essence and His existence is true existence. He is more deserving than all else of having the attributes of perfection truly affirmed of Him.

This, then, is what we mean when we say, “His knowledge shares with the knowledge of created beings the reality of knowledge.” Thus, the voices heard from His servants bear no resemblance or likeness to His voice as Moses heard it, except in the same sense in which His other attributes bear resemblance or likeness to the attributes of created beings. This concerns His own speaking of the Quran, glorified and exalted is He. According to Imam Ahmad and all the other imams of the Sunnah, the Quran is His speech, which He spoke. He spoke the Arabic Quran with His own voice, and He spoke to Moses with His own voice, which is unlike any of His servants’ voices.

---

## Page 6141

Then, when we recite the Quran, we recite it only in our created voices, which do not resemble the Lord’s voice. The Quran we recite is Allah’s speech conveyed from Him, not heard directly from Him. We recite it through our movements and voices: the speech is the Creator’s speech, while the voice is the reciter’s voice, as the Book, the Sunnah, and reason indicate. Allah Most High says:

“And if any of the polytheists seeks your protection, grant him protection so that he may hear the words of Allah; then escort him to his place of safety.”

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Adorn the Quran with your voices.”

Regarding the Prophet’s saying, “He is not one of us who does not recite the Quran melodiously,” Imam Ahmad said: “He adorns and beautifies it with his voice, as in the saying: ‘Adorn the Quran with your voices.’”

Ahmad thus explicitly affirmed what the Book and the Sunnah teach: we recite the Quran in our own voices, and the Quran is entirely Allah’s speech, both its wording and its meaning. Gabriel heard it from Allah and conveyed it to Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. Muhammad heard it from him and conveyed it to humankind, who convey it to one another and hear it from one another.

It is well known that when people hear the words of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, or anyone else, and convey those words from him—as he said, “May Allah grant radiance to a person who hears a hadith from us and conveys it just as he heard it”—they have heard the wording from the Messenger in his own voice, with the letters he uttered, and have conveyed his wording in their own voices. The distinction between narrating a hadith by meaning and narrating it verbatim is well known. The wording conveyed is the Messenger’s wording, and it is the Messenger’s speech. For if the voice of

---

## Page 6142

the transmitter is not the Messenger’s voice, then the attributes and accidents subsisting in the Messenger have neither departed from him nor come to subsist in anyone else. Indeed, an attribute or an accident cannot subsist in anything other than its own subject. If this is intelligible concerning the attributes of created beings, then the Creator’s attributes are all the more worthy of every perfection and further removed from every deficiency. The distinction between the attributes of the Creator and those of a creature is greater than the distinction between the attributes of one creature and those of another. It is still more impossible for the Creator Himself and His attributes to unite with or indwell a creature than for a creature itself and its attributes to unite with or indwell another creature. These are summary points that have been elaborated elsewhere.

Moreover, the argument of the Jahmiyyah and the Mu‘tazilah that a creature’s speech when he says:

“O John, take the Scripture with determination”

is like the Creator’s speech is mistaken by everyone’s agreement—even their own. For those who say that it is created maintain that Allah created it in some physical body, whether the air or something else, just as they say that He created speech within the tree itself and Moses heard it. It is well known that those letters and sounds which Allah created are not like what is heard from a human being. Yet, according to them, those constitute Allah’s speech heard from Him. Likewise, Ahl al-Sunnah say that it was Allah who spoke, by His will, and that this is not like a human being’s voice.

---

## Page 6143

As for those who maintain that a particular instance of speech is beginningless—whether it consists of a meaning, letters, or sounds—they say that Allah created in Moses a faculty of perception by which he perceived that beginningless speech. In any case, a speaker’s speech, when heard from someone conveying it on his behalf, is not what subsists in the original speaker himself. How, then, could this not also apply to the speech of Allah Most High?

In examining “the question of divine speech,” one must therefore carefully consider two fundamental points. The first concerns Allah’s speaking the Quran and other speech: did He speak it by His will and power or not? And did He speak with speech subsisting in His own essence, or did He create it in something else? The second concerns the transmission of that speech from Allah: it is not an attribute of the person transmitting it, even though the purpose of transmission is to convey that speech. A detailed discussion of this belongs elsewhere.

Furthermore, when one of these two disputants says, “They are beginningless and have no beginning, while their vowel marks and dots came into being,” and the other says, “They are not Allah’s speech; they are created, together with their vowel marks and dots,” this may be understood to mean that by “letters” they intended written letters rather than spoken ones.

People have disputed the vowel marks and dots of written letters. When the Companions wrote out the copies of the Quran, they wrote them without vowel marks or dots, because their reliance regarding the Quran was on what they had memorized in their hearts, not on written copies. It is transmitted through mass transmission and preserved in people’s hearts. Even if the written copies ceased to exist, Muslims would have no need of them. Muslims are not like the People of the Book, who rely on books susceptible to alteration. Allah sent down the Quran to Muhammad, who received it and memorized it in his heart; He did not send it down in writing as He did the Torah

---

## Page 6144

and sent it down piecemeal, in separate portions, so that it could be memorized without needing a written copy, as Allah Most High says:

“Those who disbelieve say, ‘Why was the Quran not sent down to him all at once?’” And the rest of the verse.

Allah Most High also says:

“And a Quran which We have divided into portions.” And the rest of the verse.

“Do not hasten with the Quran.” And the rest of the verse.

“It is for Us to gather it and recite it.” And the rest of the verse.

In the Sahīh, Ibn ‘Abbās said:

“The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, used to experience great difficulty when receiving revelation, and he would move his lips. Ibn ‘Abbās said, ‘I will move them for you as the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, used to move them.’ He then moved his lips. So Allah Most High revealed: ‘Do not move your tongue with it to hasten it. It is for Us to gather it and recite it.’”

He explained: “To gather it in your heart, after which you will recite it.”

“So when We have recited it, follow its recitation.” He explained this as listening attentively and remaining silent.

“Then it is for Us to make it clear”—that is, “We shall make it clear through your tongue.”

Thus, whenever Gabriel came to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, he would listen. When Gabriel departed, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, would recite it as Gabriel had taught him.

For this reason, the Companions did not add dots or vowel marks to the written copies of the Quran. They were also Arabs who did not make errors in Arabic, so they had no need to specify the readings by adding dots. A single word could have two readings, one with yā’ and the other with tā’, such as ya‘malūna (“they do”) and ta‘malūna (“you do”). They therefore did not mark it for one reading in a way that would exclude the other.

Later, during the time of the Successors, when errors in Arabic began to appear, some of them began adding vowel marks and dots to the written copies of the Quran. They did this in red, indicating the a-vowel with a red dot above the letter, the i-vowel with a red dot below it, and the u-vowel with a red dot

---

## Page 6145

in front of it. They then elongated the dot and began indicating doubling by writing “shadd” (doubling), and lengthening by writing “madd” (lengthening). They made the sign for hamzah resemble the letter ‘ayn, because hamzah is closely related to ‘ayn. They subsequently simplified these signs until the doubling mark resembled the head of the letter sīn and the lengthening mark became abbreviated. This is like the way administrative scribes abbreviate expressions for numbers and other things, or hadith scholars abbreviate akhbaranā (“he informed us”) and haddathanā (“he narrated to us”), writing the beginning and end of the expression in forms such as “anā” and “thanā.”

The scholars differed over whether adding vowel marks and dots to written copies of the Quran is disliked. There are two well-known positions, both reported from Imam Ahmad. Yet they do not dispute that, once a copy of the Quran has been supplied with vowel marks and dots, these must be treated with respect, just as the letters must be respected. Nor do they dispute that the ink used for the dots and vowel marks is created, just as the ink used for the letters is created. They likewise agree that vowel marks indicate grammatical inflections, while dots distinguish the letters, and that grammatical inflection is an integral part of Arabic speech.

It is reported that Abū Bakr and ‘Umar said:

“Preserving the Quran’s grammatical inflections is dearer to us than preserving some of its letters.”

There is no doubt that a dot or vowel mark, considered in isolation, has neither a ruling nor sanctity of its own, and they should not be discussed in isolation. Nor is there any doubt that the grammatical inflections of the Arabic Quran are an integral part of it and must receive careful attention. Vowel marks make its grammatical inflections clear: just as written letters indicate spoken letters, written vowel marks indicate spoken grammatical inflections.

## Page 6146

Thus, when people understand these issues properly and fully, the correct view becomes clear to them, personal inclinations and partisan loyalties diminish, and they recognize the points of disagreement. Whoever sees the truth clearly in any of these matters should follow it; whoever remains uncertain should withhold judgment until Allah makes it clear to him. He should seek help in this by supplicating to Allah. Among the best such supplications is what Muslim narrated in his Sahīh from ‘Ā’ishah: whenever the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, rose to pray at night, he would say:

“O Allah, Lord of Gabriel, Michael, and Isrāfīl, Originator of the heavens and the earth, Knower of the unseen and the seen! You judge between Your servants concerning that over which they differ. Guide me, by Your permission, to the truth concerning which there is disagreement. Indeed, You guide whom You will to a straight path.”

As for the other speaker’s statement, “His speech was written with them,” this implies that by “letters” he meant both spoken and written letters. Thus the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Whoever recites the Quran will have ten good deeds credited to him for every letter. I do not mean that alif lām mīm is one letter; rather, alif is a letter, lām is a letter, and mīm is a letter.”

Al-Tirmidhī said: “An authentic hadith.” Here, by “letter,” the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, did not mean the ink itself or the shape formed by the ink; rather, he meant the spoken letter.

There are two views concerning what he meant by “letter.” According to one, it means this individual utterance. According to the other, by “letter” he meant the name, as in his words: “Alif is a letter, lām is a letter, and mīm is a letter.”

The terms “letter” and “word” have, in the Arabic language of the Prophet

—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—one meaning, and another in the terminology of grammarians.

## Page 6148

with the meaning of a complete sentence. Many grammarians—or most of them—do not know this. Rather, they suppose that their convention of dividing what they call a kalimah into nouns, verbs, and particles reflects the language of the Arabs. The accomplished among them says:

“And by ‘word,’ complete speech may be meant.”

They say that the Arabs may use kalimah for a complete sentence and may also use it for a single word. This is mistaken: in Arab speech, kalimah is never used except for a complete sentence.

A similar case is the speculative theologians’ convention that qadīm denotes that whose existence has no beginning, or that which was not preceded by nonexistence. Some of them then say that qadīm may also denote something that precedes something else, whether or not it is beginningless, as the Most High says:

“Until it becomes like an old date stalk.”

And He says:

“And since they have not been guided by it, they will say, ‘This is an old fabrication.’”

And the Most High says:

“They said, ‘By Allah, you are indeed in your old error.’”

And He says:

“Have you considered what you have been worshipping—you and your forefathers of old?”

Restricting qadīm to the first meaning is a terminological convention. There is no doubt that what has no beginning is more deserving of this designation in the Lord’s usage. Thus, in the language of the Arabs, muhdath (“new”) stands in contrast to qadīm (“old”). The Most High says:

“No new reminder comes to them from their Lord.”

This implies that what was revealed before it is not new, but earlier. This accords with the Arabic language in which the Quran was revealed.

## Page 6149

Another example is the term qadā’. In the speech of Allah and His Messenger, it means completing an act of worship, even within its prescribed time. As the Most High says:

“When the prayer has been completed, disperse throughout the land and seek Allah’s bounty.”

And He says:

“Then when you have completed your rites…”

Later, a group of jurists adopted a convention whereby qadā’ referred exclusively to performing an act of worship outside its prescribed time, while adā’ referred exclusively to performing it within that time. This distinction is entirely unknown in the Messenger’s speech. They then say that qadā’ may sometimes be used to mean adā’, thus treating the language in which the Quran was revealed as an uncommon usage.

For this reason, they dispute what the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, meant by:

“Pray whatever you catch, and complete whatever you miss (fa-qdū).”

Another wording reads:

“Complete it (fa-atimmū).”

They suppose that the two wordings differ in meaning, but that is not the case. His words “fa-qdū” mean the same as “fa-atimmū.” Neither expression means performing the act after its prescribed time. Indeed, nowhere in the speech of the Lawgiver is there a command to perform an act of worship outside its prescribed time.

There are, however, two kinds of prescribed time: a general time and a time specific to those with valid excuses. For example, when someone who has slept through a prayer or forgotten it prays upon waking or remembering, that person is praying within the time in which Allah has commanded them to pray, although it is not a prescribed time for those not in their situation.

## Page 6150

One of the greatest causes of error in understanding the speech of Allah and His Messenger is that a person grows accustomed to a later terminology, then seeks to interpret Allah’s speech according to that terminology and the usage with which he is familiar.

Regarding what is meant by kalām (speech), Sībawayh reports Arab usage in his book, saying:

“Know that anna (‘that’) occurs in Arab speech only in quotation, and what is quoted after ‘saying’ is speech—an utterance.”

Otherwise, in Arab usage, the terms kalām and kalima (word) are never used except for a complete sentence. The term harf is used for a noun, a verb, a meaningful particle, and the name of an alphabetic letter.

Thus al-Khalīl asked his companions, “How do you pronounce the zāy in Zayd?”

They answered, “Zāy.”

He said, “You have pronounced its name; the letter itself is zh.”

Al-Khalīl thus explained that these expressions called the letters of the alphabet are names. In the speech of earlier scholars, one frequently finds the expression, “This is a harf belonging to the uncommon vocabulary,” by which they mean a complete noun.

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, illustrated his words, “He will be rewarded for every harf,” by saying:

“But alif is a harf, lām is a harf, and mīm is a harf.”

On the same basis, dhālika (‘that’) is a harf, al-kitāb (‘the Book’) is a harf, and so forth. It has also been said that dhālika consists of several harfs, as does al-kitāb; an explicit explanation to this effect has been transmitted through some chains of narration.

The grammarians, however, adopted a special convention, using the term kalima to mean

---

## Page 6151

a noun, a verb, or a meaningful particle. For Sībawayh said at the beginning of his book:

“Speech consists of a noun, a verb, and a particle that conveys a meaning and is neither a noun nor a verb.”

He thus specified a particular sense of harf: a particle that conveys a meaning and is neither a noun nor a verb. Sībawayh’s contact with the language of the Arabs was still recent, and he knew that they called a noun or a verb a harf. He therefore qualified his statement by saying:

“They divided speech into a noun, a verb, and a particle that conveys a meaning and is neither a noun nor a verb.”

Sībawayh meant that speech is divided into these as a whole is divided into its parts, not as a universal is divided into its particulars. This resembles division as discussed by jurists: real estate and movable property are divided among heirs, with one group receiving a share distinct from that of another. Likewise, speech is composed of nouns, verbs, and meaningful particles, and is divided into these components. This division differs from dividing a genus into its species, as when one says, “Nouns are divided into inflected and indeclinable nouns.”

Al-Jazūlī and others subsequently objected to the grammarians on this point without understanding their words. They said:

“Whenever a genus is divided into its species or the individual members of those species, the name of what is divided must apply to those species and individuals; otherwise, they are not its subdivisions.”

They intended this as an objection to al-Zajjāj’s statement, “Speech consists of a noun, a verb, and a particle.” Yet what al-Zajjāj stated was precisely what Sībawayh and the other leading grammarians had stated. They meant the first, familiar kind of division: dividing existing things into their parts, as real estate and wealth are divided. They did not mean the division of universals—which do not exist as universals

---

## Page 6152

except in the mind—as in the division of animals into rational and non-rational beings, and of nouns into inflected and indeclinable nouns. What is divided here is a universal intellectual concept, which is universal only in the mind.

Section

The term harf refers to meaningful particles, which constitute a category alongside nouns and verbs. Examples include prepositions, jussive particles, the two future particles, and particles resembling verbs, such as inna and its sister particles. These particles have well-known classifications in works on Arabic grammar. For example, grammarians classify them, with respect to inflection, into those specific to nouns and those specific to verbs. They say:

“A particle specific to either category, without being like a part of the word itself, governs inflection.”

Thus, prepositions and inna and its sister particles govern nouns, while subjunctive and jussive particles govern verbs. This contrasts with the definite article and the two future particles, sa- and sawfa, which do not govern inflection because they are like parts of the word itself.

They also say:

“By analogy, mā (‘not’) should not govern inflection, because it introduces both nominal and verbal sentences. The people of the Hijaz, however, made it govern inflection because of its resemblance to laysa (‘is not’).”

The Quran follows their usage in His words:

“This is no human being.”

“They are not their mothers.”

---

## Page 6153

They also classify “particles” according to their meanings into interrogative particles, negative particles, particles of specification, and so forth. According to their structure, they classify them—as they do verbs and nouns—into one-, two-, three-, four-, and five-letter forms. Here, the term harf has been transferred from ordinary language into grammatical usage by restricting its meaning. In ordinary language, however, harf encompasses nouns, particles, and verbs. The alphabetic letter-names are also called hurūf, although they are nouns, as with the letters mentioned at the beginnings of surahs: what each name denotes is a letter forming part of a word.

Letters are also classified in another way, into guttural and labial letters. Those mentioned at the beginnings of surahs in the Quran constitute half the alphabet and include the nobler half of each class: half the guttural letters, the labial letters, the emphatic letters, the musmata (non-fluid) letters, and other classes of letters.

The original meaning of harf in the language is a boundary or edge, as in the expressions “the edges of a loaf” and “the edge of a mountain.” Al-Jawharī said:

The harf of anything is its extremity, edge, or boundary. Hence the expression “the harf of a mountain,” meaning its sharp summit, and the words of the Most High:

“And among people are those who worship Allah on an edge,”

through His words:

“and the Hereafter.”

Someone standing at the edge of something is not firmly established. Thus, whoever worships Allah in prosperity but not in adversity worships Him on an edge: at times he displays this worship, and at others he turns

---

## Page 6154

back, like someone standing on the edge of a mountain. The letters of speech are thus called hurūf because they constitute its extremity, boundary, and endpoint: speech originates within the speaker and reaches its endpoint at the boundary and edge formed by his lips and tongue. Hence the Most High says:

“Have We not made for him two eyes,
and a tongue and two lips?”

The word harf can therefore carry any of these three meanings. Then, when speech is written in a codex, this too is called hurūf. Here, harf may refer to the particular shape—each nation has its own distinctive forms, constituting the script in which it writes its speech—or it may refer to the material, or to both together. These written letters correspond to the spoken letters, make them clear, and signify them; they are therefore given the same names, since a person writes spoken words with his pen. Hence the first revelation Allah sent down to His Prophet was:

“Read in the name of your Lord who created,”

through His words:

“what he did not know.”

Thus, in the very first revelation, He, glorified be He, made clear that He is the Creator and Guide, who created and proportioned, and who determined and guided. As Moses said:

“Our Lord is He who gave everything its form, then guided it.”

Creation encompasses all created things other than Him. He then singled out man, saying:

“He created man from a clinging clot.”

Then He mentioned that He taught, for guidance and instruction bring created beings to their perfection. Knowledge has “three levels”: knowledge in the heart, expression by the tongue, and writing

---

## Page 6155

with the fingers;

hence it has been said that everything has four modes of existence: concrete, cognitive, verbal, and written—existence in external reality, in minds, on tongues, and through fingers.

Concrete existence, however, is the existence of things in themselves, and Allah is the Creator of everything. Mental existence, which pertains to the heart, is the knowledge of those things held in the heart. The expression of that knowledge constitutes verbal existence, while writing it constitutes written existence, produced by the fingers. Teaching writing necessarily entails teaching verbal expression, which in turn entails imparting knowledge. Thus He said:

“He taught by the pen,”

because teaching by the pen entails all three levels. He spoke of teaching in general, then specified, saying:

“He taught man what he did not know.”

People have disputed whether the existence of each thing is identical to its essence. This has been discussed at length elsewhere, where it was explained that the correct position is as follows: “existence” may mean what is established in external reality, while “essence” means what is conceived in the mind. Understood in this way, the existence of things established in external reality is not their essence as conceived in the mind. Yet Allah created what exists in external reality and knew the essences conceived in minds, as He explained in the first surah of the Quran that He revealed.

Both “existence” and “essence” may also refer to what is realized in external reality and to what is realized in the mind. If both terms mean what is realized in external reality, or what is conceived in the mind, then they are not two distinct things in external reality; rather, the one is the other. Likewise, when the mind conceives of something, that image

---

## Page 6156

is the representation conceived by the mind; this is its mental existence, as conceived by minds. This is the decisive resolution of this issue. Whoever reflects on these questions and others like them will recognize that most disagreements among rational people arise from using the same terms for different meanings.

“And he to whom Allah has not granted light—for him there is no light.”

The foundations and details of these questions have been discussed at length elsewhere. People have disputed them so extensively that it has been said: “The question of speech” has bewildered the minds of mankind.

However, the question posed by these two men does not lend itself to extensive elaboration, for they asked according to what they had heard, believed, and conceived. Once the questioner understands the basis of his question, its implications, and the ambiguous expressions and potentially confusing meanings it contains, he will recognize that some people have affirmed or denied such terms without qualification, inevitably prompting others to counter them with equally unqualified statements.

One of the general principles to understand is that expressions fall into “two types.” One type consists of expressions found in the Quran and the Sunnah. Every believer must acknowledge what these entail, affirming what Allah and His Messenger have affirmed and denying what Allah and His Messenger have denied. The wording Allah uses in affirmation or negation is true, for Allah speaks the truth and guides to the way. And the expressions

---

## Page 6157

of revelation are to be held in reverence.

Part of attaining complete knowledge is to investigate what His Messenger intended by them, so as to affirm the meanings he affirmed and deny those he denied. We must believe everything he reported and obey him in everything he made obligatory and commanded. Then, when we understand these matters in detail, our knowledge and faith increase. Allah Most High says:

“Allah will raise those of you who believe and those who have been given knowledge in rank.”

As for expressions that occur neither in the Quran nor in the Sunnah, and whose affirmation or denial was not agreed upon by the early generations, no one is obliged to agree with anyone who denies or affirms them without first asking what he means. If he intends a meaning consistent with what the Messenger conveyed, it is accepted; if he intends a meaning contrary to what the Messenger conveyed, it is rejected.

When conveying these meanings, if the wording is confusing or ambiguous, other wording should be used, or its intended meaning clarified, so that the truth is made known in a manner consistent with revelation. Much disagreement among people arises from ambiguous, newly introduced expressions and unclear meanings. Thus, you may find two men quarrelling and becoming enemies over the unqualified affirmation or denial of certain expressions, yet if either were asked what he meant by his words, he would have no clear conception of it, let alone know the evidence for it. Even if he knew its evidence, it would not necessarily follow that someone who disagreed with him was mistaken; rather, his opponent’s position may contain a measure of truth. Each may be right in one respect, or the truth may lie in a third position.

“In a clear Arabic tongue.”

The word “Trustworthy” indicates that he is entrusted with what he has been sent to convey, neither adding anything to it nor taking anything away from it. A treacherous messenger, by contrast, may alter the message. As He says in describing him in another passage:

“Indeed, it is the word of a noble messenger,”

“Possessed of strength, held in honor with the Lord of the Throne,”

“Obeyed there and trustworthy.”

His words, “sent down from your Lord,” indicate several things. Among them is the falsity of the view of those who say that it is created speech which He created in a body

---

## Page 6162

among created bodies, as maintained by the Jahmiyyah who hold that the Quran is created, including the Muʿtazilah, the Najjāriyyah, the Dirāriyyah, and others. The early generations called anyone who denied the divine attributes, declared the Quran created, and denied that Allah would be seen in the Hereafter a Jahmī. For Jahm was the first to become known for the innovation of denying the divine names and attributes, and he carried this denial to extremes. What distinguishes him in this innovation is the extremity of his denial and his pioneering role in publicizing it widely and calling others to it, although al-Jaʿd ibn Dirham had preceded him in some of this.

Al-Jaʿd ibn Dirham was the first to introduce this into Islam. Khālid ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Qasrī therefore offered him as a sacrifice at Wāsit on the Day of Sacrifice, saying:

“O people, offer your sacrifices; may Allah accept them. I am offering al-Jaʿd ibn Dirham as a sacrifice, for he claimed that Allah did not take Abraham as a close friend and did not speak directly to Moses. Exalted is Allah, far above what al-Jaʿd ibn Dirham says!”

He then descended and slaughtered him.

Although the Muʿtazilah agree with Jahm on some of these matters, they disagree with him on others, such as divine decree, faith, and even some questions concerning the divine attributes. Nor do they carry denial to the extremes that he does.

Jahm says that Allah Most High does not speak, or that He speaks only figuratively. The Muʿtazilah, however, say that He speaks in a real sense, although their position amounts in substance to Jahm’s. Jahm also denies the divine names, as do the Bātiniyyah and those philosophers who agree with them. The majority of the Muʿtazilah, however, do not deny the divine names.

## Page 6163

The point is that His words,

“Sent down from your Lord,”

make clear that it was sent down from Allah, not from any created being. Hence the early generations said, “From Him it originated,” meaning that He is the One who spoke it; it did not originate with anyone else, as those who hold it to be created claim.

Another implication of His words, “Sent down from your Lord,” is that they invalidate the view that it emanated into the soul of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, from the Active Intellect or some other source, as various groups among the philosophers and the Sabians maintain. This view is even greater in unbelief and misguidance than the preceding one.

Another implication is that this verse also invalidates the view that the Arabic Quran was not sent down from Allah but was instead created—either within Gabriel, within Muhammad, or within some other body. This is maintained by the Kullābiyyah and Ashʿariyyah who say that the Arabic Quran is not Allah’s speech; rather, His speech is only the meaning subsisting in His essence, and the Arabic Quran was created to signify that meaning.

On this account, it was either created in some physical body—air or something else—or Gabriel was inspired with it and expressed it as the Arabic Quran, or Muhammad was inspired with it and expressed it as the Arabic Quran, or Gabriel took it from the Preserved Tablet or elsewhere. These previously mentioned views are thus ramifications of this position, for this Arabic Quran must have had a speaker who first spoke it before it reached us.

## Page 6164

This position agrees with that of the Mu'tazilah and others like them in affirming that the Arabic Quran is created, as is the Hebrew Torah, but differs from it in two respects.

This is the position of their leading authorities and the majority of them. A group of their later scholars, however, said that the word “speech” applies to both in distinct senses. Most people, however, say that, upon examination, the proponents of this position have not truly affirmed any speech for Him apart from created speech. it is the Quran; if it is expressed in Hebrew, it is the Torah; and if it is expressed in Syriac, it is the Gospel. Some of them said that it consists of five meanings.

## Page 6170

For its being written in the Preserved Tablet and in purified pages in the hands of the angels does not preclude Gabriel having brought it down from Allah, whether Allah wrote it before sending Gabriel with it or afterward. If He sent it down in written form to Bayt al-ʿIzzah (the House of Honour), all at once on the Night of Decree, then He had written all of it before sending it down.

Allah, Most High, knows what has been, what will be, and what will not be—and how it would be if it were to occur. Then He commands the angels to record those deeds after they perform them. This is what Ibn ʿAbbās and others among the early generations said, and it is true. If He has recorded what He creates as distinct from Himself before creating it, how can it be considered implausible that He should write His speech, with which He sends His angels, before sending them with it?

The claim that Gabriel took the Quran from the Book and did not hear it from Allah is false for several reasons.

Thus, the Children of Israel took Allah’s speech from the Book in which He, glorified and exalted is He, had written it. If, then, Muhammad received it from Gabriel, and Gabriel from the Book,

## Page 6172

the terms “speaking” and “revelation” each have both a general and a specific sense. Thus, speaking is the general category subdivided in His words:

Speaking, when used without qualification, is a distinct category alongside revelation in its specific sense, not a subdivision of it. Likewise, the term “revelation” may have a general sense that includes speaking in its specific sense, as in His words to Moses:

and His words:

and His words:

and similar passages indicate that it is sent down from Allah, not from anyone else. Likewise, His words:

affirm that what has been sent down to him comes from his Lord, and that his role is to convey it, as he has been commanded.

## Page 6173

—and the verses that follow—provide evidence of speech that Moses heard. ## Page 6175

will they ever cease to subsist in His essence. The call that Moses heard is eternal and beginningless; it has always existed and will remain forever.

Others say that the individual letters are eternal, but not the sounds. All these groups maintain that speaking and calling amount merely to creating perception in a creature, enabling him to hear what has always existed and will remain forever. They do not mean that Allah then utters speech by His will and power, or that an act of addressing someone takes place. Rather, in their view, His addressing someone means enabling the servant to hear what existed before he heard it. Yet their position is not that of the early generations. Their position is, however, closer to that of the early generations in one respect, while the position of those who maintain that it is created is closer in another respect.

Their position is closer because they affirm that Allah has speech subsisting in His own essence, and this is the position of the early generations. By contrast, those who maintain that His speech is created say that His speech is nothing other than what He creates in something other than Himself. Their position therefore contradicts that of the early generations. As for why the position of

## Page 6176

those who maintain that it is created is closer, it is because they say that Allah speaks by His will and power, which is the position of the early generations. The opposing group, however, holds that Allah has no power over any of His speech and that His speech is not subject to His will and choice. Rather, in their view, His speech is like His life. They say: “In our view, speech is an attribute of His essence, not an attribute of His action.” Those who maintain that it is created say that it is an attribute of His action, not of His essence. The position of the early generations is that it is both an attribute of His essence and an attribute of His action. Thus, each group agrees with the early generations in one respect but not in another.

Their disagreement concerning Allah’s speech resembles their disagreement concerning His actions, pleasure, anger, will, aversion, love, hatred, joy, wrath, and similar attributes. One group says that these are all created things, separate from Him, which amount to reward and punishment. The other group says that these are all individually eternal realities subsisting in His essence. Some of them then reduce all of these to one and the same will relating to all created things.

Others say: “Rather, they are distinct attributes.” Yet they maintain that each has a single, eternal reality, existing before the things it entails come into existence, just as they said concerning speech. Allah Most High says:

“That is because they followed what displeased Allah and hated His good pleasure.”

He thus states that their deeds displeased Him. He Most High says:

“So when they provoked Our anger, We took vengeance on them.”

That is, they angered Us. He Most High also says:

“Call upon Me; I will respond to you.”

These and similar passages make clear that He became displeased with the disbelievers when they disbelieved, and pleased with the believers when they believed.

## Page 6177

Analogous to this is their disagreement concerning His actions, exalted is He, and questions of divine decree. The Muʿtazilah say that He acts for an intended wise purpose and out of a desire to show kindness to His servants, but they do not affirm any wisdom in His action whose end relates to Him Himself. The other group says that He does not act for any wisdom or purpose whatsoever. The former affirm wisdom, but not wisdom subsisting in Him; the latter affirm neither wisdom nor purpose as an attribute of His. Neither group affirms any wisdom or intended end that relates to Him Himself.

The same applies to “speech”: the former affirm speech that is His action but does not subsist in Him. The latter say that whatever does not subsist in Him cannot confer its corresponding attribute upon Him. Both groups deny that wisdom intended by Him can subsist in Him, just as both deny that speech and action that He wills can subsist in Him.

The former group’s position is closer to that of the early generations and the jurists, insofar as they affirm wisdom and benefit in His rulings and actions, and affirm speech that He utters by His power and will. The latter group’s position is closer to that of the early generations insofar as they affirm the attributes and say that He cannot be described merely on account of something created, separate from Him, that does not subsist in Him at all. Nor can any corresponding attribute be ascribed to Him on account of something that does not subsist in Him. Thus, He cannot be one who speaks by virtue of speech that does not subsist in Him, nor can He be wise, generous, and merciful by virtue of wisdom and mercy that do not subsist in Him—just as He cannot be knowing by virtue of knowledge that does not subsist in Him, or powerful by virtue of power that does not subsist in Him. Nor can He be loving, pleased, or angry by virtue of love, pleasure, and anger that do not subsist in Him.

Thus, both the Muʿtazilah and the Ashʿariyyah, concerning questions of Allah’s speech and Allah’s actions—indeed,

---

## Page 6178

all His other attributes as well—agree with the early generations and the imams in one respect and disagree with them in another. Neither group’s position, to the exclusion of the other’s, represents that of the early generations. However, in questions of the attributes generally—indeed, in all questions of the attributes and divine decree—the Ashʿariyyah are closer to the position of the early generations and the imams than the Muʿtazilah.

If it is said:

“Allah Most High has said, ‘Indeed, it is the word of a noble messenger.’ This indicates that the messenger originated the Arabic speech.”

The reply is:

This is false, because Allah mentions this in two places in the Quran. In one, the messenger is Muhammad; in the other verse, the messenger is Gabriel.

Allah Most High says in Sūrat al-Hāqqah:

“Indeed, it is the word of a noble messenger. It is not the word of a poet—how little you believe! Nor is it the word of a soothsayer—how little you take heed! It is a revelation from the Lord of all worlds.”

The messenger here is Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. In Sūrat al-Takwīr, He says:

“Indeed, it is the word of a noble messenger, possessed of power, held in honour with the Lord of the Throne, obeyed there and trustworthy.”

The messenger here is Gabriel. Had He attributed it to the messenger because he originated its letters, or originated any part of it, the two statements would have contradicted one another. For if one of them originated its letters, the other could not have originated them.

Furthermore, He said:

“The word of a noble messenger.”

He did not say, “The word of an angel,” or “of a prophet.” The term “messenger” necessarily implies someone who sent him. This therefore indicates that

---

## Page 6179

the messenger conveys it from the One who sent him, not that he originated any part of it himself. This indicates that He attributed it to the messenger because he conveyed and delivered it, not because he originated or first uttered any part of it.

Furthermore, Allah has declared whoever regards it as the word of a human being a disbeliever, saying:

“Indeed, he thought and calculated. May he be destroyed—how he calculated! Again, may he be destroyed—how he calculated! Then he looked, then frowned and scowled, then turned away in arrogance and said, ‘This is nothing but magic handed down. This is nothing but the word of a human being.’”

Muhammad is a human being, so whoever says that it is Muhammad’s word has disbelieved. There is no difference between saying that it is the word of a human being, a jinn, or an angel. Whoever regards it as the word of any of these has disbelieved.

Yet Allah Most High has said:

“Indeed, it is the word of a noble messenger. It is not the word of a poet.”

Thus, He attributed it to the human messenger while declaring whoever says that it is the word of a human being a disbeliever. It is therefore clear that what is meant is that the messenger conveyed it from the One who sent him, not that it is speech originating from himself. It is the speech of Allah, who sent him, as Allah Most High says:

“If any of the polytheists seeks your protection, grant him protection so that he may hear the speech of Allah.”

What the messenger conveyed is therefore Allah’s speech, not the messenger’s speech.

For this reason, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, would present himself to people at the seasonal gatherings and say:

“Is there a man who will take me to his people so that I may convey the speech of my Lord? Quraysh have prevented me from conveying the speech of my Lord.”

Reported by Abū Dāwūd and others. Speech belongs to the one who

---

## Page 6180

first uttered it, not to the one who uttered it merely to convey and transmit it. Moses heard Allah’s speech from Allah without an intermediary, whereas the believers hear it from one another. Moses’ hearing was therefore unqualified, without an intermediary, whereas other people’s hearing is qualified by an intermediary.

As Allah Most High says:

“It is not for any human being that Allah should speak to him except by revelation, or from behind a veil, or by sending a messenger who reveals, by His permission, whatever He wills.”

He thus distinguished between speaking from behind a veil—as He spoke to Moses—and speaking through a messenger—as He spoke to the prophets by sending a messenger to them. People know that when the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, spoke, he uttered the words, with their letters and meanings, in his own voice. Those who convey his words then convey them through their own movements and voices, as he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“May Allah brighten the face of a person who hears a hadith from us and conveys it as he heard it.”

The listener conveys his hadith as he heard it, but in his own voice, not the Messenger’s voice. The speech is the Messenger’s speech, which he uttered in his own voice; the transmitter conveys the Messenger’s speech, but in his own voice. If this is understood regarding someone who conveys the speech of a created being, it applies all the more to the speech of the Creator.

For this reason, Allah Most High says:

“If any of the polytheists seeks your protection, grant him protection so that he may hear the speech of Allah.”

And the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Beautify the Quran with your voices.”

He thus identified the speech as the Creator’s speech, while identifying the voice in which the servant recites it as the reciter’s voice. The voices of the servants are not identical to the voice used in calling

---

## Page 6181

by Allah and used by Him in speaking, as the texts affirm. Indeed, they are not even like it, for nothing is like Allah—in His essence, His attributes, or His actions. His knowledge is not like the knowledge of created beings, nor is His power like theirs, His speech like their speech, His calling like their calling, or His voice like their voices.

Whoever says of the Quran that Muslims recite, “It is not Allah’s speech,” or, “It is someone else’s speech,” is a heretic and a misguided innovator.

Whoever says that the voices of the servants or the ink with which the Quran is written are eternal and without beginning is likewise a heretic and a misguided innovator. Rather, this Quran is Allah’s speech, recorded in written copies. It is Allah’s speech conveyed from Him and heard from the reciters, not heard directly from Him.

A person sees the sun, the moon, and the stars directly, and also sees them in water or a mirror. The latter is seeing through an intermediary, whereas the former is unqualified, direct seeing. Likewise, speech is heard directly from the one who utters it, and indirectly from the one who conveys it on his behalf. In both cases, what one seeks to hear is the speaker’s speech, just as in both cases of seeing, what one seeks to see is the object itself.

Whoever understands how these two situations coincide and differ, and what they share and do not share, will be rid of the confusion that afflicts many people concerning this matter. One group has said: “What is heard is Allah’s speech; what is heard is the servant’s voice; and his voice is created. Therefore, Allah’s speech is created.” This is ignorance, for it is heard from

---

## Page 6182

the one who conveys it, and the fact that his voice is created does not mean that the speech itself is created.

Another “group” said: “What is heard is the servant’s voice, which is created. The Quran is not created, so what is heard cannot be Allah’s speech.” This is ignorance, for what is created is the voice, not the speech itself, which is heard both from the one who utters it and from the one who conveys it on his behalf.

Yet another “group” said: “This is Allah’s speech, and Allah’s speech is uncreated; therefore, this voice is uncreated.” This too is ignorance. For when it is said, “This is Allah’s speech,” what is being referred to is the speech itself, which remains the same whether heard from Allah or from one who conveys it on His behalf. When what is heard is called Allah’s speech, it is Allah’s speech heard from one who conveys it on His behalf, not heard directly from Him. Thus, it is heard through the servant’s voice, and the servant’s voice is created. As for Allah’s speech itself, it is uncreated, however it is conveyed.

These are subtle points that have been discussed at length elsewhere.
