## Page 6210

who say that the eternal sound is heard from the reciter.

They may sometimes say that what is eternal is the very sound heard from the reciter, and at other times say that two sounds are heard from the reciter: one eternal and the other newly produced. Many—or most—of them do not maintain that the eternal inheres in what is newly produced; rather, they say that it becomes manifest in it, just as a face appears in a mirror. Others among them maintain that the eternal inheres in what is newly produced.

Neither this position nor the preceding positions was held by any of the early generations of the Muslim community or its leading scholars. Neither Imam Ahmad, nor the leading scholars among his followers, nor any other imam said this. Rather, they agree in condemning anyone who says, “My utterance of the Quran is uncreated.” What, then, of someone who says, “My voice is uncreated”? And what of someone who says, “My voice is eternal”?

As for the claim that the ink in a copy of the Quran is eternal, we have not encountered this in any book by anyone belonging to any Muslim group, nor has anyone reported hearing it from a recognized scholar. Some, however, refrain from making any affirmative or negative statement about the ink, saying: “We do not say that it is eternal; rather, we remain silent as a preventive measure.”

Some have attributed belief in the eternity of ink to those whom they call the Hashwiyya, saying: “They maintain that the ink in a copy of the Quran is eternal: while it was in the inkwell, it was newly produced, but once it was on the paper, it became eternal.”

---

## Page 6211

We have seen groups accuse these people of false reporting. It would seem that what actually happens is that those making such attributions report others’ views merely on the basis of unqualified statements that have reached them, or what they suppose those views necessarily imply, or what they have heard from people who report recklessly and without verification. They may also have heard this from some of their ordinary followers—if that did indeed occur.

This has caused errors in this matter, to the point that people have misrepresented even those whom they hold in high esteem. It was for this reason that Imam Ahmad corrected Abū Tālib concerning what he had reported from him. Abū Tālib had recited to him:

“Say, ‘He is Allah, One.’”

He then asked him, “Is this created?” Ahmad replied, “This is not created.” Ahmad subsequently learned that Abū Tālib had reported him as saying, “My utterance of the Quran is uncreated.” Ahmad became angry with him and asked, “Did I tell you, ‘My utterance of the Quran is uncreated’?”

He replied, “No. But I recited to you:

“‘Say, “He is Allah, One.”’

“Then I said to you, ‘This is uncreated,’ and you said, ‘Yes.’”

Ahmad asked, “Why, then, did you report that I told you, ‘My utterance of the Quran is uncreated’?”

He replied, “I did not report it from you; I only stated it as my own view.”

Ahmad said, “Do not say this, for I have never heard a scholar say it. Rather, say: ‘The Quran, however it is conveyed, is the uncreated speech of Allah.’”

This is why al-Bukhārī said in The Creation of Deeds that these “Lafziyya” attribute their position to Ahmad, although they do not understand the subtlety of his words. The source of the confusion is that when he says “this,” he is referring to the speech simply as speech, without regard to the servant’s movements and voice through which it is conveyed, just as

---

## Page 6212

a man who writes the name of Allah—blessed and exalted is He—and hears someone mentioning Allah speaks truthfully when he says, “This is my Lord.” If he were asked, “Do you worship this?” he would answer, “Yes”—because the reference is to the One designated by that name. Do you not know what is written?

In connected speech, a name is intended to refer to the one named. Thus, when He says:

“Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, and those with him,”

the meaning is that the person whose name is Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah—not that the actual spoken expression or written form is the Messenger of Allah.

This gave rise to the dispute over whether “the name” is the one named or something other than it. The correct approach was to disallow both unqualified assertions and instead say what Allah Most High said:

“To Allah belong the most beautiful names,”

and what the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Allah has ninety-nine names; whoever enumerates them will enter Paradise.”

Those who stated without qualification that the name is the one named basically meant that the name refers to the one named, and that mentioning the name points to its referent. When a servant says, “I praised Allah, called upon Allah, and worshipped Allah,” he means only that he worshipped the One designated by this name.

Those who denied this considered that the actual spoken expression or written form is not identical to the entities designated by it. Others distinguished between naming and the name: they treated the spoken expressions as the naming, and the entities designated by those expressions as the name. They thereby departed from the established usage of the language in which the Quran and Sunnah came.

---

## Page 6213

The underlying intent of all these groups is sound, except for those among them who used their statement to arrive at a false conclusion. Such was the Jahmiyyah’s assertion that the name is other than the one named. They used this to argue that Allah’s names are other than Him. They then said that whatever is other than Allah is created and separate from Him. Accordingly, Allah Most High would not have named Himself with any name, nor uttered any of His names, nor would He have speech that He Himself had spoken. Rather, His speech would consist only of something created and separate from Him.

When the early generations recognized that these people’s intent was false, they rejected their unqualified assertions that Allah’s speech is other than Allah, that Allah’s knowledge is other than Allah, and similar statements. This is because the expression “other” is ambiguous: it may mean something separate from another, or something that is neither identical to another nor separate from it. Thus, if someone says that it is other than Him in order to make it separate from Him, both meanings would be correct, even if the wording falls short.

Likewise, the imams rejected the statement, “My utterance of the Quran is created,” as well as, “My utterance of the Quran is uncreated.” They said, “Whoever says it is created is a Jahmī, and whoever says it is uncreated is an innovator.” They said the same regarding “recitation and reading,” because utterance, recitation, and reading may refer to the action denoted by the verbal noun—that is, the servant’s act. The acts of Allah’s servants are created. Whoever declares any of their acts, voices, or other attributes to be uncreated is therefore an innovator.

“Utterance” may also mean the very words uttered, just as recitation and reading may mean the actual speech being recited—namely, the Quran itself. And whoever says that the speech of

---

## Page 6214

Allah, which He revealed to His Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) and which the Muslims recite, is created is a Jahmī.

It is well known that when people hear a hadith scholar narrating a hadith of the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace), such as his saying:

“Actions are judged only by intentions, and each person will have only what he intended,”

they say, “This is the speech of the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace),” or, “These are his very words.” This is because they know that the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) uttered that speech, both its wording and its meaning, in his own voice. The person conveying it from him then conveyed it in his own voice. Thus, the speech belongs to the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace): he expressed its meanings and arranged its letters in his own voice, while the person conveying it did so through his own action and in his own voice.

When they say, “This is the speech of the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace),” they are referring to the actual speech—its letters, arrangement, and meanings—not to the movements and vocal sounds peculiar to the person conveying it. Rather, they attribute the voice to the person conveying it, saying, “A beautiful voice.” Whatever eloquence the speech possesses in its wording and arrangement, and whatever rhetorical power its meanings possess, are attributed only to the one who originally spoke it, not to the person conveying it. What is attributed to the person conveying it, however, is excellence of delivery, such as precise articulation of the letters and beautification of the voice.

For this reason, Allah Most High says:

“And if any of the polytheists seeks your protection, grant him protection so that he may hear the speech of Allah.”

---

## Page 6215

“And the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) would present himself to the people, saying: ‘Is there no man who will take me to his people so that I may convey the speech of my Lord?’”

The Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) also said:

“Beautify the Quran with your voices.”

And he said:

“Allah listens more attentively to a man who beautifies his voice in reciting the Quran than the owner of a singing girl listens to her.”

Thus, Allah and His Messenger have made clear that the Quran which is heard is Allah’s speech, not the speech of any created being, and that people recite it in their own voices. Whoever says that this Quran which is heard is not Allah’s speech, or that it is the speech of its reciters, makes a claim whose falsity is self-evident, both according to revelation and to reason. Likewise, whoever says that this audible voice is not the servant’s voice, or that it is Allah’s voice, makes a claim whose falsity is self-evident, both according to revelation and to reason. Rather, this is Allah’s speech and no one else’s. Gabriel heard it from Allah, the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) heard it from Gabriel, and the Muslims heard it from their Prophet. They then conveyed it to one another. None of these intermediaries has any role in it beyond conveying it through his own actions and voice. None of them originated any of its letters, its arrangement, or its meanings; rather, all of that is the speech of Allah Most High.

The fifth position:

The position of the Hishāmiyyah, the Karrāmiyyah, and those who agree with them is that Allah’s speech originates in time and subsists in His essence, after He had previously not spoken at all. Rather, they hold that He has always been capable of speech. In their view, He has always been speaking only in the sense that He has always been capable of speech. Apart from this sense, they hold that the existence of speech in pre-eternity is impossible, just as the existence of

---

## Page 6216

acts is impossible in their view and in that of the speculative theologians who agree with them, such as the Muʿtazilah and their followers.

They say that His speech consists of letters and sounds that come into being within the Lord’s essence through His power and will. They do not say that the sounds heard or the ink in the written copy of the Quran are eternal; rather, they say that these came into being.

The sixth position:

The position of the majority, the scholars of hadith, and their leading authorities is that Allah Most High has always spoken whenever He wills, and that He speaks with a voice, as the transmitted reports indicate. The Quran and the other divine scriptures are Allah’s speech, which He spoke by His will and power; it is not something created and separate from Him. They do not say that He began to speak after previously not speaking, nor that Allah Most High’s speech, considered in itself, originated in time. Rather, He has always spoken whenever He wills, although He spoke to Moses and called out to him by His will and power. His speech is inexhaustible, as He Most High says:

“Say: ‘If the sea were ink for the words of my Lord, the sea would be exhausted before the words of my Lord were exhausted, even if We brought another like it as a replenishment.’”

They affirm what the authentic prophetic texts convey and what sound, unclouded reason establishes. They do not deny Allah Most High His attributes of perfection—glorified and exalted is He—thereby making Him like inanimate objects that neither speak nor hear nor see, that neither speak to their worshippers nor guide them to any path, that give them no answer and have no power to harm or benefit them.

---

## Page 6217

Whoever maintains that Allah’s speech subsists only in something other than Allah makes that other thing the one possessing this attribute. Thus, the tree would be the one saying to Moses:

“Indeed, I am Allah.”

For this reason, the early generations vehemently condemned those who said this. They said that it was comparable to Pharaoh’s declaration:

“I am your supreme lord.”

That is, this would be speech subsisting in something other than Allah. Hence, advocates of union, such as Ibn ‘Arabī and others like him, explicitly stated the true implications of this view, saying:

“All speech in existence is His speech;
Its prose and verse are alike to us.”

Those who hold the position described above—who agree with the early generations and the leading scholars—do not say that the Lord was devoid of the attributes of perfection in eternity past, or that He was incapable of speech until He acquired the ability to speak, like a child.

Those who say that the Quran is created make speech an attribute of something other than Him, thereby denying Him the attributes of perfection. They say that in eternity past He was incapable of speech, whether created speech or otherwise. Even if they do not explicitly declare that He was incapable of speech in eternity past, this necessarily follows from their position.

The Karrāmiyyah sought to avoid the first error and affirmed that He speaks with speech that subsists in Him. Yet they did not affirm that He spoke in eternity past, or even that He was truly capable of speech in eternity past.

The Kullābiyyah and those who agreed with them, such as the Sālimiyyah and others, attributed speech to Him in eternity past. They said that He possesses this attribute eternally, without beginning or end. Yet they did not regard Him as capable of speech, or as speaking by His will and choice, or as able to bring anything into being

---

## Page 6218

through which He would address anyone else. Rather, He creates in others a perception of what has always existed, just as He removes blindness from a blind person who cannot see the sun, although it was already manifest and plainly visible—not that the sun itself has newly become manifest and visible. Many of these people say the same regarding seeing Him: it consists solely in the creation of perception; there are no veils external to the beholder, so He neither draws aside nor lifts a veil. The Quran, hadith and reason refute them, as in His words, Most High:

“It is not for any human being that Allah should speak to him except by revelation, or from behind a veil, or by sending a messenger.”

If the veil were merely the absence of vision, then revelation and the sending of messengers would also be from behind a veil.

He also says, Most High:

“When his Lord manifested Himself to the mountain, He made it crumble, and Moses fell unconscious.”

An authentic hadith states:

“When the people of Paradise enter Paradise, a caller will proclaim: ‘O people of Paradise, Allah has a promise for you that He wishes to fulfil.’ They will say: ‘What is it? Has He not brightened our faces, made our scales heavy, admitted us to Paradise and saved us from the Fire?’ He said: ‘Then He will draw aside the veil, and they will look upon Him. Nothing He has given them will be dearer to them than gazing upon Him.’”

There are many reports to this effect.

Furthermore, the Kullābiyyah’s assertion that realities of different kinds are one and the same thing, and the others’ assertion that mutually opposed sounds coexist at a single instant, are views that most scholars of sound reason regard as self-evidently false. These views have been discussed at length elsewhere.

---

## Page 6219

The purpose here is to respond to this speaker’s statement: “Some hold that it is eternal in its sounds and letters; these are the Hashwiyyah.” If he means the position that the sounds themselves coexist in pre-eternity, then this is the position of the aforementioned Sālimiyyah and others among the practitioners of speculative theology and hadith.

As for his use of “Hashwiyyah,” this term has no established referent in revelation, language or general usage. It is reported, however, that the first person to use this expression was Amr ibn Ubayd, who said: “Abd Allah ibn Umar was a Hashwī.”

The origin of this usage is that any group adopting a position contrary to that of the majority and the common people labels their view “the view of the Hashwiyyah”—meaning those considered mere rabble, whom that group does not regard as qualified. Thus, the Muʿtazilah call anyone who affirms divine decree a Hashwī; the Jahmiyyah call those who affirm the divine attributes Hashwiyyah; and the Qarāmitah—such as the followers of al-Hākim—call anyone who regards prayer, zakat, fasting and pilgrimage as obligatory a Hashwī. Similarly, the Rāfidah call the position of Ahl al-Sunnah wa-l-Jamāʿah “the view of the majority,” as do the philosophers. “The view of the majority” and “the view of the common people” are expressions of the same kind. If someone using this expression believes that the elite do not hold that view, but only the common people and the majority do, he attributes it to them and calls them Hashwiyyah.

A group is sometimes named after the man who originated its doctrine, as in the names Jahmiyyah, Ibādiyyah, Azāriqah, Kullābiyyah, Ashʿariyyah and Karrāmiyyah

---

## Page 6220

and, with reference to the imams of the legal schools, Mālikiyyah, Hanafiyyah, Shāfiʿiyyah and Hanbaliyyah. At other times, a group is named after its beliefs or practices, as with the Rāfidah, Khawārij, Qadariyyah, Muʿtazilah and others. The term “Hashwiyyah” derives from neither of these bases.

As for his statement, “Some hold that it originated in time, consisting of sounds and letters—these are the Jahmiyyah,” these are the words of someone unfamiliar with people’s doctrines.

The Jahmiyyah say: “Allah does not speak and has no speech; He merely created something that was then given expression.” Some of them say that He speaks through speech He creates in something other than Himself. This is the position of the Muʿtazilah.

The Karrāmiyyah, however, say: “The Quran is Allah’s speech, uncreated, and He speaks it with letters and sounds.” Yet they also say that it originated in time and subsists in Him. They are not Jahmiyyah; rather, they refute them most vigorously, and their differences with them are greater than those of the Ashʿariyyah. Nevertheless, they say: “The Quran originated in time within Allah’s essence.”

Some of these maintain that all of Allah’s speech originated in time, while others do not. This view is known to have been held by Abū Muʿādh al-Tūmanī, Zuhayr al-Bābī and Dāwūd ibn ʿAlī al-Asbahānī. Indeed, it is also reported from al-Bukhārī, the author of the Sahīh, and others, as well as numerous groups. Thus, not everyone who says that it originated in time is a Jahmī or says that it is created.

---

## Page 6221

As for his statement, “Some hold that it is eternal, consisting neither of sound nor of letters, but rather of a meaning subsisting in Allah’s essence—these are the Ashʿariyyah,” this is correct. However, the first person in Islam to advance this view was ʿAbd Allāh ibn Kullāb. The early Muslims and the imams affirmed attributes subsisting in Allah Most High, as well as acts connected to His will and power. The Jahmiyyah deny both. Ibn Kullāb agreed with the early Muslims in affirming eternal attributes subsisting in Him, but denied that anything connected to His will and power could subsist in Him.

Abū al-Hasan al-Ashʿarī came after him. He had been a student of Abū ʿAlī al-Jubbāʾī, the Muʿtazilī, but then abandoned the Muʿtazilī position and exposed their contradictions on numerous points. He opposed them so strongly on questions of divine decree, faith, and the promise of reward and threat of punishment that they accused him of adopting the positions of the Murjiʾah, Jabriyyah and Wāqifah. Regarding the divine attributes, he followed Ibn Kullāb’s approach. This position concerning the Quran thus originated with Ibn Kullāb and was adopted by his followers, including al-Ashʿarī and others.

And his statement:

“Concerning anyone who says that the letters and sounds uttered are identical with the eternal speech, those who uphold the truth have two opinions: one declares him an unbeliever, and the other declares him an innovator,”

up to his words:

“Let it be known that letters articulated by the tongue and letters written by the fingers are both subject to his control.”

---

## Page 6222

The response is as follows:

As for the claim that the ink used in writing is eternal, we know of no recognized person who has held it, nor have we seen it in any author’s work, whether among the followers of Abū Hanīfah, Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī, or Ahmad. Rather, we have seen works by several authors among the followers of Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī, and Ahmad rejecting the claim that ink is eternal and declaring false the reports attributing this view to them. Some of their statements indicate that the written copy of the Quran contains an eternal letter distinct from the ink.

Some of them say that it is manifest in the written copy without inhering in it, while others say that it inheres in it. Some of their statements imply that this is the form—the letter’s shape and appearance—not its material substance, namely its ink. This view, too, is false, just as the claim that any human vocal sounds are eternal is false. The latter view has been held by some followers of Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī, and Ahmad, although the majority of the followers of these imams reject it. Imam Ahmad and the majority of his followers have made many well-known statements rejecting this view.

There is no doubt that anyone who says that people’s voices are eternal is a fabricator and an innovator, subject to the same judgment as others of his kind. Likewise, anyone who says that this Quran is not Allah’s speech is a fabricator and an innovator, subject to the same judgment as others of his kind.

And whoever says that the Arabic Quran is not Allah’s speech, but rather that part of it is the speech of

---

## Page 6223

Allah and part of it is not Allah’s speech is a fabricator and an innovator, subject to the same judgment as others of his kind.

Whoever says that the Verse of the Throne, the verse concerning debt, “Say: He is Allah, the One,” and “May the hands of Abū Lahab perish, and may he perish!” all have one and the same meaning is a fabricator and an innovator, subject to the same judgment as others of his kind.

As for “declaring someone a disbeliever,” the correct position is that anyone from the community of Muhammad—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—who exercises independent judgment, intending to reach the truth, but errs is not to be declared a disbeliever. Rather, his error is forgiven. Whoever clearly understands what the Messenger brought, yet opposes the Messenger after guidance has become clear to him and follows a path other than that of the believers, is a disbeliever.

Whoever follows his own desires, falls short in seeking the truth, and speaks without knowledge is disobedient and sinful. He may be a flagrant sinner, and he may have good deeds that outweigh his misdeeds. Thus, the judgment of disbelief varies according to the individual’s circumstances. Not everyone who errs, introduces an innovation, is ignorant, or goes astray is a disbeliever—or even a flagrant sinner, or even disobedient. This is especially so in matters such as “the question of the Quran,” concerning which many leading figures of the various groups, known among people for their knowledge and religious commitment, have erred. Most of them seek an aspect of the truth and follow it, while another aspect escapes them and they fail to grasp it. Thus they know part of the truth while remaining ignorant of another part—indeed, even denying it.

From this their disagreement arose. Those who said that it is created held that

---

## Page 6224

speech occurs only through the speaker’s power and will, and that speech inseparably bound to the speaker’s essence is inconceivable. For if it is held to be a single meaning, this defies reason; the same applies if it is held to consist of beginningless sounds. They then supposed that whatever comes about through the Lord’s power and will must be separate from Him, and that whatever is separate from Him is created. For this reason, they denied that He comes, arrives, descends, or does other things mentioned in the Book and the Sunnah.

Others agreed with them on this principle they had introduced: that nothing dependent upon His will and power subsists in Him. Yet they held that speech which does not subsist in the speaker cannot be his speech. They therefore said that His speech subsists in Him.

Then “one group” considered beginningless sounds impossible, so they held that what was beginningless was the meaning. They then considered a plurality of beginningless meanings impossible, and held that it would entail the existence of an infinite number of meanings. They therefore said that it was a single meaning.

“Another group” considered it impossible for diverse meanings to be a single meaning. They also held that to say that the Lord did not utter the letters of the Quran, but instead created them in something other than Himself, was to agree with those who held that speech does not subsist in the speaker. For if they say that those letters arranged in sequence—as in the Arabic Quran—are Allah’s speech, it necessarily follows that His speech does not subsist in Him, but in something other than Him. If they say that they are not Allah’s speech, it necessarily follows that they are the speech of whatever they were created in. Thus, the Arabic speech would not be Allah’s speech, but the speech of whatever it was created in. And this

---

## Page 6225

is precisely what they condemned in those who said that the Quran is created. Those who said it was created said no more than this. Thus, they were bound to agree in substance with those who say that the Quran is created, even if they added a claim that has no basis in reality and contradicts both reason and revelation: the affirmation of a single meaning encompassing all the meanings of the Torah, the Gospel, and the Quran. Yet they said this only to escape positions they believed to be false. Their sole intention was to escape what they regarded as false, but they fell into positions whose implications likewise entail their falsity.

When this “second group” saw how these people responded, they said: “His speech consists of eternal, beginningless letters and sounds.” Others refuted them, saying: “Sounds are by their very nature mutually contrary, and two contraries cannot coexist. Yet the least that beginningless things require is that they coexist.” They also said to them: “Sounds necessarily entail movements, which in turn entail power and will. Thus, sounds can occur only through power and will, and whatever is such cannot be beginningless in its individual instances. The dispute, however, concerns whether it is beginningless in kind.”

They also said: “Sounds cannot, by their very nature, endure. Whatever cannot endure cannot be beginningless. Thus, sounds cannot be beginningless.”

“Others” said: “If that is so, then He speaks with letters and sounds that come into being through His will and power and subsist in His essence. But none of these can be beginningless, because things that come into being cannot be beginningless.” They believed that this position would save them from

---

## Page 6226

all the pitfalls into which others had fallen. There was nothing in this position for those opponents to object to except that something connected to the Lord’s will and power should subsist in His essence.

The Mu‘tazilah denied that any attributes subsist in Him, expressing this by saying that no accidents or things that come into being subsist in Him. Thus, they called the knowledge, power, and life that subsist in Him “accidents,” and the acts of creating, bestowing goodness, coming, arriving, and descending that subsist in Him “things that come into being.” They said to the early generations of the Muslim community, its imams, and the majority of its members:

“If you say that particular speech is inseparable from Him, then you have said that accidents subsist in Him. If you say that He speaks by His choice and power, then you have said that things that come into being subsist in Him.”

These people replied:

“The Mu‘tazilah’s assertion that these things do not subsist in Him is false, contrary to the Book, the Sunnah, and the consensus of the early generations of the Muslim community. It also contradicts the plain dictates of reason, for affirming one who knows without knowledge, one who is powerful without power, and one who is living without life is impossible according to the plain dictates of reason. Likewise, affirming a creator who does not create, one who is just without justice, an agent in whom no action subsists, and a Lord who cannot Himself act, but is instead like an inanimate object, denies Him the attributes of perfection—just as affirming a Lord who neither knows nor has power denies Him the attributes of perfection.”

---

## Page 6227

These people said:

“If we say that He spoke—uttering speech with both its letters and its meanings—by His will and power, we avoid these pitfalls without affirming anything objectionable according to either revelation or reason.”

The “seventh group” replied:

“But you have made Him incapable of speech in eternity past, bereft of perfection. Your position necessarily invites the following objection: if He did not speak from eternity past to eternity future, and then spoke, that would be a new occurrence requiring a newly occurring cause. The same argument would apply to that occurrence as to the first, necessarily entailing an infinite regress of events. If that is impossible, your position is invalid. If it is possible, then say that He has always spoken whenever He wills, as the imams of the Sunnah and the great majority of hadith scholars have said. You would then be describing your Lord as possessing the attributes of perfection eternally, without beginning or end.”

They added:

“This position is better than all the others, besides agreeing with reason and authentic transmitted evidence.”

Those others replied:

“This entails events with no beginning, which is impossible.”

The former answered:

“This is an innovated assertion that you have merely taken from the Mu‘tazilah. Neither the Book nor the Sunnah teaches it; none of the early generations of the Muslim community or its imams asserted it; nor does reason establish it. Rather, reason establishes its opposite.

“Those among the Mu‘tazilah who advanced this position, and their followers among the Karrāmiyyah and Ash‘ariyyah, thought that through it they could establish that the world came into being. They based this on the premise that bodies cannot be devoid of accidents that come into being, and that whatever cannot be devoid of things that come into being is

---

## Page 6228

brought into being. This very position gave the “eternalist philosophers,” who hold that the world has always existed, leverage against them. For the position they adopted and claimed necessarily entailed that the world came into being actually contradicts the world’s coming into being; indeed, it contradicts establishing the existence of the Maker. They thus sought to defend Islam by means incompatible with the religion of Islam. This is why the early generations so frequently condemned such reasoning: it is the foundation of the “condemned speculative theology” censured by the early generations of the Muslim community and its imams.

“This is because anything whose existence and nonexistence are both possible can exist only through a cause that necessarily entails its existence. If it could exist without such a cause, created things—whose existence and nonexistence are both possible—could have come into existence without an agent. Contingent things therefore require a necessarily existent being through whom they come to exist. When the fully sufficient cause exists, their existence and nonexistence are no longer both possible; rather, their existence becomes inevitable. For whatever Allah wills comes to pass, and whatever He does not will does not come to pass. When the Lord wills something, it cannot fail to exist; rather, it must exist by the will of the Lord Most High, which necessarily entails His power.”

They said:

“If that is so, then consider an event whose existence and nonexistence are both possible. If it comes into being without a newly occurring cause, while bearing the same relation to every moment in time, and while all events and moments bear the same relation to the Lord’s will and power, it follows that certain events are singled out to occur, and certain

---

## Page 6229

times are singled out for events to occur in them, without a determining factor that necessitates this and without a newly occurring cause that necessitates their occurrence.

“Besides being patently invalid according to sound reason, this also invalidates the argument they used to establish the Maker’s existence. Events must therefore have a newly occurring cause; hence every event is preceded by another event.

“This entails that, if Allah speaks by His will and power, it is possible that He has always spoken by His will and power. He cannot have begun to speak after never having spoken at all, for that would entail an event coming into being without a newly occurring cause, which is impossible. It would also entail His newly acquiring attributes of perfection that He could have possessed from eternity, which is likewise impossible. This is because the attributes of perfection that the Lord can possess cannot depend upon anything other than Him. Otherwise, that other would be the one who bestows attributes of perfection upon Him, and whoever bestows attributes of perfection upon another is more entitled to be the Lord Most High. Yet the Lord of the worlds—the Creator of everything besides Him, upon which He bestows attributes of perfection—cannot have anyone else as His lord in any respect. Glorified and exalted is He above that. Thus, the attribute of speaking whenever He wills must belong to Him eternally, without beginning or end.”

These people said:

“This principle invalidates the argument of the eternalist philosophers that

---

## Page 6230

they used to establish the eternity of the world, and which you, O Muʿtazilah, and your followers among the speculative theologians who maintain that a perpetual succession of events is impossible, were unable to answer. For their argument is binding upon you according to your own principles: you posited the existence of a being who does not speak by His will and power and does nothing. Indeed, you held that, in eternity without beginning, no speech or action could possibly proceed from Him.

They said: ‘If we posit the existence of such a being, and that He continues indefinitely without speaking or doing anything, but then speaks and acts, there must be a cause that necessitated the occurrence of this speech and action—whether the emergence of power, will, knowledge, or some other cause. But if His state throughout eternity to come is assumed to be just as it was throughout eternity past, then no speech, action, or anything else can arise anew in Him.’

This, then, is the philosophers’ argument against you, and you have answered them only through obstinate denial or by turning the argument back on them.

‘Obstinate denial’ consists in your claim that events occur without any newly occurring cause. Indeed, you have made the eternal power or will itself single out one of two identical alternatives rather than the other, without any cause whatsoever, even though its relation to all identical alternatives is the same. Besides being self-evidently invalid, this closes off your route to ‘establishing the Maker’s existence.’ For that argument rests on the principles that events must have an originator, that whatever is determined in a particular way must have a determining factor, and that one alternative’s prevailing over another must have a factor that makes it prevail—when that determining factor or the factor that makes one alternative prevail is itself contingent or newly originated.

As for ‘turning the argument back on them,’ this is your statement that this difficulty is binding upon the philosophers just as it is

---

## Page 6231

binding upon us. For if events cannot arise from an eternal, fully sufficient cause—and you recognize nothing but an eternal, fully sufficient cause—it follows that events have no originator.

As for us, if we follow the path of the early generations of this community and its leading scholars, we say to these philosophers:

Rather, Allah created the heavens and the earth in six days, as the messengers reported. They came into being through causes that had arisen before that. If we say that He has always spoken whenever He wills—and that

“His command, when He wills a thing, is only to say to it, ‘Be,’ and it is”—

then whatever comes into being does so through whatever of His speech He wills to utter, especially if an analogous position is held regarding His will—glorified and exalted is He.

We can also offer the philosophers another answer, combining our position with yours. We say to them: Is the existence of a succession of events without a beginning possible or impossible?

If you say it is impossible, you must acknowledge that the world came into being, and it then becomes possible that the position of the Karrāmiyyah and others like them is correct.

If you say it is possible, the reply is: Then it is possible that this world came into being through a cause that arose before it, and likewise that this cause arose through another, and so on without end.

These matters are discussed at length elsewhere. The “purpose here” is to draw attention to the fact that these are subtle and difficult matters

---

## Page 6232

that have caused division and disagreement within the community. When a person strives to follow the Messenger and believe what he brought, but errs concerning subtle matters that perplex even intelligent believers, Allah forgives his errors, in fulfilment of His words:

“Our Lord, do not take us to task if we forget or make a mistake.”

It is established in the Sahīh that Allah said: “I have done so.”

As for the statement:

“And whoever says, ‘Allah’s speech is free of the marks of temporal origination, since sound and letters necessarily originate in time; just as His essence is exalted above the marks of createdness, so too is His true speech.’”

He should be told: There is no disagreement among Muslims—indeed, among the adherents of all religions and other rational people—that the Creator is free of the marks of temporal origination. His beginninglessness is self-evident, so there can be no proof that He came into being. A “mark” means a sign or proof.

However, the majority of people dispute your position concerning sound and letters. None of the various groups has agreed with the Kullābiyyah on their position: neither the Jahmiyyah, the Muʿtazilah, the Dirāriyyah, the Najjāriyyah, the Karrāmiyyah, nor the Sālimiyyah; neither the majority of the Murjiʾah and the Shia, nor the majority of the scholars of hadith, jurisprudence and Sufism; nor the philosophers—whether theists or naturalists, in all their different varieties.

Among their opponents are those who say that letters originate and are created in a locus separate from Allah, just as the Kullābiyyah themselves say. But these opponents say: “This is Allah’s speech; Allah has no

## Page 6233

speech other than this, just as the Muslims unanimously agree that this is Allah’s speech. Indeed, all nations agree that speech can only be understood in this way.”

If you say, “We call both this and that Allah’s speech, both literally, with the same expression bearing different meanings,” you are told:

and your leading scholars have acknowledged that most schools are committed to this position.”

## Page 6235

As for the statement:

“Just as His essence must be declared free of the characteristics of created beings, so too must His true speech.”

This is akin to the rhymed prose of soothsayers, which establishes no truth and refutes no falsehood. Would you say that every one of His words or other attributes possesses every attribute with which the Lord is described?

When it is said that the Lord, exalted is He, is God, powerful, the Creator, and worshipped, must any of His words or attributes therefore be God, powerful, a creator, and worshipped?

This statement resembles that of the Christians who say:

“Just as the hypostasis of existence is God, so too are those of the Word and the Spirit.”

Thus they ascribe to the attributes the divinity they ascribe to the essence. Now the Lord, exalted is He, has speech that subsists in a locus and cannot exist apart from it, for speech must have a locus without which it cannot exist. Must the Lord therefore depend on a locus in which to subsist, just as speech does?

His speech must, however, be declared free of every deficiency and flaw, for He is worthy of perfection in His essence, attributes, and actions. It is impossible for Him to lack the attributes of perfection—life, knowledge, power, speech, and other such attributes—when some of His creatures possess them. The One described by these attributes, whose existence is necessary and who is eternal and without beginning, has a greater right to the attributes of perfection than created beings do. Every perfection possessed by a created being comes from the Creator, who bestowed it upon that being and granted it. The One who bestows and grants perfection is Himself more entitled to it and more worthy of it.

---

## Page 6236

This is something that every group expresses in its own terminology. Even the philosophers say:

“Every perfection possessed by an effect derives from the perfection of its cause.”

It is well known that a created being, brought into existence after having been nothing, possesses absolutely nothing of itself. Rather, everything it possesses comes from its Creator, glorified and exalted is He.

As for his statement:

“Know that both the letter articulated by the tongue and the letter inscribed by the fingers are bound by time, which governs them. The Lord speaks before time, and His speech is exalted above being encompassed by the vicissitudes of time.”

He is already aware that his opponents dispute this, yet he offers nothing beyond a bare assertion. He knows that most rational people regard the very notion asserted as self-evidently false, and that the argument for it consists of premises disputed by the majority of rational people. Ultimately, these lead back to premises they received from their Muʿtazilite teachers, for the Kullābiyyah and the Ashʿariyyah took the premises and substance of this argument from them. Their position in this regard is well known.

As for his statement, “The Lord speaks before time”: if he means that He, glorified and exalted is He, existed before the heavens and the earth, before night and day, and before all created things, then this is true. But what grounds does he have for claiming that everything He has said to His servants, and will say to them on the Day of Resurrection, must have existed before all created things?

And what grounds does he have for claiming that, before creating the world, He was calling out to Moses, saying to him:

“Indeed, I am Allah. There is no deity except Me, so worship Me and establish prayer to remember Me”?

---

## Page 6237

But if he means that He, glorified and exalted is He, is before anything described as “before,” this is impossible, for He, glorified is He, is Himself described as the First, before everything. If he means that time is the measure of action and motion, and that this is impossible in eternity past, he already knows that the leading authorities of religions and schools of thought dispute this with him, despite the agreement of the religious communities that Allah created the heavens and the earth in six days.

As for his statement:

“Letters and sounds are two means of expressing the meaning subsisting in Allah’s essence, just as a person expresses a request within himself—sometimes with his fingers, sometimes with his tongue, and sometimes with his head—when asking someone to leave or to come. This is the true doctrine and the sound course.”

The response to him is:

There are several objections to this.

The first is to ask: What is this meaning subsisting in the essence? Is it one single meaning, as al-Ash'arī says, which, according to him, is what the Torah, the Gospel, and the Quran signify, what the Verse of the Throne and the verse on debt signify, and what Sūrat al-Ikhlās and Sūrat al-Kawthar signify? Or does it consist of multiple meanings?

If he adopts the first position, its falsity is self-evident. He should then be told: Assenting to something presupposes conceiving it. We cannot conceive of this, so explain its meaning to us; then discuss the proof for its existence.

If he says, “It is analogous to the meanings existing within us,” this statement would be false even if we set aside whatever likening and comparison of Allah to creation it might entail. For the meanings within us are many and varied. As for a single meaning that is a command to do everything commanded and a statement about everything spoken of, this is inconceivable.

---

## Page 6238

Second: It may be said: Grant that it is conceivable. What is the evidence for its existence? And what is the evidence that it has no beginning?

Third: It may be asked: When you say, “Sound and letters express it,” do you mean the sounds heard from reciters or the letters present in recitation and written copies of the Quran, or do you mean letters and sounds other than these?

If you mean the first, this is false for several reasons:

First: Anyone proficient in recitation would express what is within Allah without Allah having expressed what is within Himself. The created being would thus be more capable than the Creator.

Second: Many reciters—or most of them—do not understand most of the meanings of the Quran. Expressing what is within oneself presupposes knowing it. How, then, can someone who does not understand all the meanings of the Quran—the speech of Allah—express those meanings?

Third: People understand the meanings of the Quran only through its words signifying those meanings. When they hear its words and reflect upon it, the wording guides them to the meanings. Someone who infers from the wording the meaning intended by the speaker cannot himself be the one expressing that meaning in those words, for someone who expresses a meaning in words first knows the meaning

---

## Page 6239

then conveys it to others in words. With the Quran, people are in precisely the opposite position; they therefore cannot be the ones expressing those meanings through it.

Fourth: Each of them knows that he learned the Arabic Quran from someone else, and that his role is only to memorize, convey, and recite it. Indeed, he knows that if he memorizes the speeches of orators and the poetry of poets, he is not thereby the one expressing what is within them through those words. Rather, the words remain theirs; he has merely memorized, recited, and conveyed them. How much more so with the speech of the Lord of all worlds!

Fifth: Everyone knows with immediate certainty that the Arabic Quran itself existed before any of the reciters came into being, and that people received it only from Muhammad—may Allah’s blessings and abundant peace be upon him, his family, and his Companions. In short, the proofs that this view is false are too numerous to enumerate.

If you say: “Rather, the letters and sounds used to express the meanings Allah intended are letters and sounds that existed before the reciters came into being; each reciter, however, memorized that Arabic arrangement of words which existed before him,” you are told: “Then there were letters and sounds other than these sounds heard from reciters and other than the ink written in copies of the Quran, and this is

---

## Page 6240

the truth on which all creation agrees.”

Thus, the claim that there is nothing but the meaning subsisting in His Essence or these letters and sounds is false. He is then asked: “Are those letters and sounds part of the speech that Allah Himself spoke, or are they created things that He created in something other than Himself?”

If you say, “They are part of Allah’s speech,” you must accept what you were trying to evade, since you have acknowledged that Allah has speech consisting of letters and sounds, as the majority of Muslims affirm. If you say, “They are not Allah’s speech,” then the same applies all the more to these. This Quran would therefore not be Allah’s speech—a conclusion whose falsehood is necessarily known in the religion of Islam.

As for his statement, “Whoever says, ‘My utterance is the very speech of Allah,’ has cast off the bonds of reason and drowned in a sea of blindness and ignorance,” the response is:

The statement, “My utterance is the very speech of Allah,” is ambiguous. Lafz (utterance) is originally the verbal noun of lafaza–yalfizu (to utter), just as tilāwah and qirā’ah (recitation) are originally the verbal nouns of talā–yatlū and qara’a–yaqra’u (to recite). Yet the terms “utterance” and “recitation” are also used to refer to the actual speech uttered or recited.

When people say, “An utterance indicates a meaning,” they do not mean the act of uttering, but rather what is uttered. Likewise, when they say to someone whom they have heard speaking, “These are fine expressions,” they mean what he utters. As Allah Most High says: “He utters no

---

## Page 6241

word without a vigilant observer standing ready.” The word lafz may refer to the act itself, or it may refer to the actual words uttered by the speaker. This is like the word “Quran,” which may denote the verbal noun—recitation—or the speech being recited.

Allah Most High says:

“It is for Us to gather it and to recite it. So when We have recited it, follow its recitation.”

Here, qur’ān is a verbal noun, as indicated by Ibn ‘Abbās’s explanation of the verse: “It is for Us to gather it in your heart, then for you to recite it with your tongue. When Gabriel recites it, listen to his recitation. Then it is for Us to explain it.”

The word “Quran” may also refer to the actual speech being recited, as when He says:

“When the Quran is recited, listen to it and remain silent.”

And:

“Indeed, this Quran guides to what is most upright.”

Allah Most High also says:

“Had We sent down this Quran upon a mountain, you would have seen it humbled and split apart from fear of Allah.”

And He says:

“Say: If mankind and the jinn came together to produce the like of this Quran, they could not produce its like.”

There are many similar examples.

This being so, when someone says, “My utterance is the very speech of Allah,” if he means the act of uttering, he is mistaken. His actual movements are not Allah’s speech, and no one who understands what he is saying would claim this. But if he means the “latter” sense, then his meaning is that this Quran which he recites is the very speech of Allah. This is what people mean when they say: “What is recited by

---

## Page 6242

the reciters is the very speech of Allah; what we hear from the reciters is the very speech of Allah; and what is recited in prayer is the very speech of Allah.” No one intends thereby to identify people’s movements with His speech itself.

Moreover, whoever says this agrees with the words of Allah Most High:

“If any of the polytheists seeks your protection, grant him protection so that he may hear the speech of Allah.”

Indeed, it is necessarily known as part of the religion of Islam that what Muslims recite and write in their copies of the Quran is the speech of Allah, not the speech of anyone else. Sometimes it is heard directly from Him, as Moses son of ‘Imrān heard it; at other times, it is heard from those who receive it from Him, as the Companions heard it from the Messenger. Thus, what we hear is Allah’s speech, received from Him and heard from the one conveying it on His behalf.

Allah Most High says:

“This Quran has been revealed to me so that I may warn you with it and whoever it reaches.”

And He says:

“O Messenger, convey what has been sent down to you from your Lord. If you do not, you will not have conveyed His message.”

And He says:

“So that He may know that they have conveyed the messages of their Lord.”

People know that speech belongs to the one who first uttered it, issuing its commands and relating its reports—not to someone who merely conveys and delivers it from another. People recite the Quran, but it is not their own speech; rather, it is speech they recite through their own actions and voices. If, when people narrate, convey and recite the speech of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, or of anyone else, it remains the speech of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, or of the other speakers who uttered it—and the Prophet

---

## Page 6243

may Allah bless him and grant him peace, uttered its wording, arrangement, and meaning, speaking it in letters and sounds, even though the narrators’ voices are not the voice of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace—then the Quran, when people recite and convey it through their voices and actions, has all the more right to be called the speech of Allah, even though they have not heard it from Allah, but from created beings.

It should also be understood that the statement of Allah, His Messenger, and the believers, “This is the speech of Allah,” is true. Indeed, people’s statement concerning speech conveyed from created beings, “This is so-and-so’s speech,” is likewise true, as everyone agrees.

However, confusion arose among many of those given to hair-splitting. They failed to distinguish between hearing speech from the one who uttered it and hearing it from someone else. Thus, they thought that His saying:

“Grant him protection so that he may hear the speech of Allah”

meant hearing Allah’s speech in the same way that Moses heard it.

One group therefore said: “What is heard is the voices of Allah’s servants. Allah’s speech is not the voices of His servants, so what is heard cannot be Allah’s speech.”

Another group said: “Rather, this is Allah’s speech, and this is created; therefore, Allah’s speech is created.”

Yet another group said: “Rather, this is Allah’s speech, and Allah’s speech is uncreated; therefore, this is uncreated.”

---

## Page 6244

And this is true when they state it in general terms. Some of them, however, said: “This is my utterance, my recitation, or my voice; therefore, my utterance, my recitation, or my voice is uncreated.” Thus they went astray, just as others had. Had they been rightly guided, they would have known that when we say, “This is Allah’s speech,” we are not referring to what distinguishes one reciter from another. For it is known that what is heard from every reciter is Allah’s speech, while it is also known that one reciter’s voice is not another’s. What is heard is therefore one and the same insofar as it is Allah’s speech, but differs insofar as the reciters’ voices differ. It is Allah’s speech by virtue of the reality that remains the same, not by virtue of the differing circumstances of the reciters.

This is because what is intended by speech is its wording and meaning, and its wording consists of the recited letters in their ordered arrangement. Even if letters are segmented sounds, or the endpoints of segmented sounds, they constitute speech by virtue of their particular form of segmentation and composition, not by virtue of the vocal material shared by all who produce sounds. Thus, whatever speech contains of eloquence, clarity, fine composition and arrangement, perfection of meaning, and other such qualities belongs to the one who spoke its wording and meaning; it does not belong merely to the qualities of the person who conveyed and delivered it.

As for the statement: “Anyone who says that the doctrine of Jahm ibn Safwān is the doctrine of al-Ashʿarī, or is close to it, or identical to it, is ignorant of the doctrines of both groups; for the Jahmiyyah

---

## Page 6245

affirm the createdness of the Quran and of all . . . (1) Al-Ashʿarī, however, maintains that the Quran is eternal and that human speech is created by the Most Merciful. Thus, each of the three doctrines is clear to the discerning reader.”

The response is:

There is no doubt that the position of Ibn Kullāb, al-Ashʿarī, and others who affirm the divine attributes is not the position of the Jahmiyyah, nor even that of the Muʿtazilah. Indeed, they have written works refuting the Jahmiyyah and the Muʿtazilah and explaining the error of those who deny these attributes. Sometimes they declare the Jahmiyyah and the Muʿtazilah unbelievers, and sometimes they declare them misguided.

This is especially so since Jahm went further than anyone in denying the attributes—and even the Most Beautiful Names. His position is of the same kind as that of the esoteric Qarmatians. It is even reported that he would not call Allah “a thing,” or use any other designation also applied to created beings, because he claimed that this constituted an inadmissible likening of Allah to His creation. This is the position of the esoteric Qarmatians. It is also related that he would describe Him only as “possessing power and acting,” because, in his view, the servant has neither power nor agency; he was, after all, the foremost proponent of determinism.

His position on faith is worse than that of the Murjiʾah, for he regards faith as nothing more than the heart’s assent. Ibn Kullāb—the leading authority of the Ashʿariyyah—disagrees more strongly with Jahm and is closer to the early generations

> **Footnotes:**
> (1) Blank in the original.

---

## Page 6246

than al-Ashʿarī himself. Al-Ashʿarī, in turn, is closer to the early generations than Judge Abū Bakr al-Bāqillānī.

Judge Abū Bakr and others like him are closer to the early generations than Abū al-Maʿālī and his followers, for the latter denied attributes such as rising over the Throne, the Face, and the two Hands. They then differed over whether to interpret them figuratively or entrust them to Allah, adopting two positions or approaches. Abū al-Maʿālī’s earlier position was to interpret them figuratively, as he stated in al-Irshād. His later position was to prohibit such interpretation, as he stated in al-Risālah al-Nizāmiyyah, citing the consensus of the early generations as evidence that figurative interpretation is neither permissible nor obligatory.

As for al-Ashʿarī himself and the leading authorities among his followers, their position remained consistent in affirming the attributes known through transmitted revelation and refuting those who interpreted them figuratively—for example, those who say that “rose over” means “took control.” This is stated in all his books, including al-Mūjaz al-Kabīr, al-Maqālāt al-Saghīrah and al-Maqālāt al-Kabīrah, al-Ibānah, and others. This is also how everyone else reported his position. Even later scholars, such as al-Rāzī and al-Āmidī, report that he affirmed the attributes known through transmitted revelation; they do not attribute two positions on this matter to him.

Whoever claims that al-Ashʿarī denied these attributes and held two positions regarding their figurative interpretation has falsely attributed this to him. Rather, this was the approach of some of his later followers, such as Abū al-Maʿālī and others like him, who introduced elements of Muʿtazilī doctrine into his school.

---

## Page 6247

And al-Ashʿarī was afflicted by two groups: one that hated him and another that loved him. Both falsely attributed things to him, saying that he wrote these books only to conceal his true beliefs and outwardly profess agreement with the people of hadith and Sunnah, whether Hanbalīs or others. This is a false allegation against the man. No private position of his has been found that contradicts the positions he publicly professed, nor has anyone among his closest followers or anyone else transmitted from him anything that contradicts these positions recorded in his writings. The claim that he concealed beliefs contrary to those he professed is therefore rejected on both religious and rational grounds. Indeed, anyone who carefully considers his statements on this subject in various places will know with certainty that he defended what he publicly professed.

However, those who love him yet disagree with his affirmation of the attributes known through transmitted revelation seek to deny that he held this position, lest it be said that they have contradicted him—even though, in the positions they adopted that accord with the Sunnah, they followed his argument, which they continually invoke and on which they rely.

The other group denied that he held this position because they saw those affiliated with him professing only its opposite, and because they accused him of concealing his true beliefs. But this was not the case. Rather, he defended the well-known positions of the people of the Sunnah on which the Muʿtazilah opposed them, such as seeing Allah, divine speech, the affirmation of the attributes, and similar matters. His knowledge of speculative theology, however, was detailed, whereas his knowledge of the Sunnah was general. Consequently, he agreed with the Muʿtazilah on some of their foundational principles, which had led them to adopt positions contrary to the Sunnah, and he believed that he could reconcile those principles with championing

---

## Page 6248

the Sunnah, as he did regarding seeing Allah, divine speech, the attributes known through transmitted revelation, and other matters.

His opponents among the people of the Sunnah and hadith, the Muʿtazilah, and the philosophers say that he is inconsistent: the positions in which he agrees with the Muʿtazilah contradict those in which he agrees with the people of the Sunnah. Likewise, the Muʿtazilah are inconsistent in their defence of Islam, for they have based many of their arguments on principles that contradict much of the religion of Islam.

Indeed, most of al-Ashʿarī’s opponents, both those who affirm the attributes and those who deny them, say that his positions on seeing Allah and divine speech are self-evidently false to reason. Hence his followers say that no other group agrees with their position on “the question of seeing Allah and divine speech.”

Since his discourse contains a mixture of both positions, some have come to say that it contains an element of Jahmism. Anyone who says that his position is identical to Jahm’s has spoken falsely; and anyone who says that it contains nothing of Jahm’s position has also spoken falsely. Allah loves speech grounded in knowledge and justice, giving everyone their due, and according people their proper standing.

Jahm’s position is the absolute denial of Allah’s attributes, exalted is He. This is the essence of the position held by the esoteric Qarmatians and deviant adherents of philosophy, such as al-Fārābī and Ibn Sīnā. As for the more moderate philosophers, such as Abū al-Barakāt, author of al-Muʿtabar, and Ibn Rushd al-Hafīd, their positions contain affirmations that make them better than Jahm’s position, for they are well known for affirming the names

---

## Page 6249

—the Most Beautiful Names—and affirming what the attributes entail. Thus, on the whole, their position is better than Jahm’s, while the position of Dirār ibn ‘Amr al-Kūfī is better than theirs.

As for Ibn Kullāb, al-Qalānisī and al-Ash‘arī, they do not belong to this category. Rather, they are known as affirmers of the attributes and renowned for their doctrine of affirmation. Their positions, however, contain elements of Jahmī principles on account of which, people say, they fall into inconsistency, combine opposites and make unintelligible assertions. They therefore regard them as wavering between the two sides, belonging to neither. This explains why some identify elements of Jahmī doctrine in their positions. Similarly, the imams—such as Ahmad and others—used to say:

The Jahmiyyah have split into “three groups”: one group says that the Quran is created; another suspends judgment, saying neither that it is created nor that it is uncreated; and another says that our utterances of the Quran are created.

It is well known that they meant only their division over “the question of the Quran” specifically. Otherwise, many of these people affirm the attributes, seeing Allah, and His rising over the Throne. They classified a person as a Jahmī in certain matters—meaning that he agreed with the Jahmiyyah on those matters—to expose the weakness of his position, not to say that he was like the Jahmiyyah or that the same ruling applied to him as to them. No one who understands what he is saying would make such a claim.

Hence, Ahmad’s statements generally classify those who say that their utterances of the Quran are created as Jahmīs; he hardly ever declares them unbelievers without qualification, as he does those who say that the Quran is created. This view has been attributed to several people known for their adherence to the Sunnah and hadith, such as al-Husayn al-Karābīsī and Nu‘aym

---

## Page 6250

ibn Hammād al-Khuzā‘ī, al-Buwaytī and al-Hārith al-Muhāsibī. Some have also attributed this view to al-Bukhārī.

The view that “the utterance is uncreated” has been attributed to Muhammad ibn Yahyā al-Dhuhlī and Abū Hātim al-Rāzī. Some even attribute it to Abū Zur‘ah as well, saying that he and Abū Hātim shunned al-Bukhārī when Muhammad ibn Yahyā al-Dhuhlī shunned him. The account of this is well known. After Ahmad’s death, disputes arose over this among some of his followers, and between them and groups outside their circle. The inhabitants of the frontier region, together with Muhammad ibn Dāwūd al-Missīsī, Abū Dāwūd’s teacher, held this view.

When Sālih ibn Ahmad was appointed judge of the frontier region, Abū Bakr al-Marwadhī asked him to make “Abū Tālib’s question” known to its inhabitants, since Sālih and ‘Abd Allāh, Ahmad’s two sons, al-Marwadhī, Fawrān and others had witnessed it. Al-Marwadhī wrote a book refuting those who said, “My utterance of the Quran is uncreated.” He also wrote concerning this to the scholars of Mecca, Medina, Kufa, Basra, Khurasan and elsewhere, and they agreed with him. Abū Bakr al-Khallāl mentioned this in his Kitāb al-Sunnah and discussed it at length.

Nevertheless, groups who identify themselves with the Sunnah and with following Ahmad—such as Abū ‘Abd Allāh ibn Mandah, Abū Nasr al-Sijzī and Abū Ismā‘īl al-Ansārī

---

## Page 6251

, Abū al-‘Alā’ al-Hamdānī and others—say: “Our utterance of the Quran is uncreated.” They maintain that this is Ahmad’s position. They reject—or some of them reject—the report transmitted by Abū Tālib, claiming that it was fabricated and attributed to Ahmad, or that he retracted that position, as Abū Nasr al-Sijzī mentioned in his well-known book al-Ibānah.

The matter is not as they claim. Those who transmitted this from Ahmad were the most knowledgeable about him, the closest to him, and the most truthful in reporting from him. The people of Khurasan, however, did not know Ahmad’s statements as well as the people of Iraq, who were closer to him.

The controversy over “utterance” was most intense in Khurasan, where partisan hostility was directed against al-Bukhārī despite his eminence and standing as an imam. Although those who opposed him were also eminent imams, al-Bukhārī—may Allah be pleased with him—was among the most distinguished of men. If their intentions were good, and both he and they exercised their best judgment, Allah rewards him and them for their good intentions and their efforts. Even if he or they committed some error or mistake, Allah forgives them all.

Yet some ignorant people do not know how events unfolded. Indeed, I saw the following in the handwriting of a shaykh possessed of knowledge and religious devotion: “Al-Bukhārī died in the village of Khartank. Ahmad then sent word to the villagers, instructing them not to offer the funeral prayer over him because of his position on the ‘question of utterance.’”

This is one of the most blatant lies about Ahmad and al-Bukhārī, and whoever fabricated it knew nothing of their circumstances. For al-Bukhārī—may Allah be pleased with him—died in the year fifty-six, having outlived Ahmad by fifteen

---

## Page 6252

years, for Ahmad died in the year forty-one. Ahmad held al-Bukhārī in honour and esteem. As for the esteem in which al-Bukhārī and others like him held Ahmad, this is too well known to need mentioning. In his book on the creation of actions, al-Bukhārī stated that neither group understood Ahmad’s words.

Among the other group, who profess adherence to the Sunnah and affiliation with Ahmad’s followers, are Abū Nu‘aym al-Asbahānī, Abū Bakr al-Bayhaqī, and others who say that they follow Ahmad and that their position on the “question of utterance” agrees with his. A dispute arose between Ibn Mandah and Abū Nu‘aym over this, leading Abū Nu‘aym to write his Refutation of the Hurūfiyyah Hulūliyyah, while Abū ‘Abd Allāh wrote his Refutation of the Lafziyyah.

Those who champion the Sunnah among the scholars of speculative theology and jurisprudence—such as al-Ash‘arī, Judge Abū Bakr ibn al-Tayyib, Judge Abū Ya‘lā, and others—agree with Ahmad in censuring both groups: those who say, “My utterance of the Quran is created,” and those who say, “My utterance of the Quran is uncreated.” They maintain, however, that the reason for this disapproval is that the Quran is not “uttered,” because lafz (utterance) means casting or throwing.

Some of these deny that Allah speaks with a voice, while others affirm it. Indeed, some say that the sound heard is the eternal sound. Nevertheless, they censure anyone who says, “My utterance of the Quran is uncreated,” because they suppose that the disapproval

---

## Page 6253

in this matter stems from its connotations of casting and throwing. But the matter is not as they supposed.

Imam Ahmad and the other imams did not object to someone saying, “My utterance of the Quran is created,” or “uncreated,” because “utterance” means casting. Had that been the case, they would have objected only to derivatives of the verb “to utter.” Yet that was not so. Rather, they objected to anyone saying, “Recitation and reading are created,” and to anyone saying, “My recitation and reading are uncreated,” even though Muslims may legitimately say, “I read the Quran and recited it.”

Moreover, one may say, “I uttered the words,” or “I spoke them,” as Allah, Exalted is He, says:

“Not a word does he utter without a watchful observer ready beside him.”

However, Imam Ahmad and the other imams of the Sunnah said: “Whoever says, ‘My utterance of the Quran and my recitation or reading are created,’ is a Jahmī. Whoever says that it is uncreated is an innovator.”

This is because “utterance,” “recitation,” and “reading” may denote the verbal nouns of the verbs “to utter,” “to read,” and “to recite.” What the verbal noun denotes is the servant’s action and movements, which are not eternal, according to the agreement of the early generations of the Muslim community and its imams. Even the Qadariyyah, who say that people’s actions are uncreated, say that this is not eternal. They also say that it is created by Allah.

The early generations and the imams—such as Hammād ibn Zayd, al-Mu‘tamir ibn Sulaymān, Yahyā ibn Sa‘īd al-Qattān, Ahmad ibn Hanbal, and others—censured those who said that

---

## Page 6254

people’s words and actions are uncreated. Yahyā ibn Sa‘īd said:

“I have always heard our companions say that people’s actions are created.”

Some of these scholars said:

“Whoever says that this is uncreated is like someone who says that Allah’s heaven and earth are uncreated.”

“Recitation,” “reading,” and “utterance” may also mean the Quran itself, which Allah sent down to His Prophet Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him, and which is Allah’s speech. Whoever says that Allah’s speech, which He sent down to His Prophet, is created is a Jahmī. Hence Ahmad and others among the early generations said:

“The Quran is Allah’s speech and is uncreated, however it is conveyed.”

None of the early generations or the imams said that people’s voices when reciting the Quran are uncreated or eternal. Nor did any of them say that the ink with which the Quran is written is eternal or uncreated. Whoever says that any of people’s voices, actions, movements, or ink is eternal or uncreated is therefore a misguided innovator who contradicts the consensus of the early generations and the imams. Ahmad ibn Hanbal declared even those whose position was less objectionable than theirs to be innovators, and instructed that they be shunned if they did not abandon their innovation.

People have fallen into great confusion over “the question of the Quran,” to the point that some have said, “The question of divine speech has bewildered human minds.” Most of them have in view one aspect of

---

## Page 6255

the truth, while another aspect escapes them. The statements of the imams are among the strongest—those of Ahmad ibn Hanbal, the Muslim imams who preceded him among the Companions and those who followed them in righteousness, and all the other imams held in lasting esteem within the Muslim community:

Such as Sa‘īd ibn al-Musayyib, ‘Alī ibn al-Husayn, ‘Alqama, al-Aswad, al-Hasan al-Basrī, Ibn Sīrīn, and other Successors; Mālik, al-Thawrī, al-Awzā‘ī, al-Layth ibn Sa‘d, Hammād ibn Zayd, Hammād ibn Salama, Abū Hanīfa, Ibn Abī Laylā, Sharīk, and their peers among the Successors of the Successors; and al-Shāfi‘ī, Ahmad ibn Hanbal, Ishāq ibn Ibrāhīm, Abū ‘Ubayd, and their peers in the generation following the Successors of the Successors.

These are the imams of the people of the three generations included in the praise of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, when he said:

“The best generation is the generation among whom I was sent, then those who follow them, then those who follow them.”

Whoever reflects on the statements of the Muslim imams and others on this subject will find them to be the strongest statements, in agreement with clear reason and sound transmitted evidence. This general point cannot be elaborated here; it has already been explained at length elsewhere. It has also been shown that the “blameworthy discourse” censured by the early generations is false discourse that contradicts sound transmitted evidence and clear reason; and that matters established by conclusive proofs can never conflict or contradict one another. Thus, two proofs that yield certainty can never conflict, whether both are based on reason

---

## Page 6256

or on transmitted revelation, or one on reason and the other on transmitted revelation. Whoever supposes that they conflict is mistaken, because he believes one of them to yield certainty when it does not—especially when neither yields certainty.

Much of people’s disagreement on this subject and others consists of “differences reflecting diversity”: one person intends something true in what he affirms, while another intends something true in what he refutes, and both are speaking truthfully. Yet they imagine that there is a substantive disagreement between them when there is not. Much dispute concerns the use of expressions rather than the meanings apprehended by reason. Those with the soundest approach use expressions consistent with those of revelation and intend sound meanings that accord with revelation and reason. . . . (1).

The fundamental source of disagreement among Muslims on this subject is that the speculative theologians—the Jahmiyya, the Mu‘tazila, and their followers—adopted a method of proving that the world had a beginning and that the Creator exists which was an innovation in religion and rationally incoherent. They made this method obligatory, claiming that the Creator could be known only through it. This method contains equivocal premises yielding equivocal conclusions. Consequently, many who followed it misunderstood both the Lawgiver’s intent and the implications of reason. They neither understood what the prophetic texts conveyed nor precisely established what rational proofs entailed. For they said:

“It is impossible to know
