> (1) A blank space in the original.

---

## Page 6257

the Creator except by establishing that the world had a beginning, and it is impossible to establish that the world had a beginning except by establishing that bodies had a beginning.”

They said that the way to do this is to infer, from the origination of accidents, the origination of the things in which those accidents subsist. Some argued from motion and rest alone; others appealed to spatial states, which they define as combination, separation, motion, and rest. Still others appealed to accidents generally. Their proof rests on the premise that whatever is never devoid of events must itself have had a beginning, since events without a first are impossible.

Their opponents—adherents of religious traditions and others, including both those who hold that the heavens and the earth were brought into existence from nothing and those who hold that the celestial spheres are beginningless and eternal—say to them: “The occurrence of events after their previous nonexistence is itself an event. It must therefore have a newly arising cause; otherwise, one of the two alternatives of a contingent thing would be favored without a determining factor.”

Those among the adherents of religious traditions and others who hold that the celestial spheres had a beginning also say to them:

“You have established that the world had a beginning by a certain method, yet the world’s having a beginning is possible only if the contrary of what you have established is true. What you have presented as proof that the world had a beginning therefore does not prove that it had a beginning; indeed, it does not even entail this. A proof must necessarily entail what it proves, such that whenever the proof holds, what it proves must also hold. Rather, your proof is incompatible with the world’s having a beginning and contradicts it. It implies that the world could not have come into being—indeed, that there could be no coming into being of

---

## Page 6258

anything whatsoever. This entails that your proof is invalid in itself and that, even if it were sound, it would establish only the opposite of what you seek to prove and the opposite of what every rational person affirms. For every rational person knows that events do occur, whether or not they hold that the celestial spheres are beginningless. Your proof rests on the claim that an agent endowed with power favors one of two things within his power over the other without a determining factor, and that the eternal will—which bears the same relation to everything willed—favors one willed thing over another without any determining factor other than one whose relation to all determining factors is identical, without differentiation. Yet it is self-evidently contrary to reason to maintain that a contingent thing’s existence is favored over its nonexistence without a determining factor, or that one of two equivalent alternatives is favored over the other without a cause that requires this.

Even if this were conceded to be valid, it would invalidate the proof used to establish the existence of the Creator and that the world had a beginning. For that proof rests on the premise that whatever comes into being must have a cause that brings it into being. This entails that favoring its coming into being over its nonexistence requires a determining factor. Moreover, something must have newly proceeded from that originating, determining cause which necessarily entails the existence of the originated thing it has brought into being. If its existence did not follow necessarily, its existence would remain possible and contingent: it could either exist or not exist. Favoring existence over nonexistence therefore requires a determining factor that brings it into being. Thus, everything

---

## Page 6259

that can come into being will not do so unless something occurs that necessarily entails its coming into being. Whatever Allah wills inevitably comes to be, and its existence becomes necessary through His will. Whatever He does not will does not come to be; indeed, its existence is impossible without Allah Most High willing it. Whatever Allah wills to bring into being must therefore come into being, necessarily so through His will, not in itself. Whatever He does not will to bring into being cannot come into being and must necessarily remain nonexistent, because the will of Allah that would necessarily entail its coming into being has not occurred.

Then the eternalist philosophers, who maintain that the world is beginningless, said:

“The proof you have presented does not establish that the world had a beginning; rather, it entails that it had no beginning. For it is impossible for events to come into being after not existing, proceeding from an essence that had always been inactive. Thus, the world must be beginningless.”

They expressed this by saying that if all the conditions required for His being an agent existed from eternity, His action must necessarily have existed from eternity. Otherwise, the effect would fail to follow from its fully sufficient cause. In that case, if they came to exist subsequently, this would entail favoring one alternative without a determining factor. If, however, those conditions did not exist from eternity, their subsequent existence would itself be something newly occurring and would therefore require something newly occurring to account for it. Otherwise, something would come into being without a cause bringing it into being. This would then entail an infinite regress of events, since the same reasoning applies to this event as to any other. This is something the Muʿtazilah and the speculative theologians who agree with them deny.

They said:

“You therefore face two alternatives: either affirm an infinite regress of events or affirm that one alternative can be favored without a determining factor. Yet both are impossible according to you.”

---

## Page 6260

The philosophers then claimed, on the basis of this argument, that the world is beginningless. Those who followed the path of the early Muslim generations and the imams established what the messengers affirmed—that the world had a beginning—through rational proof admitting no contrary conclusion. They explained the error of the speculative theologians among the Muʿtazilah and similar groups, who departed from the early generations and the imams by introducing an innovation contrary to revelation and reason. They also explained that the philosophers’ error in maintaining the beginninglessness of the world, and their opposition to reason and revelation, were greater than those of these theologians. They further showed that proving that the world had a beginning does not require the method followed by those theologians. Rather, this can be established through other sound rational methods that conflict with neither sound reason nor authentic transmitted evidence.

This establishes that everything other than Allah was brought into being, coming to exist after not existing, whether it is called a body, an intellect, a soul, or anything else.

Since the argument of those speculative theologians among the Muʿtazilah and their followers established only that the bodies of the world had a beginning, the philosophers and those later scholars who agreed with them—such as al-Shahrastānī, al-Rāzī, al-Āmidī, and others—said: “You have offered no proof ruling out the existence of anything other than bodies. Consequently, establishing that the bodies of the world had a beginning does not entail that everything other than Allah had a beginning, unless you establish that everything other than Him is a body. Yet you have not established this.”

For this reason, some later scholars—such as al-Urmawī and those in Egypt who agreed with him, including Abū ʿAbd Allāh al-Qushayrī—came to hold that the bodies of the world had a beginning. As for intellects and souls, however, they refrained from affirming that they had a beginning and maintained that they were beginningless

---

## Page 6261

although their position actually amounts to saying that He is their necessitating cause by His very essence, and that He brings bodies into existence through certain conceptions and volitions arising in souls, which then become a cause of bodies coming into existence. Just as this view is known to be false according to revelation, it is also known to be false according to reason, as we shall explain, if Allah Most High wills.

We therefore say: The proof establishing that everything other than Allah had a beginning encompasses both of these categories.

“Furthermore,” if He is a necessitating cause by His very essence, then the bodies of the world coming into existence at that particular time, rather than before or after it, requires a determining factor. Nothing whose occurrence is confined to one time rather than another can proceed from a cause that necessitates its effects by its very essence. For if that were possible, He would not be a necessitating cause by His very essence, and it would be possible for the world to come into existence from Him.

Moreover, according to most philosophers, the souls they posit are accidents subsisting in the body of the celestial sphere; thus, they cannot subsist in it without the sphere existing. According to Ibn Sīnā and a group of others, however, the soul is a substance subsisting in its own right, but connected to the body through governing and directing it. In that case, if it existed without any connection to the body, it would not be a soul, but rather an intellect. It is therefore clear that the existence of the soul necessarily entails the existence of the body.

Thus, if these people say that the soul is beginningless while bodies are not, then this view would be

---

## Page 6262

false according to plain reason, although no rational thinker before these people is known to have held it. They were driven to this position only by their belief in the soundness of the speculative theologians’ proof that bodies had a beginning, and in the philosophers’ assertion that there are existents and contingent beings other than bodies, together with their affirmation of a cause that necessitates its effects by its very essence.

Having based their position on the false premises of both groups, they were committed to this consequence, even though combining these two positions involved a contradiction. For the speculative theologians’ principal argument rests on ruling out a beginningless succession of events, whereas the philosophers’ principal argument rests on causal efficacy being inseparable from the Being whose existence is necessary in itself. If they affirm a beginningless soul with an infinite succession of conceptions and volitions, they must admit the possibility of an infinite succession of events. This invalidates the speculative theologians’ fundamental premise on which they based their assertion that bodies had a beginning. Their agreement with the speculative theologians would then have no rational proof to support it. It is thus clear that they have combined two contradictory positions.

Abū 'Abd Allāh Ibn al-Khatīb and others like him were more accomplished than these people and recognized that these two positions could not be reconciled. They therefore did not adopt this contradictory position. Yet they did not find their way to the position of the early Muslim generations and the imams, although elsewhere they mention its fundamental principles and establish that most rational thinkers are committed to them. Had they recognized Allah’s speech and acts, which subsist in His essence and are connected to His will and power, and His ever possessing the attribute of perfection, they would have escaped these perplexities.

---

## Page 6263

We shall now indicate some of the rational arguments by which it is known that everything other than Allah Most High had a beginning.

We say: One of the “arguments” by which this is known is as follows: If anything other than Allah were beginningless, it would proceed from a complete cause that necessitates its effect by its very essence and necessarily entails it, whether or not that cause is held to possess will or choice. For a beginningless, eternal contingent being, which does not exist independently, cannot conceivably exist unless there is, from all eternity, a complete cause necessarily entailing its existence.

Not only is this known by rational necessity, but rational thinkers do not dispute it. No one says that a beginningless, eternal being proceeds from an agent whose effect does not necessarily accompany it. Nor does anyone say that it proceeds from an incomplete cause necessitating something other than its own effect; or from a cause that necessitates by its very essence, yet is not accompanied by what it necessitates and brings about; or from an agent acting by choice whose effect may be delayed.

For if its effect could be delayed, then it would be possible for that beginningless, eternal being to be beginningless and eternal. Its existence from all eternity would thus be contingent, while nothing would exist from all eternity to necessitate that existence. Its existence from all eternity would therefore be impossible. For the existence of an eternal contingent being without a complete cause necessarily entailing it is impossible by rational necessity. Plain reason establishes that no contingent being exists unless the complete cause necessarily entailing its existence obtains.

---

## Page 6264

Those among the Muʿtazilah and others who dispute this, saying that it does not reach the level of necessity, but that reason favors existence over nonexistence, nevertheless do not dispute that a particular effect produced by an agent possessing power and choice cannot be beginningless and coexist with that agent. Indeed, neither they nor anyone else disputes this. It is therefore clear that, if anything other than Allah were beginningless, it would necessarily have a complete cause entailing its existence from all eternity—whether this is called a complete cause or a cause that necessitates by its very essence, or is conceived as an agent acting by will whose particular willed effect is beginningless and coexists with it.

That being so, we say:

The existence of a beginningless complete cause is impossible. A beginningless complete cause necessarily entails its effect; no part of its effect can fail to accompany it. If any part failed to accompany it, it would not be a complete cause of its effect. Thus, one and the same thing cannot necessitate an effect by its very essence while that effect, or any part of it, fails to accompany it. For whatever necessitates something by its very essence must coexist with the entirety of what it necessitates. A complete cause is one whose effect accompanies it, with no part of that effect coming later. If any part of its effect came later, it would not be a complete cause of that delayed part.

The philosophers concede that there is no complete cause from all eternity for all the events that arise one after another, for that would entail a contradiction. It is impossible for a beginningless complete cause to produce something that originates from it and is not itself beginningless.

---

## Page 6265

Or, if you wish, you may say:

It is impossible for anything, by its very essence, to necessitate from all eternity something that comes into being and is not beginningless, whether it does so through an intermediary or without one. If that intermediary is beginningless, whatever necessarily follows from it must also be beginningless. If it comes into being, the same argument applies to it as to whatever comes into being through its mediation. What they have conceded here is also known by plain reason. The premise is therefore both demonstratively established and conceded.

Yet they say that it is a complete cause of what is beginningless—such as the celestial spheres, according to them—but not a complete cause of temporal events. This too is false.

For anything said to be beginningless, such as the celestial spheres, either must coexist with temporal events—as they say of a celestial sphere, that motion must necessarily accompany it and that it has always been moving—or need not coexist with any temporal event. If the former is the case, it follows that the cause must be a complete cause of temporal events. Yet its being a complete cause of temporal events is impossible.

For whatever coexists with temporal events and is never free of them, but is necessarily accompanied by them, cannot proceed from its necessitating cause without them. It is impossible for something to exist without that which necessarily accompanies it. If motion necessarily accompanies a celestial sphere, as they say, then the sphere’s existence without motion is impossible. Thus, that which necessitates by its very essence and is a complete cause of the celestial sphere must also be a complete cause necessitating whatever inseparably accompanies it, and a complete cause from all eternity of the sphere together with its motion. But a beginningless complete cause cannot be a beginningless complete cause of temporal events, whether motion or anything else, because its effect—which is what it necessitates and entails—must exist

---

## Page 6266

from all eternity, with nothing that it necessitates, entails, or causes lagging behind it. Neither motion, which occurs progressively, nor any other temporal event occurring in succession is beginningless. Rather, each comes into being and is preceded by another. None, therefore, can be an effect of a beginningless complete cause, since no temporal event can be beginningless. Nor can the totality of temporal events exist from all eternity. Furthermore, whatever necessarily entails temporal events cannot exist except together with an individual temporal event or with their totality. Since neither can be beginningless, nothing that necessarily entails temporal events can be beginningless either.

Thus, neither any temporal event nor anything that necessarily entails temporal events can have a beginningless complete cause. Consequently, temporal events—whether taken collectively or individually—and whatever necessarily entails them cannot proceed from a beginningless complete cause. Hence, nothing that is never free of temporal events can proceed from a complete cause existing from all eternity. It follows that the celestial sphere, which coexists with temporal events, cannot be a complete cause existing from all eternity, without beginning. Were it beginningless, it would proceed from a beginningless complete cause. Thus, it can be beginningless only if its complete necessitating cause exists from all eternity; yet the existence of such a complete necessitating cause is impossible, just as its own beginninglessness is impossible.

If, however, it is said that what is beginningless neither coexists with temporal events nor necessarily entails them—for example, that what is beginningless consists of motionless entities constituting the first effect—then the reply is: either a new state can arise, whether in that effect, from it, or otherwise, or it cannot.

---

## Page 6267

If, then, a new state can arise for it, that temporal event cannot proceed from a beginningless complete cause—that is, a cause that necessitates its effect by its very essence—as explained above and as is known and agreed upon among rational people. There must nevertheless be something that brings it into being. If this is something other than Allah, then the same argument applies either to its own coming into being, if it was itself brought into being, or to its beginning to produce that event after not having done so. If it is Allah Most High, He cannot necessitate that event by His very essence, since what is beginningless cannot necessitate a temporal event by its very essence, as has been explained. The existence of such a beginningless cause is therefore impossible. If the Maker does not necessitate His effects by His very essence—and thus is not a complete cause—nothing in the world can be beginningless, since nothing can be beginningless except through a complete cause.

If it is said that no new state can arise for what is postulated to be beginningless and an effect of the First, then, besides being a position that no rational person has held, this is false for several reasons:

First: Relations and correlations newly arise for the Necessary Existent, as rational people agree. All the more, then, can they arise for anything other than Him.

Second: Temporal events are witnessed in both the upper and lower worlds. These events proceed from Allah, either through intermediaries or without intermediaries. If they proceed through intermediaries, then things have arisen from those intermediaries after not having existed. It follows that new states must arise for what is beginningless, whether it is the Maker Himself or the Maker’s intermediaries.

---

## Page 6268

If it is said, “The beginningless entity is something that does not serve as an intermediary for anything else,” the reply is: That entity must be capable of acquiring new states. For it is necessarily known, and agreed upon by rational people, that new relations and correlations can arise for Allah, Mighty and Majestic. All the more, then, is this possible for anything other than Him. If that entity is capable of acquiring such states, new states can arise for it just as they arise for other contingent beings. For it is not impossible for temporal events to proceed from Allah, either through an intermediary or without one. If, then, that entity is receptive to such states, and such things can proceed from the Maker, temporal events can arise from it or within it after not having existed.

The explanation of their coming into being is then the same as that of everything else that proceeds from Him and comes into being. Yet this is impossible with a complete cause that necessarily entails its effect. This compelling proof thus demonstrates that the First cannot be a complete cause of anything in the world. In this respect, there is no difference between the celestial sphere and anything else, whether that other thing is postulated to be a body or something incorporeal, and whether it is postulated to entail temporal events within itself or proceeding from it—as maintained by the eternalist philosophers, such as al-Fārābī, Ibn Sīnā, others like them, and their Greek predecessors.

They say that the celestial sphere necessarily entails beginningless temporal events, and that the intellects and souls necessarily entail the temporal events that proceed from them. Each of these therefore coexists with temporal events and cannot precede them, even though all of this is an effect of that which necessitates its effects by its very essence.

Once it becomes clear that neither a temporal event nor anything necessarily entailing a temporal event can proceed from all eternity from that which necessitates its effects by its very essence, the claim that the Maker of the world is a complete cause from all eternity is disproved. Once that claim is disproved, no particular entity other than Him can be beginningless. This demonstrates that everything other than Allah is brought into being, existing after not having existed, whether one holds

---

## Page 6269

that a perpetual succession of temporal events is possible or that it is impossible. For if such a succession is held to be impossible, everything inseparable from temporal events must itself have come into being. If such a succession is held to be possible, each individual event nevertheless comes into being after not having existed and is preceded by nonexistence. Every constituent of the world necessarily entails an event that comes into being after not having existed and is preceded by nonexistence. For every constituent of the world, and everything that is made and necessarily entails temporal events, its Maker cannot be a beginningless, complete cause that necessarily entails its existence. Since this is impossible, that thing cannot be beginningless. Thus, no particular entity within the world can be beginningless.

As for the Lord having always spoken whenever He wills, or having always acted, with acts subsisting in Him by His will, and similar affirmations—this is precisely what the early Muslim generations and the imams maintained. It is therefore clear that their position is the truth, consistent with both revelation and reason.

As for the philosophers’ position being even more untenable than that of the Mu'tazilites, they may be addressed as follows:

Those people allowed temporal events to proceed from an essence that had always been inactive, with no temporal event subsisting in it or proceeding from it. You, however, maintain that a perpetual succession of differing temporal events proceeds from this essence. Moreover, you went further in denying its attributes, making it absolute existence conditioned by absoluteness, or something similar. Your denial of its attributes is therefore more extreme than that of the Mu'tazilites.

---

## Page 6270

You also maintain that He necessarily produces His effect by His very essence and is a beginningless, complete cause whose beginningless effect coexists with it and does not come after it. Yet it is well known that differing temporal events proceeding from a beginningless, simple, complete cause—whose necessary consequence and effect can never fail to accompany it—is even more clearly impossible than temporal events proceeding from an agent endowed with power and choice after they had not previously proceeded from Him. If temporal events cannot arise from a beginningless being in whom no temporal event subsists, your position is even more clearly impossible. If they can, then the Mu'tazilites’ position is more tenable.

For if their position entails that temporal events have no newly arising cause, your position entails that temporal events have no originator whatsoever. Yet temporal events are observable, and their originator must exist when they exist. Everything required to bring them into being must also be present when they are brought into being. This, however, cannot proceed from a complete cause.

It thus becomes clear that the very premises with which the philosophers argued against the Mu'tazilites and their followers for the beginninglessness of the world can be used to argue that the world came into being. Their proof rests on the claim that a beginningless, complete cause necessarily entails its effect: if the Creator were not a beginningless, complete cause, things would necessarily come into being without a cause; if He were a beginningless, complete cause, His effect would necessarily coexist with Him. Thus, they conclude, the world must be beginningless.

But His being a complete cause is impossible, because the entire effect of a beginningless, complete cause coexists with it; no part of its effect comes after it. The world, however, is inseparable from temporal events that accompany it, as is necessarily evident and agreed upon by the vast majority of rational people. Whatever necessarily entails temporal events cannot be the effect of a beginningless, complete cause, since it is impossible for temporal events to arise

---

## Page 6271

from a beginningless, complete cause. For every temporal event is preceded by nonexistence, so He is not a complete cause of any such event. Every conceivable time contains a temporal event, so at no time—past or future—is He a complete cause. It is therefore impossible for Him to be a complete cause, which is what was to be demonstrated. It follows that everything other than Him came into being, whether or not a succession of temporal events is affirmed.

As for their statement, “If He is not a beginningless, complete cause, things must come into being without a cause,” they may be answered:

“This follows only if He is not One who speaks when He wills and in whom voluntary acts subsist through His power—exalted is He. Otherwise, on this supposition, He has always been and will always remain able to act, speaking whenever He wills. In that case, whatever occurs of His words and acts through His will and power is itself the cause of what follows it.”

If they say, “This entails that temporal events subsist in Him,” they may be answered, first:

“According to your own position, temporal events may subsist in a beginningless being. Those speculative theologians who deny this do so only because they believe that whatever temporal events subsist in must itself have come into being. If this belief is correct, your claim that the celestial spheres are beginningless is invalid. If it is false, the argument of those who say that temporal events cannot subsist in a beginningless being is invalid. On neither supposition, therefore, can you maintain that temporal events cannot subsist in Him. Rather, you have denied this on the basis of your denial of the divine attributes. Your position denying the attributes is utterly unsound. The unsoundness of your proof for it has been explained elsewhere, and the falsity of what you have advanced has been demonstrated.”

---

## Page 6272

And, in sum, if affirming that the world came into being entails affirming the divine attributes and acts subsisting in Allah, then the proof we have presented establishes both that the world came into being and that its Originator possesses attributes subsisting in Him and performs voluntary acts subsisting in Him. This is also indicated by the mass-transmitted divine texts conveyed by the prophets in the Quran, the Torah, and the Gospel. This illustrates the agreement of sound reason with authentic revelation. The rational principles that underlie the innate dispositions of rational beings and represent the furthest reach of their reason likewise accord with this. Consider this in light of what Abū ‘Abd Allāh ibn al-Khatīb al-Rāzī writes in his book al-Arba‘īn (The Forty), concerning the identification of the premises to which one may appeal in establishing rational propositions.

He said:

“Know that there are two premises upon which the speculative theologians and philosophers base most of their discussions. The first is the premise of perfection and imperfection, as when they say: ‘This attribute is an attribute of perfection, so it must be affirmed of Allah; this attribute is an attribute of imperfection, so it must be denied of Allah.’ Most of the positions held by the speculative theologians are based on this premise.”

He went on to say:

“As for the second premise—the premise of necessity and contingency—this

---

## Page 6273

premise is of the utmost nobility and sublimity, and represents the furthest reach of rational minds.

They said: Existence is either necessary or contingent, and the contingent must depend upon the necessary. Likewise, the Necessary must be necessary in His essence and attributes, for if He were contingent, He would depend upon another cause.

[As for the first premise—that He is necessarily existent in Himself—it has two implications. The first is that His reality must be free of multiplicity. This, in turn, entails several things concerning His essence.

First, He cannot occupy space, because whatever occupies space is divisible, and whatever is divisible cannot be indivisible. Since He does not occupy space, He is not in any direction.

Second, there cannot be more than one Necessary Existent. Were there more than one, the two would share necessity while differing in their particular identities. That which they share is distinct from that which differentiates them. Each would therefore be composite in itself, although we have supposed it to be indivisible. This contradicts the second implication of His being necessarily existent in Himself: that He neither inheres in another nor serves as a locus of inherence. And acts are dependence . . .” (1)

I say: Someone might respond: This is the philosophers’ foundational principle concerning divine oneness, by which they denied His attributes, exalted is He, and it is exceedingly weak.] (*)

## Page 6274

The principle on which they based this is exceedingly weak, although it has caused confusion among many later scholars.

By saying, “The Necessary Existent can only be one,” they intended to deny that He has knowledge, power, life, speech, or any other attributes subsisting in Him. For, they argued, if He did, there would be more than one necessary existent. Similarly, the Muʿtazilah say that He has no eternal attributes subsisting in His essence, because otherwise there would be more than one eternal existent.

The terms “necessary” and “eternal” may refer to God, the Creator—glorified is He—who necessarily exists and is eternal. In this sense, there is only one. They may also refer to His beginningless attributes, which are eternal and necessary by virtue of the pre-existence and necessary existence of the One they qualify. This does not entail that they must be like Him, nor does it make them deities, just as a prophet’s attribute is not itself a prophet, and an attribute of a human or an animal is neither a human nor an animal. Likewise, if an attribute of something that came into being also came into being, their both having come into being does not imply that they are alike. The argument they have offered for their claim is weak.

Thus, if they say:

“If He had knowledge that was necessary by virtue of the necessary existence of the Knower, there would be more than one necessary existent,”

they may be answered:

“Why do you say that there cannot be more than one necessary existent, when the necessarily existent essence is one God endowed with the attributes of perfection?”

---

## Page 6275

Their argument is:

“If there were more than one necessary existent, the two would share necessity but differ in their individuation. What they share is distinct from what differentiates them; hence each would be composite in itself, although we have posited it [as necessary].”

Many have refuted this argument. Its proponent may be asked in reply: “When you say that they share necessity but differ in their individuation, do you mean that the necessity peculiar to each is shared by the other, or that they share necessity in the absolute, universal sense?” The first is false; no rational person would intend it.

As for the second, the reply is:

Their sharing an absolute universal is like their sharing individuation in the absolute, universal sense. For one has an individuation peculiar to it, while the two individuations share individuation in the absolute sense. Likewise, one has a reality peculiar to it, and the other has a reality peculiar to it, while both share reality in the absolute sense. Similarly, one has an essence peculiar to it, and the other has an essence peculiar to it, while both share essence in the absolute sense. The same applies to all other terms that are general when left unrestricted and particular when qualified, such as “existent,” “self,” “quiddity,” and others.

That being so, it is clear that they share necessity in the absolute sense, while each is distinguished by its own necessity through an individuation peculiar to it.

Accordingly, there is no difference between necessity and individuation in this respect.

Thus, the statement, “They share necessity in the absolute sense but differ in their particular individuation,”

---

## Page 6276

is like saying, “They share individuation in the absolute sense but differ in their particular necessity.” Clearly, this is unavoidable, whether or not it is called composition. No existent, whether necessary or otherwise, can be devoid of such commonality and distinction. Whatever is inseparable from existence cannot possibly be denied of necessary existence.

“Furthermore,” the shared, absolute universal is universal and shared only in the mind, not in external reality. Accordingly, neither contains anything that the other shares with it in external reality. Rather, whatever attribute one possesses, the other does not possess that very same attribute or share in it; indeed, it does not resemble or match it in that respect. Since this commonality exists only in the mind, neither would be composed of a shared element and a distinguishing element. Rather, each would possess an attribute peculiar to it, in which the other does not resemble it, and an attribute in which the other does resemble it. There is nothing objectionable in this.

Furthermore, it may be said:

This is refuted by the case of existence. Necessary existence and contingent existence both fall under the designation “existence,” while each is distinguished from the other by its particular character. It would therefore follow that necessary existence is composed of that which they share and that which distinguishes them. Whatever answer is given to this would also answer the earlier argument.

“Furthermore,” it may be said: Grant that you call this composition. Why, then, do you say that

---

## Page 6277

this is impossible for any existent, whether necessary or contingent? Yet your opponent maintains that the very feature you have denied and called composition is inseparable from every existent.

They say: “But we have assumed it to be a single entity.”

The reply is: “Granted that you have assumed it to be so. But your mere assumption does not establish that it is a single entity in the sense you claim, unless there is evidence to support that claim.”

## Page 6279

“a glorious Quran, in a Preserved Tablet.” It is as He Most High says:

## Page 6280

The Muslim must therefore adhere to the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—and that of his rightly guided caliphs, the earliest forerunners among the Emigrants and the Helpers, and those who followed them in righteousness. Regarding matters over which the Muslim community has disputed and become divided, he should resolve the dispute with knowledge and justice if he can. Otherwise, he should hold firmly to the general principles established by the revealed texts and scholarly consensus, and turn away from those who have divided their religion and become sects. Most division and disagreement arise from following conjecture and what people’s souls desire, although guidance has come to them from their Lord.

I have discussed questions of this kind at length in several places, explaining the position of the early generations of the Muslim community, which both reason and revelation affirm, and clarifying the ambiguities, confusion, and errors that arise in this subject. Here, however, we shall give a brief overview suited to the questioner’s circumstances. The duty is to instruct ordinary people in the general principles established by the revealed texts and scholarly consensus, and to prevent them from delving into details that cause division and disagreement among them. Division and disagreement are among the gravest things Allah and His Messenger have forbidden.

The brief explanation is as follows:

Whoever believes that the ink in the copy of the Quran and the voices of human beings are eternal and without beginning is misguided and mistaken, contradicting the Book, the Sunnah, and the consensus of the earliest forerunners and all other scholars of Islam. Nor has anyone ever maintained this view from among

---

## Page 6281

the Muslim scholars—whether followers of Imam Ahmad or others—that such things are eternal. Anyone who attributes this view to a scholar among the followers of Imam Ahmad or others like them is either mistaken in his attribution or deliberately lying.

Rather, Imam Ahmad and the majority of his followers are explicitly reported to have declared anyone who said, “My utterance of the Quran is uncreated,” an innovator, just as they classified anyone who said, “Utterance of the Quran is created,” as a follower of the Jahmiyyah. Abū Bakr al-Marwadhī—the closest of Imam Ahmad’s disciples—composed a lengthy, detailed treatise on this subject. Abū Bakr al-Khallāl transmitted it from him in his Book of the Sunnah, in which he collected the statements of Imam Ahmad and other leading scholars of the Sunnah on matters of belief.

At that time, some scholars of hadith had stated without qualification, “My utterance of the Quran is uncreated,” in opposition to those who said, “My utterance of the Quran is created.” When Imam Ahmad heard of this, he condemned it vehemently, declared anyone who said it an innovator, and stated that none of the scholars had said such a thing. What, then, of someone who claims that a human being’s voice is eternal? More reprehensible still is someone who attributes to certain scholars the view that the ink in a copy of the Quran is eternal. All the leading scholars among Imam Ahmad’s followers, as well as others, rejected this. I know of no scholar who says such a thing; we have only received reports of it from some ignorant people among the Kurds and others like them.”

Allah distinguishes in His Book between speech and ink. He, Most High, says:

“Say, ‘If the sea were ink for the words of my Lord, the sea would be exhausted before the words of my Lord were exhausted, even if

---

## Page 6282

We brought the like of it as a supplement.’”

This, then, is an error on this side of the issue. Likewise, anyone who claims that the Quran is preserved in hearts just as Allah is known in hearts, recited by tongues just as Allah is mentioned by tongues, and written in the Quran’s pages just as Allah is written of—and equates the Quran’s presence in hearts, on tongues, and in written copies with that of the Essence of Allah Most High in these places—is also mistaken. For there is a clear and evident distinction between how entities are represented in a written copy and how speech is recorded in it.

Existing things have four levels of existence: in external reality, in minds, in speech, and in writing. Knowledge corresponds to the entity, spoken expression corresponds to knowledge, and writing corresponds to spoken expression.

Thus, when an entity is said to be in Allah’s Book, as in His words:

“Everything they have done is in the records,”

it is understood that what is in the records is only writing corresponding to spoken expression, which in turn corresponds to knowledge. Between the entities and the written copy, therefore, are two levels: spoken expression and writing. As for speech itself, there is no intervening level between it and the written copy; rather, the speech itself is placed in the book, although there is a difference in another respect between a spoken letter and a written letter—unless what is meant is that the written copy contains a mention of that speech and an account of it, as in the words of the Most High:

“Indeed, it is a revelation from the Lord of the worlds.”

“The Trustworthy Spirit has brought it down”

---

## Page 6283

“upon your heart,” down to His words:

“And indeed, it is in the scriptures of the former peoples. Is it not a sign to them that the scholars of the Children of Israel know it?”

What is in the scriptures of the former peoples is not the Quran itself that was sent down to Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. This Quran was not sent down to anyone before him, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. Rather, those earlier scriptures contain mention of the Quran and information about it, just as they contain mention of Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and information about him. Likewise, people’s deeds are in the records, as the Most High says:

“Everything they have done is in the records.”

One must therefore distinguish between these things being in the records and speech itself being in the records, as the Most High says:

“Indeed, it is a noble Quran, in a well-guarded Book.”

And the Most High says:

“Reciting purified scriptures, containing upright writings.”

Whoever says that the ink is eternal without beginning is mistaken. Whoever says that Allah’s speech is not in the written copy of the Quran, and that it contains only ink representing Allah’s speech, is also mistaken. Rather, the Quran is in the written copy just as other speech is on paper. This is the consensus of the Muslim community and accords with Muslims’ innate understanding.

Each level has its own distinctive status. The presence of speech in a book is not like the presence of an attribute in the one possessing it—for example, knowledge and life being present in their respective subjects—such that one could say that Allah’s attribute has come to dwell in something other than Him or has become separated from Him. Nor is its presence there that of a mere indication, like the existence of the world that points to the Creator, Most High, such that one could say: “It contains nothing but a sign pointing to the speech of Allah, Mighty and Majestic”;

---

## Page 6284

rather, it is another kind of presence. Anyone who fails to give each mode expressed by locative language its due—distinguishing a body’s presence in a spatial region or a place from an accident’s presence in a body and an image’s presence in a mirror, and distinguishing seeing something with the eyes while awake from seeing it with the heart while awake or asleep, and so forth—will become confused about these matters.

Likewise, asking whether what is in the written copy of the Quran originated in time or is eternal without beginning is an ambiguous question. First, the term “eternal without beginning” has not been transmitted from the early Muslim generations. Rather, what they agreed upon is that the Quran is Allah’s speech, uncreated. It is Allah’s speech wherever it is recited and wherever it is written. It is one Quran and one speech, even though the forms in which it is recited and written vary: the voices of His servants and their ink.

For speech is the speech of the one who originally spoke it, not of the one who transmits it. Thus, when we hear a hadith narrator relating the Prophet’s words, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“Actions are judged only by intentions,”

we say, “This is the speech of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, in both wording and meaning,” although we know that the voice is that of the transmitter, not that of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. The same applies to anyone who transmits another person’s speech, whether poetry or prose.

When we say, “This is Allah’s speech,” referring to what we hear from the reciter and see in the written copy of the Quran, we are referring to the speech itself, setting aside what accompanies its transmission: the transmitter’s voice and the scribe’s ink.

---

## Page 6285

Thus, whoever says, “The reciter’s voice and the scribe’s ink are Allah’s uncreated speech,” has erred. This is the distinction that Imam Ahmad explained to a man who questioned him after reciting:

“Say: He is Allah, the One.”

The man asked, “Is this Allah’s speech, uncreated?” Ahmad replied, “Yes.”

The questioner then reported that Ahmad had said, “My utterance of the Quran is uncreated.” Ahmad summoned him, rebuked him severely, and called for him to be punished and disciplined. He asked, “Did I tell you, ‘My utterance of the Quran is uncreated’?”

The man replied, “No, but when I recited, ‘Say: He is Allah, the One,’ you told me, ‘This is Allah’s speech, uncreated.’”

Ahmad said, “Then why do you attribute to me something I did not say?”

Imam Ahmad thus explained that when someone says of what he hears from those conveying and reciting the Quran, “This is Allah’s speech,” he is referring to the actual speech that Allah spoke, even though we hear it only through the reciter’s conveyance, movements, and voice. But if someone points to any attribute of a created being—his utterance, his voice, or his action—and says, “This is uncreated,” he has gone astray and erred.

What must be said, therefore, is: “The Quran is Allah’s speech, uncreated.” The Quran is in its written copies just as other speech is in written documents. It must not be said that any of the ink or paper is uncreated; rather, all paper and ink in the world are created. It is also said: “The Quran in the written copy is Allah’s speech, uncreated,” and “The Quran that Muslims recite is Allah’s speech, uncreated.”

This answer will become clearer through the discussion of “the second question,” namely, his words:

---

## Page 6286

“Does Allah’s speech consist of letters and sound, or not?”

Giving an unqualified answer to this question, whether negative or affirmative, is an error. This question is among the newly devised innovations that arose after the third century AH, when some speculative theologians who affirmed the divine attributes said:

“Allah’s speech—what He revealed to His prophets, such as the Torah, the Gospel, and the Quran; what He did not reveal; the words by which He brought created things into being; and the words containing His commands, prohibitions, and reports—is nothing more than a single meaning, constituting one attribute subsisting in Allah. If expressed in Hebrew, it is the Torah; if expressed in Arabic, it is the Quran. Command, prohibition, and report are descriptions of this attribute, not subdivisions of it. The letters of the Quran are created: Allah created them but did not speak them, and they are not part of His speech, for His speech does not consist of letters and sound.”

Others who affirmed the divine attributes opposed them, saying:

“Rather, the Quran consists of letters and sounds.”

Some mistakenly supposed that by ‘letters’ they meant ink, and by ‘sounds’ they meant the voices of human beings. No scholar, however, has said this.

The correct position held by the early generations of the Muslim community—including Imam Ahmad, al-Bukhārī, the compiler of the Sahīh, in his Book of the Creation of Human Actions and elsewhere, and all the imams before and after them—is adherence to the established texts and the consensus of the early generations of the Muslim community. That position is

---

## Page 6287

that the Quran in its entirety—its letters and its meanings—is Allah’s speech. None of it is the speech of anyone else; rather, He sent it down to His Messenger. The term “Quran” does not refer to meaning alone or to letters alone, but to both together. Likewise, all other speech consists neither of letters alone nor of meanings alone, just as a human being endowed with articulate speech is neither a soul alone nor a body alone, but both together.

Allah Most High speaks with sound, as established by authentic hadiths, and that sound is unlike the voices of His servants, whether the reciter’s voice or anyone else’s. Nothing is like Allah, whether in His essence, His attributes, or His actions.

Just as His knowledge, power, and life do not resemble the knowledge, power, and life of a created being, so His speech does not resemble created speech. Its meanings do not resemble the meanings of created speech, nor do its letters resemble its letters; nor does the Lord’s voice resemble the servant’s voice. Whoever likens Allah to His creation has deviated concerning His names and signs, and whoever denies what He has affirmed of Himself has deviated concerning His names and signs.

In my detailed, comprehensive response, I have set out the spectrum of views held by people throughout the world on this matter. The philosophers claim that Allah’s speech has no existence except within the souls of the prophets: meanings emanate to them from the Active Intellect and become letters within their souls. Likewise, in their view, Allah’s angels are the luminous forms that arise within the souls of the prophets. This is akin to the statement of the philosopher of Quraysh, al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīrah:

“This is nothing but the speech of a human being.”

Thus, what their position really amounts to is that the Quran is the composition of

---

## Page 6288

the noble Messenger; yet it is noble speech issuing from a pure soul. These are the Sabians, and the Jahmiyyah drew close to their position, saying:

“Allah has never spoken and does not speak, nor has speech ever subsisted in Him. His speech is only what He creates in the air or elsewhere.”

Some speculative theologians who affirm the divine attributes adopted part of this view, saying:

“Rather, half of it—its meaning—is Allah’s speech, while the other half—its letters—is not Allah’s speech but something He created.”

Those who affirm the divine attributes and hold that the Quran is uncreated have disagreed: should it be said that it is eternal, without beginning, and not subject to His will? Or should it be said that He speaks when He wills and remains silent when He wills? These are two well-known positions concerning this matter, as well as hearing, sight, and similar attributes. Al-Hārith al-Muhāsibī reported both positions from Ahl al-Sunnah, and Abū Bakr Abd al-Azīz reported both from Ahl al-Sunnah among the followers of Imam Ahmad and others.

Similar disagreement on questions of this kind exists among the scholars of hadith, the Sufis, and the various schools of jurists—the Mālikīs, Shāfiʿīs, Hanafīs, and Hanbalīs—and indeed among the schools of speculative theologians and philosophers. This is not the place to discuss that at length. This is the wording of the answer in the Egyptian fatwa.

## Page 6289

The imam and eminent, discerning scholar Abū al-Abbās Ahmad ibn Taymiyyah—may Allah Most High have mercy on him and be pleased with him—also said:

All praise is due to Allah, Lord of all worlds. May Allah bless our master Muhammad, his family, and all his Companions.

To proceed: this is “A Section on the Sending Down of the Quran” and on the term “descent” wherever it occurs in the Book of Allah Most High. Many people have interpreted descent in certain passages of the Quran as meaning something other than its familiar meaning, because its meaning in those passages was unclear to them. This has then served as an argument for those who interpret the sending down of the Quran according to the interpretation of the people of religious innovation.

Some of the Jahmiyyah say that “He sent down” means “He created,” as in His saying, Most High:

“And We sent down iron, wherein is great military might.”

Or they say: “He created it in a high place, then sent it down from that place.”

---

## Page 6290

And among the Kullābiyyah are those who say that its descent means making it known and enabling the angel to understand it, or the angel’s descent with what he has understood. What they have said is false on linguistic, scriptural, and rational grounds. “The purpose here” is to discuss descent.

We say, then—and success comes from Allah—that descent in the Book of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is of “three kinds”: descent specified as being from Him; descent specified as being from heaven; and descent not qualified in either way.

The first occurs only in reference to the Quran, as He, Most High, says:

“Those to whom We have given the Scripture know that it has been sent down from your Lord in truth.”

And He, Most High, says:

“The Holy Spirit has brought it down from your Lord in truth.”

And He, Most High, says:

“The revelation of the Book is from Allah, the Almighty, the All-Wise.”

There are two grammatical interpretations of this. “The first” is that nothing is omitted: His words, “The revelation of the Book,” form the subject, and its predicate is “from Allah, the Almighty, the All-Wise.” “The second” is that it is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: “This is the revelation of the Book.” On either interpretation, it is established that it has been sent down from Him. The same applies to His saying:

---

## Page 6291

“Hā Mīm. The revelation of the Book is from Allah, the Almighty, the All-Wise.”

Likewise:

“Hā Mīm. A revelation from the Most Compassionate, the Most Merciful.”

“Hā Mīm. The revelation of the Book is from Allah, the Almighty, the All-Knowing.”

“Revelation” here denotes what is sent down: the verbal noun is used to name its object, a common usage. Hence the early generations said: “The Quran is the speech of Allah, uncreated; from Him it originated.” Ahmad and others said: “And to Him it returns.” That is, He is the One who speaks it. He also said: “Allah’s speech is from Allah; it is not separate from Him.” That is, He did not create it in something else, such that it would originate in, and be sent down from, that created thing. Rather, it is sent down from Allah, as He has stated. It originated from Allah, not from a created being: He is the One who spoke it to His creation.

As for descent “specified” as being from heaven, this occurs in His saying:

“And We sent down from heaven.”

“Heaven” is a generic term for everything above. When qualified by a particular referent, its meaning is restricted accordingly. Thus, His words “from heaven,” occurring in several passages, are unqualified, referring to what is above. He then clarifies this elsewhere by saying:

“Is it you who bring it down from the clouds?”

And:

“Then you see the rain emerge from within them.”

That is, it is sent down from the clouds. Resembling the descent of the Quran is His saying:

“He sends down the angels with the inspiration of His command upon whomever He wills of His servants.”

The angels’ descent is thus their descent with revelation from His command, which is His speech. Likewise, His saying:

“The angels and the Spirit descend therein,”

corresponds to His saying:

“Therein every wise decree is made distinct—a command from Us. Indeed, it is We who send messengers.”

This resembles His saying:

“Say: The Holy Spirit has brought it down.”

## Page 6292

A group of scholastic theologians—including Abū al-Hasan al-Ash'arī and those who followed him among the adherents of Mālik, al-Shāfi'ī, and Ahmad—regarded descent, arrival, and coming as an event that He brings about separate from Himself. That, according to them, constitutes His coming and His rising over the Throne. They therefore said that His rising over the Throne is an act He performs in the Throne, whereby He becomes established over it, without any act

---

## Page 6294

subsisting in the Lord. Most people, however, disagreed with them, saying:

It is well known that no attribute or accident comes except through the coming of something else. When people say, “The cold has come,” or “The heat has come,” it is the air carrying the heat and cold that has come, and air is a self-subsisting entity.

When they say, “The fever has come,” fever is heat or cold subsisting in a concrete entity, caused by bodily humours that move and pass from one state to another, thereby producing heat and cold. This differs from an accident that arises without any movement of its bearer, such as the colour of fruit. In this case, people do not say, “Redness, yellowness, and greenness have come”; rather, they say that it is red, yellow, or green.

Since this is so, His sending down justice, tranquillity, drowsiness, and trustworthiness—qualities that subsist in His servants—takes place only when He conveys them to them. Concrete entities are described as descending, just as the angels are described as descending with revelation and the Quran. When the angels descend with these things, they are said to have descended.

The same applies when something other than the angels descends, such as air that descends through the operation of causes. Allah then produces from it the vapour that gives rise to drowsiness. Thus He, glory be to Him, has sent down drowsiness by sending down that which carries it.

He, glory be to Him, has also mentioned sending down iron, although iron is created in mineral deposits. As for the report from Ibn ‘Abbās, may Allah be pleased with them both, that Adam, peace be upon him

---

## Page 6295

descended from Paradise carrying five iron objects—an anvil, tongs, a basin, a hammer, and a needle—it is a lie; no such report is established. Likewise, the hadith that al-Tha‘labī narrated from Ibn ‘Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“Allah sent down four blessings from heaven to earth: iron, water, fire, and salt.”

This is a fabricated, falsely attributed hadith. Its chain of transmission includes Sayf ibn Muhammad, the son of Sufyān al-Thawrī’s sister, may Allah have mercy on him, who is among the notorious liars.

Ibn al-Jawzī said:

“He is Sayf ibn Muhammad, the son of Sufyān al-Thawrī’s sister. He narrates from al-Thawrī, ‘Āsim al-Ahwal, and al-A‘mash. Ahmad, may Allah have mercy on him, said, ‘He is a liar who fabricates hadith.’ On another occasion, he said, ‘He is worthless as a narrator.’ Yahyā said, ‘He was a vile liar,’ and on another occasion, ‘He is not reliable.’ Abū Dāwūd said, ‘A liar.’ Zakariyyā al-Sājī said, ‘He fabricates hadith.’ Al-Nasā’ī said, ‘He is neither reliable nor trustworthy.’ Al-Dāraqutnī said, ‘He is weak, and his narrations are abandoned.’”

People can plainly see that these tools are made from iron extracted from mineral deposits.

If it is said that Adam, peace be upon him, descended with all these tools, this is a denial of what is plainly observable. If, instead, it is said that he descended with a single tool, and that this tool is unknown, then what benefit does this offer the rest of humanity? Moreover, what use could he make of these tools if there was no iron available to be hammered with them? Once Allah creates iron, these tools can be made from it, even though

---

## Page 6296

the transmitted account states:

“The first to write and sew was Idrīs, peace be upon him.”

Adam, peace be upon him, did not sew a garment, so what would he do with a needle?

Furthermore, Allah stated that He sent down iron. The principal purpose of mentioning iron was its use in making weapons for jihad—swords, spearheads, blades, and similar implements by which Allah and His Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, are supported. These did not descend from heaven. If it is said that the implement used to forge them descended, the reply is: Allah stated that He sent down iron for the purposes already mentioned. The implement alone is insufficient; there must also be material from which weapons for jihad can be made.

However, the expression “sending down” puzzled many people, to the point that Qutrub, may Allah have mercy on him, said that it means He made it a provision for hospitality (*nuzul*), as in the expression, “He bestowed the matter upon so-and-so as a good provision”—that is, He made it a provision. He said that a similar example is Allah’s statement:

“And He sent down for you eight pairs of livestock.”

This interpretation is weak, for *nuzul* applies only to what is eaten, not to what is used in fighting. Allah Most High says:

“Then a welcome of scalding water.”

Hospitality is called *nuzul* because a guest customarily arrives riding, then alights at a place where refreshments are brought to him. It is thus called *nuzul* because of his alighting (*nuzūl*). One also says, “A guest alighted among such-and-such a clan.” This is why Noah, peace be upon him, said:

“My Lord, let me land at a blessed landing place, and You are the best to grant a landing.”

For he was aboard the Ark. The places where travellers stop are called *manāzil* because they travel mounted and then alight; those travelling on foot follow the mounted travellers in this usage. Dwellings are also called *manāzil*.

---

## Page 6297

Some have understood the sending down of iron to mean its creation, because He brought it out of its mineral deposits and taught people how to work it. Iron is created only in mineral deposits, and these occur only in mountains. Thus Allah sends iron down from its deposits in the mountains so that the children of Adam may benefit from it. Allah Most High says:

“And He sent down for you eight pairs of livestock.”

This, too, has puzzled some people. Some say that “sent down” means “made”; others say it means “created,” on the grounds that livestock are created from water, since water produces the vegetation whose source—water—descends from heaven. Qutrub said: “We made it a provision for hospitality.”

There is no need, however, to depart from the expression’s familiar linguistic meaning. Livestock descend from their mothers’ wombs, and from their fathers’ loins they enter their mothers’ wombs. The verb “to send down” is also used of a man discharging semen; when he ejaculates, a full ritual bath becomes obligatory for him. Yet a man generally ejaculates while lying on his side, whether during intercourse or in a wet dream. How much more, then, does this apply to livestock, which generally discharge semen while standing on their legs, raised above the females’ backs?

This is further clarified by the fact that He did not use the expression “sending down” for things He created in lower places. He did not say that He sent down vegetation or pasture. Rather, He used it for things created in an elevated place, which Allah then sent down from that place, such as iron and livestock. Allah Most High says:

“O children of Adam, We have sent down to you clothing to cover your nakedness and adornment”—to the end of the verse.

There are two readings of this verse. In one, the accusative is used, so that the garment of righteousness is also

---

## Page 6298

sent down. In the nominative reading, however, it is not. Both are true. It has been said that the expression means “We created it,” or “We sent down the means of producing it,” or “We inspired them with the knowledge of how to make it.” These explanations are weak.

The vegetation they mentioned is not described with the words “We sent down,” nor is this expression used for everything that is made. He did not say, “We sent down houses,” or “We sent down cooked food,” and so forth. Nor did He say, “We sent down every kind of clothing and furnishings.”

It has been said that rīsh and riyāsh both mean luxurious clothing, the two having the same meaning, just as lubs and libās both mean clothing. It has also been said that they mean wealth, abundance and livelihood; the expression irtāsha fulān means that someone’s circumstances have improved. The correct view is that rīsh means furnishings and household goods. Abū ʿUmar said: “The Arabs say, ‘So-and-so gave me his rīsh,’ meaning his clothing and equipment.”

Another said: “In Arabic usage, riyāsh means furnishings and such visible possessions as clothing, bedding and the like.” Some Quran commentators have called it wealth, but what is meant is a particular kind of wealth. Ibn Zayd said: “Adornment.” This is because the word derives from a bird’s plumage, which clothes it and protects it from heat and cold. A bird’s beauty lies in its plumage. The same applies to the bedding in which a person sleeps, what he spreads beneath him, and similar things. The Quran means coverings generally, whether worn on the body or used in homes, as Allah Most High says:

“And Allah has made your homes a place of rest for you”—to the end of the verse.

Thus He, glorified be He, reminded them of His favor in providing livestock from which they obtain clothing and furnishings. This—and Allah knows best—is the meaning of His sending it down, for He causes it to descend

---

## Page 6299

from the backs of livestock: the wool, fur, and hair that clothe these animals and that human beings use for clothing and furnishings.

He has thus sent this clothing down to them. Most people on earth clothe themselves in animal hides, which afford greater protection against heat and cold than clothing made from cotton and flax. In Surah al-Nahl, Allah Most High mentions His favors to His servants. At the beginning of the surah, He mentions the fundamental blessings without which human beings cannot live; later, He mentions the blessings that complete these favors and without which their lives cannot be pleasant. At its beginning, He mentions the provision they cannot do without, and the clothing that protects them against cold, saying:

“And He created livestock for you; in them you have warmth and other benefits, and from them you eat.”

Then, later in the surah, He mentions their dwellings and the benefits these afford: the homes of settled people and nomads, and the lodgings of travelers. He, Most High, says:

“And Allah has made your homes a place of rest for you”—to the end of the verse.

Then He mentions His favor in providing shade that protects them from heat and danger, saying:

“And Allah has made shade for you from what He has created, and has made shelters for you in the mountains”—through to His words:

“Thus He perfects His favor upon you, so that you may submit to Him.”

He does not mention protection against cold here because He has already mentioned it at the beginning of the surah, among the fundamental blessings. Cold kills: no one can live in cold lands without warmth. Heat, by contrast, causes discomfort but does not kill as cold does. Protection against heat can be found in shade, clothing, and other things. Moreover, people living in hot climates do not need protection to the same extent as those exposed to cold; even minimal protection suffices them, and at night and at either end of the day they

---

## Page 6300

do not suffer greatly from the heat; indeed, at times they have no pressing need for protection. He therefore brings the two together in His words:

“Garments that protect you from the heat and garments that protect you in battle.”

There is neither any omission in the wording nor any deficiency in the meaning, as imagined by those who have not properly grasped the true meanings of the Quran. Rather, its wording is the most complete wording, and its meaning the most perfect of meanings.

Since clothing and furnishings descend from the backs of livestock, and the coverings of livestock themselves are sent down from loins and wombs, as explained above, they are sent down in both respects. For human beings cannot benefit from these coverings while they remain on the animals’ backs; they must first come down.

It has thus become clear that every occurrence of the word “descent” in the Quran and the Sunnah carries the familiar meaning of descent. This is what befits the Quran, for it was revealed in the language of the Arabs, and the Arabs know descent only in this sense. Had another meaning been intended, they would have been addressed in a language other than their own. Moreover, that would mean using a word with a recognized meaning in a different sense without explanation. This is impermissible for the reasons we have mentioned.

In this way, the intended meaning of the Quran and its language is conveyed—the meaning which Allah Most High has stated that He has made clear and made a guidance for mankind.

Let this be its conclusion. All praise belongs to Allah alone. May Allah bless our master Muhammad and all his family and Companions, and grant them abundant peace.

None of these indicates that a creature’s attribute is the Creator’s attribute, or even that it resembles it. Rather, they indicate the distinction between the Creator’s attributes and those of created beings.

Thus, His speech is not like a creature’s speech; its meaning is not like the meaning of a creature’s speech; its letters are not like the letters of a creature’s speech; and His voice is not like a creature’s voice. Likewise, His knowledge is not like a creature’s knowledge, His power is not like a creature’s power, His hearing is not like a creature’s hearing, and His sight is not like a creature’s sight. For there is nothing like Allah, whether in His essence, His attributes, or His actions.

## Page 6308

No scholar endowed with sound reason and religious commitment disputes this distinction.

Section

As for His saying, Most High:

“Indeed, it is the word of a noble messenger,”

He mentions this in two places. In Sūrat al-Hāqqah, He says:

“Indeed, it is the word of a noble messenger.”
“Nor is it the word of a poet; little do you believe.”
“Nor the word of a soothsayer; little do you reflect.”

The messenger here is Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. In Sūrat al-Takwīr, He says:

“Indeed, it is the word of a noble messenger,”
“Possessed of power, held in honour with the Lord of the Throne,”
“Obeyed there and trustworthy.”
“And your companion is not mad.”
“And he certainly saw him on the clear horizon.”

The messenger here is Gabriel. Thus, He attributed it at one point to the human messenger and at another to the angelic messenger, using the designation “messenger.” He did not say, “It is indeed the word of an angel,” or “of a prophet,” because the term “messenger” makes clear that he is one who conveys

---

## Page 6309

on behalf of another, not one who originates it himself.

“The Messenger’s duty is only to convey the message.”

Thus His saying, “Indeed, it is the word of a noble messenger,” is equivalent to saying that it is conveyed by a messenger, transmitted by a noble messenger, brought by a noble messenger, or heard from a noble messenger. It does not mean that a noble messenger originated it or brought it into being, or originated or brought into being any part of it. If he originated it, he would not be a messenger with respect to what he himself originated and initiated; he is a messenger only with respect to what he conveys and delivers. It is well known that the pronoun refers to the Quran without qualification.

(Moreover, if either of the two messengers had originated its letters and composition, the other messenger could not have been their originator and composer. It is therefore untenable to say that it is attributed to the messenger because he brought its wording and composition into being. If this attribution could be based on the messenger’s having brought it, or any part of it, into being, we could say that it is the word of a human being. ## Page 6311

These two foolish innovations sparked turmoil and intensified animosity, although the adherents of both positions may explain them in ways that confuse many people. For example, someone who maintained that the sound heard from a person, or part of it, is eternal explained this by saying that the eternal had manifested in what was brought into being, without dwelling within it.

As for “human actions,” I have seen a later writer claim that they are eternal, both good and evil. He explained this by saying that divine legislation is eternal and divine decree is eternal, and that these actions are governed by that legislation and decree. He did not distinguish between divine legislation, which is Allah’s speech, and what it governs, namely what is commanded or forbidden. Nor did he distinguish between divine decree, which is Allah’s knowledge and speech, and the things decreed, which are His creations.

All rational people know as a self-evident truth that commands and statements are two kinds of speech, in both its wording and its meaning. Commands and statements are not attributes of a single subject. Whoever makes commands, prohibitions, and statements attributes of speech rather than kinds of speech contradicts what reason knows necessarily.

In this respect, these people are like someone who claims that existence is one, failing to distinguish between unity in kind and identity as a single entity. For the division of “what exists” into the eternal and the originated, the necessary and the contingent, the Creator and the created, and what subsists by itself and what subsists in another is like the division of “speech” into commands and statements, or into non-declarative and declarative speech, or into commands, prohibitions, and statements. Whoever says that speech is a single meaning that is both command and statement is like someone who says that existence is one and is both the Creator and the created, or both the necessary and the contingent. Just as the true import of this position amounts to denying the Creator, so the true import of

“I am your lord, the Most High.”

up to His words:

## Page 6314

do you reflect! It is a revelation from the Lord of the worlds.”

Thus He combined His statement, “Indeed, it is the word of a noble messenger,” with His statement, “Indeed, it is a revelation from the Lord of the worlds.” Both pronouns refer to the same thing. Had the messenger originated and composed it, it would not have been a revelation from the Lord of the worlds; rather, it would have been a revelation from the messenger.

As for anyone who takes the pronoun here to refer to something other than the referent of the other pronoun—even though nothing in the wording requires different referents—or who says that this is an expression of Allah’s speech, tell him:

Is what you recite an expression of the expression which, according to your claim, the angelic or human messenger originated? Or is it that very expression itself? If you make this an expression of that expression, then Gabriel’s or the Messenger’s expression could likewise be an expression of Allah’s expression. In that case, the dispute remains merely verbal. For once he says that Muhammad heard all of it from Gabriel, that Gabriel heard all of it from Allah, and that the Muslims heard all of it from the Messenger, he has spoken the truth. After this, his use of the term “expression” is intended to distinguish between the act of conveying and the one whose speech is conveyed, as we shall explain.
