The latter seems more likely, for the Arabs say insāʿa al-māʾ when water flows over the surface of the ground, and insāʿa al-jāmid when a solid substance melts. Perhaps, therefore, what is meant is looseness of the bowels. Allah knows best.

---

## Page 6354

If it is objected, “But it has been reported that He commands a herald to call out,” the reply is: This is not found in the Sahīh. If it is authentic, the two reports can be reconciled: He Himself calls out and also commands a herald to call out. However, this report cannot be used to contradict the authentic, widely transmitted report whose authenticity hadith scholars have unanimously affirmed and which they have accepted, especially since it explicitly states that Allah Most High Himself says:

“Who is calling upon Me, that I may answer him? Who is asking Me, that I may give him? Who is seeking My forgiveness, that I may forgive him?”

Likewise, Jahm denied the names of Allah Most High. He would not call Him a thing, living, or anything else except metaphorically. He said, “Calling Him by a name also applied to a created being would amount to likening Him to creation.” Jahm was also a determinist, saying that the servant does nothing. Thus, it is reported that he called Allah Powerful, since, in his view, the servant has no power.

Then the Mu‘tazilah, who followed ‘Amr ibn ‘Ubayd’s position on divine decree and the threat of punishment, adopted Jahm’s doctrine. They affirmed the names of Allah Most High but did not affirm His attributes. They said, “We say that Allah truly speaks.” They sometimes even cite the Muslims’ consensus that Allah truly speaks, lest the view that He does not speak be attributed to them. Yet, in their view, His being a speaker—glory be to Him—means that He created speech in something other than Himself. Thus, their doctrine and that of the Jahmiyyah are identical in substance. The former, however, say that He truly speaks, whereas the latter deny that He truly speaks. The true import of both groups’ position is that He is not

---

## Page 6355

a speaker, for no one can be conceived of as a speaker unless speech subsists in him, or as willing unless will subsists in him, or as loving, pleased, hating, or merciful unless will, love, pleasure, hatred, and mercy subsist in him. Many of the Mu‘tazilah who followed Abū Hanīfah in jurisprudence agreed with them on this. Among the other imams of the Muslims, none espouses the Mu‘tazilah’s positions on denying the attributes, divine decree, the intermediate position between the two positions, or carrying out the threat of punishment.

The Mu‘tazilah and the Kullābiyyah then disputed the true meaning of “speaker.” The Mu‘tazilah said: A speaker is one who produces speech, even if he brings it into being in another. This allowed them to say that Allah creates speech in another and is its speaker.

The Kullābiyyah said: A speaker is one in whom speech subsists, even if he does not speak by his will and power and performs no act at all. Rather, they regarded a speaker as analogous to a living being in whom life subsists, even if his life is not by his will or power and does not result from any act of his.

As for the early generations, their followers, and the majority of rational people, a speaker, as they understand the term, is one in whom speech subsists and who speaks by his will and power. A speaker in whom speech does not subsist is inconceivable, as is a speaker who speaks without his will and power. Thus, each of these two groups of innovators adopted only part of what characterizes a speaker: the Mu‘tazilah held that he produces speech, while the Kullābiyyah held that he is the subject in whom speech subsists. The Mu‘tazilah then claimed that he could produce speech in another. They also claimed, together with those followers of the Kullābiyyah who agreed with them, such as Abū al-Hasan

---

## Page 6356

and others, that an act does not subsist in its agent. The early generations and the majority of rational people rejected this, saying that an agent can only be one in whom the act subsists, and that a distinction must be made between the agent, the act, and what the act produces. In his book Khalq Af‘āl al-‘Ibād (The Creation of the Acts of the Servants), al-Bukhārī reported the scholars’ consensus on this.

Those who held that an act does not subsist in its agent, yet also held that Allah is the agent of the servants’ acts—as did Abū al-Hasan and others—that the servant performs no act, and that everything the servant creates is an act of His, ascribe to Him attributes of action that are separate from Him. They divide His attributes into attributes of essence and attributes of action, although, in their view, these actions are the effects produced separately from Him. Their position therefore entails that He be characterized by the injustice and evil deeds He creates, despite their assertion that He is not characterized by the speech and other things He creates. This was a contradiction on their part, which the Mu‘tazilah exploited against them.

When they affirmed a principle of Ahl al-Sunnah—that when a quality subsists in a subject, a name is derived from it for that subject and not for another, as with the name “speaker”—the Mu‘tazilah challenged them with the names “Creator” and “Just.” They offered no sound answer to this objection. The principle upheld by the early generations and the imams, however, is consistent throughout.

Among the proofs they cited that the Quran is uncreated was the saying of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, invoked by Imam Ahmad and others:

“I seek refuge in Allah’s perfect words.”

They said that refuge is not sought in anything created. They were then challenged with his saying:

“I seek refuge in Your pleasure from Your wrath, in Your granting well-being from Your punishment, and in You

---

## Page 6357

from You.” The early generations and the imams consistently applied their principle, saying: His granting well-being is His act, which subsists in Him, whereas the well-being found in people is what His act produces.

They likewise said: Allah is the Creator of the servants’ acts. The servants’ acts, which subsist in them, are effects produced by Him, not His own act; they are the servants’ own acts. In reality, those people’s position amounted to denying both the Lord’s act and the servant’s act. Thus, the Mu‘tazilah gained the upper hand against them on “the question of divine speech and predestination,” exposing their contradictions just as they themselves had exposed the contradictions of the Mu‘tazilah.

This is the greatest benefit to be derived from the statements of disputing parties whose positions are false: the statements of each party expose the unsoundness of the other’s position. The seeker thereby recognizes the unsoundness of those positions, and this prompts him to seek the truth. You will find that the truth invariably accords with what the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, brought, and that what the Messenger brought invariably accords with sound reason. The seeker thus becomes one who has a heart, or listens with full attentiveness—one who has a heart with which to understand and an ear with which to hear—unlike those who said:

“If only we had listened or reasoned, we would not have been among the inhabitants of the Blaze.”

Many scholars of hadith and Sufism, as well as jurists affiliated with the four imams, agreed with the Kullābiyyah’s position. Yet none of the four imams

---

## Page 6358

or comparable imams of the Muslims held their view.

Alongside the Kullābiyyah and their like, other groups emerged among scholars of jurisprudence, hadith, and speculative theology, including Karrāmiyyah and non-Karrāmiyyah. They said that He, glorified be He, speaks by His will and power, with speech that subsists in His essence, and that He speaks with letters and sounds by His will and power. In this way, they sought to escape the two innovations of the Muʿtazilah and the Kullābiyyah. Yet they said that it had not been possible for Him to speak in pre-eternity; rather, speech became possible for Him after having been impossible for Him, without any cause arising that necessitated its becoming possible or His becoming able to speak.

Many scholars of speculative theology, jurisprudence, and hadith agreed with the Karrāmiyyah on this position. However, no such view has been transmitted from any of the four imams or comparable imams of the Muslims. In this, they shared the position of the Jahmiyyah and the Muʿtazilah, for all these groups say that speech had not been possible for Him in pre-eternity, but then became possible for Him after having been impossible for Him, without any cause arising that necessitated its becoming possible.

The Jahmiyyah and the Muʿtazilah, however, say that He created speech in something other than Himself, without any speech subsisting in Him. For if speech subsisted in Him by His will and power, temporal occurrences would subsist in Him. They say that temporal occurrences do not subsist in Him.

The Jahmiyyah and the Muʿtazilah explain that temporal occurrences fall within the category of attributes that they call accidents. In their view, no attributes subsist in Him. They argue that attributes are accidents, and an accident can subsist only in a body, whereas He is not a body. This is because a body is never free of temporal occurrences, and whatever is never free of temporal occurrences is itself originated in time.

---

## Page 6359

The Kullābiyyah, however, said: Attributes do subsist in Him, but temporal occurrences do not. We do not call attributes accidents, because, in our view, an accident does not persist for two successive moments, whereas Allah’s attributes endure.

They also said: If temporal occurrences subsisted in Him, He would never be free of them, because whatever is receptive to something cannot be devoid of both that thing and its opposite. Whatever is never free of temporal occurrences is itself originated in time.

The majority who opposed both groups replied: As for their assertion that attributes do not subsist in Him because they are accidents, that an accident can subsist only in a body, and that He is not a body: calling whatever subsists in something else an “accident” is a newly introduced convention. Likewise, calling anything that can be pointed to a “body” is also a newly introduced convention. In Arabic, jism means the body—the badan or jasad—as several authorities on the language have stated, including al-Asmaʿī and Abū ʿAmr. Thus, the word jism is similar in meaning to jasad, referring to that which is thick and dense. The Arabs say, “This is jasīm (bulky),” and “This is ajsam (bulkier) than that,” meaning thicker than it. Allah Most High says:

“And has increased him abundantly in knowledge and stature.”

And He Most High says:

“When you see them, their bodies impress you, and when they speak, you listen to their words.”

The word “body” may denote thickness and density themselves, or it may denote that which is thick and dense. Similarly, speculative thinkers sometimes use “body” to mean magnitude, which they may call the “mathematical body.” At other times, they mean the thing possessing magnitude, which is the natural body. Magnitude abstracted from that which possesses it is like number abstracted from that which is counted, and this exists only

---

## Page 6360

in the mind, not in external reality. Likewise, a surface, line, or point abstracted from the subject in which it subsists exists only in the mind.

They said: If this is the meaning of “body” in Arabic, then it is narrower than “that which can be pointed to.” For the Arabs do not call the spirit, which subsists in its own right, a body. Rather, they say, “His spirit has left his body,” and, “He is body and spirit.” They do not call the spirit a body, nor do they call the breath that leaves a person a body. The speculative theologians, however, adopted the convention of calling everything that can be pointed to a “body,” just as they adopted the convention of calling everything that subsists in its own right a “substance.” They then disagreed over whether everything that can be pointed to is composed of indivisible atoms, or of matter and form, or of neither. These three positions have been discussed at length elsewhere. Hence many of them would say: In our terminology, a body is that which subsists in its own right, or that which exists—not that which is composite.

The scholars who adhere to the Sunnah said: When the Jahmiyyah and other deniers of the attributes say that attributes can subsist only in a body, and that Allah Most High is not a body, they are answered: If by “body” you mean something composed of indivisible atoms, or something composed of matter and form, we do not concede your “first premise,” namely, your assertion that attributes can subsist only in something of that kind. You are told: The Lord Most High subsists in Himself. His servants raise their hands to Him in supplication and direct their hearts toward Him. He is the Most High, the Most Exalted—glory be to Him—and the believers will see Him directly with their own eyes on the Day of Resurrection, just as they see the moon on the night of

---

## Page 6361

the full moon. If you say, “Whatever is like this is a body and has come into being,” this would be an innovation contrary to language, revelation, and reason. If you say, “We call whatever is like this a body and say that it is composite,” the reply is: This designation you have invented is among the names for which Allah has sent down no authority.

Anyone who takes realities known through revelation and reason and gives them repellent names to turn people away from them is told: The dispute concerns meanings, not words—even if those words conform to the language. How, then, when they are your own inventions? Clearly, realities established by revelation and reason cannot be dismissed by such groundless verbal disputes.

As for their claim that anything in which attributes subsist, toward which hands are raised, and which people can see with their own eyes must necessarily be composed of indivisible atoms or of matter and form, this is not conceded. Indeed, the majority of rational thinkers—including speculative thinkers, jurists, and others—consider it false, as has been explained at length in its proper place.

The majority said: As for the Kullābiyyah’s distinction between realities unconnected with His will and power and realities connected with His will and power—the latter being termed “temporal occurrences,” while some of them call attributes “accidents” on the grounds that an accident does not endure for two successive moments—the reply is as follows:

The claim that an accident, such as blackness, whiteness, length, shortness, and the like, does not endure for two successive moments is a doctrine newly introduced into Islam, which none of the early generations or the imams upheld. It contradicts the position held by the vast majority of rational thinkers across all

---

## Page 6362

groups; indeed, some hold that its falsity is self-evident, as has been explained at length elsewhere.

As for calling the attributes “accidents,” this is a terminological convention adopted by those speculative theologians who use it, not the customary usage of Arabic speakers or of other scholars. Realities known through revelation and reason are unaffected by differences in terminology; rather, these are merely verbal disputes. In such disputes, the soundest usage is that which accords with the language of the Quran, the Messenger, and the early generations. The Muslims agree that expressions used by the Messenger and the Companions may be used. As for expressions they did not use, there is disagreement and a need for distinctions that are beyond the scope of this discussion.

As for the Kullābiyyah’s claim, “Whatever admits temporal occurrences is never free of them, and whatever is never free of temporal occurrences has itself come into being,” the majority of rational thinkers have disputed both premises. Even their own later followers disputed them on this point and acknowledged the invalidity of the rational arguments their predecessors advanced to deny that temporal occurrences subsist in Him. Later leading scholars among the Ashʿariyyah, the Shiʿah, the Muʿtazilah, and others acknowledged this, as has been explained at length elsewhere.

Another group arose among the Sālimiyyah and others—including people versed in speculative theology, jurisprudence, hadith, and Sufism, many of whom affiliate themselves with

---

## Page 6363

Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī, and Ahmad ibn Hanbal—and this became widespread among some later adherents of Ahmad ibn Hanbal—and they combined the positions of the Muʿtazilah and the Kullābiyyah. They agreed with the latter that it is eternal, and with the former that it consists of letters and sounds. They introduced an innovated doctrine—as others had done—saying:

The Quran is eternal, consisting of eternal, beginningless letters and sounds, inseparable from Allah Himself, exalted is He, throughout eternity, past and future. They supported its eternity with the arguments of the Kullābiyyah, and its consisting of letters and sounds with the arguments of the Muʿtazilah.

When they were told that some letters are preceded by others—bā precedes sīn, and sīn precedes mīm—whereas what is eternal cannot be preceded by anything else, and that sound cannot conceivably persist, let alone be eternal, they replied: Speech has both existence and essence. This resembles the position of those among the Muʿtazilah and others who distinguish between existence and essence.

They said: Speech has an order in its existence and an order in its essence. The temporal [precedence] of bā over sīn pertains to its existence, whereas in its essence bā coexists with sīn, without preceding it in time, although it precedes it in position. This is like some written letters preceding others: a scribe may write the end of the Quranic codex before its beginning, yet once he has written it, its beginning precedes its end in position.

The majority of rational thinkers replied to them: This is something whose invalidity is self-evident, for sound cannot conceivably persist, and the claim that an essence exists apart from what exists in external reality is a claim

---

## Page 6364

that is invalid, as has been explained at length elsewhere. The arrangement in the Quranic codex is an arrangement of letters written in ink. Ink is corporeal, so its arrangement resembles that of the parts of a house or a human being: the first part exists alongside the second. Sound is different: its second part does not exist until the first has ceased to exist, just as with motion. Drawing an analogy between the two is therefore invalid.

Some of these people use the term “eternal” without understanding its meaning. Others say that by “eternal” they mean that it originated from Allah and is uncreated. This meaning is correct. However, those who disputed whether it is eternal did not intend this meaning. Anyone who tells them that it is eternal, intending this meaning, intends something correct, but is ignorant of what people mean, misleads those he addresses with these words, and introduces innovations into both religious law and language.

Many of these people then say that the eternal letters and sounds are neither the sounds heard from reciters nor the ink in the Quranic codex. Others say, rather, that the sounds heard from reciters are the eternal sound. Still others say that two things are heard from the reciter: the eternal sound, which is indispensable to the existence of speech, and the newly produced sound, which is whatever exceeds that.

These people say that the ink in the Quranic codex is created, but that the eternal letters are not the ink; rather, they are the shapes and dimensions made visible by the ink. These may also be engraved in stone or cut into paper. Some of them forbid saying of the ink that it is eternal or

---

## Page 6365

created. He may say, “I do not prohibit this; indeed, I know that it is created. But I close the door to delving into this matter.” Yet he shuns those who speak the truth and explain the correct position that accords with the Quran, the Sunnah, and the consensus of the early generations of the Muslim community—even though it also accords with the clear dictates of reason and rebuts the outrageous accusations they level at one another.

People have engaged in much discussion and dispute over this subject, which we have treated at length elsewhere. Our purpose here is only to offer a concise yet comprehensive statement explaining the sound positions indicated by the Quran and the Sunnah and upheld by the early generations of the Muslim community concerning the question of divine speech, which has bewildered human minds. And Allah Most High knows best.

---

## Page 6366

Shaykh al-Islām, the mufti of mankind, Taqī al-Dīn Abū al-‘Abbās Ahmad ibn Taymiyyah, was asked about people who say:

“The speech of human beings and others is eternal—whether true or false, obscene or otherwise, verse or prose—and there is no difference between Allah’s speech and theirs in respect of eternity, except with regard to reward.”

Some of them—indeed, most of them—also say that the sounds made by donkeys and dogs are likewise eternal. When what was transmitted from Imam Ahmad in refutation of their position was read to them, they reinterpreted it, saying that Ahmad had said this only out of fear of people. Are these people correct or mistaken? Must the ruler—may Allah Most High grant him success—restrain them from this or not? Do they become disbelievers by persisting in it or not? And is what was transmitted from Ahmad true, as they claim, or not?

He replied—may Allah be pleased with him:

All praise is due to Allah. Rather, these people are mistaken in this, committing an error that is forbidden by the consensus of the Muslims. They have uttered an abominable statement and a falsehood—indeed, disbelief and absurdity. They must be forbidden from saying this, and the rulers must punish any of them who do not desist, as recompense for what

---

## Page 6367

they have earned, as an exemplary punishment from Allah. This statement is contrary to reason and religion, contradicting the Quran, the Sunnah, and the consensus of the believers. It is a “monstrous innovation” that no Muslim scholar has ever professed—neither scholars of the Sunnah nor scholars of innovation. Nor would any sane person who understands what he is saying profess it. However, those who have professed it have fallen prey to a misconception, which we shall explain, if Allah Most High wills.

When a statement’s falsity is self-evident to reason, there is no need to appeal to anything transmitted from an imam, except to demonstrate that its rejection and denunciation have been transmitted from the imams, and that whoever professes it opposes the Muslim community and introduces an innovation into religion. This also dispels the misconception of anyone who imagines that their position necessarily follows from a statement of one of the early generations, making him aware that they oppose the positions of the revered imams who are followed as exemplars. It also makes clear that the opposite of their statement is expressly affirmed by the imams followed in the Sunnah, and that this is not a matter on which they remained silent, neither affirming nor denying it.

There is no doubt that Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal, and the imams before and after him, expressly stated, without qualification, that human speech is created. Indeed, Ahmad and many other imams expressly affirmed this regarding “the acts of Allah’s servants” generally and “human speech” specifically. They did not refrain from making this unqualified statement because of the misconception that befell these dissenting innovators. Thus, neither they nor anyone else can say: “One should call it neither created nor uncreated,” on account of their misconception or because speaking about

---

## Page 6368

this is an innovation. Rather, the statement that human speech is created, not pre-eternal, is expressly transmitted from the imams whose leadership in religion and the Sunnah is agreed upon. Some expressly affirmed this when discussing “matters of divine decree” and “the creation of human acts”; others when discussing “people’s recitation of the Quran and their utterance of it”; and others cited it to establish the distinction between the Creator’s speech and the speech of created beings.

Abū Bakr Ahmad ibn Hārūn al-Khallāl—who compiled Ahmad’s statements on the foundations of religion, the principles of jurisprudence, every branch of jurisprudence, manners, character, asceticism, heart-softening exhortations, hidden defects in hadith, history, and other Islamic sciences—related in his Kitāb al-Sunnah (Book of the Sunnah), in the discussion of the Lafziyyah, from Abū Bakr ibn Zanjawayh, who said:

“I heard Ahmad ibn Hanbal say: ‘Whoever says, “My utterance of the Quran is created,” is a Jahmī; and whoever says it is uncreated is an innovator who is not to be spoken to.’”

Al-Khallāl said:

“Abū Dāwūd al-Sijistānī also informed us, saying: ‘I heard Abū ‘Abd Allāh discussing the Lafziyyah and denouncing their statements. I also heard Ishāq ibn Rāhawayh mention the Lafziyyah and their innovations.’”

Al-Khallāl also said: “I heard Ibn Sadaqah say: ‘I heard Yahyā ibn Habīb ibn ‘Arabī say: “I heard a man ask Mu‘tamir ibn Sulaymān: ‘We have

---

## Page 6369

a Qadarī imam behind whom I pray.’ He replied: ‘Whoever claims that his utterance is uncreated is like someone who claims that Allah’s sky is uncreated.’”’”

Al-Khallāl said: “Abū Bakr al-Marwazī informed me: Muhammad ibn Yahyā al-Azdī narrated to us: Musaddad narrated to me, saying: ‘I was with Yahyā al-Qattān when Yahyā ibn Ishāq ibn Tawbah al-‘Anbarī arrived. Yahyā said to him: “Tell this man”—meaning Musaddad—“what Hammād ibn Zayd said about it”—that is, the question under discussion. He said: “I asked Hammād ibn Zayd about someone who says that human speech is uncreated. He replied: ‘This is the speech of the disbelievers.’” Yahyā ibn Ishāq also said: “I asked Mu‘tamir ibn Sulaymān about someone who says that human speech is uncreated. He replied: ‘This is disbelief.’”’”

These reports and others like them were relied upon by those renowned for their adherence to the Sunnah, such as al-Marwadhī, al-Khallāl and others. Likewise, Imam Abū ‘Abd Allāh ibn Battah relies on these reports and similar ones in his book al-Ibānah al-Kabīr (The Greater Exposition).

I say: Hammād ibn Zayd was one of the eminent imams of the Sunnah, belonging to the same generation and holding a comparable standing as Mālik, al-Thawrī, al-Awzā‘ī, Hammād ibn Salamah and al-Layth ibn Sa‘d. Indeed, the scholars of the Sunnah considered him more firmly grounded in the Sunnah than al-Thawrī, although al-Thawrī surpassed him in knowledge and asceticism. Hadith scholars considered him more proficient in retaining hadith than Hammād ibn Salamah, although the latter was better known for asceticism and more active in calling people to the Sunnah. He was the leading imam of Basra at a time when Basra was the gathering place of Islamic learning. The scholars of the Ummah, the heirs of the prophets and the successors of the messengers, in that age

---

## Page 6370

—the age of the Successors of the Successors—were these Muslims and others like them, who belonged to the praised third generation.

Al-Mu‘tamir ibn Sulaymān was also one of the distinguished imams, though he ranked below Hammād ibn Zayd. Imam Ahmad, Ishāq ibn Rāhawayh and others met him, and he was one of Imam Ahmad’s teachers. As for Hammād ibn Zayd, Imam Ahmad missed the opportunity to meet him. He said: “I missed Hammād ibn Zayd, so Allah compensated me with Ismā‘īl ibn ‘Ulayyah; and I missed Mālik ibn Anas, so Allah compensated me with Sufyān ibn ‘Uyaynah.”

As for Yahyā ibn Sa‘īd al-Qattān, he was one of the scholars of the Sunnah and the leading hadith scholar in assessing the authenticity of hadith, their hidden defects, their narrators and the accuracy of their transmission. Ahmad even said: “I have never seen anyone like him”—meaning in that discipline. ‘Alī ibn al-Madīnī learned this discipline from him, and al-Bukhārī, the compiler of al-Sahīh, learned it from ‘Alī. Al-Tirmidhī stated that he had never seen anyone equal to Muhammad ibn Ismā‘īl al-Bukhārī in knowledge of the hidden defects of hadith.

These eminent scholars denounced those who said that human speech and utterances are uncreated, when the Qadariyyah innovators emerged and claimed that the servants’ acts were not created by Allah: neither their words nor any of their other deeds, whether good or evil. Rather, they say: “These acts came into being; the servant brought them into being, but they were not created by anyone.” Or they say: “The servant created them, just as he brought them into being”; for they may disagree over affirming

---

## Page 6371

creation by anyone other than Allah. Nevertheless, there was no disagreement within the Muslim community that these acts have a beginning, coming into existence after not having existed. No one said that they were eternal. However, the “Qadariyyah” among the Mu‘tazilah and others believed that Allah did not create the voluntary acts of angels, jinn and humans—whether acts of obedience or disobedience—or the acts resulting from them.

They argued that, had He created them, this would necessarily mean that the servant was compelled to act, and that religious accountability, promise and warning, reward and punishment would all be nullified. They also argued that the servant knows with self-evident certainty that he himself brings his acts into being. They supported this with reasoned arguments.

When they introduced this “doctrine,” the imams of the Sunnah denounced it, just as the Companions—may Allah be pleased with them—had denounced the beginnings of this innovation when the Qadariyyah emerged towards the end of the Companions’ era. Ibn ‘Umar, Ibn ‘Abbās, Wāthilah ibn al-Asqa‘ and other Companions refuted them. The imams explained that anyone who holds that something which has come into existence, such as the servants’ acts or anything else, was not created by Allah is like someone who denies that Allah created other things that have come into existence, such as the heavens and the earth.

For Allah is the Lord of all worlds, the Sovereign of all dominion and the Creator of all things. Nothing in all the worlds lies outside His lordship, nothing in all dominion lies outside His sovereignty, and nothing that has come into existence lies outside His creation. Allah Most High says:

“Allah is the Creator of all things, and He is the Guardian over all things.”

“To Him belong the keys of the heavens and the earth.”

And Allah Most High says:

“Or have they assigned to Allah partners who created as He created, so that it became difficult to distinguish

one creation from the other? Say, ‘Allah is the Creator of all things.’” And Allah Most High says:

“That is Allah, your Lord; there is no deity but Him, the Creator of all things. So worship Him, and He is the Guardian over all things.”

“No vision can encompass Him, but He encompasses all vision.”

And Allah Most High says:

“That is Allah, your Lord, the Creator of all things; there is no deity but Him. How then are you turned away?”

And Allah Most High says:

Thus, the adherents of the Sunnah and the united community—the people of hadith—were the ones who followed Allah’s Book and believed in what these texts entail. They held that Allah is the Creator, Lord, Owner, Sovereign and Guardian of everything that comes into existence: all entities and attributes, all direct acts and acts resulting from them, and every movement, whether natural, voluntary or forced. They also held that He, glorified be He, has power over all things and knows all things. They therefore believed in His all-encompassing knowledge, His perfect power, His all-embracing will and His complete lordship. For this reason,

## Page 6373

Ibn 'Abbās said:

“Belief in divine decree is what holds belief in Allah’s oneness together. Whoever affirms Allah’s oneness and believes in divine decree has perfected his belief in His oneness; whoever affirms Allah’s oneness but denies divine decree has nullified his belief in His oneness through that denial.”

As for Allah’s attributes, they are included in what His explicit names and the pronouns referring to Him denote. When you say, “I worshipped Allah,” “I called upon Allah,” or “You alone we worship,” nothing of His attributes—His knowledge, mercy, speech or any other attribute—is excluded from this designation. For this reason, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Whoever wishes to swear an oath, let him swear by Allah or remain silent.”

He also said:

“Whoever swears by other than Allah has committed shirk.”

Yet it is authentically established that he swore “by Allah’s might” and used the oath “By Allah’s life.” It is therefore clear that this is not swearing by other than Allah.

They thus gave these explicit verses their due by accepting the universal scope they expressly affirm: that Allah is the Creator of all things. For it is known that Allah Himself is not included among created things, and that His attributes are not excluded from what His name denotes.

As for the Mu'tazilah, who combined Jahmī and Qadarī doctrines, they excluded from these verses’ scope things unquestionably encompassed by the expression: the actions of angels, jinn, human beings and animals, whether acts of obedience or otherwise. These constitute a considerable part of Allah’s dominion and His signs. Indeed, they are among the finest features of His dominion and the greatest of His signs and creations. Yet they included His speech among created things because it is called a “thing,” as in His saying:

“When they said, ‘Allah has not sent down anything to any human being.’ Say, ‘Who sent down the Book that Moses brought?’”

They failed to consider that this is like His calling His knowledge a “thing” in His saying: “And they do not encompass

---

## Page 6374

anything of His knowledge except what He wills,” and His calling Himself a “thing” in His saying:

“Say, ‘What thing is greatest in testimony?’ Say, ‘Allah is witness between me and you.’”

Nor did they consider that the scope of His words, “all things,” depends on the surrounding statement, for a term’s scope varies according to its qualifications.

Thus, His saying, “He has knowledge of all things,” includes Himself, since He can be known. His saying, “He has power over all things,” includes everything that can be subject to power, encompassing everything whose existence is intrinsically possible. It may also be said that this includes everything called a “thing” in the sense of “something willed,” for shay’ (“thing”) was originally a verbal noun bearing the meaning of mashī’ (“something willed”). Thus, He has power over everything that can be willed. Alternatively, you may say: He has power over everything that can be subject to power. What is intrinsically impossible is not a thing, as all rational people agree.

Regarding His saying, “Allah is the Creator of all things,” it is known that the Creator is not the creation and is not included within the term’s scope here. Rather, it encompasses every created thing—that is, everything that has come into existence.

At the same time, Ahl al-Sunnah affirm that the servant has will, ability, and volition, and truly performs his own acts. They warn against using the term “compulsion,” because it suggests that Allah forces the servant to act against his own will, just as a woman may be forced into marriage. This is not the case. Rather, the servant chooses and acts by his own choice and will, willingly and out of love. He is not compelled and devoid of will, and Allah is the Creator of this

in its entirety. These things are contingent and have come into existence, so the evidence that Allah created them is like the evidence that He created other things that have come into existence. The point here is simply that the imams refuted those who excluded people’s words and deeds from Allah’s creation, treating this as equivalent to claiming that the heavens and the earth were not created by Allah.

The first is making something that has come into existence and been fashioned into a beginningless attribute of Allah, after the manner of the Christians and those like them.

The second is excluding what Allah has created and what lies within His power from His creation and power, as the Qadariyyah maintained, after the manner of the Magians and those like them.

The third is denying that the servant’s act, what lies within his power, and his acquisition are within his power or constitute his own acquisition and action, after the manner of the polytheistic Jabriyyah-Qadariyyah. This was the point of those imams’ statements on this matter.

other evidence, the statements of those early scholars. The imams in question included al-Bukhārī, the imam and compiler of the Sahīh; Abū Bakr al-Marwazī, the imam and companion of Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal; many others in his time; and Abū Bakr al-Khallāl and others like him.

The purpose here is to draw attention to the underlying issue from which the divisions within the Muslim community on this subject arose: the “question of utterance.”

Section

The “question of the utterance of the Quran” has caused confusion among people possessed of knowledge, virtue, religious commitment, and sound intellect. It has led to disputes and estrangement among the adherents of hadith and the Sunnah, to the point that Ibn Qutaybah said, in words to this effect: “The adherents of hadith have not differed over any of

---

## Page 6377

their doctrines except the ‘question of utterance.’” He explained that this was due to the obscurity surrounding the issue; in many instances, their disagreement was merely verbal. People did not dispute that human speech which Allah Most High has not revealed is brought into being and created. There was, however, disagreement concerning the “letters of the alphabet” and the “names of created things.” It was this disagreement that led these ignorant people into the absurdities they embraced, as we shall explain, Allah Most High willing. This response does not permit a detailed exposition of the “question of utterance,” but we shall address it briefly, saying:

Allah Most High sent His messengers, revealed His Books to them, and commanded them to convey to people the revelation and speech He had sent down to them. Some people believed in Allah and His messengers, accepted as true what they brought from Allah, and obeyed their commands. These are the believers in every age and era, and they are the people of Paradise and felicity. As Allah Most High says:

“Race toward forgiveness from your Lord and a Garden as wide as heaven and earth, prepared for those who believe in Allah and His messengers.”

And Allah Most High says:

“Indeed, those who believed, the Jews, the Christians, and the Sabians—whoever believed in Allah and the Last Day and did righteous deeds—will have their reward with their Lord. No fear will be upon them, nor will they grieve.”

Others disbelieved in the messengers and declared them liars, such as the nations whose accounts Allah has related to us: the people of Noah, ʿĀd, Thamūd, the people of Lot, the dwellers of the Thicket, and Pharaoh

---

## Page 6378

and the Arab polytheists, as well as all those who do not believe in messengership itself—among the Indians, the Brahmins and others, the Turks, the black peoples, and other unlettered nations who have no scripture—whether they declare the messengers liars or turn away from following them. For disbelief is the absence of faith in Allah and His messengers, whether accompanied by outright denial or, instead, by doubt and uncertainty, or by turning away from all of this out of envy, arrogance, or obedience to desires that divert one from following the divine message. Nevertheless, the disbeliever who declares the messengers liars is more extreme in disbelief, as is one who repudiates and rejects them out of envy despite being certain of their truthfulness. All the Meccan surahs address these people.

This is why He, glorified be He, says:

“The people of Noah denied the messengers.”

For they denied all the messengers and did not believe in messengership itself. Allah Most High said when He sent their father Adam down:

“He said, ‘Go down from it, both of you, all together, as enemies to one another. Then if guidance comes to you from Me, whoever follows My guidance will neither go astray nor suffer misery.

But whoever turns away from My remembrance will have a life of hardship, and We will raise him blind on the Day of Resurrection.’

He will say, ‘My Lord, why have You raised me blind when I used to see?’

He will say, ‘Just as Our signs came to you and you neglected them, so today you will be neglected.’

Thus do We recompense whoever transgresses and does not believe in the signs of his Lord. And the punishment of the Hereafter is more severe and more lasting.”

He thus declares that when guidance comes to them from Him—the Reminder He revealed to His messengers—whoever follows it is rightly guided and attains happiness in this world and the Hereafter, while whoever turns away from it suffers misery and becomes blind.

Thus, in the Quran, Allah addresses both the unlettered peoples who have not followed any messenger and the People of the Book who affirm some of the messengers, as in His saying:
