## Page 6386

Section

Among the nations were disbelievers and hypocrites who rejected some of the message but not all of it, whether in respect of its extent or its character, just as there were disbelievers and hypocrites who rejected the message altogether. Among those who rejected the message altogether were some who claimed that the Messenger was a poet, a sorcerer, a soothsayer, someone taught by others, a madman, or a fabricator. Such was al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīra, “the Peerless,” the chief, philosopher, and sage of Quraysh, who is mentioned in the words of Allah Most High:

“Leave Me with the one I created alone, and to whom I granted abundant wealth and sons by his side, and for whom I made ample provision. Yet he desires that I give him more. No! He has stubbornly opposed Our signs. I shall burden him with an arduous ascent. He thought and calculated. May he be destroyed—how he calculated! Again, may he be destroyed—how he calculated! Then he looked; then he frowned and scowled; then he turned away in arrogance and said, ‘This is nothing but magic passed down; this is nothing but the word of a human being.’”

He acted as a philosopher opposed to the messengers acts: first he thought—that is, he sought to proceed from conceiving the two terms of a proposition to the premises that necessitate assent, in order to discover the middle term. Then, secondly, he calculated. This calculation is “syllogistic reasoning”: proceeding from the premises to the desired conclusion through a logical syllogism based on subsumption. And, by my life,

---

## Page 6387

it is indeed sound if its premises are sound, even though its conclusions generally concern mental universals that exist in minds, not in external reality, as with mathematical knowledge concerning numbers and magnitudes. For number abstracted from the things numbered, and magnitude abstracted from bodies, exist only in the mind. But how can its premises be sound when most of those used in metaphysics are mere claims whose universality is asserted, and whose propositions are taken as conceded without proof? Whenever a syllogism lacks a proposition known to be universal, it does not establish the desired conclusion. They confuse unquantified propositions, which have the force of particular propositions, with universally applicable, conceded propositions; alternatively, they assert their universality through some form of analogical reasoning.

It is well known that every syllogism must contain a “universal proposition.” Yet most of the “universal propositions” they use to establish their metaphysical conclusions are not known to be universally applicable. Their universality is supposedly established only through analogical reasoning, which may be among the most unsound forms of reasoning, entailing the likening of Allah to His creation. Thus they say, “From one, only one proceeds.” Yet they have nothing to support this except likening the Creator of the heavens and the earth, the Lord of all worlds, to natural properties, such as those of water and fire.

Moreover, the “one” they posit in metaphysics—and likewise in logic, where they treat the proposition concerning species as composed of it, namely “genus” and “differentia”—has no reality and exists only in minds, not in external particulars. We have discussed this at length elsewhere. We have explained that the intelligible entities they posit, namely the “intellectual substances” abstracted

---

## Page 6388

from matter—namely, intellect, soul, matter, and form, which are neither bodies nor accidents—have no reality in the external world; they are conceived only in minds, not in external particulars. Likewise, the “one” they posit as an attribute of the Necessary Existent, and the “one” from which they hold species to be composed, exist only in minds, not in external particulars.

The “rational inference” they employ as proof must contain a universal proposition. Inference is of two kinds: “syllogistic reasoning” and “analogical reasoning.” People disagree about what the term “inference” denotes. Some hold that it applies literally to analogical reasoning and figuratively to syllogistic reasoning, as stated by Abū Hāmid, Abū Muhammad al-Maqdisī, and others. Others hold the reverse, as stated by Ibn Hazm and others who reject analogical reasoning. Still others hold that the term encompasses both; this is the view of the majority.

The term “rational inference” includes both kinds. Some, however, have supposed that “analogical reasoning” does not yield certainty and cannot be used in rational matters. This was the position of Abū al-Ma‘ālī, Abū Hāmid, al-Rāzī, Abū Muhammad, al-Āmidī, and other adherents of logic. The majority, by contrast, regard the two forms of inference as equivalent, and this is correct: both ultimately amount to the same thing, differing only in the arrangement of

---

## Page 6389

the argument.

For if someone says, “The disputed fermented drink is forbidden because it is intoxicating, and is therefore forbidden by analogy with grape wine,” he must establish that intoxication is the basis of prohibition. In analogical reasoning, this is called the “basis,” the “effective cause,” the “indicator,” the “common factor,” the “posit,” and similar terms.

For the analogy to be valid, he must provide evidence that intoxication is the basis of prohibition, such that wherever intoxication is present, prohibition follows. If he formulates the argument syllogistically—“This fermented drink is intoxicating, and everything intoxicating is forbidden”—then intoxication is the repeated middle term in this formulation, just as it is the effective cause in analogical reasoning. In this syllogism, he must establish the universal major premise: “Everything intoxicating is forbidden.” Whatever establishes this proposition in the syllogistic formulation also establishes intoxication as the basis of prohibition in the analogical formulation. There is no difference between them.

If someone says that establishing the attribute’s determining effect and its being the basis of the ruling is the foundation of analogical reasoning, that this answers the “demand for proof” and demonstrates that the attribute, in its full scope, is the basis of the ruling, and that this can be established only through evidence yielding probability, the reply is:

Establishing the universality of the major premise is likewise the foundation of syllogistic reasoning. The minor premise is generally known, just as the presence of the attribute in the case under consideration is known. If establishing the presence of the attribute in that case sometimes requires proof, then, as has been said, so too does

---

## Page 6390

the minor premise. Establishing the major premise is possible only through evidence yielding probability. The very evidence that establishes the universality of the proposition also establishes the determining effect of the shared attribute; there is no difference whatsoever between the two.

In matters concerning Allah, both forms of reasoning may be used only as a fortiori arguments. This is the “method” employed by the Quran and followed by the early generations of the Muslim community and its leading scholars. For nothing that exists is comparable to Allah—glorified is He—in “analogical reasoning,” nor can He be included in “syllogistic reasoning” whose individual instances are on an equal footing. Rather, whatever perfection is established for others, involving no deficiency whatsoever, He is all the more entitled to possess; and whatever imperfections others are declared free of, He is all the more entitled to be declared free of. As the Most High says:

“To those who do not believe in the Hereafter belong evil attributes, while to Allah belong the highest attributes.”

And the Most High says:

“He presents to you an example from yourselves: do you have, among those whom your right hands possess, any partners in what We have provided for you, so that you share equally in it, fearing them as you fear one another?”

We have discussed this at length elsewhere and explained that, in most matters, what is learned through “syllogistic reasoning” may be learned without it. Thus, the judgments concerning the particulars included in the syllogism can be known without knowing the judgment expressed by the universal proposition. For example, it is said: “The whole is greater than the part,” and “Two contraries cannot coexist.” Yet, for any particular whole and any particular pair of contraries, once it is known that one thing is part of another and that one thing is contrary to another, it is known that the whole is greater than its part and that the two contraries cannot coexist

---

## Page 6391

without a universal proposition ever coming to mind—that no two contraries can coexist and that every whole is greater than its part. Likewise, when it is said, “Two contradictories cannot both be true or both be false,” any pair recognized as contradictories is also known to be incapable of both being true or both being false, without calling to mind the universal proposition that this holds for every pair of contradictories.

Thus, most questions can be resolved without syllogistic reasoning involving a major premise, which necessarily requires a universal proposition. Particular things cannot be known through rational inference alone; such inference establishes only what they share with other things. They themselves concede this.

We have explained that the proofs pointing to the Maker are signs that, in themselves, point to His holy Self. We have also explained the difference between the indicative force of signs and that of syllogistic reasoning: these proofs are more perfect and beneficial, while the syllogistic method is subordinate to them and inferior in benefit and perfection. The Quran employs both approaches. For knowledge of divine matters, prophethood, and other subjects, the former approach is more perfect and complete.

Yet these people claim that no truth accessible to our innate nature can be attained except through syllogistic reasoning, which necessarily requires a universal proposition. A universal proposition, however, yields only a universal concept apprehended by the intellect; it does not yield knowledge of any particular thing. Everything that exists is particular. How, then, can any rational person nevertheless claim that knowledge can be attained only by this method?

Moreover, in their error, they suppose that the knowledge of the prophets—indeed, even the knowledge of the Lord, glorified is He—was acquired only

---

## Page 6392

through syllogistic reasoning, and that a prophet possesses an intuitive faculty by which he discovers the middle term of a syllogism without a teacher, making him more perfect than others. They place his knowledge of the unseen in this category. Yet knowledge of natural science, arithmetic, and the like has not been attained through such syllogisms. On what basis, then, do they claim that no knowledge can be attained except through them? And on what basis do they claim that there are no grounds for certainty beyond those a claimant possesses: familiar outward and inward intuitions, familiar self-evident truths, mass-transmitted reports, and familiar empirical findings?

Familiar intuitions, inward and outward perception, experience, and the like yield, by themselves, knowledge only of a specific particular, which is unsuitable as a premise in a syllogism. Its universal application, however, is known either through analogical reasoning or through non-inferential knowledge that Allah creates directly in the heart. If He creates non-inferential knowledge universally applicable to a set of particulars, then creating knowledge of some of those particulars is easy. Rarely does their method yield knowledge of a conclusion without that conclusion also being knowable through the same means by which the premises were known, or through an easier means. Their syllogisms thus add nothing but prolixity, intimidation, and misguidance.

Elsewhere, we have discussed “Greek logic” at length, explaining what is true and false, beneficial and harmful in it. To deny that knowledge can be attained except through such syllogisms, and that syllogisms can yield certainty except through these premises, is to speak without knowledge and to reject what one has not fully grasped. Hence, the method of the Prophet and the early generations was to employ “a fortiori reasoning” in the study of divine matters, as Allah Most High says: “And to Allah belongs

---

## Page 6393

the highest description.” For the Creator and the created do not fall under a universal proposition whose individual instances are equal, nor are they alike in anything. Rather, it is known that every perfection established for a created being—which involves no deficiency whatsoever—belongs more fittingly to the Creator, and every deficiency that must be denied of a created being must all the more be denied of the Creator. Such “rational arguments” belong to the kind of comparisons set forth in the Quran, and to Allah belongs the highest description. We have discussed this at length elsewhere.

Since those who disbelieved in the revealed message held the views described above, some who disbelieved in part of it came to share certain aspects of those views.

Thus, the Jahmiyyah denied that Allah speaks, says anything, loves, or hates, and denied all His other attributes conveyed by the messengers. They thereby denied part of the very reality of the revealed message, which is Allah’s speech, and denied some of the attributes of Allah conveyed in that message.

The first to proclaim this within Islam—although it had existed among other nations before Islam—was al-Ja'd ibn Dirham, the teacher of al-Jahm ibn Safwān. He was reportedly from Harrān, whose people included leading philosophers. From them Abū Nasr al-Fārābī learned much of the philosophy he acquired, according to what 'Abd al-Latīf ibn Yūsuf al-Baghdādī related.

Khālid ibn 'Abd Allāh al-Qasrī then slaughtered al-Ja'd as a sacrifice at Wāsit, in the days of scholars among the Successors and other Muslim scholars. Among those still living from the Successors at that time were al-Hasan al-Basrī and others, who praised him for what he had done and expressed their gratitude. He said: “O people, offer your sacrifices; may Allah accept your sacrifices! For I am sacrificing al-Ja'd

---

## Page 6394

ibn Dirham, for he claimed that Allah did not take Abraham as a close friend and did not truly speak to Moses—exalted is Allah far above what al-Ja'd says!” He then descended and slaughtered him.

They based this on the principle of the innovators among the Sabians who deny some of what the messengers brought and describe the Lord only through negative or relational attributes, or attributes combining the two. In this negation of the divine attributes, they in fact agree with Pharaoh, the leader of the disbelievers, who denied the Maker altogether; for denying His attributes necessarily entails denying His very essence.

Thus they agreed with Pharaoh in rejecting Moses’ statement that his Lord is above the heavens. Pharaoh said:

“O Haman, build me a tower so that I may reach the ways—”

“The ways into the heavens—and look upon the God of Moses, though I certainly think he is a liar.”

This contrasts with Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, who confirmed Moses when he was taken up to his Lord. He reported that he found Moses there and went back and forth between his Lord and Moses. Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, thus affirmed Moses’ statement that his Lord is above the heavens, whereas Pharaoh denied it. People are either followers of Muhammad and Moses or followers of Pharaoh: Pharaoh denied Moses’ statement that Allah is above and that Allah had spoken to him, just as he denied the existence of the Maker, while Muhammad affirmed Moses in all of this.

These pure Sabians among the philosophers say that Allah does not truly have speech. Rather, according to those among them who outwardly profess belief in the messengers, His speech is what emanates into the souls of the prophets: it is something brought into being within their souls, without

---

## Page 6395

there being, in their view, any speech of Allah outside their souls. Likewise, al-Jahm initially used to say that Allah has no speech. Then, for the sake of the Muslims, he found it necessary to say that Allah does have speech, but would say, “It is figurative.”

For this reason, Imam Ahmad and the other imams understood their intent: their aim was to deny the divine attributes, and they were zindīqs (heretics)—a zindīq being a hypocrite. Thus, you find the imams describing them as heretics in their writings. Imam Ahmad, for example, wrote Refutation of the Heretics and the Jahmiyyah, and al-Bukhārī entitled the final book of his Sahīh “The Book of Divine Oneness and the Refutation of the Heretics and the Jahmiyyah.” ‘Abd Allāh ibn al-Mubārak used to say, “We can indeed recount the statements of the Jews and Christians, but we cannot bring ourselves to recount the statements of the Jahmiyyah.”

The pure Sabians—who professed faith outwardly and inwardly believed in only part of the Scripture—say that “Allah’s speech” is a name for what emanates into the prophet’s heart from the “Active Intellect” or something else, and that “Allah’s angels” is a name for the luminous forms that take shape within his soul. They may say that Gabriel is the “Active Intellect,” or that he is one of the imaginary forms appearing within the prophet’s soul, like those a sleeper sees.

Hence, these people say that what distinguishes a prophet is his ability to evoke images in the imagination, and that the prophets outwardly expressed the contrary of what they inwardly held for the benefit of the common people. Through their words, they imparted not knowledge but imaginative representations that benefited the common people. They regard this as one of the finest things, praising and venerating the prophets for it.

---

## Page 6396

And we have discussed this at length elsewhere. In their view, neither speech nor any angel exists outside the prophet’s soul. Such is the claim made by those philosophers and polytheistic Sabians who hold this view. They claimed to be believers and said that they combined prophethood with philosophy. This is what al-Fārābī, Ibn Sīnā, and other philosophers do, as do the esoteric Qarmatians among the Ismā‘īlīs and others like them, who took the ideas of the Greek and Persian philosophers and presented them in the guise of Shiism and Rāfidism. The Imāmīs, Zaydīs, and other Shiites know that these people are disbelievers.

Likewise, Ibn Sab‘īn and others who outwardly profess Sufism while following this path take these people’s ideas and clothe them in Sufi expressions. The knowledgeable Sufis know that they are disbelievers. Indeed, the great Sufi masters—such as al-Fudayl ibn ‘Iyād, Ibrāhīm ibn Adham, Abū Sulaymān al-Dārānī, ‘Amr ibn ‘Uthmān al-Shiblī, al-Junayd ibn Muhammad, Sahl ibn ‘Abd Allāh al-Tustarī, Abū ‘Abd Allāh Muhammad ibn Khafīf al-Shīrāzī, and others like them, may Allah be pleased with them—were among those most emphatic in declaring these people disbelievers.

For even if the position of these heretics contains faith in another respect, they in fact agree with their predecessor, al-Wahīd (“the solitary one”), who said:

“This is nothing but the word of a human being.”

Yet that man rejected him entirely, both outwardly and inwardly, whereas these people may believe in him outwardly and may inwardly believe in some of his attributes: that he is obeyed and held in high esteem, that he is the leader of the human race, and that this speech which

---

## Page 6397

he brought is speech of great worth, issuing from a pure soul perfected in knowledge and action, possessing three qualities that distinguish it from others: exceptional powers of intuition and knowledge; the power to influence the lower world through his own soul; and an imaginative faculty that corresponds to realities, enabling him to hear sounds within himself and see forms that imaginatively represent those realities. They also hold that his speech may be attributed to Allah and called Allah’s speech, on the grounds that He commanded it through an imagined command.

In fact, in their view, the knowledge and words that flow into all other pure souls are likewise Allah’s speech, just as this is Allah’s speech. This, however, is nobler, and his discourse indicates that he is the Messenger to creation, whom they must obey as the messengers have taught. Nevertheless, they describe him as speaking.

For this reason, they say that “prophethood” can be acquired. More than one of them therefore aspired to become a prophet, as did al-Suhrawardī, Ibn Sab‘īn, and other heretics.

We have explained the foundations of their views and their falsity elsewhere, as in our refutation of their claim that the prophets’ miracles are powers of the soul.

As for the Mu‘tazilah and others like them, they agree with these people that Allah does not speak in the real sense in which people understand someone to speak. Rather, His speech is separate from Him, though they claim that this is speech in the literal sense. His speech, in their view, amounts to nothing more than His creating in the air or elsewhere

---

## Page 6398

sounds heard by whomever He wills among His angels and prophets, without any speech subsisting in Him, whether meaning or letters. They dispute whether this created thing is a body, an accident, or something described as neither.

When these people appeared, the early generations—the Successors and their followers—declared them disbelievers and refuted them in statements well known from those generations. The discerning imams among the scholars recognized that the reality of these people’s doctrine was the denial of Allah’s attributes and heresy, even though their ordinary followers did not understand this. Likewise, they recognized that the reality of the doctrine of the Qarāmitah and Ismā‘īliyyah was the denial of Allah’s attributes and heresy, even though their ordinary followers professed only Rāfidism.

The Jahmī ordeal unfolded, and the imams were put to the test. “Imam Ahmad”—the imam of the Sunnah, the community’s champion of truth in his time, the successor to the messengers and heir to the prophets—stood firm. Through him, Allah strengthened Islam and the Quran, preserved knowledge and faith for the community, and repelled the people of unbelief, hypocrisy, and tyranny who believed in part of the Scripture and disbelieved in another.

Thus, the people of the Sunnah, the great majority of the Muslim community, those who upheld its unity, and the leading figures of the faith throughout its eastern and western lands remained firmly committed to the faith that the messengers brought from Allah and that the Seal of the Prophets brought, confirming the Scripture that preceded him and serving as a guardian over it: namely, that the Quran, the Torah, and the Gospel are Allah’s speech, and that Allah’s speech cannot be something created and separate from Him, just as a speaker’s speech cannot be separate from him. For this amounts to denying His speech, which

---

## Page 6399

is His message, and rejecting the reality of what the messengers proclaimed and their nations knew, deviating from the truth concerning Allah’s names and signs, and likening Him to what is nonexistent and lifeless. For life, knowledge, power, speech, and the like are attributes of perfection, and the Lord Most High is more entitled to every perfection. It is therefore impossible for a created being to possess any perfection without the Creator being more entitled to it, just as it is impossible for a created being to be free of any deficiency without the Creator being more entitled to freedom from it. How could it be otherwise, when He creates perfection in those endowed with it?

“Furthermore,” anything that does not possess the attributes of perfection—life, knowledge, hearing, sight, power, speech, and so forth—must either be capable of possessing them but lack them, or be incapable of possessing them.

If it is capable of possessing them but lacks them, then, by the agreement of all rational people, it is characterized by attributes of deficiency, such as death, ignorance, blindness, deafness, incapacity, and muteness. For they agree that whatever is capable of either of two opposing attributes must possess one when it lacks the other. If, however, it is said to be incapable of possessing these attributes, then it is more deficient than something capable of possessing them but lacking them. Thus, a living creature that can sometimes hear and sometimes be deaf, sometimes see and sometimes be blind, sometimes speak and sometimes be mute, is more perfect than an inanimate thing incapable of either condition.

Thus, whoever does not ascribe the attributes of perfection to Him must either ascribe these deficiencies to Him or hold that He is more deficient than one characterized by them. This is because the “philosophers”

---

## Page 6400

have conventionally divided “opposites involving negation and affirmation” into contradictories and what they call “privation and possession.” By “privation,” they mean the absence of an attribute from something naturally capable of possessing it, as with blindness and muteness: these are the absence of sight and speech from something naturally capable of seeing and speaking. Inanimate things, however, they describe in neither way.

“Their specious argument” has confused some of those engaged in rational inquiry. They supposed that if He is not described by the attributes of perfection—life, knowledge, hearing, sight, and speech—it does not necessarily follow that He possesses attributes of deficiency, because the two stand opposed as “privation and possession,” not as contradictories.

They may be answered: First, this is your own terminological convention. Others do describe inanimate things as dead, lifeless, and the like, as in His words:

“Those whom they invoke besides Allah create nothing, but are themselves created.”

“They are dead, not living.”

They may also be answered: “Second,” what must be considered is the realities apprehended by reason. It is known that the absence of these attributes necessarily entails the deficiency constituted by their absence.

They may further be answered: “Third,” if you say that He possesses neither of the two opposing attributes because He is incapable of possessing either, then this deficiency is greater than the deficiency of blindness, deafness, and muteness. For that which is incapable of

---

## Page 6401

possessing the attributes of perfection is more deficient than one who is capable of them and can possess them. For it originated from Him—not, as the Sabians and those Jahmiyyah who agree with them claim, from the Prophet’s own soul, the “Active Intellect,” or the “air.” Rather, it is a revelation from One who is All-Wise, Praiseworthy. And to Him it will return when it is taken away by night from the written copies and people’s hearts.

Imam Ahmad became a guiding authority for those of Ahl al-Sunnah who came after him, across all their groups. They all agree with his main teachings and the fundamental principles of his doctrine, because he preserved for the Muslim community its inherited faith and prophetic foundations against those who sought to distort and alter them. He did not institute a religion that Allah had not authorized. What he taught is what the other eminent imams taught; indeed, his very statements are explicitly reported from their leading figures. However, he brought together their scattered teachings, strove against those who opposed them, and demonstrated how the Quran and Sunnah supported them. His statements concerning the Jahmiyyah, and those of the imams before and after him, are numerous and well known.

The Jahmiyyah are those who deny Allah’s attributes and follow the misguided Sabians. Offshoots of Jahmism began to circulate in many people’s minds. Some who were known for adhering to the Sunnah and hadith said: “We say neither that it is created nor that it is uncreated; rather, we withhold judgment.” Inwardly, most of them held it to be created, but in their hearts they feared the believers more than they feared Allah.

---

## Page 6402

And “another group” said: “We say that Allah’s speech which He has not sent down is uncreated. As for the Quran which He sent down to His Messenger, and which Gabriel, Muhammad, and the believers recited, it is created.” These are the “Lafziyyah.”

The Muslim community therefore turned to its imam at that time for help, and Ahmad would tell them: “The Jahmiyyah have split into ‘three groups’: one says, ‘The Quran is created’; another says, ‘It is Allah’s speech,’ and says nothing further; and another says, ‘Our utterances and our recitation of the Quran are created.’”

What this last group’s position really entails is that the Quran which Gabriel brought down upon the heart of Allah’s Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, is a created Quran which Allah did not speak. Their specious argument rested on the fact that our actions and voices are created, and that we recite it only through our movements and voices. Some of them might even say: “All we have are our utterances and our recitation. There is no Quran on earth other than this, and this is created.”

They were opposed by people who intended to uphold the Sunnah but fell into innovation. They answered falsehood with falsehood and countered one unsound position with another, saying: “Our recitation of the Quran is uncreated, and our utterances of it are uncreated, because this is the Quran, and the Quran is uncreated.” They failed to distinguish between what an unqualified designation denotes and what a qualified designation denotes, or between the referent considered on its own and that referent when coupled with something else and qualified.

Imam Ahmad therefore also condemned those who said that people’s recitation, reading, utterances, and voices were uncreated. He ordered that they be shunned, just as he had declared the former group to be Jahmiyyah and innovators. And reports from him

---

## Page 6403

on this matter were transmitted by his son ʿAbd Allāh, Sālih, al-Marwadhī, Fawrān, Abū Tālib, Abū Bakr ibn Sadaqah, and a great many of his companions and followers. After his death, his closest follower, Abū Bakr al-Marwadhī, took up this matter and compiled his statements alongside those of leading scholars among his companions and others, including ʿAbd al-Wahhāb al-Warrāq, al-Athram, Abū Dāwūd al-Sijistānī, al-Fadl ibn Ziyād, Muthannā ibn Jāmiʿ al-Anbārī, Muhammad ibn Ishāq al-Sanʿānī, Muhammad ibn Sahl ibn ʿAskar, and other scholars of Islam. He explained the innovation of those who say that people’s recitation and utterances of the Quran are uncreated. Al-Khallāl mentioned this in The Book of the Sunnah and discussed it at length.

Al-Khallāl said:

Abū Bakr al-Marwadhī told me: Word reached Abū ʿAbd Allāh that Abū Tālib had written to the people of Nisibis, saying, “My utterance of the Quran is uncreated.” Abū Bakr said: Sālih ibn Ahmad came to us and said, “Come with me to my father.” We went and entered upon Abū ʿAbd Allāh, finding him intensely angry, with anger plainly visible on his face. He said, “Go and bring me Abū Tālib.” I brought him, and he sat trembling before Abū ʿAbd Allāh, who said, “Did you write to the people of Nisibis, telling them on my authority that I said, ‘My utterance of the Quran is uncreated’?”

He replied, “I was only speaking for myself.”

He said, “This is not permissible, whether as your own statement or mine. I have never heard any scholar say this.”

Abū ʿAbd Allāh said, “The Quran is Allah’s speech, uncreated, however it is conveyed.” Then Abū Tālib was told, “Go out and announce

---

## Page 6404

that Abū ʿAbd Allāh has forbidden saying, ‘My utterance of the Quran is uncreated.’”

Abū Tālib went out, met a group of hadith scholars, and told them that Abū ʿAbd Allāh had forbidden him to say, “My utterance of the Quran is uncreated.”

Despite this, each of the “two groups”—those who say, “Our utterance of the Quran is uncreated,” and those who say, “Our utterance and recitation are created”—claims allegiance to Abū ʿAbd Allāh, attributes its own position to him, and maintains that he held its view. This is because he is an imam accepted by all, and because Ahmad affirms whatever truth each group holds and rejects whatever falsehood each group condemns in the other.

Thus Muhammad ibn Dāwūd al-Missīsī—one of the hadith scholars and one of Abū Dāwūd’s teachers—and a number of his contemporaries, such as Abū Hātim al-Rāzī and others, would say, “Our utterance of the Quran is uncreated.” A group followed them in this, including Abū ʿAbd Allāh ibn Hāmid, Abū Nasr al-Sijzī, Abū ʿAbd Allāh ibn Mandah, Shaykh al-Islam Abū Ismāʿīl al-Ansārī, Abū al-ʿAlāʾ al-Hamdānī, Abū al-Faraj al-Maqdisī, and others. They say, “Our utterances of the Quran are uncreated,” and report this from Ahmad, claiming that he subsequently adopted this position, as Abū Nasr mentioned in his book al-Ibānah (The Clarification).

These, however, are weak reports with unknown chains of transmission. They cannot stand against what has been mass-transmitted from him through his closest companions, his household, and trustworthy scholars—especially since it is known that, during his lifetime, he declared Abū Tālib mistaken in what he reported from him, until Ahmad made him retract it, and became intensely angry with him.

---

## Page 6405

I have seen some of these people challenge those firmly established reports from him, while others have altered their wording. As for distorting their meanings, various groups have done so.

Those who accepted the reports from him as authentic and agreed with his rejection of both positions include the majority of the people of the Sunnah, as well as speculative theologians who affiliated themselves with them, such as Abū al-Hasan al-Ash'arī and others like him. In “The Doctrines of the People of the Sunnah and Hadith,” al-Ash'arī states that they condemn both those who say, “My utterance of the Quran is created,” and those who say, “My utterance of it is uncreated,” and that he himself holds this position.

Some of these people, however, interpreted the statements of Ahmad and others on this matter as prohibiting the assertion that the Quran is uttered. This interpretation was advanced by al-Ash'arī, Ibn al-Bāqillānī, Judge Abū Ya'lā, and the latter’s followers, such as Abū al-Hasan ibn al-Zāghūnī and others like him.

Among those who interpreted his statements in this way, some affirmed the very meaning that Ahmad had condemned in those who said, “My utterance of the Quran is created.” This was the position taken by al-Ash'arī and his followers. Others instead affirmed the meaning that Ahmad had condemned in those who said, “My utterance of it is uncreated.” This was the position taken by the judge, Ibn al-Zāghūnī, and others like them.

For Ahmad and all the other imams reject the claim that any part of Allah’s speech—whether its letters or its meanings—is created; that the meaning of the Torah is the same as the meaning of the Quran; or that Allah’s speech is the Quran when expressed in Arabic and the Torah when expressed in Hebrew. They also reject the claim that the revealed Quran is not itself Allah’s speech, or that it be asserted without qualification

---

## Page 6406

that what is Allah’s speech is created. Ahmad and the other imams also reject the claim that any human actions or voices are uncreated, let alone eternal. Ahmad’s statements on the questions of recitation, faith, and the Quran follow a consistent pattern: he prohibited declaring without qualification that these are created, because this entails saying that some of Allah’s attributes are created and opens the door to that assertion. He likewise prohibited declaring without qualification that they are uncreated, because of the innovation and misguidance this involves.

Since Ahmad had become the imam of the Sunnah, those who came after him and affiliated themselves with the Sunnah acknowledged him as their imam. Al-Ash‘arī mentions this in his book al-Ibāna and elsewhere, saying:

“If someone says, ‘You have rejected the positions of the Jahmiyyah, the Mu‘tazilah, the Khawārij, the Rāfidah, and the Murji’ah. Tell us, then, the position you uphold and the religion you profess,’ he is told: ‘The position we uphold and the religion we profess consist in adhering to the Book of our Lord, the Sunnah of our Prophet, and what has been transmitted from the Companions and the Successors. We affirm what Abū ‘Abd Allāh Ahmad ibn Hanbal affirmed, and shun whatever contradicts his teachings. For he is the consummate imam and eminent leader through whom Allah made the truth manifest, clarified the path, and suppressed the innovations of the innovators, the deviations of those who stray, and the doubts of the doubters.’”

He then mentioned a number of doctrinal points.

---

## Page 6407

For this reason, those who came after him disagreed on this issue. The group who say, “Our utterance and recitation are uncreated,” identify themselves with him and claim that this was the later of his two positions. Alternatively, they challenge reports from him that contradict this, or interpret his words in ways he did not intend.

The group who say that recitation is created, that the revealed Quran brought down by Gabriel is created, and that Allah did not speak the letters of the Quran, claim that this is Ahmad’s position and that they agree with him. Abū al-Hasan al-Ash‘arī did this in what he reported from Ahmad, how he interpreted his words, and his declaration that he agreed with him. Likewise, Judge Abū Bakr al-Bāqillānī sought to clear his fellow adherents of contradicting the Sunnah and its imams, such as Imam Ahmad. Abū Nu‘aym al-Asbahānī did the same in his well-known book on this subject, as did Abū Dharr al-Harawī and Judge ‘Abd al-Wahhāb al-Mālikī.

Similarly, some people falsely alleged that al-Bukhārī, the imam and compiler of the Sahīh, used to say, “My utterance of the Quran is created.” They classed him among the “Lafziyyah,” until a dispute arose between him and his fellow scholars, such as Muhammad ibn Yahyā al-Dhuhlī

## Page 6408

and Abū Zur‘ah, Abū Hātim, and others over this matter. Personal inclinations and suspicions played a part in the affair, until he composed The Creation of Acts. In it, he included his report from Abū Qudāmah, from Yahyā ibn Sa‘īd al-Qattān, who said: “I have always heard our companions say, ‘The acts of Allah’s servants are created.’”

He also stated therein what accords with what he mentioned at the end of his Sahīh: that the Quran is Allah’s speech, uncreated, and that Allah speaks with a voice and calls out with a voice. He presented authentic hadiths and reports on this subject which this is not the place to discuss at length. He explained the distinction between the voice with which Allah calls out and the voices heard from His servants, and that the voice with which Allah spoke is not the voice heard from the reciter. He set out the evidence for this, explaining that the acts and voices of Allah’s servants are created, whereas Allah Most High, His action, and His speech are uncreated.

Concerning His words,

“No reminder comes to them anew from their Lord,”

he said that its newness is unlike that of created beings. He also cited the words of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“Allah introduces whatever commands He wills, and among what He has introduced is that you must not speak during prayer.”

He related from the scholars of the early generations that the Lord’s act of creating the world is not the created thing itself; rather, His action, which subsists in Him, is uncreated. It was also related from Nu‘aym ibn Hammād al-Khuzā‘ī that action is inseparable from life, and that whoever is living must be active. He mentioned other points of this kind, demonstrating his knowledge and that of the early generations of the truth that accords with authentic transmitted reports and clear reason.

## Page 6409

He also mentioned that each of the two factions of the Lafziyyah—those who affirm and those who deny—claims allegiance to Abū ‘Abd Allāh; that much of what is transmitted from Ahmad ibn Hanbal is falsely attributed to him; that they failed to understand some of his statements because of their subtlety and obscurity; and that what he himself and Imam Ahmad said is the position of the imams and scholars, supported by the Quran and Sunnah.

I saw the following in the handwriting of Judge Abū Ya‘lā—may Allah have mercy on him—on the back of his handwritten copy of The Book of al-‘Uddah:

> I copied from the end of al-Bukhārī’s Book of the Epistle, concerning the distinction between reciting and what is recited. He said:
>
> “Reports from Ahmad ibn Hanbal have reached me in twenty-two versions, all contradicting one another. What I consider authentic is that he said: ‘I have never heard a scholar say: My utterance of the Quran is uncreated.’”
>
> He said: “Ahmad ibn Hanbal’s followers split into some fifty groups.”
>
> Abū ‘Abd Allāh al-Bukhārī said: “Ibn Hanbal said: ‘A Lafzī is someone who says: The Quran as uttered by us is created.’”

Toward the end of Abū ‘Abd Allāh’s lifetime, there had also emerged members of the Kullābiyyah and similar groups—the followers of Abū Muhammad ‘Abd Allāh ibn Sa‘īd ibn Kullāb al-Basrī, who composed works refuting the Jahmiyyah, the Mu‘tazilah, and others. He was one of the speculative theologians who affirmed the divine attributes, and his approach inclined toward the position of the people of hadith and Sunnah. Nevertheless, it contained an element of innovation, because he affirmed that the attributes subsist in Allah’s essence but did not affirm that matters dependent on His will subsist in His essence. Yet, in refuting the Jahmiyyah—those who deny the divine attributes and Allah’s exaltedness—he presented such evidence, arguments, and extensive discussion as demonstrated his distinction

---

## Page 6410

in this field and his refutation of the doctrines of those who deny the attributes through various forms of proof and argument. What he presented became an aid and support for many people of understanding, delivering them from those specious arguments. He thus became an exemplar and leader for those who came after him who affirmed the attributes and refuted those who denied them. Nevertheless, they shared some of the deniers’ unsound foundational principles, which rendered some of their statements rationally unsound and contrary to the Messenger’s Sunnah.

Among his followers were al-Hārith al-Muhāsibī and Abū al-‘Abbās al-Qalānisī, followed by Abū al-Hasan al-Ash‘arī, Abū al-Hasan ibn Mahdī al-Tabarī, Abū al-‘Abbās al-Duba‘ī, Abū Sulaymān al-Dimashqī, Abū Hātim al-Bustī, and others who affirmed the attributes, affiliated themselves with the Sunnah and hadith, and bore the title “the speculative theologians of the people of hadith.”

Many later followers of Mālik, al-Shāfi‘ī, and Ahmad adopted Ibn Kullāb’s approach of distinguishing between “inherent attributes,” such as life, and “attributes dependent on His will,” holding that the former, but not the latter, subsist in the Lord. These included members of the Tamīmī family: Abū al-Hasan al-Tamīmī, his son Abū al-Fadl al-Tamīmī, and his grandson Rizq Allāh al-Tamīmī. In discussing Ahmad’s beliefs as part of his account of Ahmad’s virtues, Abū Bakr al-Bayhaqī relied on al-Fadl’s creed, which al-Fadl stated was Ahmad’s creed. Likewise, this approach of Ibn Kullāb was adopted by Abū al-Hasan ibn Sālim and his followers

---

## Page 6411

—the “Sālimiyyah”—and by Judge Abū Ya‘lā and his followers, such as Ibn ‘Aqīl and Abū al-Hasan ibn al-Zāghūnī. This was also the approach of Abū al-Ma‘ālī al-Juwaynī, Abū al-Walīd al-Bājī, Judge Abū Bakr ibn al-‘Arabī, and others. Although they shared the distinction established by Ibn Kullāb, they divided into two positions concerning the Quran and certain other questions. Their views have been discussed at length elsewhere.

Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal and other imams of the Sunnah warned against this principle introduced by Ibn Kullāb and against his followers. This was why Imam Ahmad warned against al-Hārith al-Muhāsibī and other Kullābīs like him.

When these people emerged, there also appeared among those who professed to affirm the divine attributes some who said, “Allah has not spoken with a voice.” Ahmad rejected this and declared those who said it to be Jahmīs. He said, “These heretics seek nothing but the negation of the divine attributes.” He transmitted reports establishing that Allah speaks with a voice. He likewise condemned those who said that the letters were created.

‘Abd Allāh ibn Ahmad ibn Hanbal said in the Book of the Sunnah:

“I said to my father, ‘There are people here who say that Allah does not speak with a voice.’ He replied, ‘My son, these people are Jahmīs and heretics. They seek nothing but the negation of the divine attributes.’ He then cited reports contradicting their claim.”

---

## Page 6412

Likewise, al-Bukhārī, compiler of the Sahīh, and the other imams also rejected this. At the end of the Sahīh and in The Creation of Actions, al-Bukhārī transmitted the reports concerning this matter and explained the distinction between Allah’s voice with which He speaks and the voices of His servants reciting the Quran. In agreement with Imam Ahmad and the other imams, he explained that Allah speaks with a voice, as the reports establish, and that this is not the voice of the servant reciting; that voice, rather, is the servant’s own. He expressly stated all of this in several places.

The imams of the Sunnah and hadith generally affirm this and uphold this distinction. They do not agree with those who claim that divine speech contains neither letters nor sound, nor with those who claim that the voices heard from reciters and their utterances are beginningless. Nor do they say that the Quran consists of nothing but letters and sounds.

I have recorded Imam Ahmad’s statements and explicit pronouncements, along with the statements of the imams before and after him, elsewhere, since the answer to this question does not allow for extensive elaboration. Neither Imam Ahmad nor the other imams stated that the voice with which Allah spoke was beginningless. Rather, they say, “Allah has always been One who speaks.” They may also say, “Allah has always been One who speaks whenever He wills, saying whatever He wills,” as Imam Ahmad, Ibn al-Mubārak, and others have said.

Likewise, in their time and afterward, their followers and others disputed the meaning of the Quran’s being uncreated: whether what is meant is that speech itself is beginningless

---

## Page 6413

and eternal, like His knowledge, or that Allah has always possessed the attribute of speaking whenever He wills. There are two views on this. Al-Hārith al-Muhāsibī reported both views from the adherents of the Sunnah, as did Abū Bakr ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz from the followers of Imam Ahmad in his book al-Shāfī. Abū ʿAbd Allāh Ibn Hāmid also mentioned them in his book Usūl al-Dīn (The Foundations of Religion).

This dispute exists among the various groups adhering to the Sunnah and hadith. It rests on the underlying question of “attributes pertaining to voluntary acts.” This question is disputed among all the groups devoted to hadith, the Sunnah, jurisprudence, and Sufism, including those adherents of the four legal schools who joined them, as well as among the other sects—even among the philosophers. I have examined this thoroughly elsewhere.

This is the source of disagreement among those who agreed with the early generations that the Quran is Allah’s speech, uncreated. They differed over whether the Lord speaks by His will and power, holding two views.

Those who agreed with Ibn Kullāb said that He does not speak by His will and power; rather, His speech is inseparable from His essence, like His life. Some among them recognized that individual letters and sounds cannot be beginningless. They therefore could not say that what is beginningless consists of letters and sounds, because these can only occur in succession, and a sound does not persist for two moments, let alone be beginningless.

They therefore said that what is beginningless is a single meaning, since an infinity of meanings is impossible, as is singling out one number rather than another. Thus, they said that it is a single meaning. They also said that Allah does not speak in Arabic or Hebrew, and that the meaning of the Torah, the Gospel, the Quran, and all of Allah’s other speech is one and the same

---

## Page 6414

and that the Verse of the Throne and the Verse of Debt have one and the same meaning, along with other implications that most rational people regard as self-evidently false.

Some of these people recognized that Allah spoke the Arabic Quran and the Hebrew Torah, that He called out to Moses with a voice and calls out to His servants with a voice, and that the Quran—both its letters and its meanings—is Allah’s speech. Yet they also believed that it is beginningless in its particular existence and that Allah did not speak by His will and power.

They therefore committed themselves to the view that it consists of letters and sounds whose individual existence is beginningless: they have always existed and always will. They said that the letter bā did not precede the sīn, nor did the sīn precede the mīm, and that all the letters coexist in a beginningless conjunction that has always existed and always will. They said, “They are ordered in their reality and essence, but not in their existence.”

Many of them also said that, despite this, they are one thing, along with other “implications” that most rational people regard as self-evidently false.

Some of these people say, “It is beginningless,” without understanding what “beginningless” means. When asked about this, they say, “They are beginningless in divine knowledge,” not realizing that created things, such as heaven and earth, are likewise so, despite being created. Others call it “ancient,” meaning that it precedes other things, without realizing that those who say it is created do not dispute its being ancient in this sense. Still others say, “By saying that it is beginningless, we mean that it is uncreated,” without understanding that, on this view, it is also eternal and has always existed. These people heard

---

## Page 6415

from those who agreed with them that it is uncreated: “It is beginningless.” They therefore agreed that it is beginningless without understanding what they were saying. Likewise, some people said, “It is uncreated,” meaning that it is not fabricated. This is something people have never disputed, just as they have never disputed that it is ancient in the sense of preceding other things.

The second position is that Allah speaks by His will and power, while His speech is uncreated. This is the position of the great majority of the people of Sunnah and rational inquiry, and of the leading authorities in Sunnah and hadith. Some of them, however, believed that Allah could not have spoken by His will in beginningless eternity, just as, in their view, He could not have done anything in beginningless eternity. They therefore committed themselves to saying that He spoke by His will after not having spoken, just as He acted after not having acted. This is the position of many scholars of speculative theology, hadith, and Sunnah.

As for the early generations and the leading authorities, they said that Allah speaks by His will and power, while His speech is nevertheless beginningless in kind—meaning that He has always spoken whenever He wills. Speech is an attribute of perfection: one who speaks is more perfect than one who does not speak; one who speaks by his will and power is more perfect than one who does not speak by his will and power; and one who has always spoken by his will and power is more perfect than one for whom speech becomes possible only after having been impossible—even supposing that this were possible. How much more so, then, if

---

## Page 6416

this is impossible? For it is impossible for the Lord to become capable after not having been so, or for speaking and acting to become possible after having been impossible. This has been explained at length elsewhere.

The “Lafziyyah khalqiyyah” among the scholars of hadith—those who held utterances to be created—used to say: “We say that our utterances of the Quran are created, that recitation is distinct from what is recited, and that reading is distinct from what is read.” The “affirming Lafziyyah” say: “We say that our utterances of the Quran are uncreated, that recitation is itself what is recited, and that reading is itself what is read.”

As for the position explicitly reported from Imam Ahmad, his leading followers, and the other leading authorities in Sunnah and hadith, they say neither that these utterances are created nor that they are uncreated. Nor do they say without qualification that recitation is itself what is recited, or that it is distinct from what is recited, just as they do not say that a name is itself the thing named or that it is distinct from the thing named.

For “recitation” and “reading,” like “utterance,” may be used as verbal nouns in the sequences “recited, recites, recitation,” “read, reads, reading,” and “uttered, utters, utterance.” What the verbal noun denotes is the servant’s action and movements. What is meant by the terms recitation, reading, and utterance in this sense is created; it is not the speech that is heard, which is what is recited.

“Utterance,” however, may mean what is uttered; “recitation,” what is recited; and “reading,” what is read. This is the speech that is heard, and that is what is recited. It is well known that the recited Quran, which the servant recites and utters

---

## Page 6417

is uncreated. These terms may also refer to both things together. It is therefore impermissible either to describe the whole as created or to deny that any of it is created.

Ibn Kullāb came to mean by “recitation” the Arabic Quran, and by “what is recited” the meaning subsisting in the divine essence. When these people say, “Recitation is distinct from what is recited, and it is created,” it is as though they mean that Allah did not speak the Arabic Quran. Rather, they hold that the Arabic Quran is created. None of the leading authorities in Sunnah and hadith said this. These people think that they agree with al-Bukhārī or others who may distinguish between recitation and what is recited, but that is not the case.

Others say, “Recitation is itself what is recited,” meaning that the very letters and sounds that Allah spoke are the sounds heard from reciters. They thus identify the voice heard from the servant with the voice of the Lord. These people say that the created being’s own voice and attribute are identical to the Creator’s attribute. They are “advocates of union and indwelling with respect to the attributes,” resembling Christians in some respects. None of the leading authorities in Sunnah said this. These people think that they agree with Ahmad, Ishāq, and others who condemn the “Lafziyyah,” but that is not the case.

For this reason, the position explicitly reported from Imam Ahmad and the leading authorities in Sunnah and hadith is that one must not say, “Our utterances of the Quran are created,” or, “They are not

---

## Page 6418

created.” Nor should one say without qualification that recitation is identical to what is recited, or that it is distinct from what is recited. The terms “utterance” and “speech” may encompass both. Thus, speech is sometimes treated as a category alongside action, rather than as part of it, as in Allah’s words:

“To Him ascends good speech, and righteous deeds raise it up.”

At other times, speech is included within action, as in His words:

“So by your Lord, We will surely question them all about what they used to do.”

A group of the early Muslims explained that this refers to saying, “There is no god worthy of worship but Allah.” Another example is the Prophet’s statement (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) in an authentic hadith:

“Envy is warranted only in two cases: a man whom Allah has granted the Quran, who recites it throughout the night and day, whereupon another man says, ‘If I had been given what this man has, I would do as he does.’”

For this reason, Ahmad’s followers differed over whether someone who swore not to perform any action that day would break his oath by speaking. There are two opinions, both mentioned by al-Qādī Abū Yaʿlā and others.

The “Lafziyyah who affirmed createdness” did not deny that the Quran—its letters and meanings—is Allah’s speech, or that Allah speaks with a voice. Indeed, they might say that the entire Quran, its letters and meanings, is Allah’s speech, for Allah speaks with a voice, as Ahmad, al-Bukhārī, and other leading authorities explicitly affirmed, and as the transmitted reports attest. Yet they say that the letters and meanings sent down to earth are not the very speech of Allah, which is uncreated. They may instead call them a reproduction of Allah’s speech, as Ibn Kullāb does, or an expression of Allah’s speech, as al-Ashʿarī does. They may also call them Allah’s speech, since the intended meaning is understood among them.

---

## Page 6419

But when Abū Muhammad ibn Kullāb emerged and debated the Muʿtazilah using a method of logical inference, he conceded premises that they themselves had devised: that Allah Most High cannot speak in letters, and that “volitional attributes”—actions, speech, and other things connected to His will and power—cannot subsist in His essence. Their reasoning was that this would entail that He had not been free of originated events, and whatever is not free of originated events is itself originated. These concessions compelled him to say that Allah’s speech is nothing but meaning alone, and that letters are not part of Allah’s speech.

Abū al-Hasan al-Ashʿarī followed him in this, although they disagreed over whether the Lord had been commanding and prohibiting from eternity or came to command and prohibit after not having done so. They also disagreed over whether “speech” is one attribute, as al-Ashʿarī maintained, or five attributes, as Ibn Kullāb maintained.

These men thus differed from the leading authorities of the Sunnah and hadith in two respects. (The first is that, in their view, half of the Quran is Allah’s speech, while the other half is not Allah’s speech. Rather, Allah created it in the air or in the Preserved Tablet, or Gabriel or Muhammad—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—brought it into being.

By holding that half of the Quran is created, these men agree with those who maintain that it is created. Yet these say that this created half is Allah’s speech, while those say that it is created, separate from Allah, and is His speech. Those, however, do not affirm that Allah has any speech connected to Him and subsisting in His own being—neither meanings nor letters. These, on the other hand, say that Allah has speech subsisting in Him

---

## Page 6420

and connected to Him, consisting of meaning. Thus, the former are more extreme in their innovation in denying that Allah truly speaks and in declaring His speech created.

The latter are more extreme in their innovation in excluding from Allah’s speech what actually belongs to it. In this they agree with part, though not all, of what al-Wahīd said, namely, in their claim: “Half of the Quran is not Allah’s speech, but human speech.”

Some of them may argue that, since it is attributed to the Messenger, he must have brought its letters into being. Yet anyone making this argument has failed to reflect and recognize that Allah attributes it on one occasion to a messenger who is Gabriel, and on another to a messenger who is Muhammad. In the first passage, He says:

“Indeed, it is the word of a noble messenger,
possessed of power and securely established with the Lord of the Throne,
obeyed there and trustworthy.”

This is Gabriel. In the other passage, He says:

“Indeed, it is the word of a noble messenger.
It is not the word of a poet—little do you believe!
Nor is it the word of a soothsayer—little do you take heed!”

This is Muhammad. If its attribution to the Messenger meant that he originated its letters and brought them into being, it could not properly be attributed to both of them, since it is impossible for each of them to have brought its letters into being.

Furthermore, He says:

“Indeed, it is the word of a messenger.”

This is a statement about the Quran—a designation more properly applied to its meaning, both in their view and in that of the people of the Sunnah. Had the Messenger originated it, the Quran would have come from him, not from Allah. Allah attributed it to the Messenger only because he conveyed it, delivered it, and brought it from Allah. Hence He said:

“The word of a messenger,”

rather than “the word of an angel” or “a prophet.” Instead, He used the designation “messenger” to make clear

---

## Page 6421

that he is an intermediary and an envoy in conveying it. Speech is properly attributed to the one whose attribute it is and who originates and produces it, not to one who utters it merely to convey and deliver it. This applies to all human speech—how much more so to Allah’s speech?

This follows the well-known interpretation, which accords with the apparent meaning of the Quran: the messenger in one passage is Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and in the other, Gabriel, peace be upon him. According to those who take the messenger in both passages to be Gabriel, the second response applies. This affirmation is, in fact, evidence for those who say that he merely utters Allah’s speech and speaks His words, for Allah describes the messenger as speaking the words of Allah with which He sent him. The meaning is certainly intended here, just as the wording is also intended.

Furthermore, these people regard the speech that is Allah’s attribute as a single meaning, which is command, prohibition, statement, and inquiry. They hold that, if expressed in Arabic, it is the Quran; if expressed in Hebrew, it is the Torah; and if expressed in Syriac, it is the Gospel. The overwhelming majority of rational people agree that the falsity of this is self-evident.

The “second point” on which they differ from the people of the Sunnah and the community is their assertion that the Quran sent down to earth is not Allah’s speech—neither its letters nor its meanings. Rather, in their view, it is created. They say that it is an expression of the meaning subsisting within Him, because

---

## Page 6422

an expression does not resemble what it expresses, unlike a reproduction and its original. This involves additional innovations not found in the position of the “Lafziyyah” among the people of hadith, whom the imams of the Sunnah denounced and called “Jahmiyyah.” For these people hold that the letters originated with the Messenger and are in no way among the words Allah spoke. They also say that Allah has no speech on earth.

Likewise, none of the early “Lafziyyah” who said, “Our utterance of the Quran is uncreated,” maintained that a servant’s voice is uncreated, that the eternal voice is heard from a servant, that this voice is Allah’s voice, or that Allah’s voice is heard alongside it. Only the extremists among them introduced this notion, just as the extremists of the other group introduced the claim that the letters of the Quran are not Allah’s speech. These two heinous “innovations” had not yet appeared among those deviants of the two groups whose views Imam Ahmad and others denounced. The latter extremists also held that the Quran is nothing more than a meaning subsisting within Him, and that Allah’s speech in the Torah, the Gospel, and the Quran all amounts to that meaning.

The “other” group recognized that the letters of the Quran are part of Allah’s speech, and that the Quran—both its letters and its meanings—is Allah’s speech. They recognized that a single meaning cannot be command, prohibition, statement, and inquiry, and that the Torah, the Gospel, and the Quran cannot all convey one and the same meaning. They knew that, if we translated the Torah into Arabic, its meaning would not become the meaning of the Quran, and that these claims are known to be false

---

## Page 6423

as a matter of self-evident knowledge. Some of them opposed these claims on the grounds that the Quran consists of letters and sound. Some believed that the Quran, and speech generally, consists of nothing but letters and sounds, whereas the other group says that speech is nothing but the meaning subsisting within the self.

Both these newly introduced denials contradict the position of the imams, such as Imam Ahmad, and other imams and leading scholars of the various groups. In their usage, speech denotes both letters and meanings, just as “the human being,” endowed with speech, denotes both body and soul. Whoever says that the human being is nothing but this visible physical whole is like someone who says that speech is nothing but articulated sounds. Whoever says that the human being is nothing but a subtle entity beyond this body is like someone who says that speech is nothing but a meaning beyond these letters and sounds. Both positions deny part of the realities designated by these terms and reject the bounds of what Allah has revealed to His Messenger.

Section

Furthermore, the offshoots of the “negating Lafziyyah,” who say that the letters of the Quran are not part of Allah’s speech, report that their opponents say: “The Quran is nothing but the sounds heard from a servant and the ink written on paper,

---

## Page 6424

and that these sounds and this ink are both eternal.” No one who says that the Quran consists of nothing but letters and sounds has made this claim. Rather, they have denied and rejected it, and accused those who attribute to them the belief that ink is eternal of lying. Yet ignorant extremists may say such things, as is reported of some prominent individuals among them, such as the inhabitants of certain mountains: that the paper, the leather binding, the peg, and the surrounding portion of the wall are Allah’s speech—or similar nonsense that no Muslim or rational person would utter.

The offshoots of the “affirming Lafziyyah,” who say that the Quran consists of nothing but letters and sound, report that their opponents hold that the Quran is not preserved in hearts, recited by tongues, or written in copies of the Quran. This, too, is not their opponents’ position. Rather, they agree that the Quran is preserved in hearts, recited by tongues, and written in copies of the Quran. However, when the ignorant and extreme among them reflect on the true implications of their more moderate members’ position—that Allah did not speak the Arabic Quran; that it is nothing but a single meaning subsisting in His Essence; that the sounds produced by servants and the ink in copies of the Quran signify that meaning; that there is no actual speech of Allah on earth, but only that which signifies Allah’s speech; that He has said only what signifies Allah’s speech; that Allah’s speech, if expressed in Arabic, is the Quran, if expressed in Hebrew, is the Torah, and if expressed in Syriac, is the Gospel; that it is a single meaning admitting neither multiplicity nor division; and that the Lord does not speak by His will and power; and so on to

---

## Page 6425

other such implications of the more moderate members’ position—they strip the written copy of the Quran of its sanctity, sometimes trampling it underfoot, and sometimes writing it with excrement or other substances. These people are more deeply steeped in disbelief and hypocrisy than those who say that the leather binding and paper are Allah’s speech. The latter believe in the truth but add falsehood to it, whereas the former deny the Book and that with which Allah sent His messengers. They will come to know, when shackles and chains are around their necks and they are dragged through boiling water, then burned in the Fire.

As for those who understand this doctrine and believe in the revealed law, they venerate the written copy of the Quran, recognize its sanctity, and uphold the rulings that the revealed law prescribes concerning it. Although their position contains an element of error and innovation, and their doctrine contains such Jahmism and misguidance that they deny some of Allah’s attributes and some of the attributes of His speech and His messengers, reject some of what Allah revealed to His messengers, and become the effeminate counterparts of the male Jahmiyyah who deny all the attributes, they nevertheless base their position on interpretation and intend to attain the truth.

Despite this Jahmism of theirs, they say:

“The Quran is written in the written copy of the Quran just as Allah is written in it; it is recited by tongues just as Allah is mentioned by tongues; and it is preserved in hearts just as Allah is known in hearts.”

This position contains its share of misguidance, hypocrisy, and ignorance of the bounds of what Allah has revealed to His Messenger. It is what has led the ignorant to disregard the sanctity of

---

## Page 6426

Allah’s verses and names, to the point that they deviated concerning His names and verses.

Similarly, the former group’s unqualified assertion that the Quran has no reality other than letters and sounds, their failure to distinguish between Allah’s voice heard from Him and the reciter’s voice, and their assertion that the Quran is eternal led the ignorant among them, and those who lied about them, to report that they held that people’s voices and the ink in the written copy of the Quran are eternal, and that the letters constituting Allah’s speech are the ink itself. Yet they did not say this; rather, they rejected it, just as Allah distinguished words from ink in His saying:

“Say, ‘If the sea were ink for the words of my Lord, the sea would be exhausted before the words of my Lord were exhausted, even if We brought its like as a supplement.’”

These people made “two errors”: an error concerning their own doctrine and an error concerning the revealed law. As for the error in their “representation of their doctrine,” they should have said that the Quran is in the written copy just as knowledge and meanings are on paper. Just as one says, “Knowledge is in this book,” one says, “Speech is in this book.” For, in their view, speech is the meaning subsisting in the essence. Its analogue should therefore be knowledge subsisting in the essence, not the essence itself.

As for the error concerning “the revealed law,” they should be told: The Quran is in written copies just as Allah’s name is in written copies. For the Quran is speech: it is preserved in hearts just as speech is preserved in hearts, and it is mentioned by tongues just as mention is made of

---

## Page 6427

speech by tongues. It is written in copies of the Quran and on sheets, just as speech is written in copies of the Quran and on sheets. Speech, understood as verbal expression, corresponds to meaning and signifies it, while meaning corresponds to existing realities.

Whoever says, “The Quran is preserved just as Allah is known; it is recited just as Allah is mentioned; and it is written just as the Messenger is written,” has erred by two levels in his analogy and comparison. For he has equated the existence of entities that subsist in themselves with the existence of an expression signifying a meaning that corresponds to those entities. Muslims know the difference between His saying, exalted is He:

“Indeed, it is a noble Quran, in a protected Book,”

and His saying, exalted is He:

“And indeed, it is in the scriptures of the former peoples.”

The Quran was not sent down to anyone before Muhammad—neither its wording nor the entirety of its meanings. Rather, Allah sent down mention of it and information about it, just as He sent down mention of Muhammad and information about him. Thus, the Quran is mentioned in the scriptures of the former peoples just as Muhammad is mentioned in those scriptures, and he is written about in the Torah and the Gospel they possess.

Allah and His Messenger are known in hearts, mentioned by tongues, and written about in the written copy of the Quran, just as the Quran was known to those before us, mentioned to them, and written about in their scriptures. That was only mention of it and information about it. As for us, the Quran itself has been sent down to us, and the Quran itself is written in our copies, just as the Quran itself is in the protected Book and in the purified scriptures.

For this reason, a distinction must be made between His saying, exalted is He:

“And everything they have done is in the records”

---

## Page 6428

and His saying, exalted is He:

“By a Book inscribed on parchment unrolled.”

For deeds are in the records just as the Messenger and the Quran are in the scriptures of the former peoples. As for “the Book inscribed on parchment unrolled,” this is like speech itself being written on a sheet. How different the two are!

This is because everything has “four levels” of existence: existence in external reality, existence in minds, existence in speech, and existence in writing—that is, concrete, cognitive, verbal, and written existence.

For this reason, the first words Allah revealed of the Quran were:

“Read in the name of your Lord who created.”

In this passage, He mentioned that He, glorified is He, bestows both forms of existence. He said:

“Read in the name of your Lord who created—created man from a clinging clot.”

This is existence in external reality. Then He said:

“Read, and your Lord is the Most Generous, who taught by the pen—taught man what he did not know.”

Thus, He mentioned that He bestowed cognitive, mental existence. He mentioned teaching by the pen because it necessarily entails teaching words and expression, and teaching words and expression necessarily entails teaching meaning. By mentioning the last level, He thus indicated the first. Had He mentioned the first level alone, or spoken simply of teaching, that would not have indicated universality and comprehensiveness.

Since this is so, the Quran is speech, and speech occupies “the third level”; there is no other level intervening between it and the paper. Rather, speech itself is recorded in the book, as Allah, exalted is He, said:

“Indeed, it is a noble Quran, in a Book

---

## Page 6429

well-protected.” And He, exalted is He, said:

And He said:

“Even if We had sent down to you a book on a sheet of paper.”

It may be said that it is written in them, just as one may say without qualification that it is in them, as He, exalted is He, said:

“By the Mount, and a Book inscribed on parchment unrolled.”

As for the Lord, glorified is He, His Messenger, or any other entity, only the name appears in the scriptures, and that name is speech. Hence He said:

“Those who follow the Messenger, the unlettered Prophet, whom they find written of in the Torah and the Gospel in their possession.”

What is in the Torah is merely the written record of him, his mention, description, and name. This is the “fourth level” of his existence. How, then, can the Quran or speech being in scriptures or on paper be likened to Allah, His Messenger, the sky, or the earth being in scriptures or on paper? If someone were to say, “Allah or His Messenger is in the scriptures or on paper,” that would be rejected unless accompanied by contextual indications clarifying the intended meaning, as in His saying:

“Everything they did is in the records.”

And His saying:

“Indeed, it is in the scriptures of the former peoples.”

What is meant is its mention and written record. Zubur is the plural of zabūr. Zabūr follows the pattern faʿūl with the meaning of mafʿūl—that is, mazbūr, meaning “written.” Thus, the word zabūr denotes writing. This is like what appears in the well-known hadith reported by Maysara al-Fajr, who said: “I said, ‘O Messenger of Allah,

## Page 6430

when did you become a prophet?’—or, in another narration, ‘When were you recorded as a prophet?’ He replied, ‘While Adam was between spirit and body.’” Reported by Ahmad.

This “being” refers to his being recorded and decreed, which is the “fourth level,” as explained above. This level, with Allah and with whomever He wills among His creation, precedes the existence of created beings, although it may also come afterward. For:

“Allah recorded the decrees of all created beings fifty thousand years before He created the heavens and the earth.”

Muslim related this in his Sahīh from ‘Abd Allāh ibn ‘Amr, from the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him. Hence, regarding His words,

“Indeed, We were having all that you did transcribed,”

Ibn ‘Abbās said that Allah commands the angels to copy from the Preserved Tablet what He has recorded of the divine decree, and commands the recording angels to write down the deeds of Adam’s descendants. They then compare the two records, and they match exactly. Ibn ‘Abbās would then say: “Are you not Arabs? Can a copy be made from anything but an original?”

Decreeing and recording proceed from the general to the detailed. When Allah Most High decreed the destinies of created beings fifty thousand years before creating the heavens and the earth, He did not disclose that decree to the angels. When He created Adam, before breathing the spirit into him, He disclosed to them what He had decreed, just as He discloses it to them concerning each child. Thus, it is related in the Sahīh from Ibn Mas‘ūd that the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“The creation of each of you is brought together in his mother’s womb for forty days as a drop of sperm, then he becomes a clinging clot for a similar period, then

## Page 6431

he becomes a lump of flesh for a similar period. Then Allah sends the angel to him, who breathes the spirit into him and is commanded to record four things: his provision, his lifespan, his deeds, and whether he will be wretched or blessed.” Through another chain, and in another narration:

“Then He sends the angel to him, who is commanded concerning four things and told: ‘Record his provision, his deeds, his lifespan, and whether he will be wretched or blessed.’ Then he breathes the spirit into him.”

In this authentic hadith, the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, thus explained that the angel is commanded to record a person’s provision, lifespan, deeds, and whether he will be wretched or blessed after the body of that descendant of Adam has been created, but before the spirit is breathed into him. Allah’s recording of the prophethood of Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him—the foremost of Adam’s descendants—after creating Adam’s body but before breathing the spirit into him was of this same kind.
