This and similar cases concern the existence of individual entities in written records.

The existence of speech in written records, however, is a different matter. Thus, Ibn Qutayba reported that the position of the people of hadith and the Sunnah is that the Quran is in the written copy in a real sense, not metaphorically, as some speculative theologians claim. One of the “Jahmī doctrines” that Ahmad denounced—and the gravest of them—was the claim of those who alleged that the Quran is neither in people’s hearts nor in written copies, and that anyone who affirms its presence in hearts and written copies has adopted the Christians’ position, as was reported to him concerning Mūsā

## Page 6432

ibn ‘Uqba al-Sūrī—one of those who recorded hadith at that time, not the author of al-Maghāzī (The Military Expeditions), who was an earlier figure associated with the Successors. For the Christians say that the Word—which, in their view, is a divine substance and a Lord who is worshipped—clothed itself in human nature and united with it as water and milk unite; or dwelt within it as water dwells in a vessel; or mingled with it as fire and iron mingle. Muslims do not say that the Quran is a self-subsisting substance that is worshipped. Rather, it is Allah’s speech, which He spoke; nor do they say that it united with a human being.

As for describing it as indwelling in written copies and hearts, many of those affiliated with the Sunnah, among the people of Khurāsān and elsewhere, use this expression. Others, among the Iraqis and elsewhere, deny this and say that it is present in them by way of manifestation, not indwelling.

## Page 6433

and some neither affirm nor deny this, but say: The Quran is in hearts and written copies; it should be described neither as indwelling nor as not indwelling, because both affirmation and denial may suggest a false meaning. They do not disagree that Allah’s speech does not separate from His essence, and that neither His speech nor any of His attributes becomes detached from Him. How, then, could any rational person imagine that Allah’s speech separates from Him and transfers to someone else?

For this reason, Imam Ahmad said:

It is well known that a created being’s speech does not separate from the one in whom it subsists. Everyone knows that transferring and passing on speech means conveying it, as He said:

He also said:

“Convey from me, even if only a single verse.”

Speech on paper is not present in it in the way an attribute inheres in that which it qualifies

---

## Page 6434

and an accident in a substance, so as to become an attribute of it. Nor is it present there as a body is present in the space to which it has moved from another space. Nor is it present there merely as a sign, like the world, which is a sign of the Maker. Rather, it belongs to another category, intelligible in its own right. Not everything that exists must have a counterpart matching it in every respect. By their innate disposition, people understand what it means for a speaker’s speech to be on a sheet of paper. They know that the speech subsisting in him has not separated from his being and come to dwell in something else. They also know that what is on the sheet is not merely a sign pointing directly to a meaning in his mind. Rather, what is on the sheet corresponds to his utterance, his utterance corresponds to his meaning, and his meaning corresponds to external reality.

What is in his mind may also be known through natural signs and voluntary movements that he did not intend to convey anything. Yet no one calls these the speaker’s speech in the same way as the speech heard from him. If speech were so called merely because it signifies something, every sign would share that designation. We shall discuss this, Allah willing.

If what is in a written copy of the Quran required reverence merely because it signifies something, every sign would require reverence. Indeed, that which points to the Maker and His attributes is greater than that which points to His speech, yet it does not possess the sanctity of a written copy of the Quran. As for indications of the meaning within a person’s mind, that meaning may sometimes become known without his choosing. It may become known through natural sounds, such as weeping; through movements not intended to convey anything; through movements intended to convey meaning, such as gestures; or through utterances intended to convey meaning.

## Page 6435

Section

Thus, when these people—who declared the doctrine of the “Lafziyyah” erroneous yet added much evil to it—say that “reading” is distinct from what is read, “recitation” from what is recited, and “writing” from what is written, they mean by reading only the readers’ voices, and by “writing” the writers’ ink. They mean that these are distinct from the meaning subsisting in His essence, which is Allah’s speech, and are merely an indication of it and an expression of it. In their view, there is nothing but reading and what is read. Thus, nothing remains except sound, ink, and a meaning subsisting in His essence; there is no Quran beyond these.

They have excluded the letters of Allah’s speech that He spoke, and the reality of the Quran’s meanings in Allah Himself, exalted is He. They have also excluded the Quran’s meanings in the souls of its readers and listeners. For there is no doubt that the Quran we read contains letters and meanings—letters that are spoken and written. If, in their view, there is nothing but the servant’s voice and the ink in the written copy of the Quran, where are the meanings? And where are the letters of the Quran that Allah sent down, even if they regard them as created?

How can it be conceived that all the Books Allah Most High sent down have only a single meaning, which is a command, a prohibition, a promise, and a threat

---

## Page 6436

and these are its attributes, not its divisions?

For these people say that the meanings of all Allah’s speech are a single meaning. Thus, the meaning of “May the hands of Abū Lahab perish” is the meaning of “Say: He is Allah, One,” and the meaning of the Torah is the meaning of the Quran and the Gospel. They may then reduce all the meanings of speech to assertion, and may identify the meaning of assertion with knowledge, while treating knowledge of one thing as distinct from knowledge of another.

For this reason, most rational people say that the falsity of this is self-evident. They say that command, prohibition, and assertion are relational attributes of speech, not its types and divisions. Allah’s speech is far greater than the speech of created beings. The speech contained in the written copy of the Quran belongs to this last category, not the preceding categories. How much more so, then, when that wording possesses such distinctive qualities that it is said of it:

“Say: If mankind and jinn gathered together to produce the like of this Quran, they could not produce its like, even if they helped one another.”

However, some things signify something else intentionally, while others signify something else without any intention on their part to do so, such as inanimate things: they serve purposes other than signifying the Creator. Other things are intended solely to signify, such that mentioning them for their intended purpose amounts to mentioning their referents—as with a name and that which it names. What is intended by a name is the thing named; hence, when the name is mentioned, the thing named is intended. The same applies to “wording” in relation to the meaning it signifies, and to “writing” in relation to wording. Thus, what is intended by writing

---

## Page 6437

is simply the wording, and what is intended by written letters is the spoken letters. This is why the term “letter” applies to both.

Thus, when one says, “the speech in the book,” it is understood that what is intended among the book’s contents is the speech, not anything else. Hence, this enjoys a distinctive sanctity not shared by things intended both to signify and to serve other purposes. And Allah knows best.

Section

Those who misrepresented the doctrine of the “affirmative Lafziyyah”—who say, “Our utterance of the Quran is uncreated,” and say that “recitation” is the thing recited and “writing” is the thing written—have reached the point where one of them maintains that the eternal sound is heard from the reciter. Their conception of the Quran extends no further than what they imagine concerning letters and sounds. They lead those who disagree with them to believe that the very sound heard from the servant is the very sound with which Allah spoke. They deny that the meanings of the truths expressed in the Quran are part of Allah’s speech, and do not include meaning within Allah’s speech.

The early generations used to say, “The Quran is Allah’s speech, uncreated,” and, “Whatever form the Quran takes, it is Allah’s speech, uncreated.” And the “innovating affirmative Lafziyyah,” whom Imam Ahmad and others condemned

only said, “Our utterance of it is uncreated.” They did not say, “eternal.”

And what, then, of saying, “My voice when uttering it is uncreated,” or, “My voice when uttering it is eternal,” or, “Part of the sound heard is eternal,” and similar statements?

Whoever reflects on Imam Ahmad’s statements on this subject will find them among the soundest and clearest explanations. He will also find that each group claiming adherence to the Sunnah has held fast to certain statements among them. The disputes among people throughout the world and the immense, almost unmanageable confusion concerning this subject stem from “two fundamental issues”: the question of Allah’s speaking the Quran and the rest of His speech, and the question of His servants’ uttering Allah’s speech.

Allah has explained this in His Book and in the Sunnah of His Messenger. He, the Exalted, says:

In this verse, He singles out some of them as those to whom He spoke. In the other verse, He explicitly states that He spoke to Moses directly. ## Page 6443

and His intention, when they affirm them, are affirmed only in a universal sense, without singling out anyone. The sound a person hears may also originate outside his own soul, coming from the True One, exalted is He, through the tongue of one of His angels or someone other than an angel. This is what the Jahmiyyah among the Muʿtazilah and others have recognized, believing that Allah has no way of speaking other than this. It falls within the category of revelation, which is one of the forms of divine speech, or a category parallel to speech through a messenger. This is “the second category,” as the Exalted says:

“Or He sends a messenger who reveals, by His permission, whatever He wills.”

This is revelation conveyed by the messenger. It differs from the first kind of revelation from Allah, which is one of the forms of divine speech in its broader sense. Revelation conveyed by the messenger also takes various forms. In the two Sahīh collections, ʿĀʾishah, may Allah be pleased with her, reported that al-Hārith ibn Hishām asked the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, “How does revelation come to you?”

He replied: “Sometimes it comes to me like the ringing of a bell, and this is the hardest form for me. Then it ceases, and I have grasped what was said. At other times, the angel appears to me in the form of a man and speaks to me, and I grasp what he says.”

ʿĀʾishah, may Allah be pleased with her, said: “I have indeed seen him

## Page 6444

receive revelation on a bitterly cold day; when it ceased, his forehead would be streaming with sweat.”

He, peace and blessings be upon him, thus explained that the angel’s descent upon him sometimes takes place inwardly, with a sound like the ringing of a bell, and sometimes with the angel appearing in the form of a man who speaks to him. Thus Gabriel would come in the form of Dihyah al-Kalbī, just as he appeared to Mary as a man of perfect form, and just as the angels came to Abraham and Lot in human form, as Allah has related in several places. Allah has called both these forms of the angel’s conveying his message and speaking “revelation,” because of the concealment involved: when the recipient sees him, he needs to know that he is an angel; and when he comes with something like the ringing of a bell, the recipient needs to understand what the sound conveys.

The “third category” is speaking from behind a veil, as Allah spoke to Moses, peace be upon him. Hence Allah described this as “calling” and “private discourse.” The Exalted says:

“We called him from the right side of the Mount and brought him near for private discourse.”

The Exalted also says:

“When he came to it, he was called, ‘O Moses!’”

“Indeed, I am your Lord, so remove your sandals. You are in the sacred valley of Tuwā.”

“And I have chosen you, so listen to what is revealed.”

This manner of speaking is particular to certain messengers, as the Exalted says:

“Those messengers—We favored some over others. Among them were those to whom Allah spoke.”

The Exalted also says:

“When Moses came at Our appointed time and his Lord spoke to him.”

And after mentioning His revelation to the prophets, He says:

“And Allah spoke directly to Moses.”

Thus, whoever regards this as belonging to the first kind of revelation—as some adherents of philosophy maintain

## Page 6445

and those who discuss Sufism following their approach, as in “The Niche of Lights” and “The Book of Removing the Sandals,” and in the statements of the Ittihādiyyah, such as the author of “The Bezels” and others like him—his misguidance and opposition to the Book, the Sunnah, and scholarly consensus, indeed even to plain reason, are among the clearest of matters.

Likewise, anyone who claims that Allah’s speaking to Moses was merely a form of inspiration and revelation, and that any one of us may hear Allah’s speech just as Moses heard it—as is found in the statements of some of the Kullābī and similar offshoots of the Jahmiyyah—is also among the most misguided of people.

Allah’s Book indicates that the terms “revelation” and “speech,” as used therein, each have a general and a specific sense. When either is used generally, it includes the other. Thus revelation falls within speaking in its general sense in this verse, while speaking falls within revelation in its general sense where the Exalted says:

“So listen to what is revealed.”

As for speaking in its specific, full sense, it does not include the particular, concealed form of revelation shared by prophets and others. Likewise, this particular form of revelation shared by them does not include speaking in its specific, full sense. Thus the Exalted said to Zechariah:

“Your sign is that you will not speak to people for three nights, though sound in health.”

Then the Exalted said:

“So he came out to his people from the sanctuary and signaled to them.”

Such “signaling” is not speaking, nor does it contradict what has been said. As for His words in the other verse:

“You will not speak to people for three days except by gestures”—

if

---

## Page 6446

the exception is understood as disjunctive, “speaking” has the same meaning in both verses. If it is understood as connected, “speaking” is like that mentioned in Sūrat al-Shūrā: speaking in its general sense.

It has become clear that He spoke to Moses in a specific, full sense, as indicated by His words:

“Among them were those to whom Allah spoke.”

This is understood alongside the knowledge that He revealed to all of them and spoke to them in the general sense. It is also established by His distinguishing His speaking from His revelation to the prophets; by the verbal noun emphasizing His speaking; by His making speaking from behind a veil a category distinct from His revelation; and by the reports transmitted through numerous independent channels from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and his Companions concerning His speaking specifically to Moses, directly from Him to Moses. It is established that He spoke to him with a voice that Moses heard, as related in reports from the early generations of the Muslim community and its leading scholars, in accordance with what the Book and the Sunnah indicate.

Here, “the third group,” the Kullābiyyah, erred. They believed that He merely revealed to Moses, peace be upon him, a meaning without sound. They disagreed over whether it could be heard. Some said that Moses heard that meaning through a subtle faculty He created within him. They maintained that hearing, sight, smell, taste, and touch are attributes that can have anything that exists as their object, as al-Ashʿarī and a group of others held.

Others said that Moses did not hear Allah’s speech, since, in their view, it is a meaning, and a meaning cannot be heard. This was the position of al-Qādī Abū Bakr and a group of others.

What they have affirmed falls within the general category of revelation which Allah, Mighty and Majestic, distinguished

---

## Page 6447

from His speaking to Moses, peace be upon him, when He said:

“Indeed, We have revealed to you as We revealed to Noah and the prophets after him,”

through to His words:

“And Allah spoke to Moses directly.”

He also distinguished His revelation from His speaking from behind a veil when He said:

“Except by revelation or from behind a veil.”

Likewise, He distinguished the messenger to whom He spoke from others in His words, Most High:

“Among them were those to whom Allah spoke.”

Nevertheless, these people affirm that Allah has speech consisting of a meaning subsisting in His own being, which He speaks. In this respect, they are better than those who affirm no speech for Him other than the meaning He revealed within the prophet’s soul, or the newly produced sound the prophet heard. Yet, in taking their refutation of these people too far, they claimed that nothing could possibly be Allah’s speech except what subsists in Him, and that nothing subsists in Him except meaning. Thus, they denied that letters could be Allah’s speech or that the Arabic Quran could be Allah’s speech.

Then the “fourth group” came and refuted their claim that speech is meaning alone. Some of them claimed that speech consists only of letters or sounds, and that meanings on their own are not called speech at all. This is not so. Rather, speech, without qualification, designates meanings and letters together. Either may be called speech when qualified, as when grammarians say: “Speech consists of nouns, verbs, and particles.” What is being classified here is verbal expression.

Likewise, al-Hasan al-Basrī said: “People of knowledge have always brought speaking to bear upon reflection, and reflection upon contemplation, and conversed with their hearts until they spoke.” And as stated by

---

## Page 6448

al-Junayd:

“Affirming Allah’s oneness” is the heart’s utterance, and “reliance on Allah” is the heart’s action.

They thus attributed speech and power to the heart, just as the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, attributed inner speech to the soul when he said:

“Allah has pardoned my community for what they say to themselves”—then he added—“so long as they neither speak of it nor act upon it.”

It is therefore clear that “speech,” without qualification, consists of letters corresponding to meaning, although, when qualified, the term may apply to other things. Indeed, they may call any intentional communication or indication an utterance, whether conveyed through words, gestures, or finger positions—bending the fingers.

They may also call an indication an utterance even when it is unintentional, as with the indications given by inanimate objects. Thus, they say:

“It said: ‘The breadth of his belly.’”

And:

“The cistern filled and said, ‘Enough, enough!
Gently now—you have filled my belly.’”

And:

“His two eyes said to him, ‘We hear and obey.’”

This is called “the language of circumstance” or “indication through circumstance.” An example is their saying:

“Ask the earth: Who made your rivers gush forth, watered your fruits, and planted your trees? If it does not answer you in words, it answers you through reflection.”

Another example is their saying:

“The eyes tell me what the heart conceals;
There is no good in bashfulness and sidelong glances.”

Another example is their saying:

---

## Page 6449

“I asked the dwelling to tell me
What had become of my loved ones.
It said to me, ‘The people camped
For some days, then departed.’”

This may also be called testimony. Some have claimed that the glorification of Allah by created things mentioned in the Quran belongs to this category: their pointing to the Creator, Most High. The correct view, however, is that there is another glorification beyond their pointing to Him, as explained elsewhere. Yet all these usages require qualification and contextual indication.

Thus, speech and utterance can rightly be denied of these things, as Allah Most High says:

“Did they not see that it could neither speak to them nor guide them to any way?”

And He says:

“Do they not see that it returns no word to them and has no power to harm or benefit them?”

And Abraham, Allah’s intimate friend, peace be upon him, said:

“So ask them, if they can speak.”

And Allah Most High says:

“This is a Day when they will not speak, nor will they be permitted to offer excuses.”

And He says:

“They will not speak, except those whom the Most Merciful permits and who say what is right.”

And He says:

“They do not precede Him in speech, and they act by His command.”

It is known self-evidently and through mass transmission that utterance and speech may be denied of a living being who is silent or unable to speak—how much more so of inanimate things! It is also known that Allah Most High possesses the attributes of perfection to the highest degree, and that the messengers affirmed that He speaks with speech that is complete and perfect to the highest degree. Whoever regards His speech as merely meaning, merely letters, or merely letters and sounds has not esteemed Allah as He deserves. And whoever regards His speech as only that which subsists

---

## Page 6450

in something other than Him has stripped Him of perfection and likened Him to lifeless things. The same applies to whoever does not affirm that He speaks by His will; or affirms that He speaks by His will and power, but regards speech as one of the created things and describes Him by His creations; or holds that He became a speaker after not having been one. Although each of these positions affirms some truth, it also rejects some truth and detracts from the perfection that Allah deserves.

Section

Each of these groups has grasped some truth concerning the degrees and kinds of speech. The same applies to “the second principle,” namely, our utterance of Allah’s speech.

The Book, the Sunnah, and scholarly consensus establish that what Muslims recite is Allah’s speech, not the speech of anyone else. If someone were to say that a single letter or meaning within it was not part of Allah’s speech, or that it was the speech of someone other than Allah, and the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, or any of his Companions heard him say this, it would be known with certainty that they would respond to him as they responded to people of denial and misguidance. Indeed, people universally agree on the same principle regarding all speech.

Thus, all people who know that the verse

“Indeed, everything apart from Allah is vain”

---

## Page 6451

is from the poetry of Labīd know that these are Labīd’s words, and that the verse,

“Halt, you two, and let us weep at the memory of a beloved and a dwelling,”

is among the words of Imru’ al-Qays, although they know that they heard these verses only from someone else, in that person’s voice.

Then the believers came forward with some of the truth but not all of it and said: “This is nothing but the servant’s voice and utterance—or, we hear nothing else.” The “deniers” then said: “The servant’s utterance has come into being and is not Allah’s speech. Therefore, what is heard has come into being and is not Allah’s speech.”

The “affirmers” said: “Rather, this is Allah’s speech, yet it is nothing but the servant’s utterance or voice. His utterance or voice must therefore be Allah’s speech. Allah’s speech is uncreated or eternal, so his utterance or voice must be uncreated or eternal.”

People know, as a necessary truth of the Muslim community’s religion—and indeed through reason itself—that each group is mistaken in some of what it says and has introduced an innovation in that respect. This is why the imams rejected such claims. If any of them returns to his innate disposition, he will recognize the difference between pointing to the speech being heard and saying, “These are Zayd’s words,” and saying, “This is Zayd’s voice.” He will find that his innate disposition affirms the former and rejects the latter.

Allah Most High says:

“And if any one of the polytheists seeks your protection, then grant him protection so that he may hear Allah’s speech.”

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Beautify the Quran with your voices.”

Everyone knows by his innate disposition what the Book and the Sunnah indicate: that the speech

---

## Page 6452

is the speech of the Creator, while the voice is the reciter’s voice. This is why Imam Ahmad, when Abū Tālib recited to him, “Say, ‘He is Allah, One,’” told him, “This is uncreated.” Abū Tālib then reported that Ahmad had said, “My utterance of the Quran is uncreated.” Ahmad asked him, “Did I tell you, ‘My utterance is uncreated’?” He replied, “No. But I recited to you, ‘Say, “He is Allah, One,”’ and you said, ‘This is uncreated.’”

Ahmad thus clarified the difference between saying, “This speech is uncreated,” and saying, “This speaker’s utterance is uncreated.” The expression “my utterance” is ambiguous: it encompasses both the speaker’s action and his voice. Thus, saying, “My utterance, recitation, or reading is uncreated,” or, “It is the very thing recited,” suggests that the servant’s action and voice are eternal, and that the meaning and sound subsisting in him are identical to the meaning and sound subsisting in Allah.

Conversely, saying, “My utterance of the Quran, my recitation of the Quran, the utterance of the Quran, or its recitation is created,” or, “The recitation is other than what is recited,” or, “The reading is other than what is read,” implies that the letters of the Quran are in no respect part of Allah’s speech, and that half of the Quran is Allah’s speech while the other half is someone else’s speech. It also implies that Allah’s reading of the Quran is separate from what He reads, and His recitation of the Quran is separate from what He recites; likewise, that the servant’s reading of the Quran is separate from what he reads, and his recitation of it is separate from what he recites.

It further implies that what has been sent down to us is not Allah’s speech. For what is read and recited is Allah’s speech, and, according to these people, difference entails separation. Whatever is separate from His speech cannot be speech of His; thus, what He has sent down would not be His speech.

---

## Page 6453

Since speech occurs only through movement and action that give rise to letters and meanings, it sometimes falls within the terms “action” and “deed,” when considered as movement and action, and sometimes falls outside them, when considered as letters and meanings. Thus, in the Quran and Sunnah, speech is sometimes treated as a kind of action, as in the Most High’s words:

“There is no private conversation among three but He is their fourth, nor among five but He is their sixth, nor fewer than that nor more but He is with them wherever they may be. Then, on the Day of Resurrection, He will inform them of what they did.”

At other times, it is treated as a category distinct from action, as in the Most High’s words:

“To Him ascends good speech, and righteous deeds raise it.”

For this reason, scholars disagreed over whether someone who swears not to perform any action in a particular place breaks his oath by speaking there, when neither his intention nor the circumstances of the oath clarify its scope. There are two views on this within the school of Imam Ahmad and elsewhere; both are reported from Ahmad.

For this reason, Abū Muhammad ibn Qutayba stated, in the book he wrote to explain “utterance,” that recitation is both Quran and action, neither of which can be separated from the other. Whoever says that it is Quran speaks truthfully, and whoever swears that it is an action is truthful in his oath. Whoever declared without qualification that recitation is created was mistaken, as was whoever claimed that it is uncreated. He charged both parties with limited knowledge and inadequate understanding, for the subtlety of this issue had prevented either party from grasping it. One party found that recitation is called Quran and therefore denied that it is created; the other found that recitation is an action for which the reciter is rewarded and therefore affirmed that it comes into being.

---

## Page 6454

I say:

Error concerning this principle lies at two extremes, just as it does concerning the first principle. Regarding the first principle, some say that He has no speech subsisting in Him, while others say that His speech is nothing but an abstract meaning or nothing but sound.

Regarding this principle, some say that no one else utters His speech, or that it cannot be heard from anyone else. Others say that when someone else conveys and delivers His speech, its condition is the same as when it is heard from Him and recited. Rather, His messengers and servants utter His speech, speak it, recite it and read it. It remains His speech however it is conveyed, wherever it is recited and wherever it is written. His speech is uncreated however it is conveyed.

Nevertheless, its condition when His servants recite and write it is not the same as when Allah recites it and they hear it from Him. Nor is someone who hears it from a reciter in the same position as Moses son of ʿImrān, who heard the speech of the Lord of the worlds from Him. As stated in the hadith:

“When creation hears the Quran from Allah on the Day of Resurrection, it will be as though they had never heard it before.”

Indeed, even the Messenger’s recitation and hearing it from him are not like another person’s recitation and hearing it from that person. Nor is one person’s recitation and hearing it from him like another person’s recitation and hearing it from him. In all its conditions, it is the speech of Allah Most High, which is uncreated, even though its conditions differ.

The following must also be understood concerning the declaration of Allah, His Messenger and the believers about what Allah has revealed, “This is Allah’s speech”; indeed, concerning people’s declaration about human speech they hear, “These are so-and-so’s words,” as when they say of a statement such as his saying, “Actions are only according to intentions, and for each

---

## Page 6455

person is only what he intended,” “These are the words of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace”; and of a verse such as:

“Behold, everything apart from Allah is vain,”

“This is Labīd’s poetry.”

When they say, “This is that very thing,” they do not mean merely that the two are of the same kind, as when someone says, “This blackness is the same as that blackness.” For they use this expression of two utterances, two instances of knowledge, two powers or two individuals that happen to match. In such cases they say, “One thought coincides with another as one hoofprint coincides with another.” In reality, however, one is merely like the other, as Allah Most High says:

“Likewise, those before them said the like of what they say.”

They say, “This is that very thing,” when the two agree in their attributes, and may even do so when there are differences between them that are irrelevant to the point intended. Similarly, they say of a single entity whose attributes have changed, “This is the very same thing.”

Nor is this like adopting someone else’s words, whether verse or prose—for example, when a man adopts another’s saying and thus speaks those words himself, following the example of the original speaker. This is like our saying something that someone else has said, agreeing with that speaker that the statement is true.

For this reason, the jurists said that whoever utters words matching the wording of the Quran by way of

---

## Page 6456

remembrance and supplication—such as saying “In the name of Allah” when beginning an action, or “Praise be to Allah” when eating, and the like—is not thereby reciting the Quran, and may do so while in a state of major ritual impurity. Hence the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“The best speech after the Quran consists of four phrases, which are themselves from the Quran: Glory be to Allah; praise be to Allah; none has the right to be worshipped except Allah; and Allah is the Greatest.”

Narrated by Muslim. He thus described them as the best speech after the Quran and stated that they are from the Quran. They are indeed from the Quran, yet someone who says them by way of remembrance is not thereby reciting the Quran.

In this case, however, the words may be attributed to the original speaker even if the second speaker does not intend to convey his words, because the first speaker originally brought the utterance into being, while the second spoke it in imitation. Thus, if a man adopts the poet’s saying, even without intending to convey his poetry:

“Behold, everything apart from Allah is vain,”

he is told, “These are Labīd’s words.” Yet the second speaker may intend only to say this on his own behalf because he believes its meaning to be true.

This is the basis of the scholars’ disagreement concerning the “letters of the alphabet,” the “names” revealed in the Quran, and “words” in the Quran when someone uses them without intending to recite the Quran. Should they be described as uncreated because they are from the Quran? Or should it be said that, if he does not intend them as the Quran and the speech of Allah, they are not part of Allah’s speech and would therefore be

---

## Page 6457

created? On this there are two views among Ahl al-Sunnah.

As for someone who utters another person’s speech intending to convey and deliver it, or to speak it while believing that he intends only to utter that other person’s speech—the person whose commands and statements these are, and who originally spoke its letters and meanings—then the speech is unquestionably that of the first speaker. It is not the second speaker’s speech in any respect; it has merely reached people through him.

Speech has no counterpart resembling it in every respect to which it can be assimilated. Rather, it is intelligible in its own right. For example, even if Zayd, a created being, has ceased to exist, and the attribute that subsisted in him has also ceased to exist, when another narrator relates his speech and we say:

“This is Zayd’s speech,”

we are referring to the reality that Zayd originated and that was an attribute of his. This is that very same reality—I mean the formal reality, not the matter. For sound as such, in relation to distinct articulated letters, stands in the relation of matter to form. It was not the first speaker’s speech because of sound as such, which is shared by the sounds of human beings, speechless animals, and inanimate objects. Rather, it was his speech because of the form that Zayd composed, together with his composition of its meanings. The existence of this form in the two instances of matter is not like the existence of species and individuals in concrete entities, nor like the existence of accidents in substances, nor

---

## Page 6458

is it like other forms in their substantial matter. Rather, it is a reality in its own right, and not every reality has a counterpart matching it in every respect.

When people say, “This is Labīd’s poetry,” they refer to both its wording and its meaning. Yet if someone were to say, “I originated the wording of this poetry,” or “This wording is my own composition,” or “My utterance of this poetry is my own creation,” everyone would declare him a liar and say to him:

“Rather, you transmitted it and recited it. But to claim that you originated its wording, that it came into being last night through your uttering it, or that your utterance of it came into being last night—that is false. The wording of this poetry has existed for a very long time, even though you have delivered it through your movements and your voice. Movement and sound are natural phenomena that you share with living beings, both speaking and speechless. You therefore have no share in it insofar as it is speech, nor insofar as it is that poet’s speech; for its being speech, or the speech of a particular speaker, belongs exclusively to that speaker. You have merely delivered it by means of an instrument that you share with speechless animals and inanimate objects.

“Yet praise belongs to Allah, who has granted you reason and discernment by which you find your way and direct your tongue, while He has not granted this to speechless animals. He has thus made your actions and qualities help you understand speech and speak it, without making the actions and qualities of speechless animals do likewise.”

If this holds for a created being conveying the speech of another created being like himself, then what of the speech of the Creator—exalted is His majesty—whose superiority over all other speech is like Allah’s superiority over His creation?

---

## Page 6459

For it has a unique character of its own: conveying it cannot be likened to conveying any other speech, just as it is itself unlike any other speech. No created being can produce its like, whereas the human speech that people convey can be matched. Thus, this speech that is heard—the Quran—may in no way be attributed to anyone other than Allah, except in the sense of conveying it, as in His statement, exalted is He:

“Indeed, it is the word of a noble messenger.”

Allah, glorified is He, has addressed us through it by means of the Messenger, as explained above. I have discussed these matters at length in their appropriate place: matters that bewilder minds and over which people have fallen into confusion. This, however, is an answer to a request for a fatwa, so it is appropriate here only to indicate the broad principles and establish that speech must be attributed to the one from whom its wording and meaning originated, not to the one who transmitted and delivered it on his behalf. It truly is the speech of the one who originally spoke it and whose attribute it is, whether it is heard from him or from someone conveying and delivering it through his own actions and voice. At the same time, it must be understood that people’s actions and attributes are created, and that the statement of Allah, His Messenger, and the believers—“This is Allah’s speech, and what lies between the two covers is Allah’s speech”—is literally true, beyond doubt. The “Quran” that Muslims recite, write, and memorize is the speech of Allah Most High; and Allah’s speech, however conveyed, is uncreated. As for the human actions and attributes accompanying its transmission and recitation, these are created.

Yet this matter involves ambiguities and difficulties whose precise clarification and detailed explanation lie beyond the scope of this fatwa. The person requesting it is ready to leave and in a hurry to take it, and because in

---

## Page 6460

this matter there are subtleties and obscurities that require citing the relevant texts, explaining their meanings, and giving examples to clarify the reality of the matter. This is not the place for that. What is known “in general,” however, is that Imam Ahmad and the great imams who are widely held in high esteem throughout the Muslim community did not disagree on anything in this subject. Rather, some had greater knowledge of it and were more diligent in fulfilling its obligations than others. Groups of even the most eminent figures have erred in some of these matters. Imam Ahmad, together with the other imams, refuted most of the innovations concerning this subject.

The Jahmiyyah first introduced the doctrines that “the Quran is created” and that “the divine attributes are to be denied.” Those of the Successors who were alive at that time rejected these doctrines, as did the generation following the Successors and the imams after them. They declared those who professed them to be unbelievers.

Then some scholars of hadith and scholastic theology who debated the Jahmiyyah introduced the doctrine that the revealed Quran is created, that it is not Allah’s speech, or that it is neither in the written copies of the Quran nor in people’s hearts. Some of them denied that the letters of the Quran are Allah’s speech or that Allah spoke with a voice. Imam Ahmad and the imams of his time rejected this.

In opposition to them, another group of scholars of scholastic theology and hadith claimed that people’s utterances and voices are uncreated, or maintained that some human actions or attributes are uncreated, or that the Quran heard from people is like what is heard

---

## Page 6461

from Allah Most High in every respect, and similar claims. Imam Ahmad, the imams of his time generally, his companions, and other scholars rejected this. Their denunciations and refutations of all these innovations are recorded in reliably transmitted works, such as The Book of the Sunnah by al-Khallāl, al-Ibānah (The Elucidation) by Ibn Battah, the books on the ordeal transmitted by Hanbal and Sālih, The Book of the Sunnah by ‘Abd Allāh ibn Ahmad, The Sunnah by al-Lālakā’ī, The Sunnah by Ibn Abī Hātim, and numerous other works.

As for refuting the Jahmiyyah, who deny the divine attributes and maintain that the Quran is created, much concerning this is found in the statements of the Successors, those who followed them, and the renowned imams. There are very many transmitted reports concerning the question of the Quran.

Among these is what Ibn Abī Hātim, Ibn Shāhīn, al-Lālakā’ī, and others narrated through several chains of transmission from ‘Alī ibn Abī Tālib—may Allah be pleased with him—that he was told on the day of Siffīn, “You appointed two men as arbitrators.” He replied, “I did not appoint a created being as arbitrator; I appointed only the Quran.”

‘Ikrimah reported: Ibn ‘Abbās was attending a funeral. When he had placed the deceased in the burial niche, a man stood up and said, “O Allah, Lord of the Quran, forgive him.” Ibn ‘Abbās sprang towards him and said, “Stop! The Quran is from Him.”

Another version reads: “The Quran is Allah’s speech and is not subject to lordship. From Him it came forth, and to Him it will return.”

‘Abd Allāh ibn Mas‘ūd said: “Whoever swears by the Quran owes an expiation for every verse. Whoever disbelieves in a single letter of it has disbelieved in it all.”

---

## Page 6462

Among the widely transmitted reports is that narrated by Sufyān ibn ‘Uyaynah from ‘Amr ibn Dīnār—though some transmitters attribute it only to Sufyān, the former being the well-known version—who said:

“For seventy years, I have known our shaykhs and the people to say: ‘The Quran is Allah’s speech, uncreated. From Him it came forth, and to Him it will return.’”

‘Amr’s shaykhs were the Companions and Successors whom he met.

It is also reported from ‘Alī ibn al-Husayn Zayn al-‘Ābidīn and his son Ja‘far ibn Muhammad:

“The Quran is neither a creator nor created; rather, it is Allah’s speech.”

Similar statements are transmitted from al-Hasan al-Basrī, Ayyūb al-Sakhtiyānī, Hammād ibn Abī Sulaymān, Ibn Abī Laylā, Abū Hanīfah, Ibn Abī Dhi’b, Ibn al-Mājishūn, al-Awzā‘ī, al-Shāfi‘ī, Abū Bakr ibn ‘Ayyāsh, Hushaym, ‘Alī ibn ‘Āsim, ‘Abd Allāh ibn al-Mubārak, Abū Ishāq al-Fazārī, Wakī‘ ibn al-Jarrāh, al-Walīd ibn Muslim, ‘Abd al-Rahmān ibn Mahdī, Yahyā ibn Sa‘īd al-Qattān, Mu‘ādh ibn Mu‘ādh, Abū Yūsuf, Muhammad, Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal, Ishāq ibn Rāhawayh, Bishr ibn al-Hārith, Ma‘rūf al-Karkhī, Abū ‘Ubayd al-Qāsim ibn Sallām, Abū Thawr, al-Bukhārī, Muslim, Abū Zur‘ah, Abū Hātim, and countless others.

Abū al-Qāsim al-Lālakā’ī—after naming the scholars of the most virtuous generations and those who followed them, from whom he transmitted in his book that the Quran is Allah’s speech, uncreated—said:

“These are five hundred and fifty individuals from among the Successors, the followers of the Successors, and the imams

---

## Page 6463

held in esteem—apart from the Companions—across different ages and through the passing years. Among them are some hundred imams whose opinions people accepted and whose schools they followed. Had I undertaken to transmit the statements of the hadith scholars, their names would have numbered many thousands. Thus, I have transmitted from these scholars, generation after generation, without anyone objecting to them. Anyone who rejected their position was called upon by them to repent, or they ordered his execution, exile, or crucifixion.”

He said:

“There is no disagreement within the Muslim community that the first to say that the Quran is created was al-Ja‘d ibn Dirham, followed by Jahm ibn Safwān. Both were executed by the Muslims.”

Among those who issued rulings that such people should be put to death were Mālik ibn Anas, Muhammad ibn ‘Abd al-Rahmān ibn Abī Laylā, Sufyān ibn ‘Uyaynah, the caliph Abū Ja‘far al-Mansūr, Ma‘mar ibn Sulaymān, Yahyā ibn Sa‘īd al-Qattān, ‘Abd al-Rahmān ibn Mahdī, Mu‘ādh ibn Mu‘ādh, Wakī‘ ibn al-Jarrāh and his father, ‘Abd Allāh ibn Dāwūd al-Khuraybī, Bishr ibn al-Walīd—the associate of Abū Yūsuf—Abū Mus‘ab al-Zuhrī, Abū ‘Ubayd al-Qāsim ibn Sallām, Abū Thawr, Ahmad ibn Hanbal, and other imams.

Likewise, condemnation of “those who suspend judgment”—those who say neither that the Quran is created nor that it is uncreated—and the declaration that they are misguided are reported from the majority of these imams, including Ibn al-Mājishūn, Abū Mus‘ab, Wakī‘ ibn al-Jarrāh, Abū al-Walīd, Abū al-Walīd al-Jārūdī—the associate of al-Shāfi‘ī—Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal, Abū Thawr, and Ishāq ibn Rāhawayh,

---

## Page 6464

and others whose number none but Allah can count.

As for the second innovation concerning the revealed Quran—that relating to people’s recitation of it, known as the “Lafziyyah controversy”—the imams of their time condemned the innovation of the Lafziyyah, who say that reciting, reading, and uttering the Quran are created. They counted them among the Jahmiyyah and explained that their position entails saying that the Quran is created. In many of their statements, they declared them disbelievers.

The same applies to those who say that this Quran is not Allah’s speech, but merely a representation or expression of His speech; or that it is present in written copies of the Quran and in people’s hearts only as Allah and His Messenger are present in those copies and hearts; and similar claims. This condemnation is recorded from Imam Ahmad, Ishāq, Abū ‘Ubayd, Abū Mus‘ab al-Zuhrī, Abū Thawr, Abū al-Walīd al-Jārūdī, Muhammad ibn Bashshār, Ya‘qūb ibn Ibrāhīm al-Dawraqī, Muhammad ibn Yahyā ibn Abī ‘Amr al-‘Adanī, Muhammad ibn Yahyā al-Dhuhlī, Muhammad ibn Aslam al-Tūsī, and so many other imams and guides of Islam that none but Allah can count them.

Likewise, the innovation of the “affirming Lafziyyah”—those who say that people’s utterance of the Quran, or their voices when reciting it, are uncreated, or that recitation, which is the person’s own act and voice, is uncreated—was condemned by the imams who had heard of this

---

## Page 6465

innovation: Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal, Abū ‘Abd Allāh al-Bukhārī, compiler of the Sahīh, and Abū Bakr al-Marwadhī, the closest of Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal’s associates. On this matter, al-Marwadhī obtained responses from the Muslim scholars of that time in Baghdad, Basra, Kufa, the two Holy Sanctuaries, Syria, Khurasan, and elsewhere. These included ‘Abd al-Wahhāb al-Warrāq, Abū Bakr al-Athram, Muhammad ibn Bashshār Bundār, Abū al-Husayn ‘Alī ibn Muslim al-Tūsī, Ya‘qūb al-Dawraqī, Muhammad ibn Sahl ibn ‘Askar, the hadith master Muhammad ibn ‘Abd Allāh al-Mukharrimī, Muhammad ibn Ishāq al-Sāghānī, al-‘Abbās ibn Muhammad al-Dūrī, ‘Alī ibn Dāwūd al-Qantarī, Muthannā ibn Jāmi‘ al-Anbārī, Ishāq ibn Ibrāhīm ibn Habīb ibn al-Shahīd, Muhammad ibn Yahyā al-Azdī, al-Hasan ibn ‘Abd al-‘Azīz al-Jarawī, ‘Abd al-Karīm ibn al-Haytham al-‘Āqūlī, Abū Mūsā ibn Abī ‘Alqamah al-Nafrūnī and other scholars of Medina, Muhammad ibn ‘Abd al-Rahmān al-Muqri’, Abū al-Walīd ibn Abī al-Jārūd, Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn al-Qāsim ibn Abī Murrah and other scholars of Mecca, Ahmad ibn Sinān al-Wāsitī, ‘Alī ibn Harb al-Mawsilī, and as many other imams of Ahl al-Sunnah and scholars of hadith as Allah Most High willed, from among Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal’s associates and others.

They condemned anyone who regarded a person’s utterance of the Quran, his voice when reciting it, or any other human attributes connected with the Quran as uncreated. They called for such a person to be punished by shunning and other means. Abū Bakr al-Khallāl compiled some of their statements on this matter in his Book of the Sunnah.

## Page 6471

As for Ahmad’s and the imams’ denunciation of those who say, “This Quran is created,” and “Recitation is created”; their regarding as grave the assertion, “There is no Quran in people’s hearts or in the written copies”; and the allegation made by some that whoever says this has adopted the position of the Christians and the proponents of divine indwelling—Ahmad’s and others’ denunciations of these views are numerous, widely known, and recorded in many books. This fatwa did not require establishing this principle, so there was no need to discuss it in detail, unlike the other principle. Elsewhere, we have mentioned as much of this as Allah enabled us to mention.

Were I to recount the statements of Ahmad, the leading scholars among his followers, and others refuting those who say that the servant’s utterance or voice is uncreated, or that the voice heard from the reciter is eternal, the discussion would be lengthy.

Consider Abū Nasr al-Sijzī, who wrote the well-known al-Ibānah (The Clarification). He was among the strongest proponents of the view that recitation is what is recited, that uttering the Quran is the Quran itself, and that it is uncreated. He rejected reports attributing any other view to Ahmad. Nevertheless, he said:

“If our opponents object, saying, ‘Although you say that recitation is the Quran and the speech of Allah, you do not declare that the voice heard from the reciter is Allah’s voice. Rather, you attribute it to the reciter. Since you cannot make that declaration, this indicates that it is something other than the Quran.’”

Abū Nasr said: “The answer is that, in this matter, we adhere to the apparent meaning of revelation

---

## Page 6472

and our position concerning recitation and voice is consistent. When a reciter recites the Quran, one does not say, ‘This is Allah’s recitation,’ nor permit such a statement in any way. Rather, one attributes the recitation to the reciter by extension, because it is he who effects the change. One says only that the reciter’s recitation is Quran. This is established in revelation, as everyone agrees.

“For al-Ashʿarī, despite his disagreement with us, says, ‘What is heard from the reciter is Quran.’ We have explained that distinguishing between recitation and the Quran on the point at issue between us is impossible. Likewise, he says that the voice heard from someone reciting the Quran is both recitation and Quran. Revelation requires the position we have stated, and I know of no disagreement among Muslims concerning this.”

Section

As for Imam Ahmad’s explicit statements that “human speech is created” and that “the acts of servants are created,” these occur in many places, just as the other imams explicitly affirmed this. There is no disagreement among Ahl al-Sunnah on this matter.

Thus Yahyā ibn Saʿīd al-Qattān, Imam Ahmad’s teacher, said, “I have always heard our companions say, ‘The acts of servants are created.’” Imam Ahmad was asked, “Are the acts of servants created?” He replied, “Yes.” He explicitly affirmed this concerning human speech in the report transmitted by Ahmad ibn al-Hasan al-Tirmidhī, as will be discussed, and in his work refuting “the heretics and the Jahmiyyah,” which is

---

## Page 6473

transmitted through his son ʿAbd Allāh from a written text he found (1). Al-Khallāl also included it in his Kitāb al-Sunnah, and Judge Abū Yaʿlā and others quoted from it. Several scholars have reported universal consensus on this, including Abū Nasr al-Sijzī in al-Ibānah, despite his being among the strongest critics of anyone who says that people’s utterances of the Quran are created, or that what is heard from the reciter is not the Quran.

Abū Nasr said:
“As for attributing voices to reciters—as we have done in this chapter and elsewhere in this book—and attributing recitation to them, although those who deviate may rejoice at this, it provides them with no proof. For we have never disagreed about attributing a voice to a person, or about his voice being created when he shouts, speaks human speech, or calls out to someone.”

He said:
“There is no ambiguity about this. The disagreement concerns only what a person listening to a reciter of the Quran actually hears.”

He continued the discussion to its conclusion. Elsewhere, he also mentioned consensus on this.

Section

I have drawn attention to the fundamental position of Imam Ahmad and the other imams of the Sunnah and scholars of hadith concerning the question of our recitation of the Quran only because it lies at the root of the confusion

---

## Page 6474

and dispute in this area, including the question of “faith”—whether it is created or uncreated—and the questions of the “light of faith,” “guidance,” and similar matters over which the scholars of hadith and the Sunnah frequently disagree. Each group clings to part of the truth, until they become like those who were given a portion of the Scripture yet differed over it, each resembling someone who believes in part and disbelieves in part. Most of them are beset by ignorance and injustice: ignorance of the true nature of faith and truth, and injustice toward others. These disputes lead members of the Muslim community to declare one another unbelievers and curse one another, delighting Satan and angering the Most Merciful. Those who do this fall into the division and disagreement Allah has forbidden, departing from the unity and harmony He has commanded.

The root of this is the close connection between what Allah Most High has sent down of the Quran and faith—which pertains to His attributes—and the actions and attributes of His servants. Because distinguishing between them is difficult, some people incline toward excessive affirmation, while others incline toward excessive negation.

For this reason, the position of Imam Ahmad and the great imams was to prohibit blanket affirmation and blanket negation. Rather, one may refrain from both—which is more appropriate for people at large and constitutes the broad outlines of belief. Precise, well-founded distinctions, however, are for believers who possess knowledge, just as the former approach is for believers generally.

This question rests on two foundational principles:

---

## Page 6475

The first is that “the actions of Allah’s servants are created.” This was explicitly affirmed by the imams—Ahmad and others—and by all the imams of Ahl al-Sunnah wa-l-Jamā‘ah who opposed the Qadariyya. The Muslim community has unanimously agreed that people’s actions are brought into being.

The second principle concerns the question of “reciting the Quran, reading it, and uttering it”: should this be described as created or uncreated? Imam Ahmad explicitly rejected both statements, as did all the earlier and later imams of the Sunnah. His rejection of the “negationist Lafziyya,” however, was more frequent, more widely known, and more forceful, for two reasons.

The first is that their position leads to further denial of Allah’s attributes and further negation; the tendency toward negation is always worse than the tendency toward affirmation. The messengers brought detailed affirmation of Allah’s attributes and negation in general terms. They described Him as possessing knowledge, mercy, power, wisdom, speech, highness, and other attributes. As for negation:

“There is nothing like Him.”

“And there is none comparable to Him.”

By contrast, those who depart from the true substance of the messengers’ teachings—Sabians, philosophers, polytheists, and others, including those among the prophets’ followers who adopted Jahmī doctrines—follow the method of “detailed negation”: He is not this, He is not that. Their affirmation, however, remains general. Hence the saying: “The denier of Allah’s attributes is blind, while the one who likens Him to His creation is dim-sighted.” Thus, despite their misguidance, those who liken Allah to His creation are better than those who deny His attributes.

The second reason is that Ahmad was specifically tried by the Jahmiyya who denied Allah’s attributes, for they were his opponents,

---

## Page 6476

so his efforts were directed toward refuting their doctrines, rather than those who affirmed Allah’s attributes. At that time and place, no one was advocating excessive affirmation, whereas advocates of excessive negation had emerged. Refutation is undertaken as the need arises. When al-Bukhārī was tried by the “affirmationist Lafziyya,” his denunciation of them became evident, as seen in the chapter headings near the end of his Sahīh and in The Creation of Actions. Yet he denounced as a liar anyone, from any region, who reported that he had said, “My utterance of the Quran is created.” I believe he swore an oath to that effect, and he was truthful and righteous.

Section

Ahmad explicitly addressed this very “question” on several occasions. Abū al-Qāsim al-Lālakā’ī related in Foundations of the Sunnah:

Al-Hasan ibn ʿUthmān informed us, saying: ʿAmr ibn Jaʿfar narrated to us, saying: Ahmad ibn al-Hasan al-Tirmidhī narrated to us, saying:

I said to Ahmad ibn Hanbal, “People have become embroiled in controversy over the Quran. What should I say?”

He said, “Are you not created?”

I said, “Yes.”

He said, “Then your speech is from you and is created?”

I said, “Yes.”

He said, “Is the Quran not part of Allah’s speech?”

I said, “Yes.”

He said, “And Allah’s speech is from Allah?”

I said, “Yes.”

He said, “Could anything from Allah, then, be created?”

---

## Page 6477

Ahmad explained to the questioner that speech comes from the speaker and subsists in him. Speech cannot be detached from the speaker or fail to subsist in him, as is evident from the fact that your speech, O created being, comes from you, not from anyone else. Since you are created, your speech must also be created. Since Allah Most High is uncreated, whatever comes from Him and subsists in Him cannot be created.

His purpose was to refute the Jahmiyya, who claim that Allah’s speech neither comes from Allah nor is connected to Him. He thus explained that this conception of speech does not convey what it means for a speaker to speak, nor does it reflect the reality of speaking. Nor is it what the messengers and believers mean when they report that Allah spoke and speaks, uttered the Quran, called out, spoke privately, and summoned, and other such things that His messengers have reported about Him and that believers in Him from every nation have agreed upon.

Hence Allah Most High says:

“But the word from Me has come into effect.”

And He says:

“The revelation of the Book is from Allah, the Almighty, the All-Wise.”

And Allah Most High says:

“Indeed, you receive the Quran from One who is All-Wise, All-Knowing.”

And Allah Most High says:

“Alif Lām Rā. A Book whose verses have been perfected, then set out in detail, from One who is All-Wise, All-Aware.”

The Quran is not a self-subsisting entity such that one could say that this is like His statement:

“And He has subjected to you whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth—all from Him.”

Rather, it is an attribute, like knowledge, power, mercy, anger, will, seeing, hearing, and the like. Such an attribute can subsist only in that which possesses it. Every quality that has a name

---

## Page 6478

and subsists in a subject requires that a name be derived from it for that subject, and not for any other. Thus, when life, knowledge, and power subsist in a subject, the names “living,” “knowing,” and “powerful” must be derived from them for that subject. These names cannot be applied to anyone other than the one in whom knowledge and power subsist. Likewise, when utterance, speech, love, hatred, pleasure, mercy, anger, will, and volition subsist in a subject, the corresponding name and verb must be derived from them for that subject. Thus, one says: He is the Truthful, the Witness, the Wise, the Loving, the Merciful, and the One who commands. No name derived from these attributes can be applied to anyone else.

If Allah, glorified and exalted, were not Himself the One saying:

“I am Allah; there is no deity except Me,”

but instead brought these words into being in something else, He would not be the One issuing these commands or conveying this statement. Rather, the subject in which these words subsisted would be the one issuing this command and conveying this statement. That subject would be either the air or something else. Thus, that created subject would be the one saying to Moses:

“Indeed, I am Allah; there is no deity except Me, so worship Me.”

For this reason, the early generations used to say concerning this verse and others like it: “Whoever says that it is created has disbelieved.” They regarded the assertion that this verse and others like it were created as even graver than the same assertion concerning other verses. They considered it an enormity for anyone other than Allah Most High to claim divinity and lordship.

For this reason, the view of the great majority of “the people of the Sunnah and knowledge”—which is the well-known view among the followers of Imam Ahmad and Abū Hanīfa, and others among the Mālikīs and Shāfiʿīs

---

## Page 6479

and the Sufis, the scholars of hadith, and groups among the speculative theologians, including the Karrāmiyya and others—is that Allah’s being Creator, Provider, Giver of life, Bringer of death, Resurrector, Inheritor, and so forth belongs to His attributes of action and also to the attributes of His Essence. One who creates is not like one who does not create. The majority hold that creation is distinct from what is created: creation is Allah’s act, which subsists in Him, whereas what is created consists of the creatures separate from Him.

Groups among the “speculative theologians”—the Muʿtazila, the Ashʿarīs, and those who agree with them among Hanbalī, Shāfiʿī, Mālikī, and other jurists—hold that none of Allah’s acts constitutes an attribute of His Essence. Rather, creation is identical with what is created, or is merely a relation and attribution. This is the position chosen by Ibn ʿAqīl and the earlier of al-Qādī Abū Yaʿlā’s two positions. According to them, the Essence is in the same state whether it creates and provides or neither creates nor provides.

On this basis, the Muʿtazila challenged the consistency of their opponents among the Ashʿarī affirmers of the attributes and others like them. When those affirmers appealed to the previously mentioned “noble principle,” the Muʿtazila said: “Your principle is contradicted by the names Creator, Provider, and other names denoting actions. Creation and provision subsist in something other than Him, yet the names Creator and Provider are derived from them and applied to Him, even though no attribute of action subsists in Him at all. The same therefore applies to the Truthful, the Wise, the One who speaks, the Merciful, and the Loving.”

This objection does not hold against the great majority of the Muslim community and the general body of Ahl al-Sunnah wa-l-Jamāʿah, for they apply the same principle throughout. Nor does this amount to asserting that His creatures or the things He brings into being are eternal, whether it is said that only His act itself, which subsists in Him, is eternal—as is maintained by many among these

---

## Page 6480

Hanafīs, Mālikīs, Shāfiʿīs, Hanbalīs, scholars of hadith and speculative theology, and Sufis—or whether they maintain that He has states and relations when He brings creatures into being, as do many jurists, scholars of hadith, Sufis, and speculative theologians of all groups.

For the same reasoning applies here as applies to His will and volition. Although Ahl al-Sunnah and all other affirmers of the attributes hold that His will is eternal, the things He wills are not eternal. The same applies to the attribute of creation and bringing into being. Both revelation and reason indicate that the Creator, Provider, Originator, Giver of life, Bringer of death, Guide, and Helper is not in Himself in the same state as He would be had He not brought these things into being. Hence He, glorified and exalted, says:

“Is He who creates like one who does not create?”

The distinction between one who creates and one who does not create is like the distinction between one who has power and one who does not. The opposing view maintains that He is described only by power, which encompasses both what He creates and what He does not create, and that He is in Himself the same whether He creates or does not create. On this view, His being Creator entails no “positive attribute”—neither an attribute of perfection nor even any existential attribute—as His being powerful does.

The texts of the Quran and Sunnah require that His names denoting His acts belong to His most beautiful names, for which He deserves praise, commendation, and glorification. This entails that they are attributes of perfection. The purpose here, however, is not to discuss this “issue,” but merely to carry through the argument of

---

## Page 6481

Imam Ahmad, other trustworthy imams of the early generations, and all other affirmers of the attributes. Thus Imam Ahmad said, as reported by Hanbal in “The Book of the Ordeal”: “Allah has always been All-Knowing, Speaking, and All-Forgiving.” He thus affirmed Allah’s knowledge—a purely essential attribute—His “forgiveness,” which is among the “attributes of action,” and His speech, which shares features of both. He stated that Allah has always possessed these attributes and names.

In his “Refutation of the Heretics and the Jahmiyyah,” Imam Ahmad mentioned Jahm’s statement, “He speaks, but His speech is created.” Ahmad said:

“We said to him: ‘Likewise, the speech of human beings is created. According to your doctrine, there was a time when Allah did not speak, until He created speech. Likewise, human beings do not speak until He creates speech for them. You have thus combined disbelief with likening Allah to His creation.’”

They also related in “The Ordeal” the evidence Imam Ahmad cited during the debate. He argued from Allah’s words:

“But the word from Me will come to pass.”

He said: “If the word is from anyone other than Allah, then it is created.”

Section

As for the claim that Ahmad said this only out of fear of people, its falsehood is known to every rational person who has heard anything of Ahmad’s life. Whoever says this is in greater need of severe punishment for his slander against the imams than of an answer. For

---

## Page 6482

Imam Ahmad became a byword for enduring trials and remaining steadfast upon the truth, undeterred by anyone’s blame in the cause of Allah. Indeed, the title “Imam” became inseparable from his name on everyone’s lips: “Imam Ahmad said”; “This is the position of Imam Ahmad.” This accords with the words of Allah Most High:

“And We made from among them leaders guiding by Our command when they were patient and had certainty in Our signs.”

He was granted such patience and certainty as entitled him to leadership in religion. “Three caliphs,” whose power extended from east to west, successively subjected him to persecution. They were supported by scholars of speculative theology, judges, ministers, informers, commanders, and governors whose numbers Allah alone could reckon. Some imprisoned him; others subjected him to dire threats of death and other punishments, inducements of authority and wealth to whatever extent Allah willed, and beatings; still others drove him from his home and banished him. Throughout this, people at large abandoned him—even his own companions among the scholars, the righteous, and the devout. Yet he did not concede a single word of what they demanded. He neither abandoned what the Quran and Sunnah taught, nor concealed knowledge, nor resorted to concealing his beliefs for his own protection.

Rather, he made known the Sunnah of Allah’s Messenger—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—and the reports concerning him, and repelled innovations contrary to them, to a degree unmatched by any of his peers and fellow scholars, earlier or later. Thus, one of the shaykhs of Syria said: “No one has made known what the Messenger—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—brought as Ahmad ibn Hanbal did.” How, then, could anyone suppose that he feared for himself over this statement, which was of no consequence?

## Page 6483

Moreover, one of his principles was not to advance any innovated view in religion. Furthermore, Ahmad ibn al-Hasan al-Tirmidhī was among his closest and most distinguished companions. What reason, then, would he have to conceal his true beliefs from him?

These people’s specious argument rests on their finding that others had discussed “the letters of the alphabet” and “the names of created things.”

Those who profess adherence to the Sunnah discussed the letters of the alphabet as they occur outside the Quran and the divine scriptures. Some groups among them—such as Ibn Hāmid, Abū Nasr al-Sijzī, al-Qādī in the better-known of his two opinions, Ibn ʿAqīl, and others—said that they are created. They said: “Letters are of two kinds.”

Another view was held by groups comprising many people from Syria, Iraq, and Khurāsān, such as al-Qādī Yaʿqūb al-Barzabīnī and al-Sharīf Abū al-Fadā’il al-Zaydī al-Harrānī. This is also reported from Shaykh Abū al-Husayn ibn Samʿūn. ## Page 6487

intended only recitation. Some, however, hold that his prayer is invalid, as Abū Hanīfah does. This category also includes prompting the imam, alerting someone entering by means of a Quranic verse, and similar matters.

The reason is that meaning is included in what the term “speech” denotes; it does not denote wording alone. Meaning may be performative or informative, and performative speech includes commands and prohibitions. Clearly, Zayd’s command is not ʿAmr’s command, nor does it have the same status, even when the wording is identical. Likewise, Zayd’s choice is not ʿAmr’s choice, nor does it have the same status, even when the wording is identical.

When a wise person whose commands are obeyed issues a command, it has a different status from the same command issued by someone ignorant and powerless, even if their wording is identical. Likewise, when a knowledgeable, truthful witness reports something, his report has a different status from the same report given by someone ignorant and untruthful, even if their wording is identical.

Accordingly, if someone incorporates into his speech wording that another person has incorporated into his own speech, this does not entail that this wording belongs to that other speaker’s speech, even though the two expressions resemble each other. This is like someone writing letters resembling those in a copy of the Quran but using them to write something else: that does not make them letters of the Quranic text.

Others said that mere agreement in wording does not require that the ruling on

one expression be applied to the other. But if one speaker originated the statement and the other merely followed his pattern and example, the wording and speech are attributed to the first. This is like someone quoting Labīd’s words:

or quoting a familiar proverb, such as:

Such a person has uttered these words to express his own intended meaning, not to convey someone else’s words. Nevertheless, they remain attributed to their original speaker. The same applies to the letters found in Allah’s speech: even when people incorporate them into speech of their own, they originally derive from the speech of Allah Most High.

## Page 6489

the revealed scriptures. The Arabs likewise used these letters and names before the Quran was revealed, and Allah Most High revealed it in the language they had spoken before its revelation.

The same applies when someone does this with complete sentences—and applies all the more clearly here. The rulings of Islamic law support this.

The other group—those who maintain that the letters of the alphabet are uncreated without qualification—said: “We have two views concerning names found outside the Quran.” Some of them hold that all names are uncreated, just as they maintain concerning letters. Others do not hold this view.
