## Page 6633

is created, insofar as the underlying premise of their doctrine is concerned. For their fundamental premise is that nothing involving choice subsists in the Lord. Thus, neither speech nor action subsists in Him by His choice and will. They said:

“These are occurrences that begin in time, and no such occurrences subsist in the Lord.”

They thereby contradicted authentic revelation and clear reason. They believed that by this they were refuting the philosophers and establishing that the world came into existence. But they were mistaken: they neither defended Islam nor defeated the philosophers. They claimed that, in eternity past, the Lord had no power to utter speech or perform an act, and that He became able after having been unable, without anything new occurring. Or they change their wording and say, “He has always had power.” Yet they say:

“What was within His power was impossible, and acting became possible for Him after it had become impossible for Him, without anything new arising.”

They sometimes express this by saying:

“In eternity past, He had power over what would be possible in the unending future, not over what was impossible in eternity past.”

They thus combine two contradictory claims, affirming that He had power while maintaining that what He had power over was impossible. They failed to distinguish between speech and action as kinds and particular instances of them, just as the philosophers failed to distinguish between the two. Rather, the philosophers claimed that a particular thing He produced was coeternal with Him. In this they went astray and contradicted clear reason and authentic revelation. For the evidence does not establish the eternity of any particular thing in the world. Rather, it establishes that everything other than Allah is created and comes into existence after not having existed, since He acts by His power and will, as is shown by the proofs

---

## Page 6634

that are conclusive. Clear reason and the general agreement of rational people establish that nothing produced by an agent acting by his will is necessarily inseparable from his essence. Indeed, this holds for every agent: none of his effects is necessarily inseparable from his essence, nor is it conceivable that a particular effect should be simultaneous with him—even supposing that he acts without will. How much more, then, does this apply to an agent who acts by will!

The claim that an effect is simultaneous with its cause is valid only for causes that function as conditions. A condition need not precede what depends upon it; rather, it may accompany it, just as life accompanies knowledge. An agent, however—whether called a cause or not—must precede the particular act, and none of the effects of that particular act can be simultaneous with it. Rational people have never known an agent from whom a particular effect is necessarily inseparable. The statement, “I moved my hand, so the ring moved,” concerns a condition, not an agent.

Furthermore, if the world were eternal, its agent would necessarily produce its effect by virtue of his very essence from eternity, and what he necessitated and entailed would not come after him. Were that so, no event could ever come into being. This contradicts what is observed—even if He, glory be to Him, has always had the power to speak and act; indeed, has always spoken whenever He wills, done whatever He wills, and possessed the attributes of perfection and the qualities of majesty and honor.

The world contains order and precision that demonstrate the Lord’s knowledge; particular features that demonstrate His will; goodness that demonstrates His mercy; praiseworthy outcomes that demonstrate His wisdom; and it contains

---

## Page 6635

events that demonstrate the power of the Lord Most High, even though the Lord is intrinsically worthy of the attributes of perfection. He is worthy of every perfection whose existence is possible and which entails no deficiency, and He is free of every deficiency. He, glory be to Him, has no equal in any respect. He is therefore described in detail by the attributes of perfection, without being likened or equated to others in them, and He is absolutely free of deficiencies. Indeed, attributing deficiencies to Him is among the greatest falsehoods. His perfection is inseparable from His holy essence; He does not acquire it from another. Rather, He bestows His favors upon His creation by bringing them into existence and endowing them with the attributes of living beings. The Creator of the attributes of perfection is all the more worthy of them, and He has no equal in them.

The root of people’s confusion over “the question of Allah’s speech” is that, when the Jahmiyyah and the Muʿtazilah debated the philosophers over “the question of the world’s having a beginning,” they believed that anything in which successive attributes and acts subsist must itself have come into being, on the premise that the infinite cannot exist. They consequently accepted that, in pre-eternity, the Lord was incapable of acting and speaking; indeed, that both were impossible for Him, and that He was inactive in both respects.

They sometimes express this by saying that, in pre-eternity, He had the power to act in the everlasting future, although acting in pre-eternity was impossible for Him. Thus, they combine two contradictories, ascribing power to Him while what that power concerns is intrinsically impossible. For an act necessarily entails having a beginning, whereas pre-eternity has no beginning; affirming and denying a beginning at the same time is to combine two contradictories.

---

## Page 6636

They failed to distinguish between what necessarily entails a beginning and coming into existence—namely, a particular act and its particular effect—and what does not, namely, acting and speaking as such. The latter can be perpetual even though each individual instance comes into being, just as they can continue perpetually into the future even though each individual instance passes away. This is unlike a creator whose particular creation is perpetually inseparable from him: that is false according to clear reason and authentic revelation. Hence, the natural dispositions of rational people concur in rejecting it. Only a handful of philosophers disputed this, such as Avicenna and his like, who claimed that a contingent thing produced by an agent could be beginningless and necessarily existent through another. In this they opposed the vast majority of rational people, as well as their predecessors, Aristotle and his followers. The latter did not maintain this, although they held the celestial spheres to be beginningless.

Aristotle was the first of the Peripatetic philosophers to maintain that the spheres were beginningless, basing this on the affirmation of a final cause for the celestial sphere’s motion, which the sphere moves to imitate. They did not affirm an originating agent for it, nor did they affirm anything contingent that was beginningless and necessarily existent through another. Although they were more ignorant of Allah and more deeply steeped in unbelief than their later followers, they conceded to the majority of rational people that whatever is contingent in itself must have come into being after not existing.

They were therefore compelled to say: “His speech is created and separate from Him.”

Another group agreed with them that the existence of an infinity is impossible, but held that acts of choice subsist in Him. They therefore said that in pre-eternity He did not speak, and indeed speech was not even within His power; then He began to speak, with speech subsisting in Him, without any new occurrence. This is the position of the Hāshimiyyah, the Karrāmiyyah, and others.

---

## Page 6637

Another group maintained that if the Quran is uncreated, it must be beginningless as a particular entity and inseparable from the Lord’s essence, so that He does not speak by His will and power. Some of them then said: “It is a single, beginningless meaning.” They thus made the Verse of the Throne, the Verse of Debt, all the other verses of the Quran, the Torah, the Gospel, and every utterance Allah speaks a single meaning admitting neither multiplicity nor division. Others said that it consists of letters and sounds existing simultaneously and inseparable from His essence.

These, too, agreed with the Jahmiyyah and the Muʿtazilah on their fundamental claim that He speaks with speech that does not subsist in Him by His will and power, and that no acts of choice subsist in Him. They also held that He did not rise over His Throne after creating the heavens and the earth; that He will not come on the Day of Resurrection; that He did not call Moses when He called him; and that sins do not anger Him, acts of obedience do not please Him, and the repentance of those who repent does not bring Him joy.

Concerning His words:

“Say, ‘Do deeds! Allah will see your deeds, and so will His Messenger and the believers,’”

and similar passages, they said that He does not see those deeds when they come into existence. Rather, either He has always seen them, or nothing existent has newly arisen, but only a nonexistent relation. They made other such statements in which they contradicted the explicit texts of the Book and the Sunnah, as well as clear reason.

What drove them to this was their agreement with the Jahmiyyah’s fundamental claim that He, glorified be He, had no power in pre-eternity to act or speak. They opposed the early generations and the leading scholars, who said: “Allah has always spoken whenever He wills.” They then divided into four factions, as mentioned above: the Khalqiyyah, the Hudūthiyyah, the Ittihādiyyah, and the Iqtirāniyyah.

---

## Page 6638

Worse than these are the Sabians and the philosophers who say that Allah has never spoken—neither with speech subsisting in His essence nor with speech He utters by His will and power: neither speech beginningless in kind nor speech beginningless as a particular entity, neither originated nor created. Rather, His speech, in their view, is what emanates into the souls of the prophets. They say that He spoke to Moses from the heaven of his intellect. They may also say that He, exalted be He, knows universals but not particulars, for He knows them only in a universal manner. Yet they also say that He knows Himself and knows what He does.

Their statement that He knows Himself and what He has brought into existence is true, as He, exalted be He, says:

“Does He who created not know, when He is the Most Subtle, the All-Aware?”

But their further claim that He does not know particular individual entities is ignorance and contradiction. His holy Self is a particular entity, the celestial spheres are particular entities, and everything that exists is a particular entity. If He did not know particulars, He would know nothing that exists, since universals exist as universals only in minds, not in external reality. Thus, whoever knows only universals knows nothing that exists. Exalted is Allah, far above what the wrongdoers say!

What drove them to this deviation was their attempt to avoid affirming the occurrence of new states in the Creator, exalted be He. Yet these same people say that temporal events subsist in that which is beginningless and that temporal events have no beginning. They denied this of the Creator, however, because they believed that He has no attributes, but is instead absolute existence. They said that knowledge is identical with the knower, that power is identical with the one who possesses it, that knowledge and the knower are one and the same, and that the one who wills and the will

---

## Page 6639

are one and the same. Thus they identified each attribute with the others and identified the attributes with the One described by them. Some go further, saying that knowledge is the entirety of what is known, as al-Tūsī, author of Sharh al-Ishārāt (Commentary on the Pointers), maintains. He criticized Ibn Sīnā for affirming that He knows Himself and what proceeds from Himself. Ibn Sīnā was closer to the truth, yet he nevertheless contradicted himself by denying that attributes subsist in Him, identifying the attribute with the One described by it, and identifying every attribute with every other.

Thus these thinkers went further in monism and heresy than those who say that the meanings of speech are one and the same. Yet they argued that their position necessarily followed from the latter’s view, saying: “If multiple meanings can be one and the same, then knowledge can be identical with power, and power with will.” The most astute among the latter acknowledged that there was no answer to this argument.

They then said: “And if one attribute can be identical with another, then the attribute can be identical with the One described by it.” Then came Ibn ʿArabī, Ibn Sabʿīn, al-Qūnawī, and other heretics like them, who said: “If one attribute can be identical with another, and the attribute with the One described by it, then the necessarily existent, beginningless Creator can be identical with the contingently existent, originated creature.” They therefore said that the existence of every creature is identical with the existence of the Creator, and said: “Existence is one.” They did not distinguish between being one in kind and being one

---

## Page 6640

and the same entity, just as those others failed to distinguish between one individual instance of speech and speech of a single kind.

Those who deviated concerning speech ultimately arrived at this negation of the divine attributes, unbelief, and union professed by the proponents of monism, indwelling, and union between the Creator and created beings. Likewise, those who failed to distinguish between speech as a kind and its individual instances, and said that He speaks with beginningless letters and sound, initially maintained that He does not speak by His will and power, and that the letter bā does not precede the letter sīn. Rather, when He called to Moses and said:

“Indeed, I am Allah. There is no deity except Me, so worship Me.”

“Indeed, I am Allah, Lord of the worlds.”

the hamza, the nūn, and everything between them had existed together from all eternity, each simultaneous with the others, inseparable from the essence of Allah Most High, without beginning or end.

Then a group among them said that this beginningless speech is identical with the sounds heard from the reciters. Others said, rather, that two sounds are heard: one beginningless and the other originated. Some said that the shapes traced in ink are beginningless and eternal. Others said that the material bearing the ink is beginningless and eternal. It is also related that some of them said that the ink itself is beginningless and eternal.

Most of them use the term qadīm (beginningless) without understanding its meaning. Some think it means that it is beginningless in His knowledge; others think it means that it precedes something else; and others think that the word means uncreated. Still others make no distinctions in what they say. Thus these people became proponents of indwelling and union with respect to the attributes, and some of them affirm indwelling and union in

---

## Page 6641

the essence and the attributes. Both groups ultimately arrived at negation.

The correct position on this matter and others is that of the early generations of the Muslim community and its leading scholars:

He, glorified be He, has always spoken whenever He wills, and He speaks by His will and power. His words have no end. He called to Moses with a voice that Moses heard, and He called to him only when he came, not before that. The Lord’s voice does not resemble the voices of His servants, just as His knowledge does not resemble their knowledge and His power does not resemble their power.

He, glorified be He, is distinct from His creatures in His essence and attributes. Nothing of His essence or of His attributes that subsist in His essence is within His creatures, nor is anything of His creatures within His essence. The views of the proponents of negation and union, who deny the divine essence, attributes, speech, or acts, are false. Likewise, the views of the proponents of indwelling, who affirm indwelling with respect to the essence or the attributes, are false.

These matters are discussed at length elsewhere, and we have expounded them in al-Wājib al-kabīr. Allah knows best what is correct.

---

## Page 6642

He—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked:

“What should be done with an old copy of the Quran if it becomes torn? If someone writes something from the Quran and then washes it off with water or burns it, does it retain its sanctity or not?”

He replied:

Praise be to Allah. An old copy of the Quran, or one that has become so torn that it can no longer be used for reading, should be buried somewhere it will be protected, just as a believer’s body is honoured by being buried somewhere it will be protected.

If something from the Quran or words of remembrance is written in a vessel or on a tablet, then washed off with water or something else, there is no harm in drinking the resulting liquid. Ahmad and others explicitly stated this. They also reported that Ibn ‘Abbās—may Allah be pleased with him and his father—used to write words from the Quran and words of remembrance and instruct that the resulting liquid be given to someone suffering from an illness to drink. This implies that it contains a blessing.

The water used by the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, for ablution was likewise blessed water. Some of it was poured over Jābir when he was ill, and the Companions used to seek blessings through it. Nevertheless, the Prophet would perform ablution over the earth and elsewhere. No prohibition against pouring such water onto the earth or similar places has reached me, nor do I know of any prohibition concerning this. Once erased, the traces of the writing no longer constitute writing, and someone in a state of major ritual impurity is not forbidden to touch it. It is well known that it does not

---

## Page 6643

have the same sanctity as it does while the Quran and words of remembrance remain inscribed. Likewise, if silver, gold or copper were fashioned into the shapes of letters spelling out the Quran or words of remembrance, or a stone were engraved in that form, and the metalwork and stone were subsequently altered, the material would no longer be entitled to the sanctity it had while bearing the writing.

Al-‘Abbās ibn ‘Abd al-Muttalib used to say concerning Zamzam water:

“I do not permit its use for bathing, but it is freely lawful for anyone to drink.”

It is also reported that he said:

“For a drinker and one performing ablution.”

For this reason, scholars differed over whether bathing and performing ablution with Zamzam water are disliked, mentioning two views reported from Ahmad. Al-Shāfi‘ī cited the report from al-‘Abbās as evidence, while those who permitted it cited a hadith stating that:

“The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, performed ablution with Zamzam water.”

The Companions also performed ablution with the water that flowed from between his fingers, despite its blessed nature; however, that was a time of need.

The correct view is that al-‘Abbās’s prohibition concerned bathing alone, not ablution. The distinction between bathing and ablution rests on this consideration: bathing resembles the removal of physical impurity. Thus, whatever must be washed to remove physical impurity must also be washed when purifying oneself from major ritual impurity. Accordingly, there are grounds for protecting these blessed waters from physical impurities, unlike protecting them from earth and other pure substances. And Allah knows best.
